Explicitly excluded is thermoregulatory shivering that arises as a direct physiological response to reduced environmental temperature or pathological lowering of core body temperature (hypothermia), as this represents a distinct thermoregulatory mechanism rather than a symptom of internal pathological disturbance.
clinical_rationale: Chills is a symptom complex that may arise from pharmacological causes, such as a drug-induced fever or acute drug reaction, or as a symptom accompanying certain drug-related conditions (e.g., drug-induced neutropenia leading to infection, or cytokine release syndrome after immunotherapy). While the phenotype itself is quite broad, chills as part of drug-induced pathology is biologically plausible and well-documented in cases of pyrogenic responses, infusion reactions, and some adverse immune phenomena. The description excludes environmentally driven thermoregulatory shivering or hypothermia, focusing instead on chills as the expression of systemic pathophysiological processes, which supports its use as a symptom-based inclusion or covariate in pharmacovigilance surveillance. The breadth of etiologies means that instances of chills may not always be drug-related, but they remain relevant when the symptom arises due to a drug-adverse reaction mechanism.

source_definition: Cholecystitis is an inflammatory condition of the gallbladder caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by one or more gallstones, resulting in mucosal injury, transmural inflammation, and progressive gallbladder wall thickening or fibrosis. The condition encompasses both acute presentations â€” characterized by sudden-onset right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, Murphy's sign, and associated systemic inflammatory response â€” and chronic presentations marked by recurrent biliary pain with pathological evidence of persistent low-grade inflammation and fibrotic remodeling of the gallbladder wall. The diagnosis requires evidence of active or established gallbladder wall inflammation attributable to gallstone disease. Excluded are: acalculous cholecystitis (gallbladder inflammation arising in the absence of gallstones); symptomatic cholelithiasis or biliary colic without demonstrable gallbladder wall inflammation; and acute cholangitis, which involves inflammatory or infectious involvement of the bile ducts rather than the gallbladder itself.
clinical_rationale: Cholecystitis, as defined, is an inflammation of the gallbladder secondary to obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstones. Acute cholecystitis often presents with sudden right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, and systemic signs of inflammation, while chronic cholecystitis involves recurrent biliary pain and gallbladder wall fibrosis. This definition explicitly excludes acalculous cholecystitis and symptomatic biliary colic without inflammatory findings. Drug-induced cholecystitis has been reported, with mechanisms including drug-induced lithogenesis or direct injury to the gallbladder wall, making drug-related causality plausible. Thus, it is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. Diagnosis of cholecystitis requires imaging evidence or procedural confirmation, as clinical symptoms alone lack specificity.

source_definition: Cholestasis is a pathophysiological state characterized by the reduction or cessation of bile flow at any level of the biliary system, encompassing both intrahepatic mechanisms â€” impaired hepatocyte bile formation or secretion and dysfunction of intrahepatic bile ducts â€” and extrahepatic mechanisms involving mechanical obstruction of the common bile duct or its branches. The phenotype is defined by the presence of a cholestatic biochemical pattern, specifically elevation of alkaline phosphatase (ALP), gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT), and/or conjugated (direct) bilirubin, irrespective of whether clinical manifestations such as jaundice, pruritus, pale stools, or dark urine are present. All etiologies qualify, including drug-induced, obstructive (e.g., choledocholithiasis, biliary stricture, malignancy), infectious, autoimmune, genetic, and gestational causes such as intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, as well as cholestasis arising secondarily as a consequence of a primary systemic or hepatic disease, including sepsis-associated cholestasis, cardiac hepatopathy, and parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis. Explicitly excluded are isolated hepatocellular injury patterns in which bilirubin elevation results primarily from parenchymal damage without substantive impairment of bile flow (i.e., a predominantly cytolytic biochemical profile without cholestatic enzyme elevation), and isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemias attributable to impaired bilirubin conjugation or increased bilirubin production such as Gilbert's syndrome or hemolytic anemia, in which bile flow itself is not impaired.
clinical_rationale: Cholestasis has documented drug-attributable causes via direct hepatocyte effects (e.g., chlorpromazine, amoxicillin-clavulanate, anabolic steroids) and bile duct injury or dysfunction (e.g., immunotherapy-related autoimmune cholangitis). While the definition spans diverse etiologies, drug-induced cholestasis is both plausible and observed, making this a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. Cholestasis is primarily transient unless complications (e.g., fibrosis) arise or chronic conditions like cholangiopathies are present. Diagnosis requires biochemical evidence, with alkaline phosphatase, GGT, and conjugated bilirubin as hallmark biomarkers. Incidental symptoms may not always be coded discretely. Incident cholestasis is diagnosed variably in acute and outpatient contexts based on cause and severity — obstructive cholestasis often presents acutely, whereas other forms may be diagnosed in ambulatory care.

source_definition: Cholestatic liver disease is a primary hepatobiliary disorder characterized by impaired bile formation, secretion, or flow, arising from pathological processes intrinsic to the liver parenchyma, bile ducts, or biliary tract. The condition encompasses both intrahepatic cholestasis â€” in which bile transport fails at the level of the hepatocyte or intrahepatic bile ducts â€” and extrahepatic cholestasis â€” in which obstruction or structural disease of the extrahepatic biliary system impedes bile outflow. Both acute and chronic presentations are included, ranging from sudden-onset biliary obstruction or drug-induced cholestatic injury to chronic progressive diseases such as primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Mixed hepatocellular-cholestatic injury patterns are included when cholestasis represents a clinically significant component of the presentation. Excluded are conditions in which impaired bile flow is a secondary epiphenomenon of a non-hepatobiliary primary disease, such as sepsis-associated cholestasis, cholestasis attributable to heart failure, or cholestasis arising solely from total parenteral nutrition, where the underlying hepatobiliary architecture is not the primary site of pathology.
clinical_rationale: This phenotype encompasses a range of cholestatic pathologies intrinsic to hepatobiliary dysfunction, including both acute and chronic conditions. Drug-induced cholestasis is a well-documented entity related to several classes of drugs, such as anabolic steroids, NSAIDs, antibiotics, and antiepileptics, making this a pharmaceutical safety-relevant outcome. Chronic cholestatic liver diseases like primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis are persistent but may have relapsing episodes. The diagnostic process typically requires laboratory evidence (e.g., alkaline phosphatase elevation), imaging studies, or histologic confirmation. Acute presentations such as drug-induced cholestatic liver injury are often transient, but chronic manifestations demand long-term management. Mixed etiologies of hepatocellular and cholestatic injury require careful differentiation, and secondary cholestasis from non-hepatobiliary causes is explicitly excluded by definition.

source_definition: Chorea is a clinical syndrome defined by the presence of involuntary, irregular, non-rhythmic, and non-stereotyped movements that flow unpredictably and continuously from one body part to another, arising from dysfunction of the striato-thalamo-cortical circuit irrespective of underlying etiology. The phenomenology encompasses the full spectrum of this circuit dysfunction, including slow, writhing distal movements (athetosis) and large-amplitude, proximal flinging movements (ballismus and hemiballismus), which are considered pathophysiologically contiguous with classical choreiform movements. The syndrome is defined at any clinically observable severity, from subtle or fleeting movements that a patient may partially suppress or mask, to severe, continuous movements producing functional impairment. Chorea is explicitly distinguished from tics, which are stereotyped, repetitive, and partially suppressible with a premonitory urge; from tremor, which is rhythmic and oscillatory in character; from myoclonus, which consists of sudden, brief, shock-like jerks; and from dystonia, which is characterized by sustained muscle contractions producing patterned, twisting postures. No specific etiology, genetic basis, or associated neurological disease is required for inclusion; the definition rests solely on the characteristic quality of the abnormal involuntary movements.
clinical_rationale: Chorea is an involuntary movement disorder arising from dysfunction of the striato-thalamo-cortical circuit. As described, the term covers the full phenomenological spectrum of choreiform movements regardless of underlying etiology. While chorea can result from genetic (e.g., Huntington's disease), autoimmune (e.g., Sydenham's chorea), metabolic, structural, and drug-induced causes, drug-associated etiology is well-documented, particularly regarding dopaminergic agents, antipsychotics, and levodopa. The syndrome can arise acutely or progressively and may remit when the underlying trigger is removed, making it an important pharmacovigilance outcome under its drug-induced presentation. Incidence varies by severity, acute vs. chronic presentation, and the underlying etiology, influencing both diagnostic approaches and care settings.

source_definition: Chronic bleeding is a clinical state characterized by persistent or recurrent overt hemorrhage at one or more anatomical sites, arising from an acquired impairment of hemostasis â€” including defects in coagulation factor activity, platelet number, or platelet function â€” rather than from a discrete structural or anatomical lesion. The condition is distinguished from acute, self-limited hemorrhagic events by its temporal persistence or pattern of recurrence in the absence of full hemostatic recovery. Congenital bleeding diatheses are excluded. When chronic bleeding occurs in the context of a primary systemic disease known to affect hemostasis (such as hepatic or renal disease), it is included within this phenotype only when the bleeding manifests as a clinically distinguishable complication beyond what is expected from the natural course of the underlying condition.
clinical_rationale: Chronic bleeding as defined here has potential drug-attributable causes, such as anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, or medications associated with bone marrow suppression leading to thrombocytopenia. It specifically excludes congenital bleeding disorders and focuses on acquired hemostatic impairments leading to persistent or recurrent hemorrhage. The exclusion of solely structural or anatomical lesions separates this condition from other types of hemorrhage. The condition may persist and relapse with or without treatment, depending on the etiology. Diagnosis is likely to involve observation of the bleeding episodes and laboratory evidence of the hemostatic defect contributing to the condition, as required by the definition.

source_definition: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) is an acquired, idiopathic, immune-mediated disorder of the peripheral nervous system characterized by chronic demyelination of multiple nerve roots and peripheral nerves, with a disease course that is progressive, stepwise, or relapsing over a minimum of eight weeks. The condition encompasses both the typical presentation of symmetric proximal and distal limb weakness accompanied by sensory deficits, and recognized atypical variants including multifocal asymmetric demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy (MADSAM/Lewis-Sumner syndrome), distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy (DADS), pure sensory CIDP, and pure motor CIDP, all unified by a chronic inflammatory demyelinating pathophysiology. Excluded from this phenotype are demyelinating neuropathies with an identifiable systemic or secondary etiology, including those causally associated with paraproteinemia (POEMS syndrome, IgM monoclonal gammopathy with anti-MAG antibodies), HIV, viral hepatitis, connective tissue diseases, or other defined systemic inflammatory disorders. Also excluded are hereditary demyelinating neuropathies attributable to pathogenic genetic variants â€” such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1 resulting from PMP22 duplication or mutations in MPZ or LITAF â€” which represent a structurally determined, non-inflammatory pathophysiology fundamentally distinct from the acquired immune-mediated process defining CIDP.
clinical_rationale: CIDP is an acquired, immune-mediated condition characterized by chronic progressive or relapsing demyelination of peripheral nerves. While CIDP's primary pathophysiology is idiopathic and immune-driven, it can be misclassified in observational data due to diagnostic overlap with hereditary demyelinating neuropathies (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1) or systemic inflammatory conditions. Individuals with CIDP may present with symmetric or asymmetric motor and sensory deficits, and diagnosis relies on electrophysiologic criteria supported by nerve imaging or biopsy. Drug-induced or drug-exacerbated CIDP has been suggested but remains a rare phenomenon, mostly anecdotal, with insufficient evidence for a strong pharmacovigilance signal. However, as an immune-mediated condition, an immune-modulating drug effect cannot be entirely excluded. The disease course is chronic but often relapsing, with considerable diagnostic complexity, which can obscure definitive attribution to a drug exposure. The stringent exclusion in the provided definition of secondary and hereditary neuropathies strengthens the validity of the cohort but limits its scope to primary CIDP.

source_definition: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a sustained pathological state characterized by progressive loss of kidney structure or function, defined by the presence of markers of kidney damage (such as persistent proteinuria, hematuria of renal origin, or structural abnormalities on imaging or biopsy) and/or a reduction in glomerular filtration rate, persisting for a duration of three months or longer. The phenotype encompasses the full severity continuum from early-stage disease with preserved filtration function but demonstrable structural injury (G1â€“G2) through advanced functional impairment (G3â€“G4) to end-stage kidney failure requiring renal replacement therapy or transplantation (G5/ESRD). CKD arising as a downstream consequence of any chronic systemic condition â€” including but not limited to diabetes mellitus, hypertension, autoimmune disease, or chronic heart failure â€” is included within this phenotype, as the pathophysiological state of irreversible nephron loss is the defining criterion regardless of etiology. Explicitly excluded are acute kidney injury and other reversible causes of transient GFR reduction (e.g., prerenal azotemia from volume depletion) that resolve within three months without persistent structural sequelae.
clinical_rationale: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is highly relevant for pharmacovigilance as numerous drugs have been implicated in causing or accelerating the progression of CKD through mechanisms such as direct nephrotoxicity, hemodynamic changes, or toxic effects on the renal interstitium. The phenotype strictly excludes transient kidney injury, focusing on sustained structural or functional loss persisting for at least three months. The condition is inherently progressive in most cases, and while exacerbations or acute insults can occur, the overall disease state persists throughout the patient's life. Incident CKD diagnoses are typically established in outpatient settings via laboratory markers (e.g., eGFR, proteinuria) and imaging, though diagnoses are sometimes made in acute care settings for advanced or incidentally detected cases. Long-term monitoring and intervention are essential to delay progression and address complications, making CKD an important candidate for pharmacovigilance studies. Note that CKD includes secondary forms from underlying etiologies while maintaining a unified clinical-pathological definition based on nephron loss.

source_definition: Chronic liver disease is a pathological state characterized by persistent hepatic inflammation, injury, or structural remodeling of the liver parenchyma or biliary system, arising from any etiology â€” including but not limited to viral hepatitis, alcohol-related liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, drug-induced chronic injury, and hereditary or cryptogenic causes. The condition encompasses the full clinical spectrum from early chronic hepatocellular or cholangiocellular inflammation without significant fibrosis through progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and portal hypertension, including episodes of acute-on-chronic liver failure and acute hepatic decompensation occurring in the context of underlying chronic disease. Isolated acute liver injury or hepatic failure without evidence of a concurrent or pre-existing chronic process is excluded. Patients who have undergone orthotopic liver transplantation are excluded, as they represent a distinct hepatological state involving graft physiology. Patients in whom the underlying liver disease has been fully and documentably resolved â€” such as those with sustained virologic response to antiviral therapy and no residual fibrosis or hepatic dysfunction â€” are likewise excluded.
clinical_rationale: Chronic liver disease is suitable as a pharmacovigilance outcome, particularly in cases of drug-induced chronic liver injury, which can result from substances such as methotrexate, amiodarone, isoniazid, or long-term alcohol exposure. It is a persistent state, as the liver damage and associated remodeling are irreversible and progress over time. Episodes of acute-on-chronic liver failure or acute hepatic decompensation represent transient exacerbations but are dependent on the underlying chronic liver disease. Drug etiology is valid only for cases attributed to chronic injury induced by such agents. The spectrum of disease severity requires differentiation between stable chronic states and instances of acute decompensation, which influence coding practices and care settings. Finally, while symptoms such as fatigue, jaundice, or abdominal distension from ascites may occur, these are inconsistently documented as discrete symptoms prior to diagnosis.

source_definition: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is an indolent, mature B-cell lymphoproliferative neoplasm characterized by the clonal expansion and progressive accumulation of small, immunologically incompetent B lymphocytes in the peripheral blood, bone marrow, and lymphoid organs, with a peripheral blood clonal B-cell count of at least 5Ã—10â¹/L bearing a characteristic CLL immunophenotype (CD5+, CD19+, CD23+, with dim surface immunoglobulin expression). This phenotype encompasses the full natural history of CLL, including cases that undergo Richter's Transformation to a high-grade lymphoma â€” most commonly Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma â€” which is considered a progressive disease state within the CLL clinical trajectory rather than a separate malignancy. Explicitly excluded are Monoclonal B-cell Lymphocytosis, which represents a clonally related but pre-malignant precursor state below the diagnostic B-cell count threshold; Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma, which shares identical clonal biology but manifests primarily as nodal disease without significant peripheral leukemic involvement; and other mature lymphoid neoplasms that may present with peripheral blood lymphocytosis but are biologically distinct, including hairy cell leukemia, mantle cell lymphoma in leukemic phase, splenic marginal zone lymphoma, and T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.
clinical_rationale: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is a well-documented malignancy with potential drug-associated etiologies. Cases of drug-induced lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, have been reported in association with immunosuppressants (e.g., cyclosporine, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil), as well as other therapies affecting immune surveillance mechanisms. This phenotype captures the full natural history of CLL, including transformations like Richter's Syndrome. Given the persistent nature of the disease, clinical staging is critical for management but does not alter pharmacovigilance handling. Diagnostic confirmation relies heavily on immunophenotypic testing and clinical markers, making coding sensitivity contingent on such data. Clinical course is stable and lifelong unless transformed or relapsed, and initial diagnosis is typically made in outpatient oncology or hematology, though acute complications or progression may lead to hospitalization.

source_definition: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic, progressive respiratory condition characterized by persistent and largely irreversible airflow limitation resulting from a pathological inflammatory response of the airways and lung parenchyma to inhaled noxious stimuli, principally tobacco smoke and occupational or environmental pollutants. The underlying pathophysiology encompasses small airway remodeling, luminal narrowing, and emphysematous destruction of alveolar walls, which together reduce expiratory flow and trap air. The phenotype spans the full severity continuum from mild spirometric impairment to very severe disease with profound functional limitation, and includes patients with asthma-COPD overlap who exhibit fixed or partially reversible obstruction in conjunction with features of both inflammatory phenotypes. Excluded from this definition are: airflow obstruction attributable to a primary underlying genetic or post-infectious etiology (e.g., alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, bronchiolitis obliterans); structural bronchiectasis; restrictive ventilatory defects from parenchymal fibrosis or chest wall disease; and dyspnea or airway abnormalities driven primarily by cardiac dysfunction such as heart failure.
clinical_rationale: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a major chronic condition with a strong association to external exposures like tobacco smoke and environmental or occupational pollutants. Pharmacologic agents, especially certain respiratory drugs, can trigger or exacerbate COPD symptoms or progression, though direct initiation of the disease is uncommon. Exacerbations of COPD may also result from certain drug exposures, such as beta-blockers causing bronchoconstriction. COPD is a persistent and progressive disease with no cure, and the diagnostic label generally applies for life. Incident diagnoses are often made in outpatient settings, though acute exacerbations commonly lead to acute care encounters. The requirement for objective testing (such as spirometry) to confirm airflow limitation reflects best practices in care but may not be universally applied in routine practice.

source_definition: Chronic pain is a non-malignant pain state characterized by the persistence of pain beyond the expected period of tissue healing, conventionally defined as lasting three months or longer, and encompassing nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic mechanisms. The condition may arise as a primary disorder â€” including idiopathic pain syndromes and those principally driven by central sensitization â€” or as a secondary manifestation of an underlying non-malignant systemic, musculoskeletal, or neurological condition, such as diabetic peripheral neuropathy, osteoarthritis, or multiple sclerosis. No minimum pain severity threshold is required; the phenotype captures chronic pain across all intensity levels from mild to severe. Cancer-related pain is explicitly excluded irrespective of duration or mechanism. Recurrent episodic pain conditions are included within this phenotype only when there is clinical evidence of a persistent interictal pain state or central sensitization between discrete episodes, distinguishing true chronic pain from mere temporal recurrence of acute pain events.
clinical_rationale: Chronic pain is a heterogeneous entity with multiple etiologies, including primary and secondary mechanisms. Across these mechanisms, some instances are drug-attributable, such as neuropathic pain from chemotherapy, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, or chronic musculoskeletal pain exacerbated by corticosteroids. Although cancer-related pain is excluded, the condition captures non-malignant pain syndromes of varying intensity. Chronic pain is persistent, requiring ongoing management and surveillance due to its central sensitization and/or structural origins, distinguishing it from transient episodic pain. Under routine care, incident cases of chronic pain are predominantly diagnosed in outpatient settings, except for diagnoses made during acute exacerbations or linked to ongoing treatments. Diagnostic codes often lack precision regarding severity or mechanism, limiting granularity but not utility for observational studies.

source_definition: Cognitive impairment is a clinical state characterized by any measurable decline in one or more cognitive domains â€” including but not limited to memory, attention, executive function, language, visuospatial ability, and processing speed â€” relative to an individual's prior level of functioning. The decline may be detected through formal neuropsychological testing, structured cognitive screening instruments, or clinical evaluation, and may be corroborated by informant or clinician observation. The phenotype encompasses the full spectrum of severity, from subtle early-stage changes to profound deficits that preclude independent functioning. No restriction on etiology is applied; cognitive decline attributable to neurodegenerative disease, cerebrovascular disease, traumatic brain injury, metabolic or toxic causes, psychiatric conditions, normal aging, or any other mechanism is included. No restriction on reversibility is imposed; both transient states â€” such as delirium, post-ictal confusion, or medication-induced cognitive effects â€” and persistent or progressive conditions are encompassed within this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Cognitive impairment is described as encompassing a wide range of etiologies, severities, and durations, including both reversible and progressive conditions. Drug-attributable etiologies, such as cognitive decline due to medication side effects (e.g., sedatives, anticholinergics) or toxic effects, are well-documented in the literature, making this concept valid as a pharmacovigilance outcome under those circumstances. However, the definition also includes non-drug causes such as neurodegenerative diseases and age-related decline, which may complicate attribution in practice. Therefore, it qualifies as a pharmacovigilance outcome under a narrow reading focused on acute, acquired, or drug-induced cognitive impairment. Establishing the diagnosis typically requires clinical evaluation or cognitive testing. The course may be persistent or transient depending on the underlying etiology, so an assumption of spectrum-wide persistence is appropriate for classification purposes.

source_definition: Colitis is an inflammatory condition of the large bowel, defined by the presence of mucosal or transmural inflammation affecting any segment of the colon or rectum, including isolated proctitis. The phenotype encompasses the full etiological spectrum â€” including infectious (bacterial, viral, or parasitic), immune-mediated (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's colitis, microscopic colitis), ischemic, drug- or toxin-induced, and radiation-associated causes â€” and applies regardless of whether colonic inflammation is the primary presenting condition or arises as a direct complication of another underlying disease process. All clinical severity levels are included, from mild self-limiting inflammation to fulminant or life-threatening colitis.
clinical_rationale: Colitis as defined here spans a broad etiological spectrum, including infectious, immune-mediated, ischemic, drug-induced, and other causes. Drug-induced colitis is a well-recognized subset of this phenotype, caused by agents such as antibiotics (C. difficile-associated colitis), NSAIDs, checkpoint inhibitors, and chemotherapeutic agents. While this makes colitis valid as a pharmacovigilance outcome, the broad definition also includes other non-drug-related causes, necessitating careful refinement if drug etiology is under investigation. The clinical course is variable depending on the cause, but many cases are episodic and thus TRANSIENT_RECURRENT overall. The severity can range, but the diagnosis is often confirmed in acute care settings when presentations are severe or life-threatening, with milder forms diagnosed in outpatient settings. Follow-up may be required for resolution monitoring, complications, or managing chronic inflammatory causes like IBD.

source_definition: Colorectal cancer is a malignant neoplasm arising as a primary tumor from the epithelial or stromal tissues of the colon or rectum, encompassing all histological subtypes including but not limited to adenocarcinoma, mucinous adenocarcinoma, signet-ring cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and neuroendocrine carcinoma. The phenotype is restricted to invasive malignancy in which neoplastic cells have breached the basement membrane, thereby excluding non-invasive carcinoma in situ (Stage 0/Tis). Anatomically, the phenotype is confined to the large intestine from the cecum through the rectosigmoid junction and rectum, explicitly excluding primary malignancies of the vermiform appendix and the anal canal. The phenotype encompasses both incident (newly diagnosed) and recurrent disease; however, only cases without evidence of distant metastatic spread â€” that is, disease clinically staged as Stage I, II, or III â€” are included. Malignancies that are secondary to hematogenous, lymphatic, or direct-extension spread from a non-colorectal primary tumor to the colon or rectum are explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Colorectal cancer is biologically plausible as a pharmacovigilance outcome through drug-induced carcinogenesis. Drugs such as immunosuppressants (e.g., azathioprine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus) and chemotherapeutics promoting secondary malignancies, as well as hormonal agents (e.g., SERMs) acting on colorectal tissue, have documented links to cancer pathophysiology. Targeting exclusively invasive malignancies (Stages I–III) allows the phenotype to focus on cases with therapeutic management without metastatic spread, refining cohort eligibility. The exclusion of carcinoma in situ (Stage 0) ensures clarity on invasiveness. Organ-specific malignancies may require anatomical exclusions and precise staging. Diagnosis usually occurs in an outpatient setting for asymptomatic or symptomatic patients through colonoscopy, biopsy, imaging, or surgical specimens, but initial presentation may also occur in acute care for obstructive or advanced disease.

source_definition: Coma is a pathological state of sustained, unarousable unresponsiveness in which the patient exhibits no purposeful reaction to external stimuli â€” including verbal commands, tactile contact, or noxious stimulation â€” persisting for a minimum of one hour. It reflects a profound, generalized failure of the arousal and awareness systems of the central nervous system and may arise from any structural, metabolic, toxic, infectious, or anoxic mechanism disrupting normal brain function. Coma is distinguished from transient loss of consciousness (such as syncope or brief post-ictal states) by its duration criterion, and is explicitly differentiated from brain death, which represents irreversible cessation of all brain and brainstem function; from the vegetative state, which is characterized by the return of sleep-wake cycling and eye-opening in the absence of awareness; and from locked-in syndrome, in which consciousness is preserved despite near-complete motor paralysis.
clinical_rationale: Coma is a critical neurological state reflecting profound central nervous system dysfunction, which can result from drug toxicity (e.g., sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics), metabolic disturbances (e.g., severe hyponatremia), or anoxic insults, among other causes. Numerous pharmacological agents have documented associations with this condition. Clinically, coma is distinguished by unarousable unresponsiveness persisting for at least one hour, separating it from brief loss of consciousness. Incident cases are almost always recognized in acute care settings, as coma requires immediate diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. Thus, it is a clinically actionable safety outcome in pharmacovigilance, and its inclusion requires precise definition and coding to avoid confusion with related but distinct states such as vegetative state or transient syncope.

source_definition: Confusion, as a clinical phenotype, refers to any acute or subacute global disturbance in cognitive function characterized by a detectable change from the patient's established baseline, spanning the full spectrum from mild disorientation to profound unresponsiveness. The condition encompasses impairments in attention, awareness, orientation, memory, or organized thinking that arise over a short period, irrespective of underlying etiology, and thus includes neurologically or medically mediated presentations such as delirium, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, septic encephalopathy, and postictal confusion. Acute-on-chronic deterioration qualifies when an individual with a pre-existing cognitive impairment exhibits a clinically discernible acute worsening beyond their known baseline. The phenotype explicitly excludes primary psychiatric disorders in which disorganized cognition arises from a psychiatric process â€” such as acute psychosis or a manic episode â€” rather than a neurological or systemic medical etiology. It further excludes focal neurological deficits, such as expressive aphasia or hemispatial neglect, that may superficially resemble generalized confusion but represent discrete cortical or subcortical lesions without global cognitive or attentional impairment.
clinical_rationale: Confusion, particularly when acute, is a pertinent pharmacovigilance outcome due to its potential induction by drugs. Mechanisms include direct CNS toxicity (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines), metabolic abnormalities induced by drug side effects (e.g., electrolyte disturbances from diuretics or chemotherapy), and iatrogenic causes like polypharmacy or abrupt withdrawal. The presented definition aligns closely with acute confusional states, which are transient but can recur under new exposures or exacerbations. While acute care settings predominate, cases spanning mild disorientation may be identified in outpatient settings. Symptoms such as disorientation or memory troubles may be recorded independently as structured data. Diagnostic procedures, including metabolic panels and neuroimaging, are frequently required for differential diagnosis, especially to exclude psychiatric or focal neurological causes. A high proportion of cases necessitate active treatment within 30 days, including addressing the underlying etiology or removing contributing drugs, and significant follow-up may occur, either for monitoring sequelae or ensuring resolution.

source_definition: Congenital heart block is a disorder of atrioventricular (AV) conduction, present from fetal life or birth, characterized by second- or third-degree impairment of electrical impulse transmission from the atria to the ventricles. The condition may arise through immune-mediated mechanisms, in which transplacental passage of maternal anti-Ro/SSA and/or anti-La/SSB autoantibodies induces inflammation and fibrosis of the fetal AV node, or through structural mechanisms, in which AV nodal conduction is disrupted by coexisting congenital cardiac malformations such as atrioventricular discordance or heterotaxy syndromes. The phenotype excludes AV block acquired after birth due to infection, medication toxicity, or myocardial degeneration, as well as iatrogenic AV block resulting from surgical intervention for congenital or other cardiac disease.
clinical_rationale: Congenital heart block is not drug-attributable in this phenotype definition, as it excludes acquired AV block resulting from medication toxicity or other external causes. Immune-mediated congenital heart block due to maternal autoantibodies represents a distinct etiology independent of drug exposure, and structural causes are determined by anatomical malformations rather than external influences. The course is persistent, as the diagnosis remains relevant for life unless corrected structurally, and the affected AV conduction does not spontaneously normalize. Severe cases involving third-degree block are often diagnosed prenatally or postnatally through specialized testing, such as echocardiography or electrocardiography, and may require acute care at the time of diagnosis. Otherwise, long-term management in stable patients may occur in ambulatory settings.

source_definition: Constipation is a clinical state characterized by a symptom complex of difficult, infrequent, or incomplete defecation, which may include hard or lumpy stools, excessive straining, a sensation of anorectal obstruction or blockage, the need for manual maneuvers to facilitate defecation, or a subjective reduction in stool frequency. The phenotype encompasses presentations of any duration or severity, including transient, acute, and chronic forms, and includes all underlying etiologies such as functional or idiopathic disorders, drug-induced effects (e.g., opioid-induced constipation), metabolic disturbances (e.g., hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia), and neurogenic causes (e.g., Parkinson's disease, spinal cord injury). Constipation arising as the direct mechanical consequence of a structural intraluminal or extraluminal bowel obstruction â€” such as that caused by colorectal neoplasm, stricture, adhesion, or volvulus â€” is explicitly excluded, as this represents a qualitatively distinct pathophysiological state requiring structural rather than functional characterization.
clinical_rationale: Constipation is a broad clinical syndrome that includes drug-attributable etiologies, particularly opioid-induced constipation and effects from other medications such as calcium-channel blockers, diuretics, or anticholinergics. Mechanistically, drugs contribute by impairing gut motility, modifying electrolyte balance, or altering neural control of defecation. The phenotype excludes mechanical obstruction etiologies, focusing on functional or metabolic causes, which ensures the definition aligns with the scope of pharmacovigilance. While drug-induced constipation is clinically distinct, the broad definition spans both drug-attributable and non-drug-attributable causes, making this outcome conditional on narrowing to the concept of drug-induced constipation for pharmacovigilance purposes. Most cases present in outpatient settings, though severe or complicated cases requiring acute management may be seen in acute care. Diagnosis is symptom-based and does not routinely require tests, though some cases may warrant confirmatory procedures (e.g., imaging, colonoscopy).

source_definition: Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory skin condition in which an exogenous substance is the proximate cause of cutaneous inflammation, spanning the full clinical spectrum from mild localized erythema and pruritus to severe vesiculation, blistering, and ulceration. The phenotype encompasses two mechanistically distinct subtypes: allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed-type (Type IV) T-cellâ€“mediated hypersensitivity reaction requiring prior sensitization to a specific antigen; and irritant contact dermatitis, a non-immunologic, dose-dependent inflammatory response caused by direct chemical or physical disruption of the epidermal barrier without a requirement for prior sensitization. The phenotype further includes systemic contact dermatitis, wherein a previously sensitized individual mounts a generalized eczematous skin response following internal absorption of the culprit allergen via ingestion, inhalation, or injection. Explicitly excluded are all inflammatory dermatoses whose primary etiology is endogenous or non-contact-mediated, including atopic dermatitis (driven by genetic barrier dysfunction and IgE-mediated immune dysregulation), seborrheic dermatitis (driven by Malassezia yeast and sebaceous gland activity), psoriasis, and systemic drug eruptions not attributable to prior contact sensitization.
clinical_rationale: Contact dermatitis, including its allergic and irritant subtypes as well as systemic contact dermatitis, is a recognized pharmacovigilance outcome. Reactions can occur due to direct skin contact with exogenous substances such as topical drugs, cosmetics, or occupational exposures to chemicals, as well as systemic exposures through ingestion or injection in previously sensitized individuals. These mechanisms are biologically plausible and well-documented. The clinical course is transient as the condition resolves after removal or withdrawal of the causative agent. It is typically diagnosed in outpatient settings, except for severe cases. While pruritus and erythema are common symptoms, they are often either undercoded or subsumed under a broader diagnosis, leading to underrepresentation in structured data. Diagnosis is usually clinical, based on history and physical exam, with patch testing performed in some cases of suspected allergic contact dermatitis. Treatment is primarily achieved by removing the exposure source, and more severe cases may require additional interventions such as corticosteroids or other symptomatic treatments. Follow-up is generally not needed unless symptoms recur or persist due to ongoing exposure or misidentification of the trigger.

source_definition: A contusion of the lower limb is a closed soft tissue injury of the lower extremity â€” encompassing the hip, thigh, knee, lower leg, ankle, and foot â€” characterized by localized pain, swelling, tenderness, and ecchymosis resulting from damage to subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and small blood vessels without disruption of the overlying skin. The condition may arise from any mechanism, including external blunt-force trauma or non-traumatic medical causes such as coagulopathy or vascular fragility. This phenotype is restricted to isolated soft tissue contusions and excludes presentations in which a concurrent skeletal fracture, joint dislocation, or open wound is present at the same anatomical site, as these represent distinct or more severe injury states.
clinical_rationale: Contusion of the lower limb is a localized closed soft tissue injury involving pain, swelling, and bruising, arising primarily from blunt trauma but potentially associated with medical conditions like coagulopathies or vascular fragility. Drug-induced etiologies are plausible in the context of factors impairing clotting (such as anticoagulants) or causing increased vascular fragility (as with corticosteroids or other medications affecting connective tissue integrity). The exclusion of fractures, dislocations, and open wounds limits the scope to milder injuries. Incident diagnoses are nearly always recorded in outpatient settings or in acute care settings when sustained due to a clear traumatic incident. The absence of discrete recorded symptoms prior to diagnosis reflects a tendency for such injuries to be documented with history or physical examination findings rather than isolated symptoms. Imaging studies or diagnostic tests are not routinely necessary unless ruling out more severe injuries in complex presentations.

source_definition: A COPD exacerbation is an acute, sustained worsening of a patient's baseline respiratory symptoms â€” including dyspnea, cough, and/or sputum production â€” that exceeds normal day-to-day variability and necessitates a change in clinical management. The condition spans all severity tiers, from mild events requiring only escalation of short-acting bronchodilators to severe events requiring emergency care or hospitalization. The phenotype is restricted to worsening attributable to the pathophysiological mechanisms of COPD itself â€” principally heightened airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction â€” and explicitly excludes acute respiratory decompensation primarily driven by competing diagnoses such as decompensated heart failure, consolidative pneumonia as the primary precipitant, or acute bronchospastic events attributable to asthma or asthma-COPD overlap syndrome.
clinical_rationale: A COPD exacerbation is a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome because certain medications, such as beta-blockers, opioids, or inappropriate sedation, can potentially precipitate or worsen respiratory symptoms in COPD patients. The phenotype is well-defined as a transient worsening of symptoms requiring a change in management, which aligns with pharmacovigilance aims. The exclusion of other differential diagnoses such as pneumonia, heart failure, and asthma-related bronchospasms underscores the focus on COPD-specific pathophysiology, maintaining diagnostic specificity in observational data. Distinct episodes are separated by clinical stability and resolved adequately by management, meaning the condition is transient and recurrent.

source_definition: Coronary arteriosclerosis, as defined here, refers to the chronic, progressive pathological process of lipid-driven atherosclerotic plaque formation within the intima of the epicardial coronary arteries, resulting in variable degrees of luminal narrowing and endothelial dysfunction. The phenotype encompasses the full disease spectrum â€” from confirmed non-obstructive atherosclerotic lesions through hemodynamically significant obstructive disease â€” and includes acute atherothrombotic complications arising from plaque instability, such as plaque rupture or erosion and the resultant acute coronary syndromes. This definition explicitly excludes coronary artery pathology arising from non-atherosclerotic mechanisms, including inflammatory or immune-mediated arteritis (e.g., Kawasaki disease, Takayasu's arteritis), spontaneous coronary artery dissection, and radiation-induced coronary fibrosis. It further excludes conditions that may produce ischemic symptoms in the absence of epicardial atherosclerotic plaque, specifically coronary microvascular dysfunction and vasospastic (Prinzmetal's) angina.
clinical_rationale: Coronary arteriosclerosis is a central mechanism underlying ischemic coronary artery disease. Pharmacovigilance relevance arises from the potential of drugs to contribute to lipid abnormalities, endothelial dysfunction, or plaque progression (e.g., corticosteroids, antiretroviral drugs, atypical antipsychotics). Acute atherothrombotic complications like myocardial infarction are critical outcomes. Chronic coronary arteriosclerosis tends to be persistent, characterized by progressive plaque development and occasional acute complications. The clinical definition excludes non-atherosclerotic coronary artery abnormalities, microvascular dysfunction, and vasospastic angina, ensuring that the included cases reflect true atherosclerotic disease. Diagnosis is facilitated by imaging and functional studies, making objective testing essential.

source_definition: Coronary artery disease is an acquired pathological state characterized by any structural or functional impairment of coronary arterial perfusion, encompassing the full etiological spectrum including atherosclerotic plaque formation and luminal stenosis, coronary vasospasm, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, thromboembolic occlusion, and microvascular dysfunction, as well as coronary involvement arising as a secondary consequence of systemic conditions such as vasculitis or sustained hemodynamic compromise. The phenotype spans the full continuum of severity, from subclinical or incidentally detected impairment through stable symptomatic disease to acute ischemic manifestations including unstable angina and myocardial infarction, which are considered expressions of the same underlying pathophysiological process. Congenital coronary anomalies representing developmental structural variants present from birth are explicitly excluded, as these reflect a distinct biological origin unrelated to acquired disease mechanisms.
clinical_rationale: Coronary artery disease includes diverse acquired etiologies impairing coronary perfusion, including atherosclerosis as a dominant mechanism. Drugs may influence the disease through promotion of vasospasm (e.g., cocaine, triptans), aggravation of microvascular dysfunction (e.g., fluoropyrimidines), or hemodynamic compromise (e.g., hypotension from sedatives). Drug labels and case reports document these effects, so CAD has a plausible drug-attributable etiology. The condition is persistent once diagnosed due to chronic arterial pathology, but discrete ischemic episodes like unstable angina or acute myocardial infarction are transient, making overlap with related concepts a challenge in defining a stable cohort baseline. Coronary artery disease's modal diagnostic setting is outpatient care, with severity determining acute care referrals for symptomatic or advanced diseases. Congenital coronary anomalies, strictly excluded in the definition, affirm the phenotype's focus on acquired pathology.

source_definition: Coronary vasospasm is a pathophysiological state characterized by transient, reversible hypercontraction of coronary smooth muscle resulting in focal or diffuse luminal narrowing of one or more coronary arteries. It encompasses both discrete episodic events and the recurrent clinical syndrome of vasospastic angina (including Prinzmetal's or variant angina), and does not require the presence of myocardial ischemia as a necessary consequence â€” the functional coronary narrowing from smooth muscle contraction is itself the defining feature. The phenotype applies regardless of the underlying coronary substrate, spanning arteries that are angiographically normal, non-obstructively atherosclerotic, or significantly stenosed, with the coronary anatomy serving as a sub-classifier rather than an inclusion or exclusion criterion. Vasospasm arising from any triggering mechanism â€” including spontaneous endogenous hyperreactivity, exogenous pharmacological agents (e.g., cocaine, ergotamine, fluoropyrimidines), or pharmacological provocation testing â€” is included. The core phenotype is anchored to epicardial coronary artery spasm; coronary microvascular spasm, representing hypercontractility of the intramural resistance vessels, is recognized as a distinct but related sub-type within the broader phenotype. Excluded are non-vasospastic causes of transient coronary luminal compromise, including spontaneous coronary artery dissection, coronary thromboembolism, and mechanical myocardial bridging, which reduce coronary flow through structural or mechanical rather than vasomotor mechanisms.
clinical_rationale: Coronary vasospasm is clinically relevant as a potential drug-attributable condition, with established or plausible links to exogenous pharmacological agents such as cocaine, ergotamine, and fluoropyrimidines. It represents a transient, reversible state of coronary smooth muscle hypercontractility that may manifest as vasospastic angina, with or without myocardial ischemia. The clinical course can feature discrete episodic events and recurrent manifestations, making it both transient and recurrent. Diagnosis often requires clinical judgment, supported by provocative testing or angiography, although characteristic symptoms may be inconsistently documented. Acute care settings commonly capture incident cases due to symptom severity and urgency, but outpatient diagnoses are possible for milder presentations or recurrent episodes. Treatments such as calcium channel blockers or nitrates are commonly initiated, particularly post-diagnosis, and follow-up for recurrence or symptom monitoring is routine, particularly for vasospastic angina. The phenotype includes epicardial coronary artery spasm, distinguishing it from microvascular spasm or structural mechanisms of coronary compromise, such as dissection or bridging.

source_definition: Costal chondritis is an inflammatory condition of the costal cartilage â€” the hyaline cartilage segments connecting the anterior ends of the ribs to the sternum or to adjacent costal cartilage â€” characterized by localized chest wall pain and tenderness at one or more costochondral or sternocostal junctions. The condition may present as a discrete, self-limiting acute episode or as a persistent and recurring chronic state. All etiologies are encompassed, including idiopathic non-infectious inflammation, post-viral or other infectious-mediated inflammation, post-traumatic cartilage irritation, and inflammation following thoracic procedures. Tietze syndrome â€” a subtype distinguished by the additional presence of localized non-suppurative soft-tissue swelling at the affected costal junction â€” is included within this phenotype. Cases arising as a secondary manifestation of systemic inflammatory diseases, such as seronegative spondyloarthropathies or connective tissue disorders, are also included, provided that the primary clinical presentation involves costal cartilage inflammation. The diagnosis is clinical, based on reproducible tenderness on palpation of the affected costochondral or sternocostal junction(s), in the absence of an alternative explanation for the chest wall pain such as cardiac ischemia, pleuritis, or pulmonary pathology.
clinical_rationale: Costal chondritis is an inflammatory condition of the costal cartilage and may arise from multiple causes, including trauma, infections, thoracic procedures, or systemic inflammatory disorders. Drug-attributable etiologies are plausible but not common, primarily through mechanisms such as drug-induced hypersensitivity syndromes or immune-modulating drugs promoting systemic or localized inflammation. As the condition can present either as a discrete acute episode or as a chronic relapsing condition, its clinical course depends on the underlying cause. While physical examination is the mainstay of diagnosis, imaging is occasionally used to exclude alternative explanations. Diagnosis is typically made in an outpatient setting, with fewer acute admissions unless systemic pathology or severe pain occurs. The absence of pathognomonic symptoms and reliance on clinical diagnosis limit detection power in administrative data.

source_definition: Cough is a forceful, reflex-mediated expiratory maneuver arising from stimulation of afferent sensory receptors distributed throughout the upper and lower respiratory tract, including the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and pleura. The reflex is triggered by mechanical, chemical, inflammatory, or neurogenic stimuli and results in rapid glottic closure followed by explosive airflow intended to clear the airway of irritants, secretions, or foreign material. This phenotype encompasses cough of any duration, from transient single-episode events to persistent or chronic presentations, and includes both productive cough with sputum expectoration and non-productive dry cough. No restriction is placed on etiology; cough attributable to infectious, inflammatory, allergic, mechanical, iatrogenic, or neurogenic causes is included. Presentations where cough co-occurs with hemoptysis or precipitates vagally mediated syncope are included within this phenotype, as the cough reflex itself remains the primary clinical event of interest.
clinical_rationale: Cough is a symptom that can be reflexively triggered by diverse mechanisms, including drug-induced etiologies such as ACE inhibitor-related cough, which is well-documented and biologically plausible. Other drug-induced causes may involve irritant effects or hypersensitivity reactions to inhaled medications. The provided clinical definition is broad, encompassing all durations and etiologies, but cough itself can serve as a pharmacovigilance outcome only when focusing on drug-induced causes. Etiologies unrelated to drug exposure, such as infection or allergic reactions, are out of scope for drug safety surveillance unless explicitly drug-provoked. Incident cough is diagnosed across outpatient, acute, and inpatient settings, with outpatient predominance for milder or subacute cases. Diagnosis is often clinical, without discrete recorded symptoms distinct from the cough itself, and specific diagnostic tests are usually unnecessary unless secondary complications or differential diagnoses require investigation.

source_definition: COVID-19 is a systemic infectious disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2), encompassing the full spectrum of clinical manifestations attributable to this pathogen. The phenotype includes all laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections regardless of symptomatic status, spanning from asymptomatic infection through mild upper respiratory illness, moderate pneumonia, severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, and critical multi-organ dysfunction. The definition further encompasses post-acute disease manifestations directly attributable to SARS-CoV-2, including post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Long COVID), characterized by persistent or new symptoms extending beyond the acute infectious episode, and post-acute hyperinflammatory syndromes such as Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) and in Adults (MIS-A). Confirmation of SARS-CoV-2 as the causative pathogen is required; clinically similar presentations caused by other coronavirus species â€” including SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, and endemic human coronaviruses (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63, HCoV-OC43, HCoV-HKU1) â€” are explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, is a systemic infectious disease with a broad clinical spectrum ranging from asymptomatic cases to critical multi-organ dysfunction. It is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome as various drugs, including antivirals, immunomodulators, and vaccines, are associated with risks and benefits in the prevention or treatment of this condition. Post-acute sequelae, including Long COVID and hyperinflammatory syndromes (MIS-C and MIS-A), extend the disease's clinical relevance. Diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation of SARS-CoV-2. The inclusion of the full disease spectrum ensures that all relevant presentations, from acute to post-acute, are encompassed, while exclusion of other coronaviruses ensures specificity.

source_definition: Coxsackie virus disease is an acute infectious illness caused by Coxsackievirus, an RNA virus of the Enterovirus genus, comprising both Group A and Group B serotypes. The condition encompasses the full clinical spectrum of Coxsackievirus infection, including but not limited to mucocutaneous syndromes (hand-foot-and-mouth disease, herpangina), carditis (myocarditis, pericarditis), central nervous system involvement (aseptic meningitis, encephalitis), respiratory illness, pleurodynia, and neonatal sepsis-like illness. All severity levels are included, from mild, self-limited febrile illness to severe, organ-threatening disease. The phenotype is etiologically restricted to Coxsackievirus A and B; clinically similar presentations attributed solely to other enteroviruses (e.g., Echovirus, Enterovirus A71) or non-enteroviral pathogens are excluded, as are chronic sequelae no longer representing active Coxsackievirus infection.
clinical_rationale: Coxsackie virus disease encompasses a spectrum of acute infectious syndromes caused by Coxsackievirus, which is well-established as the etiologic agent in affected patients. While most manifestations are self-limiting or mild, severe presentations such as myocarditis, pericarditis, encephalitis, and neonatal sepsis-like illness are medically significant outcomes that may result in organ-threatening or life-threatening sequelae. Drug-attributable outcomes are not applicable, as Coxsackie virus disease is caused exclusively by viral infection and not induced by pharmacologic agents. However, differentiating Coxsackievirus disease from drug-associated mimics, such as drug-induced myocarditis or aseptic meningitis, can be important in safety signal discrimination. The phenotype is transient and encompasses acute episodes, with post-infectious sequelae separately classified. Diagnostic confirmation typically requires laboratory evidence (e.g., PCR or culture). Case severity and clinical presentation influence care setting, ranging from outpatient management for mild syndromes like hand-foot-and-mouth disease to acute care for more severe organ-threatening manifestations.

source_definition: Crohn's disease is a chronic, idiopathic, immune-mediated inflammatory bowel disease characterized by transmural, granulomatous inflammation capable of affecting any segment of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus. The disease is defined by its capacity to produce discontinuous, skip lesions and encompasses all phenotypic subtypes and disease behaviors, including non-stricturing/non-penetrating (inflammatory), stricturing, and penetrating disease, as well as perianal involvement, across all levels of clinical severity from mild to severe. The inflammatory process extends through the full thickness of the bowel wall and may result in downstream complications such as fistulas, abscesses, and fibrotic strictures. This definition explicitly excludes ulcerative colitis, which is limited to continuous, mucosal-only inflammation of the colon, and indeterminate/unclassified colitis, which represents unresolved diagnostic uncertainty between the two major inflammatory bowel disease entities. It further excludes granulomatous or transmural intestinal inflammation attributable to an identified infectious etiology, specifically intestinal tuberculosis, Yersinia enterocolitica ileitis, and actinomycosis, where a specific pathogen fully accounts for the histological and clinical findings.
clinical_rationale: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with idiopathic etiology, but drug-induced exacerbations or drug-induced secondary features (e.g., intestinal perforation) occasionally occur. The disease itself is not typically drug-attributable, though certain medications (NSAIDs, isotretinoin) may worsen symptoms or interact with underlying pathophysiology. The course is persistent and chronic, with episodic flares requiring management, making it relapsing by nature. Incident cases may be diagnosed in outpatient or acute care settings, depending on symptom severity and the presence of complications. Diagnostic confirmation typically requires endoscopy, imaging, and/or histopathology in combination with clinical features, and specific serological/laboratory markers may aid in diagnosis. Clinical management frequently involves condition-directed therapy like biologics (anti-TNF agents) or immunosuppressants during active disease or maintenance therapy. Follow-up care and monitoring are integral due to the risk of complications, disease recurrence, and sequelae.

source_definition: Cushing Syndrome is a pathological state arising from chronic, autonomous endogenous overproduction of cortisol, encompassing both ACTH-dependent forms â€” in which excess pituitary or ectopic ACTH drives bilateral adrenal hypersecretion â€” and ACTH-independent forms driven by primary adrenal pathology such as adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral hyperplasia. The phenotype includes both overt clinical presentations characterized by the systemic consequences of sustained glucocorticoid excess (including central adiposity, proximal myopathy, cutaneous fragility and striae, hypertension, glucose intolerance, and osteoporosis) and subclinical cases in which autonomous cortisol excess is confirmed by objective biochemical testing â€” such as abnormal late-night salivary cortisol, elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or failure of appropriate suppression on dexamethasone testing â€” in the absence of full clinical stigmata. Explicitly excluded are cases of exogenous or iatrogenic hypercortisolism resulting from therapeutic corticosteroid administration, as well as pseudo-Cushing states in which biochemical hypercortisolism is a reactive consequence of a primary condition such as major depressive disorder, alcohol use disorder, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, or morbid obesity, and where cortisol excess resolves upon adequate treatment of the underlying driver.
clinical_rationale: Cushing Syndrome is a viable pharmacovigilance outcome due to its potential drug-related etiology. Long-term administration of corticosteroids is a well-documented cause of iatrogenic hypercortisolism, although this phenotype excludes exogenous and iatrogenic cases. However, drugs that affect the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, such as psychiatric medications, are also reported to induce hypercortisolism and might contribute to endogenous Cushing Syndrome (albeit less commonly). The clinical course of Cushing Syndrome is persistent and highly morbid when untreated, as biochemical overproduction of cortisol does not spontaneously remit without specific treatment targeting the underlying endocrine pathology. Diagnosis requires biochemical confirmation and often imaging studies, given the rarity and complexity of the condition. Subclinical cases expand the scope of this phenotype but are captured under the definition due to inclusion of diagnostic criteria. Most cases will be diagnosed in outpatient or specialty care settings, though acute hospital admissions may occur due to severe complications of cortisol excess such as hypertensive crises, diabetes decompensation, or fractures.

source_definition: Cyanosis is a clinical sign characterized by a bluish or blue-grey discoloration of the skin, mucous membranes, lips, or nail beds resulting from an abnormal increase in deoxygenated oxyhemoglobin in the cutaneous or mucosal capillaries. It encompasses both central cyanosis, in which systemic arterial desaturation produces discoloration of the tongue and mucous membranes, and peripheral cyanosis, in which reduced local tissue perfusion causes discoloration of the extremities and nail beds despite potentially normal arterial oxygen saturation. The phenotype includes cyanosis arising secondary to any underlying cardiopulmonary, circulatory, or hematologic etiology. It is restricted to states of reduced oxyhemoglobin and explicitly excludes bluish or dusky discoloration caused by abnormal hemoglobin variants such as methemoglobinemia or sulfhemoglobinemia, as well as non-oxygen-related skin discolorations such as argyria, ecchymosis, or exogenous pigmentation.
clinical_rationale: Cyanosis is a clinical sign indicative of reduced oxygenation, which may result as a secondary consequence of various cardiopulmonary, circulatory, or hematologic disorders, some of which can be drug-induced. Drug-related etiologies include situations that secondarily compromise cardiac output, cause hypoventilation, paralyze respiratory muscles, or invoke hematologic dysfunction (e.g., methotrexate-related pulmonary toxicity or anticoagulant-induced hemorrhage leading to cardiopulmonary compromise), though not all underlying causes are drug attributable. Cyanosis itself, however, is not a standalone condition but rather a manifestation that needs association with an underlying disease process for phenotyping. The description excludes causes like methemoglobinemia or sulfhemoglobinemia, where drugs like dapsone or nitrates can be implicated. This restriction limits its direct suitability as a pharmacovigilance outcome, requiring careful contextual analysis. Accordingly, while cyanosis could appear in safety signal detection studies as part of a broader chain leading to cardiorespiratory compromise, the episode-based data capture of cyanosis alone lacks sufficient specificity.

source_definition: A cyst of the ovary is a benign, fluid-filled or semi-fluid-filled sac arising from and contained within ovarian tissue, encompassing the full etiologic spectrum of non-malignant cystic structures including functional cysts (follicular cysts and corpus luteum cysts resulting from aberrant or persistent follicular development), endometriomas (cysts lined by ectopic endometrial tissue), benign neoplastic cysts (such as serous and mucinous cystadenomas), and mature cystic teratomas (dermoid cysts). The phenotype applies regardless of cyst size or the presence of clinical symptoms. Explicitly excluded are cystic ovarian malignancies and borderline tumors, paraovarian and paratubal cysts of embryologic remnant origin, and the multifollicular ovarian morphology associated with polycystic ovary syndrome, which represents a distinct endocrine-driven anovulatory state rather than a discrete pathologic cystic lesion.
clinical_rationale: Ovarian cysts are non-malignant fluid-filled structures within ovarian tissue encompassing etiologies such as functional, endometriotic, benign neoplastic, and dermoid cysts. Ovarian cyst etiology may sometimes involve medication-induced mechanisms, particularly in cases such as ovulation induction drugs leading to follicular cyst formation or endometrial cyst exacerbation from hormonal alterations. The clinical course is often transient, with smaller cysts resolving spontaneously or after surgical removal. While diagnosed across care settings, larger symptomatic cysts or those necessitating surgical intervention are often identified in acute care settings. The definition explicitly excludes other types of cysts and multifollicular morphology, focusing solely on benign pathologic entities within ovarian tissue.

source_definition: Cystic fibrosis is a chronic, progressive, autosomal recessive multisystem disease caused by biallelic pathogenic mutations in the CFTR gene, resulting in a dysfunctional or absent cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein. This CFTR dysfunction impairs chloride and bicarbonate transport across epithelial surfaces, producing abnormally thick, dehydrated mucus secretions that obstruct and damage multiple organ systems. The phenotype encompasses the full classic clinical expression of CFTR dysfunction, including obstructive lung disease with chronic airway infection and progressive bronchiectasis, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with malabsorption and nutritional deficiencies, elevated sweat chloride concentrations, and hepatobiliary involvement. Downstream complications integral to the disease's natural history â€” including cystic fibrosis-related diabetes mellitus, CF-associated liver disease, distal intestinal obstruction syndrome, and CF-related bone disease â€” are considered part of this phenotype. This definition excludes phenotypically similar conditions arising from distinct etiological mechanisms, including primary ciliary dyskinesia, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and non-CF bronchiectasis attributable to other causes, as well as mild or atypical CFTR-related disorders that do not meet criteria for classic cystic fibrosis.
clinical_rationale: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is not primarily a pharmacovigilance outcome, as its etiology is genetic, occurring due to CFTR mutations. Medications, including antibiotics or CFTR modulators, do not cause the condition but are used for management of symptoms and complications. While some drugs may exacerbate CF-related conditions (e.g., worsening airway infections or hepatotoxicity), CF itself cannot arise as a drug-induced condition. The disease is persistent because its underlying genetic cause is immutable, and complications integral to CF are progressive or recurrent. Recording is mostly in outpatient specialty clinics, except during acute exacerbations, though the classic phenotype always mandates ongoing diagnosis and management under pulmonology or multidisciplinary care.

source_definition: Cystoid macular edema is a pathological state of the retina characterized by the intraretinal accumulation of fluid within the outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers of the macula, forming discrete cyst-like spaces arranged in a petaloid or honeycomb pattern as visualized on optical coherence tomography or fluorescein angiography. The condition arises from a disruption of the blood-retinal barrier â€” inner, outer, or both â€” leading to transudation or exudation of fluid into the retinal parenchyma, and may result from any underlying etiology including post-surgical inflammation, uveitis, retinal vascular occlusion, drug-related effects, or idiopathic mechanisms. The phenotype encompasses the full spectrum of disease from subclinical fluid detectable only on imaging to states associated with functional visual impairment. Explicitly excluded are: diffuse macular edema presenting as homogeneous retinal thickening without discrete cystoid spaces; subretinal fluid accumulation situated beneath the neurosensory retina, as seen in exudative age-related macular degeneration or central serous chorioretinopathy; and macular thickening attributable primarily to vitreomacular traction rather than vascular or inflammatory leakage.
clinical_rationale: Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome as certain medications, such as prostaglandin analogs or systemic mTOR inhibitors, are associated with its development due to disruption of the blood-retinal barrier. The description explicitly identifies drug-related etiologies alongside other causes such as uveitis, retinal vascular disease, and surgical trauma, emphasizing its multifactorial nature. Diagnosis typically depends on imaging modalities like optical coherence tomography or fluorescein angiography, and the condition's severity spectrum ranges from subclinical changes to functional visual impairment. Acute post-surgical presentations and drug-related cases may resolve with timely intervention, but chronic CME due to other underlying causes can persist, justifying classification as episodic recurrent disease. Most incident diagnoses occur in outpatient ophthalmology settings; however, severe cases causing marked visual disability may necessitate urgent care.

source_definition: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a systemic inflammatory response syndrome occurring as an iatrogenic complication of immune-activating therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy, bispecific antibodies, and monoclonal antibodies. It is characterized by excessive, uncontrolled release of pro-inflammatory cytokines â€” particularly interleukin-6, interferon-gamma, and tumor necrosis factor â€” driven by immune effector cell activation following therapeutic exposure. The syndrome encompasses the full spectrum of clinical severity, from Grade 1 presentations (fever without hemodynamic compromise) through Grade 4 life-threatening manifestations including refractory hypotension, severe hypoxia requiring mechanical ventilation, and multi-organ dysfunction. Concurrent immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) or macrophage activation syndrome/hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (MAS/HLH) is included within scope when these conditions co-occur with or emerge as a direct evolution of CRS in the context of immunotherapy exposure. Explicitly excluded are cytokine storm syndromes arising from infectious etiologies, sepsis-related systemic inflammation, transfusion reactions, and isolated ICANS or MAS/HLH occurring without concurrent CRS.
clinical_rationale: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a defined iatrogenic complication directly linked to immune-activating therapies, including CAR-T cells, bispecific antibodies, and monoclonal antibodies. The biologic mechanism involves excessive immune effector cell activation resulting in cytokine overproduction, with interleukin-6 playing a central mediatory role. CRS covers diverse clinical severity grades, from isolated fever to multi-organ dysfunction, and its onset follows therapeutic exposure with high consistency. Excluded are cytokine storm syndromes from infectious etiologies or other causes unrelated to pharmacological interventions, as they diverge etiologically and cannot reasonably be captured as drug-induced outcomes. Incident diagnoses nearly always occur during inpatient or acute care settings due to severity and rapid progression of the condition. Diagnosis requires clinical assessment and laboratory confirmation, and treatment is indicated promptly, often with cytokine-directed interventions like tocilizumab or corticosteroids.

source_definition: Cytolytic hepatitis is an acute or subacute (onset within 6 months) inflammatory condition of the liver characterized by predominant hepatocellular injury, defined biochemically by elevation of serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and/or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) above the upper limit of normal and a hepatocellular injury pattern confirmed by an R-ratio greater than 5 (calculated as [ALT Ã· ULN] Ã· [ALP Ã· ULN]), in accordance with RUCAM/CIOMS criteria. The phenotype is etiology-agnostic, encompassing injury from any underlying mechanism including viral, drug- or toxin-induced, autoimmune, ischemic, or metabolic causes. The presence of pre-existing chronic liver disease does not preclude classification, provided the cytolytic episode represents a distinct acute or subacute inflammatory event with aminotransferase elevation and a qualifying R-ratio. Mixed and cholestatic injury patterns (R-ratio â‰¤ 5) are explicitly excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Cytolytic hepatitis is a recognized pharmacovigilance outcome when drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is suspected or observed, typically involving drugs like acetaminophen (overdose, intrinsic toxicity), antimicrobials, or autoimmune-modulating therapies (e.g., immune checkpoint inhibitors). RUCAM/CIOMS criteria confirm the hepatocellular injury pattern by aminotransferase elevation and an R-ratio greater than 5. This phenotype is etiology-agnostic but excludes cholestatic or mixed injury patterns, narrowing its scope to cases of hepatocellular injury. Acute onset and transient resolution define this phenotype and distinguish reactive episodes from chronic liver disease. Laboratory data for ALT/AST levels and R-ratio are crucial for diagnosis, and drug exposure preceding the event is evaluated for etiologic attribution. The description aligns precisely with the phenotype name.
