source_definition: Deafness is an acquired condition, arising after birth and following the onset of language, characterized by severe-to-profound reduction in auditory sensitivity, defined as a hearing threshold of 70 decibels or greater in the better-hearing ear. The impairment may arise from pathology at any level of the peripheral auditory pathway, including the outer and middle ear (conductive loss), the cochlea or auditory nerve (sensorineural loss), or a combination of both (mixed loss), and may result from any etiology including ototoxic insult, infectious disease, autoimmune or inflammatory processes, neoplastic compression, traumatic injury, or idiopathic mechanisms. The condition encompasses both permanent and reversible episodes of hearing loss meeting the severity threshold. Explicitly excluded are central auditory processing disorders in which peripheral hearing thresholds remain intact, as well as tinnitus and hyperacusis occurring in the absence of a clinically significant elevation in hearing threshold.
clinical_rationale: Deafness, as defined here, is acquired after birth and includes severe-to-profound hearing loss caused by various mechanisms, including ototoxic drug exposure (e.g., aminoglycosides, cisplatin, loop diuretics). These drugs can cause sensorineural hearing loss, particularly affecting hair cells or cochlear structures. Other potential causes include infections, trauma, and autoimmune diseases. The inclusion of both reversible and permanent episodes makes defining recurrent episodes challenging, but most drug-induced cases will resolve or stabilize after the withdrawal of the offending agent. As the condition requires diagnostic testing (e.g., audiometry) to confirm the severity threshold, objective measurement is essential for diagnosis. Diagnoses are typically made in outpatient or subacute settings unless deafness arises acutely and dramatically (e.g., from sudden idiopathic sensorineural hearing loss or trauma).

source_definition: Death is defined as the permanent, irreversible cessation of spontaneous cardiopulmonary function in a living, post-birth individual, characterized by the complete and sustained absence of spontaneous circulatory and respiratory activity with no return of function. This phenotype encompasses all-cause mortality without restriction to any specific underlying etiology or pathophysiological mechanism. Explicitly excluded are episodes of transient cardiopulmonary cessation followed by return of spontaneous circulation (resuscitated cardiac arrest), regardless of subsequent clinical trajectory, as these represent a distinct physiological state rather than death. Also excluded are fetal death (stillbirth) and perinatal death, which constitute biologically and clinically distinct states occurring prior to or at the threshold of independent postnatal existence.
clinical_rationale: Death, as described here, is all-cause mortality in post-birth individuals, explicitly excluding fetal and perinatal deaths as well as transient cardiopulmonary cessation followed by recovery. While death is the ultimate outcome that terminates all other conditions and care trajectories, it is not a pharmacovigilance outcome by itself because attribution to a specific drug-induced mechanism cannot be determined for all-cause mortality without further context or specific investigation into causality. Pharmacovigilance outcomes must focus on intermediate or immediate causes contributing to death rather than the state of death itself. In claims and EHR data, recording of all-cause mortality is predominantly binary and nearly always conclusive, either as explicit death records or implied discontinuation of observation when known end-of-life care is documented. This concept does not exhibit discrete episodes or recurrent risk.

source_definition: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is the pathological formation of a thrombus within the deep venous system of the lower extremity, encompassing both proximal vessels (iliac, femoral, and popliteal veins) and distal calf veins (tibial and peroneal). The condition arises from one or more components of Virchow's triad â€” venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability â€” and may be provoked by systemic risk factors such as recent surgery, prolonged immobilization, active malignancy, or exogenous hormonal exposure, or may occur without an identifiable precipitating cause (unprovoked). Proximal involvement is recognized as a clinically significant severity modifier associated with increased risk of pulmonary embolism and post-thrombotic syndrome. This definition explicitly excludes thrombosis directly attributable to an indwelling venous catheter, superficial thrombophlebitis (involving the superficial venous system), and deep venous thromboses arising in non-lower-extremity territories, including upper extremity, portal, mesenteric, and cerebral venous systems.
clinical_rationale: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a recognized pharmacovigilance outcome due to its association with exogenous hormonal exposures (e.g., oral contraceptives, hormone replacement therapy) and other drug-related risks such as chemotherapeutic agents, particularly cisplatin, and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. It involves the pathological formation of thrombi in the deep venous system of the lower extremity. Exclusion of thrombosis in other venous territories clarifies the anatomical scope for surveillance; this definition focuses on lower-extremity DVT, which accounts for the majority of clinically significant cases. Laboratory testing (e.g., D-dimer and duplex ultrasonography) is essential for accurate diagnosis, and many cases are incidentally or urgently identified in acute care settings (e.g., ED or inpatient). Structured diagnostic pathways emphasize objective testing and immediate anticoagulation for provoked or unprovoked DVT episodes. Pulmonary embolism and recurrence represent notable sequelae.

source_definition: Dehydration is a pathophysiologic state characterized by a clinically meaningful net deficit of total body water, arising when fluid losses from any combination of gastrointestinal, renal, or insensible routes â€” or insufficient fluid intake â€” exceeds replenishment. The condition encompasses all osmolality patterns (isotonic, hyperosmolar, and hypo-osmolar) and spans the full spectrum of clinical severity, from mild presentations with thirst and dry mucous membranes to severe presentations involving hemodynamic compromise, oliguria, and altered mentation. Dehydration is included regardless of whether it represents a primary index condition or a secondary complication of an underlying disease process. Explicitly excluded are states of fluid maldistribution without genuine total body water deficit, including distributive conditions such as septic shock and anaphylaxis, and edema-forming states with relative intravascular depletion such as cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome, and decompensated heart failure.
clinical_rationale: Dehydration can be drug-attributable when caused by medications that increase fluid loss (e.g., diuretics), reduce fluid intake (e.g., sedatives), or impair renal function (e.g., nephrotoxic drugs). It is a transient condition, as patients are no longer described as being 'dehydrated' once the fluid deficit is corrected. However, secondary complications such as acute kidney injury or electrolyte abnormalities may require separate coding. Most cases are diagnosed clinically, and the severity reflects the spectrum from outpatient identification in mild dehydration to acute care settings for severe cases. Structured symptoms, such as mucous membrane dryness or hemodynamic signs, may be inconsistently recorded. Diagnostic criteria are predominantly clinical, although labs evaluating electrolyte or osmolality imbalances may assist. The need for active treatment within 30 days is common in moderate to severe cases, particularly in acute settings where fluid resuscitation is urgent.

source_definition: Delirium is an acute neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by a disturbance in attention and awareness, accompanied by an additional disturbance in cognition â€” such as disorientation, memory deficit, language impairment, or perceptual disturbance â€” that develops over a short period (typically hours to days), represents a change from the individual's baseline cognitive function, and tends to fluctuate in severity throughout the day. The syndrome encompasses all recognized psychomotor subtypes, including hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed presentations. Delirium superimposed on a pre-existing neurocognitive disorder or dementia is included when there is clear clinical evidence of acute deterioration beyond the patient's established cognitive baseline. The syndrome must be attributable to the direct physiological consequence of a non-substance-related general medical condition, such as infection, metabolic disturbance, or organ failure. Explicitly excluded are delirium arising primarily from substance intoxication or withdrawal, and primary psychiatric disorders â€” including acute psychosis, mania, and severe depressive episodes with psychomotor disturbance â€” that present with confusion or altered awareness in the absence of an identifiable somatic precipitant.
clinical_rationale: Delirium is a well-documented pharmacovigilance outcome due to direct drug-attributable etiologies such as anticholinergic medications, benzodiazepines, opioids, and corticosteroids, which can induce or exacerbate acute cognitive disturbances. The provided definition explicitly excludes substance-related delirium and primary psychiatric disorders, narrowing the scope to medical conditions and excluding certain substance-related causes. As this condition develops acutely and resolves with treatment or resolution of the precipitant, the clinical course is transient. Incident cases are most frequently diagnosed in acute care settings due to the urgency of underlying medical causes, although outpatient recognition may occur in less severe cases. Diagnostic criteria rely on clinical observation and patient history rather than specific tests, as it remains a predominantly clinical diagnosis requiring exclusion of alternatives. Treatment within 30 days is expected, targeting the underlying medical condition or addressing symptoms. Condition-specific follow-up is less likely unless the underlying illness generates sequelae or an ongoing predisposition for recurrence.

source_definition: A delusion is a fixed, false belief that is held with unshakeable conviction, is not amenable to correction by contradictory evidence or rational argument, and is not accounted for by the individual's cultural, religious, or subcultural background. The belief must be clinically significant, manifesting as a frank psychotic symptom that causes functional impairment or necessitates clinical evaluation. All subtypes of delusional content are included, including persecutory, grandiose, somatic, erotomanic, and nihilistic forms, regardless of the underlying etiology â€” whether primary psychiatric, neurodegenerative, or other organic cause. Explicitly excluded are overvalued ideas and ego-syntonic obsessional beliefs that fall short of full delusional conviction, as well as false beliefs arising exclusively within the context of delirium or an acute confusional state, and psychotic beliefs that are fully attributable to and temporally coincident with substance intoxication or withdrawal.
clinical_rationale: Delusions are a key feature of multiple psychiatric and organic disorders, including schizophrenia, neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's, and certain psychotic depression cases. While not a direct pharmacovigilance outcome, delusions can be related to adverse drug effects, particularly with medications such as dopamine agonists, corticosteroids, and certain psychostimulants. Delusions are considered persistent within episodes of the underlying etiology, and recurrent episodes of delusion may occur contingent upon the disease. The exclusion of beliefs exclusively tied to delirium or substance effects ensures that delusions are conceptualized within broader psychotic syndromes rather than temporary states induced by substance misuse. Diagnosis typically requires clinical assessment, and discrete symptoms like expressed false beliefs may often be captured under structured records, depending on care setting severity.

source_definition: Dementia is an acquired clinical syndrome characterized by persistent, progressive decline in cognitive function across one or more domains â€” including memory, executive function, language, visuospatial ability, or social cognition â€” of sufficient severity to impair independence in instrumental or basic activities of daily living, representing a significant decline from a previously established level of functioning. The syndrome is not restricted by etiology and encompasses neurodegenerative, vascular, mixed, and other underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. A etiological workup for reversible causes is not required for inclusion; the definition applies to all presentations meeting the syndromic threshold at the time of clinical assessment. Co-occurrence with delirium is permitted, provided the chronic and persistent nature of the cognitive decline is clinically distinguishable from the acute confusional episode. The syndrome explicitly excludes cognitive impairment that is better accounted for by a primary psychiatric disorder, such as a major depressive episode or psychotic disorder, where the cognitive deficits represent a manifestation of the underlying psychiatric condition rather than an independent neurodegenerative or vascular process.
clinical_rationale: Dementia is a persistent, progressive syndrome of cognitive decline that may arise from neurodegenerative, vascular, or mixed etiologies. While drug-induced cognitive impairment is reported (e.g., anticholinergic burden, benzodiazepines), these cases are better captured under acutely reversible conditions such as delirium or syndrome-specific cognitive impairment. The defined phenotype of dementia excludes transient drug-induced conditions and psychiatric disorders with cognitive impairment, focusing instead on chronic and progressive, generally irreversible causes. Consequently, dementia is most appropriate as a baseline covariate or as a stratification variable in pharmacovigilance studies rather than as a drug-attributable outcome itself under this definition. Diagnosis usually occurs in outpatient settings based on structured cognitive assessments, although advanced or late-stage cases may involve acute care if associated with severe complications like delirium or behavior disturbances.

source_definition: Dental caries is a chronic, progressive, bacterially-mediated infectious disease of the calcified tooth structures, characterized by the dissolution of tooth mineral through organic acids produced as byproducts of cariogenic microorganisms â€” primarily mutans streptococci and lactobacilli â€” fermenting dietary carbohydrates. The phenotype encompasses the full spectrum of lesion severity, from initial subclinical demineralization detectable as white spot lesions or radiographic enamel opacity, through progressive involvement of dentin and cementum, to frank cavitation of the tooth surface. The definition is restricted to the active caries lesion itself and does not include downstream sequelae such as pulpitis, periapical abscess, or tooth loss, even when causally attributable to caries progression. Tooth structure loss arising from non-microbial sources â€” including dental erosion secondary to gastroesophageal reflux, dietary acids, or other extrinsic chemical exposure â€” is explicitly excluded, as are non-carious structural defects such as dental fluorosis, molar-incisor hypomineralization, attrition, abrasion, and abfraction.
clinical_rationale: Dental caries is a chronic, progressive condition mediated by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrates, predominantly mutans streptococci and lactobacilli. Drug-induced side effects, especially involving reduced saliva production (e.g., dry mouth caused by anticholinergic medications, antidepressants, or antihistamines), can increase the risk of dental caries. Poor oral hygiene attributable to cognitive impairment or sedative use may also indirectly exacerbate caries risk. While the phenotype definition is focused solely on active caries lesions without their complications, the process is biologically modifiable by factors influenced by pharmacological exposure.

source_definition: Depression is a primary, non-psychotic mood disorder encompassing Major Depressive Disorder and Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia), characterized by a sustained disturbance in mood â€” manifesting as depressed mood and/or markedly diminished interest or pleasure â€” of sufficient duration and intensity to meet established threshold diagnostic criteria, across all severity levels from mild to severe. The condition arises from primary affective pathophysiology rather than as a downstream consequence of substance use, a concurrent general medical condition, or another psychiatric disorder. Excluded from this phenotype are depressive episodes occurring within the longitudinal course of Bipolar I or II disorder, depressive states causally attributable to exogenous substances or pharmacological agents, depressive disorders secondary to an identifiable general medical etiology, and any depressive episode accompanied by psychotic features.
clinical_rationale: The clinical definition explicitly restricts the phenotype to primary, non-psychotic mood disorders, excluding depressive episodes secondary to medication, substance use, medical conditions, or other psychiatric diagnoses. This restriction removes drug-attributable causes such as antidepressant-induced mood disturbances or corticosteroid-induced depression, rendering the phenotype not directly attributable to drug etiology. While depression is persistent in its labeling and natural history, it is relapsing because discrete depressive episodes meet independent diagnostic criteria. Diagnosis frequently occurs in the outpatient setting, although severe cases may present acutely to emergency care. Though depressive symptoms like low mood, anhedonia, and fatigue are highly prevalent, these are often encompassed in the diagnostic code rather than being discretely recorded or codified. Formal diagnosis typically relies on clinical interviews rather than objective testing.

source_definition: A depressive episode is a discrete, time-limited clinical state defined by the presence of sustained depressed mood and/or pervasive anhedonia, accompanied by a constellation of associated neurovegetative, cognitive, and somatic symptoms â€” including disturbances in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, and psychomotor activity, as well as feelings of worthlessness or guilt â€” of sufficient number and duration to meet recognized diagnostic threshold criteria. The phenotype encompasses episodes of any severity, from mild to severe, including those accompanied by psychotic features. No restriction is placed on etiology or clinical context: depressive episodes arising as primary mood disorders, as well as those occurring in the setting of bipolar disorder, schizoaffective disorder, substance or medication use, general medical conditions, bereavement, adjustment reactions, or as secondary mood disturbances within any primary psychiatric disorder, are all encompassed within this construct. The sole defining criterion is the presence of a clinically recognizable depressive symptom cluster meeting episodic threshold, irrespective of underlying cause, comorbid condition, or precipitating context.
clinical_rationale: A depressive episode is commonly encountered in clinical practice and is defined by a recognizable constellation of symptoms with diagnostic thresholds. The construct is very broad, encompassing episodes of diverse etiology, including drug or medication-induced causes, as well as primary mood disorders, bipolar disorder, or depression secondary to medical conditions or adjustment reactions. Drug-induced depressive episodes represent a pharmacovigilance-relevant subset. Therefore, while the broader concept encompasses non-drug-related etiologies, depressive episodes caused or exacerbated by drugs (e.g., corticosteroids, interferons, isotretinoin) warrant pharmacovigilance attention. The clinical course is transient but episodes may recur and are separated by periods of remission, aligning with a transient recurrent classification. Diagnoses are typically recorded in outpatient or mental health settings, particularly for mild to moderate episodes. Severe episodes, especially those with psychotic features, may lead to acute care diagnoses. Diagnostic confirmation relies on clinical history and structured interviews; objective testing is not required. Treatment is usually initiated within 30 days, especially for moderate to severe cases. Follow-up is necessary in most cases to monitor response to therapy or manage recurrence.

source_definition: Dermatitis exfoliativa is a pathological inflammatory skin condition characterized by clinically significant widespread shedding and desquamation of the epidermis, manifesting as erythema, scaling, and skin peeling of sufficient severity to prompt medical evaluation or intervention. The condition encompasses the full spectrum of exfoliative presentations irrespective of the extent of body surface area involvement and is etiologically agnostic, including idiopathic forms as well as those arising secondary to underlying dermatoses (such as psoriasis or atopic dermatitis), systemic diseases (such as cutaneous T-cell lymphoma or SÃ©zary syndrome), or exogenous triggers (such as drug hypersensitivity reactions). The defining feature is an aberrant keratinocyte turnover and inflammatory process resulting in pathological desquamation; normal physiologic skin shedding and trivial or incidental scaling not requiring clinical attention are excluded.
clinical_rationale: Exfoliative dermatitis is a clinically significant pathological condition characterized by widespread skin desquamation, erythema, and peeling. Drug-induced exfoliative dermatitis is well documented through hypersensitivity reactions (including reactions to anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, and certain antibiotics). The condition spans idiopathic, secondary (linked to underlying dermatoses or systemic diseases), and exogenous drug-attributable etiologies, making it suitable as a pharmacovigilance outcome under the narrower drug-related context. Its transient course and potential for recurrence depend on etiological elimination or treatment. Acute care settings are common due to severe manifestations often warranting medical intervention.

source_definition: Dermatomyositis is a systemic autoimmune inflammatory condition characterized by the co-occurrence of proximal skeletal muscle inflammation and pathognomonic cutaneous manifestations. The muscle component is defined by symmetric proximal weakness, evidence of active myositis on laboratory evaluation (elevated muscle enzymes such as creatine kinase or aldolase), and, when assessed, characteristic perifascicular inflammation on muscle biopsy or inflammatory signal on muscle imaging. The cutaneous component is defined by one or more of the hallmark skin findings: heliotrope erythema of the periorbital region, Gottron's papules or sign over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, or other DM-specific rashes such as the shawl sign or V-sign. The phenotype encompasses all ages of onset, including juvenile dermatomyositis, and includes cases where an exogenous agent (such as a checkpoint inhibitor or other drug) appears to have triggered the syndrome. It explicitly excludes clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis in which muscle disease is absent, paraneoplastic dermatomyositis arising as a direct manifestation of an underlying malignancy, polymyositis presenting without cutaneous involvement, and anti-synthetase syndrome, which is distinguished by its characteristic serologic profile and clinical constellation despite possible myositis overlap.
clinical_rationale: Dermatomyositis (DM) is a systemic autoimmune disease with both muscle and skin involvement. It is of pharmacovigilance interest due to documented cases of drug-induced dermatomyositis triggered by immune checkpoint inhibitors and other therapies. The condition is clinically and diagnostically distinct from related syndromes such as clinically amyopathic DM, polymyositis, paraneoplastic DM, and anti-synthetase syndrome, which are excluded from this phenotype definition. DM requires diagnostic differentiation using clinical, laboratory, and biopsy findings, and structured data may capture characteristic skin or muscle symptoms. Although these symptoms can be separately recorded, diagnoses typically synthesize findings into a single diagnostic label. Most patients require active treatment with immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory therapies, and close follow-up or sequelae monitoring is common due to risk of chronic complications or recurrence.

source_definition: Deviated nasal septum is a structural condition defined by the displacement or angulation of the nasal septum â€” the osteocartilaginous midline partition dividing the nasal cavity into two passages â€” away from its normal midline position. The deviation may involve the cartilaginous septum, the bony septum (perpendicular plate of the ethmoid or vomer), or both, and may present as a smooth lateral deflection, an S-shaped curvature, or a localized angulation. The phenotype encompasses deviations of any degree of severity, including those identified incidentally on physical examination or imaging in the absence of symptoms or functional impairment. All underlying etiologies are included, incorporating both congenital or developmental malalignment arising during growth and post-traumatic displacement resulting from nasal injury or fracture. This phenotype explicitly excludes other distinct septal pathologies: septal perforation (a through-and-through tissue defect), septal hematoma (blood accumulation between cartilage and perichondrium), and septal abscess.
clinical_rationale: Deviated nasal septum describes a structural condition that is typically congenital, developmental, or related to post-traumatic injury, with no established or plausible causal relationship to drug exposure. Certain medications could hypothetically influence nasal structures indirectly (e.g., corticosteroids causing tissue atrophy), but not to the degree necessary to induce septal deviation on their own. Management of symptomatic cases often occurs in an outpatient setting, though severe or traumatic cases may require acute care attention. As the deviation is a structural abnormality, the condition is persistent by definition, though its functional relevance (e.g., airway obstruction, sinus disease) can vary.

source_definition: Diabetes mellitus is a heterogeneous group of metabolic disorders characterized by a sustained state of hyperglycemia arising from any disruption of glucose homeostasis sufficient to meet established diagnostic thresholds: a fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or greater, a two-hour plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or greater during an oral glucose tolerance test, a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) of 6.5% or greater, or a random plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or greater in the presence of classic hyperglycemic symptoms. The phenotype encompasses all etiologic subtypes without restriction, including absolute insulin deficiency from autoimmune Î²-cell destruction (type 1), progressive insulin resistance with relative insulin insufficiency (type 2), monogenic forms such as maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY), secondary diabetes arising from exocrine pancreatic disease or endocrine disorders, drug- or chemical-induced diabetes, and gestational diabetes mellitus. No etiologic subtype, mechanism of onset, or duration pattern is excluded, provided the hyperglycemic state meets the diagnostic threshold. Subclinical states of glucose dysregulation that do not fulfill these criteria â€” including impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance â€” are explicitly excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Diabetes mellitus as described spans multiple etiologic subtypes, some of which are drug-attributable (e.g., glucocorticoid-induced diabetes, atypical antipsychotic-induced diabetes, or diabetes secondary to chemotherapy). Individual subtypes have distinct mechanisms; drug-induced diabetes occurs via direct interference with glucose regulation pathways, such as insulin resistance or ß-cell impairment. However, the description explicitly includes all types, even those entirely genetic, anatomical, or related to pregnancy or endocrine disorders, making this phenotype CONDITIONAL for pharmacovigilance unless restricted to drug-induced diabetes or secondary diabetes. Chronic hyperglycemia is a persistent clinical state regardless of the underlying cause; once diagnosed, the label generally remains indefinitely. Diagnosis typically occurs in outpatient care settings except in severe presentations, though acute care may document advanced complications. The presence of discrete recorded symptoms varies; classic hyperglycemia symptoms (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) may be noted but are often subsumed under the definitive diagnosis. Persistent management, laboratory surveillance, and sequelae such as cardiovascular disease are expected within one year of onset.

source_definition: Diabetic Ketoacidosis is an acute metabolic emergency occurring in individuals with diabetes mellitus, defined by the pathophysiological triad of ketonemia or ketonuria, metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap in which ketoacidosis is the primary driver, and an underlying state of absolute or relative insulin deficiency. The condition spans a full severity spectrum from mild compensated acidosis through life-threatening decompensation, and explicitly includes euglycemic presentations in which plasma glucose may be near-normal (as may occur with SGLT-2 inhibitor use or reduced carbohydrate intake) provided that insulin deficiency and ketoacidosis remain the dominant mechanism. This phenotype excludes hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, in which residual insulin activity suppresses significant ketogenesis; alcoholic ketoacidosis and starvation ketosis, which arise independent of diabetes and insulin physiology; and other primary high anion-gap acidoses (including lactic acidosis and uremic acidosis) in which ketonemia is not the principal cause of the acid-base disturbance.
clinical_rationale: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) is a critical acute outcome with well-documented drug-attributable etiologies, particularly through mechanisms such as insulin dysfunction or suppression, and ketogenesis during treatment with SGLT-2 inhibitors. It is characterized by measurable metabolic changes including ketonemia, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and insulin deficiency. DKA requires immediate acute care, as it often presents as a life-threatening emergency. The diagnosis is heavily reliant on laboratory data (e.g., serum ketones, arterial blood gas analysis, elevated anion gap). While the condition is acute and transient once resolved, subsequent episodes are new events because the underlying mechanism ceases with appropriate correction of metabolic derangements, allowing for recurrent diagnoses in new episodes. Most cases are diagnosed in acute care settings, though outpatient recognition may occur for mild compensated cases, and the characteristics including euglycemic DKA broaden the diagnostic challenges.

source_definition: Diabetic macular edema is a manifestation of diabetic microvascular disease defined by the presence of retinal thickening or intraretinal fluid accumulation in or near the macula, resulting from breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier driven by chronic hyperglycemia-induced pericyte loss, endothelial dysfunction, and increased vascular permeability. The phenotype encompasses the full anatomic spectrum of macular involvement â€” from mild thickening detectable only on retinal imaging to extensive edema with associated hard exudate deposition â€” and does not require a minimum threshold of visual acuity loss or the concurrent presence of other clinically visible diabetic retinopathy signs such as microaneurysms or hemorrhages, recognizing that macular edema may be the first or sole ocular manifestation of diabetic microvascular pathology. This definition is restricted to cases in which diabetes mellitus is established as the primary etiologic mechanism; explicitly excluded are all forms of macular edema arising from distinct non-diabetic pathophysiology, including that attributable to retinal vein or artery occlusion, intraocular inflammation (uveitic macular edema), pseudophakic cystoid macular edema following cataract surgery, vitreomacular traction, and exudative age-related macular degeneration.
clinical_rationale: Diabetic macular edema is a well-documented complication of diabetes mellitus, driven by chronic hyperglycemia-induced vascular permeability and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier. Anti-VEGF therapies and focal/grid laser photocoagulation are mainstay treatments. Drug-attributable etiologies are not included in the definition, as macular edema must be directly connected to diabetes, although some medications may exacerbate glycemic control, indirectly influencing the risk of edema. The course is persistent with stable management, as patients typically continue to be labeled as having the condition even after treatment or clinical resolution. Diagnosis relies heavily on imaging (optical coherence tomography or fluorescein angiography). Incidence is primarily identified in outpatient ophthalmology settings, as it is not inherently acute care-inducing absent major complications. The provided definition excludes non-diabetic causes, ensuring focus solely on diabetic etiology.

source_definition: Diabetic retinopathy is a progressive microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus characterized by pathological structural and functional changes to the retinal vasculature driven by chronic hyperglycemia. The condition spans a continuum from early non-proliferative disease â€” defined by breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier, microaneurysm formation, intraretinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, and cotton-wool spots â€” through severe non-proliferative disease marked by venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, to proliferative diabetic retinopathy defined by pathological neovascularization of the retina, optic disc, or anterior segment. Diabetic macular edema, the accumulation of intraretinal or subretinal fluid at the macula resulting from the same hyperglycemia-driven vascular permeability, is included within this phenotype at any stage of retinopathy severity. This definition is restricted to retinal disease in which diabetes is the established primary etiologic mechanism; excluded are all retinal vascular conditions arising from distinct non-diabetic pathophysiology, including hypertensive retinopathy, retinal vein or artery occlusion, and radiation-induced retinopathy.
clinical_rationale: Diabetic retinopathy is a well-established consequence of chronic hyperglycemia in diabetes mellitus, driven by microvascular damage and ischemia. It is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome particularly in anti-diabetic drug safety contexts, where insufficient glycemic control or drug-induced retinal toxicity may exacerbate or accelerate its progression. The combination of non-proliferative, proliferative, and diabetic macular edema stages represents a continuum of vascular damage tied exclusively to diabetes, and the definition explicitly excludes non-diabetic retinal conditions. Incident diabetic retinopathy is typically identified via ophthalmologic examination, often in outpatient settings, with a minority of cases presenting acutely due to severe proliferative or macular edema changes. The diagnostic pathway requires direct fundoscopic or imaging findings, and most cases require ongoing ophthalmologic management beyond the first year due to progression risk or persistence of macular edema. Symptoms such as visual changes may be recorded discretely in EHR systems but are inconsistent, while diagnostic procedures like optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiography are nearly universal in confirming staging and severity.

source_definition: Diarrhea is defined as the occurrence of three or more loose or watery stools within a 24-hour period, representing a pathological increase in stool frequency and liquidity attributable to impaired intestinal water absorption, hypersecretion, altered motility, or related mechanisms, regardless of etiology or duration. The phenotype is etiology-agnostic and captures events across the full spectrum of severity. It is intended to represent diarrhea as an adverse outcome and therefore excludes episodes that constitute a defining or cardinal manifestation of a concurrently diagnosed primary condition (e.g., an active inflammatory bowel disease flare or acute infectious gastroenteritis), as well as overflow diarrhea arising secondary to fecal impaction, which reflects a mechanistically distinct process of paradoxical liquid stool passage rather than true secretory or motility-driven diarrhea.
clinical_rationale: Diarrhea can arise as a drug-attributable outcome via various mechanisms, including altered intestinal motility (e.g., metoclopramide), direct mucosal irritation or damage (e.g., chemotherapy agents), hyperosmotic effects (e.g., magnesium-containing antacids), or altered electrolyte absorption (e.g., antibiotics associated with Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea). While other etiologies like infections, chronic conditions, or secondary overflow diarrhea are excluded per the definition, isolated acute diarrhea attributed to drugs fits pharmacovigilance criteria. The phenotype is transient and can recur as a new episode after resolution. Diagnosis may occur across diverse care settings, with milder cases diagnosed in outpatient care and severe cases often requiring acute care intervention. Stool frequency and liquidity are usually recorded as symptoms, but definitive diagnosis is clinical and rarely requires diagnostic tests in uncomplicated cases.

source_definition: Differentiation syndrome is a treatment-emergent, cytokine-mediated systemic inflammatory syndrome that occurs in patients with hematologic malignancies â€” most notably acute promyelocytic leukemia and IDH-mutated acute myeloid leukemia â€” receiving differentiation-inducing therapies. It arises from the rapid, therapy-driven differentiation of malignant myeloid precursors, which triggers the release of inflammatory cytokines and subsequent capillary leak. The syndrome encompasses a spectrum of clinical presentations ranging from mild to life-threatening, characterized by one or more of the following: unexplained fever, weight gain, peripheral edema, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural or pericardial effusions, hypotension, and renal impairment, occurring in temporal association with the initiation of differentiation therapy. Inflammatory syndromes with an identified infectious or septic etiology are excluded, as is cytokine release syndrome driven by immune effector cell activation (e.g., from CAR-T cell therapy or bispecific antibodies), which shares a cytokine-mediated phenotype but arises through a mechanistically distinct pathway.
clinical_rationale: Differentiation syndrome is a well-documented drug-induced outcome associated with differentiation-inducing therapies for certain hematologic malignancies, particularly acute promyelocytic leukemia and IDH-mutated acute myeloid leukemia. The pathophysiology involves cytokine-mediated inflammation and capillary leak triggered by therapy-driven differentiation of malignant myeloid precursors. It excludes infectious causes and other cytokine-mediated syndromes such as cytokine release syndrome associated with immune therapies. The condition is transient and typically resolves following prompt medical intervention, though severe cases may lead to multisystem complications. Incident cases are almost exclusively diagnosed in acute care due to the urgency of therapeutic and supportive interventions, and structured symptoms such as fever and edema are frequently recorded. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation supplemented with imaging or laboratory tests to exclude other causes of inflammation or organ dysfunction.

source_definition: Dislocation of shoulder joint refers to a complete, pathological displacement of the humeral head from its articulation with the glenoid fossa of the scapula (the glenohumeral joint), resulting in total loss of congruent joint contact that does not self-reduce without intervention. The condition encompasses dislocations arising from both traumatic mechanisms (e.g., high-energy impact, forced abduction and external rotation, or fall onto an outstretched hand) and atraumatic mechanisms (e.g., underlying glenohumeral hyperlaxity, connective tissue disorders, or recurrent instability without a discrete injury event). This phenotype is restricted to complete dislocations and explicitly excludes partial glenohumeral displacement (subluxation), as well as injuries to adjacent shoulder girdle joints, including acromioclavicular joint separation and sternoclavicular joint dislocation, which involve anatomically and pathophysiologically distinct structures.
clinical_rationale: Shoulder dislocation, whether traumatic or atraumatic, is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome under the narrow interpretation of acquired and acute dislocations, as certain medications (such as muscle relaxants, sedatives, or drugs causing weakness or altered proprioception) may increase the likelihood of atraumatic dislocations. Recurrent dislocations may also have a drug-associated component if underlying hyperlaxity is exacerbated by medication side effects. This phenotype excludes partial subluxation and adjacent joint injuries, focusing solely on complete glenohumeral dislocations. Symptom records such as severe shoulder pain or inability to move the arm may precede diagnosis but are inconsistently and variably recorded. Diagnosis is often confirmed via imaging, particularly when reduction is required, and management generally involves active treatment within 30 days, typically reduction followed by rehabilitation. Long-term follow-up may occasionally be required to manage shoulder instability or post-traumatic sequelae.

source_definition: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acute, systemic pathological state characterized by simultaneous, uncontrolled activation of the coagulation cascade and secondary fibrinolysis, triggered by an identifiable precipitating condition such as sepsis, major trauma, malignancy, or obstetric complication. The phenotype requires the concurrent presence of clinical manifestations â€” including active hemorrhage, thrombotic events, or end-organ dysfunction â€” and corroborating laboratory evidence of consumptive coagulopathy, specifically thrombocytopenia, markedly elevated D-dimer or fibrin degradation products, prolonged prothrombin time and/or activated partial thromboplastin time, and hypofibrinogenemia, consistent with ISTH overt DIC criteria. The fundamental pathophysiological hallmark is systemic thrombin generation leading to widespread microvascular fibrin deposition with depletion of clotting factors and platelets. Explicitly excluded are primary fibrinolysis, in which the fibrinolytic pathway is activated in isolation without concurrent systemic coagulation activation; thrombotic microangiopathies such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and hemolytic uremic syndrome, which produce thrombocytopenia and microvascular thrombosis through distinct mechanisms independent of consumptive coagulopathy; and all secondary coagulopathies not mechanistically attributable to systemic coagulation cascade activation, including coagulopathy of severe liver disease, dilutional coagulopathy from massive transfusion, and vitamin K deficiency, each of which may produce overlapping laboratory profiles without the defining substrate of pathological systemic thrombin generation.
clinical_rationale: DIC has a plausible drug-attributable etiology linked to medications such as cytotoxic chemotherapy, snake venom-based drugs, and less commonly certain immunotherapy agents or biological treatments that can trigger systemic coagulation activation or endothelial injury. The phenotype is acute but complex, requiring both clinical manifestations (e.g., bleeding, thrombosis, or organ damage) and laboratory corroboration per ISTH overt DIC criteria. The course is transient; resolution of DIC is possible upon treatment and withdrawal of the precipitating factor, although recurrent episodes may occur given new triggers, including reinstituted offending drugs. DIC is nearly always diagnosed in acute care settings, given its severity and the systemic instability it often induces. While discrete recorded symptoms such as thrombosis or bleeding may be present, the definitive diagnosis depends on laboratory evidence and integration of findings. The condition requires urgent medical treatment but also produces sequelae such as organ ischemia or continuing hematologic abnormalities often requiring follow-up management.

source_definition: Dizziness, as defined by this phenotype, refers specifically to disequilibrium: a clinical state characterized by impaired postural stability and an inability to maintain normal balance, in the absence of an illusory sensation of rotational movement (vertigo) or a subjective sense of impending loss of consciousness (presyncope). The phenotype is defined by the clinical recognition of abnormal postural stability in any degree or duration. It encompasses disequilibrium arising from any pathophysiological mechanism, including peripheral vestibular insufficiency, central neurological dysfunction (cerebellar, brainstem, spinal, or peripheral nerve), proprioceptive deficits, musculoskeletal impairment, as well as iatrogenic, secondary, and idiopathic causes. No minimum duration, severity threshold, or etiological restriction is imposed.
clinical_rationale: The phenotype 'Dizziness' has been specifically narrowed to refer to disequilibrium, excluding vertigo and presyncope. Drugs can plausibly contribute to disequilibrium via mechanisms such as central nervous system depression (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedatives), peripheral vestibular effects (ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides), or musculoskeletal weakness (steroid-induced myopathy, statin-related myopathy). However, this definition of disequilibrium also includes non-drug-attributable cases, such as those arising from central neurological disorders or musculoskeletal conditions. Therefore, while drug-induced disequilibrium is biologically plausible, the broader definition requires narrowing to iatrogenic or drug-related causes for pharmacovigilance relevance. The modal case of disequilibrium due to postural instability is recognized during outpatient care, though acute severe causes such as cerebellar stroke may initially present in acute care settings. Symptoms may be recorded directly (difficulty walking or maintaining balance) or inferred clinically during the diagnostic process.

source_definition: DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) is a severe, delayed drug hypersensitivity reaction occurring typically 2 to 8 weeks after initiation of a causative drug, characterized by an extensive cutaneous eruption involving more than 50% of body surface area or exhibiting characteristic morphology, fever of 38.5Â°C or higher, hematologic abnormalities defined as peripheral eosinophilia of at least 700 cells per mmÂ³ or the presence of atypical lymphocytes, and involvement of at least one visceral organ, most commonly the liver, kidneys, lungs, or heart. Both probable and definite presentations are included, encompassing cases that fulfill most but not all cardinal criteria provided the overall clinical picture is consistent with the syndrome. Viral reactivation â€” particularly of HHV-6, EBV, or CMV â€” is recognized as an expected immunological consequence of the drug-triggered hypersensitivity and does not exclude a diagnosis; visceral organ injury must represent new or worsening dysfunction temporally attributable to the drug reaction rather than solely to a pre-existing condition. Rare DRESS-AGEP overlap presentations exhibiting eosinophilia and visceral involvement are encompassed within this phenotype. The phenotype explicitly excludes Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis, which are defined by keratinocyte apoptosis and epidermal detachment without requiring visceral involvement or eosinophilia as cardinal features, as well as Adult-Onset Still's Disease, Hypereosinophilic Syndrome, and primary viral syndromes such as infectious mononucleosis that may mimic the systemic features of DRESS in the absence of a causative drug.
clinical_rationale: DRESS syndrome is a rare but life-threatening drug hypersensitivity reaction, making it a critical pharmacovigilance outcome. Causative drugs, such as anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, or antiretrovirals, are well-established, and the syndrome's hallmark features — drug exposure, fever, rash, eosinophilia, and multi-organ dysfunction — are specifically drug-attributable. It is a transient condition, typically resolving once the inciting agent is withdrawn and systemic therapy is initiated, but recurrence is possible with re-exposure. Incident cases are overwhelmingly diagnosed in acute care settings due to the severity of the systemic involvement, and diagnosis often requires detailed clinical evaluation and confirmatory testing. Overlap with conditions such as SJS/TEN is explicitly excluded in the definition, further lending clarity to its delineation as a distinct condition.

source_definition: Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is a reversible autoimmune syndrome that arises in temporally plausible association with exposure to a causative pharmacological agent in individuals with no prior history of systemic lupus erythematosus or other autoimmune connective tissue disease. It is characterized by the de novo development of lupus-like clinical features â€” including but not limited to arthralgias, arthritis, serositis (pleuritis or pericarditis), constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue), and cutaneous manifestations â€” accompanied by serological evidence of autoimmunity, most characteristically antinuclear antibody (ANA) positivity, often with antihistone antibody reactivity. The syndrome spans the full severity spectrum from isolated musculoskeletal and serological involvement to multi-system expression, provided a plausible drug etiology is present. DILE is distinguished from idiopathic SLE by its drug-temporal relationship and its expected clinical and serological improvement upon discontinuation of the offending agent. Cases occurring in patients with pre-existing autoimmune connective tissue diseases are excluded, as the attributability of new manifestations to a drug in that context cannot be clinically established with requisite specificity.
clinical_rationale: Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is a well-documented pharmacovigilance outcome associated with multiple medications, including hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, and TNF-alpha inhibitors. It is characterized by lupus-like symptoms and serological evidence of autoimmunity, with its defining feature being a temporal relationship between drug exposure and disease onset, along with resolution following drug discontinuation. DILE is distinct from idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus due to its drug-attributed etiology. Clinical course is transient and recurrent, as future episodes are possible upon re-challenge with the offending drug or exposure to other causative agents. Incident cases are typically identified in outpatient settings, though severe, multi-system cases may require hospitalization and urgent care.

source_definition: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is an acute hepatic insult arising from the direct or idiosyncratic toxic effect of an exogenous substance â€” encompassing prescription and non-prescription medications, herbal and dietary supplements, and chemical toxins â€” on the liver parenchyma or biliary system, producing clinically significant biochemical evidence of injury. The injury may present in a hepatocellular pattern reflecting predominant hepatocyte necrosis or inflammation, a cholestatic pattern reflecting impaired bile formation or flow, or a mixed pattern involving both. The severity spectrum is continuous, ranging from isolated clinically significant enzyme elevations through to acute liver failure â€” defined by superimposed coagulopathy and/or hepatic encephalopathy arising as a direct consequence of the inciting agent. This definition applies irrespective of whether the patient has pre-existing chronic liver disease, provided a plausible temporal and causal relationship between the offending substance and the hepatic injury can be established. Excluded are hepatic insults attributable solely to non-pharmacological mechanisms such as mechanical trauma or primary ischemia, and those better explained by an intercurrent viral, autoimmune, or metabolic hepatic disease in the absence of a plausible drug exposure.
clinical_rationale: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is a significant pharmacovigilance outcome, as many drugs and supplements are implicated in hepatotoxicity, including acetaminophen, antibiotics, anticonvulsants, statins, and herbal preparations. The mechanism can be direct (dose-related toxicity) or idiosyncratic (unpredictable and immune-mediated). The clinical spectrum is wide, ranging from asymptomatic liver enzyme elevations to acute liver failure. DILI presents with a variety of patterns — hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed — often requiring biochemical tests for diagnosis and monitoring of severity, and causality is determined with reference to temporal associations. Diagnosis usually excludes alternative causes of hepatic injury. Acute care is common for severe cases with systemic symptoms or liver failure, but milder cases may be diagnosed in outpatient settings. Symptom capture in structured data is inconsistent, as presenting symptoms like fatigue, jaundice, or abdominal pain may be ambiguous or non-specific.

source_definition: Dry age-related macular degeneration is a chronic, progressive, idiopathic, non-neovascular degenerative disease of the central retina arising from age-driven accumulation of extracellular debris (drusen) beneath the retinal pigment epithelium, with associated RPE dysfunction, progressive photoreceptor loss, and in advanced stages, confluent geographic atrophy of the RPE and outer retinal layers within the macular region. The phenotype spans the full atrophic disease continuum: early dry AMD (small to medium drusen, no visual impairment), intermediate dry AMD (large or confluent drusen and/or pigmentary abnormalities with early structural compromise), and late dry AMD (geographic atrophy with clinically significant central vision loss). The definition is strictly limited to the non-neovascular disease state; any affected eye with current or historical choroidal neovascularization â€” indicative of conversion to neovascular AMD â€” is excluded. Additionally, this phenotype excludes atrophic macular disease arising from inherited retinal dystrophies (including Stargardt disease and Best vitelliform macular dystrophy) and RPE atrophy that is secondary to a distinct primary ocular or systemic condition, such as chronic uveitis or toxic maculopathy, as these represent fundamentally different pathophysiological mechanisms.
clinical_rationale: Dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is not considered a drug-induced condition, as it results from age-related retinal degeneration primarily driven by genetic predisposition and environmental risk factors such as smoking and oxidative stress rather than drug exposure. The clinical definition provided explicitly excludes toxic maculopathy and atrophic maculopathies secondary to systemic or ocular conditions, removing drug-attributable retinal damage from its scope. While certain drugs like hydroxychloroquine can cause toxic maculopathy, this possibility is distinct from the idiopathic process underlying dry AMD. Therefore, dry age-related macular degeneration is not suitable as a pharmacovigilance outcome. Clinically, dry AMD is often identified during routine ophthalmologic care and is characterized by a slow, progressive course that is classified as persistent and stable, although its stages may evolve over time from early to intermediate and advanced forms, with advanced disease leading to geographic retinal atrophy and central vision loss. Follow-up care is expected for surveillance and disease management, with the use of imaging (e.g., fundus photography, optical coherence tomography) being standard practice for diagnosis and monitoring.

source_definition: Xerostomia is defined as the subjective patient-reported sensation of oral dryness, irrespective of severity, duration, or frequency of occurrence. The phenotype is based entirely on the patient's perceived experience and does not require objective confirmation of reduced salivary gland output. It encompasses dry mouth arising from any underlying mechanism, including but not limited to medication side effects, autoimmune salivary gland dysfunction (e.g., SjÃ¶gren's syndrome), head and neck radiation, systemic dehydration, or mouth-breathing. No etiological subtype is excluded; the defining characteristic is solely the subjective complaint of oral dryness.
clinical_rationale: Dry mouth, or xerostomia, is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome because many medications are known to cause oral dryness as a side effect. This includes anticholinergics, antihistamines, antidepressants, and diuretics, which can decrease salivary flow. Other causes include systemic conditions like Sjögren's syndrome, head and neck radiation, dehydration, and lifestyle factors like mouth-breathing. The description explicitly includes drug side effects within scope and encompasses cases from various etiologies without restriction. As the condition is transient and episodic in most cases, it can resolve with cessation of the offending cause, although persistent etiologies such as autoimmune salivary gland disorders may result in chronic symptoms. Diagnosis is routinely clinical, based on the patient's self-reported sensation of dryness without the need for diagnostic testing. Most cases are captured in outpatient settings, but acute care contexts may apply in rare, severe scenarios associated with systemic causes such as dehydration or radiation injury. Distinct symptom codes for dry mouth are available, but reports may also be embedded within clinical narratives, limiting the reliability of structured data alone for identification.

source_definition: Dysgeusia is a disorder of taste perception characterized by any qualitative or quantitative alteration in the normal sense of taste, encompassing the full spectrum of gustatory disturbances including parageusia (distorted or abnormal taste in response to a stimulus), hypogeusia (diminished taste sensitivity), ageusia (complete absence of taste perception), cacogeusia (persistent perception of an unpleasant or metallic taste), and phantogeusia (spontaneous taste perception in the absence of an external stimulus). The condition may arise from any underlying mechanism, including pharmacological exposure, infectious or post-infectious processes, neurological injury or disease affecting the gustatory pathway, nutritional deficiencies, local oropharyngeal pathology, or idiopathic causes, and is not restricted to any particular etiology or duration. The definition further encompasses alterations in flavor perception attributable to olfactory dysfunction, recognizing the integral role of retronasal olfaction in the overall subjective experience of taste.
clinical_rationale: Dysgeusia is recognized as a potential adverse drug reaction, with documented associations to medications such as chemotherapy agents, antibiotics (e.g., clarithromycin, metronidazole), antihypertensives (e.g., ACE inhibitors), and antidepressants, among others. These agents can alter taste perception through various mechanisms, including direct effects on taste receptor function, alterations in salivary composition, or disruption of central taste processing. The provided description spans multiple etiologies, but drug-induced and acquired causes of dysgeusia are suitable pharmacovigilance outcomes. Dysgeusia has a predominantly transient and episodic course, resolving after the removal of the causative agent or successful treatment of an underlying condition. However, distinct episodes may recur over time. The condition is usually diagnosed in ambulatory settings due to its non-critical nature. The description’s inclusion of olfactory-related taste alterations is noted but aligns with usual phenotypic practices. Other contributing factors like nutrition or neurological diseases would present separately in an etiological analysis.

source_definition: Dysphagia is a clinical state characterized by impaired or abnormal passage of a food or liquid bolus from the oral cavity to the stomach, arising at any anatomical level of the swallowing mechanism, including the oral preparatory, oropharyngeal, and esophageal phases. The condition encompasses a severity continuum ranging from mild difficulty advancing solid boluses â€” requiring compensatory behaviors such as dietary modification or increased liquid intake â€” to complete inability to swallow (aphagia). Dysphagia may result from neuromuscular dysfunction, structural abnormalities, motility disorders, or inflammatory or neoplastic processes affecting any segment of the swallowing pathway, and includes both idiopathic presentations and those arising secondary to an identifiable underlying disease process. Explicitly excluded from this phenotype are odynophagia, defined as painful swallowing in the absence of objectively impaired bolus transit, and globus sensation, defined as a subjective perception of pharyngeal fullness or tightness without demonstrable swallowing impairment.
clinical_rationale: Dysphagia refers to impaired or abnormal passage of food or liquid from the oral cavity to the stomach and can result from neuromuscular, structural, motility, inflammatory, or neoplastic causes. This phenotype excludes odynophagia and globus sensation, which are not defined by objective dysphagia. The condition may have drug-attributable etiology, such as medications causing esophageal dysmotility, esophageal strictures, or cognitive dysfunction leading to dysphagia. However, in many cases, dysphagia arises from non-drug causes like stroke, congenital conditions, or malignancy, making drug etiology only conditionally applicable. Most cases are chronic with varying severity, though specific episodes of dysphagia may arise if triggered by modifiable factors. Dysphagia is commonly recognized in outpatient settings during routine evaluations, though acute presentations requiring urgent management (e.g., obstruction or aspiration) can occur. Diagnostic tests such as videofluoroscopic swallowing studies, endoscopy, or esophageal manometry are often required to establish cause and assess severity.

source_definition: Dysphonia is a disorder of voice production characterized by any perceptible alteration in vocal quality, pitch, loudness, or the effort required to produce voice, arising from dysfunction at the level of the larynx and vocal tract. The phenotype encompasses the full spectrum of voice impairment â€” from mild hoarseness, breathiness, roughness, or strain through complete absence of phonation (aphonia) â€” regardless of the underlying etiology, which may include structural causes (e.g., vocal fold nodules, polyps, edema, or malignancy), inflammatory or infectious causes (e.g., laryngitis), neurological causes (e.g., vocal fold paralysis, spasmodic dysphonia), or functional and psychogenic mechanisms. No minimum duration or severity of impairment is required; both transient and persistent presentations are included within this phenotype. Dysarthria â€” a motor speech disorder reflecting neurological impairment of the broader speech mechanism beyond laryngeal voice production â€” is explicitly excluded, as are isolated disorders of articulation, resonance, or fluency that do not involve primary laryngeal dysfunction.
clinical_rationale: Dysphonia encompasses a wide range of vocal impairments due to dysfunction at the level of the larynx and vocal tract. While the phenotype spans structural, inflammatory, infectious, neurological, functional, and psychogenic causes, some of these etiologies may be linked to drug exposure. For example, drug-related laryngitis, vocal cord dysfunction, or vocal fold paralysis can occur with various medications. The absence of a requirement for minimum duration or severity broadens the scope, yet makes differentiation of drug-induced cases potentially challenging. Dysphonia, as described, is transient in some cases, resolving after the underlying cause is treated or eliminated, but can be persistent if related to chronic structural, neurological, or psychogenic conditions. Recognition and documentation of symptoms vary by severity; mild cases may not produce discrete records beyond a singular mention of dysphonia in the diagnosis.

source_definition: Dysplasia of the cervix is a precancerous condition characterized by abnormal proliferation and maturation of squamous epithelial cells arising at or near the cervical transformation zone, spanning a histological continuum from mild dysplasia (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 1, CIN 1), in which abnormal cells are confined to the lower one-third of the epithelium, through moderate dysplasia (CIN 2), to severe dysplasia and carcinoma in situ (CIN 3 / high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, HSIL), in which full-thickness or near-full-thickness epithelial atypia is present without breach of the basement membrane. This phenotype is restricted to squamous epithelial precursor lesions and explicitly excludes invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, glandular precursor lesions (adenocarcinoma in situ), and benign reactive or inflammatory cervical epithelial changes that do not meet histological criteria for dysplasia.
clinical_rationale: Cervical dysplasia is biologically plausible as a drug-attributable outcome via immunosuppression-related HPV persistence and progression, which has been observed with immunosuppressive drugs like tacrolimus and azathioprine, as well as HIV treatments due to drug-induced immune modulation. While most mild dysplasia (CIN 1) resolves spontaneously, moderate to severe dysplasia (CIN 2–3 / HSIL) requires active management and surveillance due to its precancerous nature, and the diagnostic label generally persists until eradication is confirmed. Histological evaluation via biopsy is critical for diagnosis, as dysplasia cannot be definitively diagnosed based on symptoms or physical exam alone. Management typically involves close monitoring, lesion excision, or ablation within 30 days in high-grade cases. The description appropriately excludes entities like invasive carcinoma or non-dysplastic conditions. Incident diagnoses may arise in either outpatient or acute care settings depending on severity.

source_definition: Dyspnea, as defined for this phenotype, is the acute onset or acute worsening of the subjective sensation of breathlessness or difficulty breathing occurring in the context of an underlying pathological process, across any level of severity from mild to severe. The phenotype is etiology-agnostic and captures breathlessness attributable to any organic mechanism, including cardiac, pulmonary, metabolic, neuromuscular, infectious, or other pathophysiological causes, and includes episodes in which dyspnea represents a secondary manifestation of a concurrent acute or chronic disease. No competing presentations of breathing difficulty â€” including stridor or hyperventilation â€” are excluded. Explicitly excluded is transient physiological breathlessness arising solely from vigorous physical exertion in otherwise healthy individuals without an identifiable underlying pathological condition.
clinical_rationale: Dyspnea is commonly an acute sensation that arises as a symptom of an underlying pathological process such as heart failure, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, asthma exacerbation, or other diseases. In the context of pharmacovigilance, dyspnea may be indirectly drug-attributable via mechanisms such as bronchoconstriction (e.g., beta-blockers in asthma), pulmonary fibrosis (e.g., amiodarone), or cardiogenic pulmonary edema (e.g., fluid retention with thiazolidinediones). However, idiopathic dyspnea without such underlying pathological mechanisms is rare, and the phenotype as described encompasses both drug-attributable and non-drug-attributable causes. Thus, the suitability of dyspnea as a pharmacovigilance outcome depends on identifying the underlying etiology. The description appropriately excludes physiological breathlessness from exertion in healthy individuals, focusing only on pathological contexts. Dyspnea can be transient and recur in relation to subsequent insults or disease progression. Incident cases are frequently recognized in both acute and outpatient care settings, depending on severity.

source_definition: Dystonia is a movement disorder phenomenologically defined by the presence of sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contractions that produce abnormal, repetitive movements, postures, or both, irrespective of anatomical distribution (focal, segmental, multifocal, hemidystonic, or generalized) or severity. The phenotype encompasses dystonia arising from any underlying etiology, including primary and idiopathic forms, monogenic and complex genetic disorders, pharmacologically-induced dystonia, structural brain pathology, metabolic disturbances, and neurodegenerative disease, provided the defining dystonic movement phenomenology is present. Explicitly excluded are other involuntary movement disorders that lack a dystonic component â€” including pure tremor, chorea, athetosis, myoclonus, and tics â€” as well as spasticity arising solely from upper motor neuron dysfunction without co-occurring dystonic features.
clinical_rationale: Dystonia is a heterogeneous movement disorder defined by sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contractions causing abnormal movements or postures. While the phenotype encompasses forms of dystonia arising from diverse etiologies—including genetic, structural, metabolic, and degenerative origins—drug-induced dystonia (e.g., caused by antipsychotics, antiemetics, or serotonergic agents) is a well-documented pharmacovigilance outcome. Idiopathic or genetic forms of dystonia are not drug-attributable, so pharmacovigilance analyses would need to focus only on acquired or secondary dystonia, specifically pharmacologically-induced cases. Diagnosis often requires clinical observation, and while laboratory or imaging studies may be used to rule out competing conditions, these are not always necessary to confirm dystonia itself. It is commonly diagnosed in outpatient or emergency settings, with follow-up guided by severity, underlying causes, and the patient's need for symptomatic or etiology-directed management.

source_definition: Dysuria is a patient-reported symptom characterized by pain, burning, or discomfort experienced specifically during the act of urination, arising from any underlying etiology including but not limited to infectious, inflammatory, obstructive, or idiopathic processes. The phenotype encompasses all presentations regardless of severity or chronicity, such that even a single documented episode constitutes a qualifying event. No etiological distinction is imposed; dysuria secondary to genitourinary infection, interstitial cystitis, urethral irritation, systemic disease, or pharmacological effect is included equally. Explicitly excluded are related but physiologically distinct lower urinary tract symptoms â€” specifically isolated urinary urgency and urinary frequency â€” when these occur in the absence of pain or burning during voiding, as these reflect neuromuscular rather than nociceptive pathology.
clinical_rationale: Dysuria is a symptom that can result from diverse etiologies, including infections, inflammation, trauma, or drug-induced injury to the lower urinary tract. Many medications are known to cause dysuria through mechanisms such as bladder irritation (e.g., cyclophosphamide), drug-induced urethritis, or the exacerbation of underlying conditions. Pharmacovigilance studies may focus on dysuria as a non-specific indicator of medication-related urinary tract effects. The description appropriately specifies the symptom of painful or burning urination, and excludes related lower urinary tract symptoms, making the definition suitable for a broad evaluation in active safety surveillance.

source_definition: Eclampsia is a severe, acute complication of hypertensive pregnancy disease characterized by new-onset seizures of any type â€” including generalized tonic-clonic, focal, or absence seizures â€” occurring in a woman with established preeclampsia (defined by new-onset hypertension with proteinuria, end-organ dysfunction, or other severe features) at or after 20 weeks of gestation, during labor, or within 48 hours following delivery. The condition arises from pathological cerebrovascular dysregulation driven by the systemic endothelial dysfunction of preeclampsia, resulting in cerebral hyperexcitability and seizure generation. Explicitly excluded are seizures in women with a pre-existing diagnosis of epilepsy or other known seizure disorder, as well as seizures causally attributable to distinct acute etiologies such as severe metabolic derangements (e.g., hypoglycemia, hyponatremia), structural intracranial pathology (e.g., hemorrhage, tumor, arteriovenous malformation), or central nervous system infection.
clinical_rationale: Eclampsia is a hypertensive emergency occurring in the context of preeclampsia and is characterized by seizures unrelated to an underlying neurological disorder or acute structural brain pathology. Several medications have been implicated in the exacerbation of hypertension or cerebral dysregulation that could precipitate eclampsia, such as corticosteroids, certain antiangiogenic drugs, and the misuse of sympathomimetic drugs. The clinical course is transient, as eclampsia resolves following effective management of seizures and the underlying preeclampsia. Post-event follow-up is common to monitor for hypertensive complications and assess maternal neurological recovery. Diagnosis typically occurs in the acute care setting, given its emergent nature, and requires both clinical examination and objective testing to exclude other causes of seizures.

source_definition: Eczematous dermatitis is a heterogeneous group of inflammatory skin conditions characterized by epidermal barrier dysfunction, cutaneous immune dysregulation, and the shared clinical features of pruritus, erythema, spongiosis, and variable degrees of scaling, vesiculation, lichenification, or excoriation. The phenotype encompasses all recognized subtypes â€” including atopic dermatitis, allergic and irritant contact dermatitis, dyshidrotic eczema, nummular eczema, and seborrheic dermatitis â€” across all severity levels from mild and intermittent to severe and chronic. Eczematous changes arising secondary to an underlying systemic condition (e.g., stasis dermatitis in the setting of chronic venous insufficiency) are included, as the cutaneous pathophysiology remains consistent with the eczematous process regardless of the initiating systemic context. Explicitly excluded are dermatophytosis and other primary infectious dermatoses, in which eczematous-appearing lesions are a direct consequence of microbial invasion rather than immune or barrier-mediated inflammation, and psoriasis, which is a mechanistically distinct condition driven by Th17-mediated keratinocyte hyperproliferation and is not considered part of the eczematous spectrum.
clinical_rationale: Eczematous dermatitis encompasses various subtypes of inflammatory skin conditions, including atopic dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, and dyshidrotic eczema, all of which share a pathophysiological basis of epidermal barrier dysfunction and immune dysregulation. Drug-induced eczematous reactions, such as allergic contact dermatitis due to topical medications or systemically triggered conditions, are biologically plausible and observed. However, the phenotype spans conditions that are not drug-induced (e.g., atopic dermatitis, stasis dermatitis secondary to venous insufficiency), suggesting the need for clinical nuance in identifying specific cases attributable to drug etiologies. Despite its frequent identification in outpatient settings, severe eczematous presentations (e.g., generalized eczema, erythrodermic atopic dermatitis) may necessitate acute care. Discrete symptoms such as pruritus, erythema, or scaling are often recorded prior to diagnosis but do not universally appear in structured data. Diagnostic confirmation is primarily clinical, and the need for ongoing management is typical in chronic subtypes.

source_definition: Edema is the clinically detectable abnormal accumulation of fluid within the interstitial spaces of peripheral tissues, manifesting as pitting swelling of the extremities, dependent body regions, or diffuse involvement of multiple body compartments (anasarca), arising from disturbances in one or more Starling forces â€” including elevated hydrostatic pressure, reduced oncotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, or impaired renal sodium and water excretion. The phenotype encompasses the full spectrum of severity, from mild 1+ pitting edema of the ankles to severe generalized fluid accumulation, provided the finding is clinically recognized. Excluded from this definition are organ-confined fluid accumulations (e.g., pulmonary edema, cerebral edema, macular edema), angioedema (rapid-onset deep dermal and submucosal swelling mediated by mast cell degranulation or bradykinin excess), and lymphedema (non-pitting accumulation of protein-rich lymphatic fluid resulting from structural or functional lymphatic insufficiency).
clinical_rationale: Edema is a clinically detectable abnormal fluid accumulation in peripheral tissues due to disturbances in Starling forces. It is a highly non-specific presentation that has diverse etiologies, including cardiac, hepatic, renal, nutritional, and vascular causes as well as iatrogenic factors such as drug-induced edema. Certain drugs, including calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and thiazolidinediones, are known to cause or exacerbate edema by mechanisms such as fluid retention or increased capillary permeability.
