Despite its broad differential, edema is biologically plausible as a pharmacovigilance outcome in drug surveillance. Mild edema is often managed in outpatient settings in less severe cases, whereas anasarca may require acute care. Diagnosis typically occurs during a physical examination, as the characteristic swelling is clinically apparent, and diagnostic tests are generally used to investigate the underlying etiology. Drug-induced edema tends to resolve upon discontinuation of the offending agent, making it transient. If the underlying cause of edema is chronic, such as heart failure or renal disease, it may be persistent. Reconciling observational data often proves challenging due to the terminological overlap with non-drug-related causes highlighted in the definition, making it critical to contextualize it properly in analyses.

source_definition: Elevated Blood Pressure is a new-onset state of pathologically elevated systemic arterial pressure, defined by a systolic blood pressure of at or above 130 mmHg and/or a diastolic blood pressure of at or above 80 mmHg, arising in an individual with no prior history of hypertension or documented blood pressure elevation. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical spectrum of incident pressure elevation, including discrete acute hypertensive episodes and the initial presentation of sustained chronic hypertension. It includes all etiological subtypes â€” primary (essential) hypertension as well as secondary hypertension attributable to identifiable underlying conditions such as renal, endocrine, or vascular pathology, including obstetric causes such as gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia. All blood pressure elevations meeting the defined threshold are included regardless of the presence of concurrent acute physiological stressors; no stressor-based exclusions are applied at the conceptual level.
clinical_rationale: Elevated blood pressure, defined as a systolic blood pressure at or above 130 mmHg and/or diastolic pressure at or above 80 mmHg, can be linked to drug-induced effects in certain situations. Secondary hypertension may arise from pharmacological causes, including medications like corticosteroids, NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, and sympathomimetics. While these are documented in case reports and mechanistically plausible, the definition encompasses a broad range of etiologic subtypes, including primary (essential) hypertension, which is multifactorial and typically not drug-attributable. Most instances of elevated blood pressure are persistent either as sustained hypertension or as subsequent episodes on top of an underlying hypertensive presentation. The phenotype's breadth poses challenges for distinguishing transient drug-induced episodes from chronic idiopathic or secondary hypertension. Diagnosis of elevated blood pressure is commonly made in outpatient settings but may also occur in acute care settings due to severe presentations. Symptoms like headache or dizziness are inconsistently documented as discrete coded records; blood pressure measurement is universally central to diagnosis. Initial treatment within 30 days is variable depending on severity, and while patients with sustained hypertension are likely to have follow-up within a year, transient episodes may not prompt long-term care.

source_definition: Encephalitis is an inflammatory condition of the brain parenchyma, defined by the presence of neurological dysfunction arising from direct or immune-mediated inflammation of brain tissue, regardless of the underlying etiology. The phenotype encompasses infectious causes (viral, bacterial, fungal, and parasitic agents that directly invade or trigger parenchymal inflammation), primary autoimmune and antibody-mediated encephalitis (including anti-neuronal antibody syndromes), para-infectious encephalitis (immune-mediated parenchymal inflammation temporally associated with a systemic infection at a remote site), paraneoplastic encephalitis (immune-mediated brain inflammation triggered by a distant malignancy), and post-vaccinial encephalitis. All severity levels, from mild neurological impairment to coma, are included. Cases in which inflammation involves both the brain parenchyma and the meninges (meningoencephalitis) are included; however, inflammatory processes confined exclusively to the meninges without parenchymal involvement are excluded. Encephalopathy due to non-inflammatory mechanisms â€” including metabolic derangement, systemic organ failure (hepatic, renal), toxic exposure, or hypoxic-ischemic injury â€” is explicitly excluded, as these represent functional brain dysfunction without primary parenchymal inflammation.
clinical_rationale: Encephalitis is pathophysiologically diverse but includes numerous drug-attributable causes, such as post-vaccinial encephalitis, paraneoplastic autoimmune encephalitis triggered by chemotherapy, and direct neurotoxic or immune-mediated effects of specific medications (e.g., immune checkpoint inhibitors associated with autoimmune encephalitis). The clinical definition clearly excludes non-inflammatory encephalopathies, narrowing the phenotype rigorously to inflammatory processes within the brain parenchyma. Incident diagnosis most commonly occurs in acute care settings due to the severe neurological dysfunction, and laboratory tests (e.g., CSF studies, imaging, serology, sometimes brain biopsy) are nearly always needed for confirmation. Reliable case identification requires attention to these diagnostic workflows and exclusion of solely meningitic or metabolic brain dysfunction.

source_definition: Encephalopathy is a clinical state of diffuse cerebral dysfunction arising from a systemic metabolic or exogenous toxic derangement, manifesting across a spectrum from mild impairment of attention and cognition to overt confusion, agitation, stupor, or coma. The underlying mechanism is a reversible or irreversible disruption of normal neuronal metabolism caused by systemic factors â€” including organ failure (hepatic, renal, respiratory), sepsis, electrolyte or glucose dysregulation, or exogenous drug or toxin exposure â€” rather than a primary structural lesion of the brain parenchyma. This definition explicitly excludes cerebral dysfunction attributable to focal or diffuse structural intracranial pathology (such as ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, intracranial neoplasm, brain abscess, or traumatic brain injury) and excludes primary central nervous system inflammatory conditions, including viral, bacterial, or autoimmune encephalitis and meningitis, which involve direct immunological or infectious attack on CNS tissue as the proximate cause.
clinical_rationale: Encephalopathy is suitable as a pharmacovigilance outcome because a drug-attributable etiology is documented, with mechanisms including direct neurotoxicity (e.g., chemotherapeutics, recreational drugs), metabolic derangements precipitated by drugs (e.g., hepatic or renal injury from acetaminophen or aminoglycosides), and indirect effects such as sepsis caused by drug-induced immunosuppression. The clinical course is transient when the underlying cause is reversible, but recurrent episodes may occur in cases of repeated exposure to exogenous toxins or fluctuating systemic derangements, meriting classification as TRANSIENT_RECURRENT. Diagnoses may span care settings but are most frequently recognized in acute care contexts. Symptoms such as confusion or agitation, while characteristic, are inconsistently recorded as distinct entities. Diagnosis universally requires clinical examination and often supportive diagnostic tests to establish the metabolic or toxic insult. Active treatment is nearly always required and follow-up is expected in most cases to manage sequelae of the underlying cause or prevent recurrence.

source_definition: End stage renal disease (ESRD) is an irreversible, chronic state of kidney failure characterized by a persistent and progressive reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) to below 15 mL/min/1.73 mÂ², representing the terminal stage of chronic kidney disease (CKD Stage 5). The condition reflects the permanent, structural loss of functional nephron mass resulting from a chronic, progressive kidney disease process, and is defined irrespective of whether renal replacement therapy â€” dialysis or kidney transplantation â€” has been initiated. Irreversibility is established through clinical documentation of a chronic, progressive kidney disease trajectory (e.g., prior CKD Stage 4 with longitudinal decline to Stage 5) rather than a mandatory fixed confirmation interval. ESRD explicitly excludes: (1) acute kidney injury (AKI) arising solely from an acute insult â€” such as sepsis, nephrotoxins, or urinary obstruction â€” where renal function recovery is possible; (2) AKI-on-CKD in which an acute precipitating event transiently drives GFR below 15 mL/min/1.73 mÂ² in a patient whose chronic baseline GFR remained above this threshold; and (3) functional or secondary renal impairment states, including hepatorenal syndrome and prerenal azotemia from volume depletion, in which GFR reduction reflects hemodynamic insufficiency rather than irreversible nephron destruction.
clinical_rationale: End stage renal disease (ESRD) is the terminal stage of chronic kidney disease characterized by irreversible loss of kidney function. A drug-attributable etiology is plausible through chronic nephrotoxicity, progression of CKD due to medication-related injuries, or the accumulation of damage from drug interactions over time, making ESRD a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. As per the definition, ESRD requires documentation of a chronic progressive trajectory, distinguishing it from AKI and transient reductions in kidney function due to acute insults or reversible conditions. The condition is persistent, as it represents a permanent state of kidney failure with an ongoing need for management either through dialysis or kidney transplantation. Incident diagnosis of ESRD is typically related to the initiation or transition to renal replacement therapy and is most often made in outpatient specialty clinics or dialysis centers, with hospitalization reserved for complications or late or emergency presentations.

source_definition: Endometrial cancer is a confirmed primary malignancy arising from the epithelial lining of the uterine corpus, encompassing all histologic subtypes of endometrial carcinoma, including Type I tumors (endometrioid adenocarcinoma and mucinous carcinoma) and Type II tumors (serous carcinoma, clear cell carcinoma, and mixed epithelial carcinomas), across all stages of invasion and spread (Stage I through Stage IV). The phenotype is restricted to tumors of primary endometrial epithelial origin and explicitly excludes malignancies involving the endometrium secondarily, including cervical carcinoma with superior extension into the endometrial cavity and metastatic deposits from extra-uterine primary sites such as ovarian, colorectal, or breast carcinoma. Non-invasive and precancerous endometrial lesions â€” including endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN), atypical endometrial hyperplasia, and endometrial intraepithelial carcinoma (EIC) â€” are excluded, as are all primary uterine mesenchymal malignancies such as endometrial stromal sarcomas and carcinosarcomas.
clinical_rationale: Endometrial cancer is a well-defined malignancy of the uterine corpus epithelial lining. Its etiology includes both endogenous hormonal and genetic factors, as well as exogenous exposures. Drug causality is biologically plausible and documented, particularly for unopposed estrogen therapies, tamoxifen, and drugs affecting the endocrine system. The phenotype explicitly excludes precancerous lesions and secondary involvement from other cancers, aligning with its definition. Diagnosis is often made in outpatient settings after evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding symptoms or incidental findings, but advanced disease may present in acute care settings. Histopathology is essential for diagnosis, requiring endometrial biopsy or curettage. Management typically involves surgery, and may include adjunct chemotherapy, radiation, or hormonal therapies.

source_definition: Endometriosis is a chronic, estrogen-dependent inflammatory condition characterized by the presence of endometrial-like glandular epithelium and stromal tissue at sites outside the uterine cavity. These ectopic implants may occur on the peritoneal surfaces of the pelvis, ovaries (forming endometriomas), rectovaginal septum, uterosacral ligaments, bowel, bladder, or, rarely, at extra-pelvic sites. The condition spans a spectrum of morphological severity from minimal superficial peritoneal lesions (Stage I) to extensive disease with dense adhesions and organ distortion (Stage IV). Regardless of stage, the ectopic tissue undergoes cyclic hormonal stimulation, driving local inflammation, fibrosis, and pain. The phenotype includes all anatomical subtypes and all severity stages of endometriosis but explicitly excludes adenomyosis, which is defined by the invasion of endometrial glands and stroma into the myometrium and represents a pathophysiologically and anatomically distinct condition.
clinical_rationale: Endometriosis is estrogen-dependent and its inflammatory pathology can be influenced by hormonal therapies, making it a valid pharmacovigilance outcome in the context of drugs affecting sex hormones (e.g., combined oral contraceptives, GnRH agonists or antagonists, aromatase inhibitors). Additionally, there are reports of iatrogenic enhanced disease progression associated with hormonal treatments. While the clinical definition accounts for anatomical and severity variation, it accurately excludes adenomyosis. Incident cases of endometriosis are predominantly diagnosed in outpatient gynecology settings, but inpatient cases may be observed in severe presentations requiring surgical intervention or hospitalization.

source_definition: Enterobiasis is an intestinal parasitic infection caused by Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm), characterized by colonization of the cecum, colon, and perianal region by this nematode. The phenotype encompasses both symptomatic presentations â€” most characteristically nocturnal perianal and perineal pruritus, sleep disturbance, and abdominal discomfort â€” and asymptomatic infection. Diagnosis may be established by parasitological confirmation (e.g., perianal tape test, stool microscopy, or direct visualization of adult worms or ova) or on clinical grounds based on a characteristic presentation. The phenotype is restricted to primary intestinal and perianal infection; ectopic manifestations arising from aberrant worm migration (e.g., vulvovaginitis, pelvic granuloma, peritoneal involvement) are excluded. Infections attributable to other intestinal helminths are excluded by organism specificity.
clinical_rationale: Enterobiasis is not typically associated with drug-induced or drug-attributable etiology. It is caused by the parasite Enterobius vermicularis and is transmitted via direct or indirect contact, with humans serving as the definitive host for the parasite. Pharmaceutical agents (anthelmintics) are used for treatment, but they do not cause enterobiasis; rather, they eliminate the infection. Symptoms such as perianal pruritus and abdominal discomfort are commonly observed and may be documented in structured clinical data. Diagnosis is established via clinical findings or diagnostic tests such as the perianal tape test, stool microscopy, or identification of adult worms. Infection is transient and usually resolves with appropriate anthelmintic treatment, though reinfection can occur. The condition is most commonly diagnosed in outpatient settings due to its mild symptoms in most cases.

source_definition: Secondary enuresis is the involuntary passage of urine â€” occurring during sleep (nocturnal), during waking hours (diurnal), or both â€” in an individual aged 5 years or older who had previously achieved sustained urinary continence for a minimum of six consecutive months. The condition represents a clinically meaningful regression from an established developmental milestone and may be precipitated by functional, behavioral, endocrine (e.g., diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus), infectious (e.g., urinary tract infection), psychological, or iatrogenic factors including post-surgical changes or medication effects. This phenotype explicitly excludes involuntary voiding attributable to neurogenic bladder dysfunction (e.g., arising from spinal cord injury, spina bifida, multiple sclerosis, or other central or peripheral neurological conditions) and structural or anatomical abnormalities of the urogenital tract (e.g., bladder exstrophy, vesicovaginal fistula, or ureterovesical anomalies), as these represent mechanistically distinct etiologies of urinary incontinence rather than a regression from previously established continence.
clinical_rationale: Secondary enuresis specifically involves a regression in urinary continence after a sustained period of normal function and excludes causes linked to neurogenic or structural abnormalities. The description identifies iatrogenic factors, including medication effects, as potential triggers, meaning that drug-induced enuresis is a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome. The prominent association with behavioral, psychological, and endocrinologic factors informs the population eligible for examination in safety studies. Although many cases can be diagnosed clinically, the differential diagnosis often requires evaluation with diagnostic tests for possible underlying conditions like diabetes, UTI, or medication side effects.

source_definition: Eosinophilia is a sustained elevation of the absolute eosinophil count (AEC) in peripheral blood, confirmed on at least two separate measurements exceeding the upper limit of normal (> 500 cells/ÂµL). The phenotype spans a severity continuum â€” mild (AEC 500â€“1,500 cells/ÂµL), moderate (AEC 1,500â€“5,000 cells/ÂµL), and severe or hypereosinophilia (AEC > 5,000 cells/ÂµL) â€” with severity treated as a descriptive modifier rather than an inclusion criterion. Both reactive (secondary) etiologies â€” encompassing atopic and allergic disease, parasitic infection, drug hypersensitivity, and systemic inflammatory conditions driven by eosinopoietic cytokines such as IL-5 â€” and primary (clonal or neoplastic) etiologies â€” including myeloproliferative neoplasms with eosinophilia, FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion-positive disease, and chronic eosinophilic leukemia â€” are included within this phenotype, with etiology serving as a sub-classification. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical continuum from asymptomatic laboratory elevation through hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES), the latter defined by persistent AEC â‰¥ 1,500 cells/ÂµL with attributable end-organ damage (e.g., eosinophilic cardiomyopathy, peripheral neuropathy, cutaneous infiltration, or gastrointestinal involvement). Tissue eosinophilia occurring in the absence of peripheral blood elevation is outside the scope of this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Eosinophilia is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome, predominantly when reactive (secondary) etiologies are causative, such as drug hypersensitivity mediated by IL-5-driven eosinophil production. Drug-related eosinophilia has been associated with numerous drugs, including antibiotics, NSAIDs, and chemotherapeutic agents, among others. The phenotype spans a wide range of severities, from asymptomatic elevation of eosinophil count to hypereosinophilic syndrome with end-organ damage. Given the possibility of multiple etiologies, it is crucial to exclude primary (clonal or neoplastic) causes, as these are unrelated to drug exposures. The clinical definition explicitly excludes non-peripheral tissue eosinophilia, which should not be considered in phenotype construction. Eosinophilia itself constitutes a laboratory diagnosis, often confirmed with repeated measurements of AEC, and may or may not require active treatment unless end-organ damage is present.

source_definition: Epicondylitis is a painful condition of the elbow characterized by tendinous and periosteal injury at the lateral or medial epicondyle of the humerus, arising from mechanical loading â€” either through cumulative repetitive microtrauma resulting in degenerative angiofibroblastic tendinopathy, or through acute overloading of the musculotendinous attachments at the epicondyle. The phenotype encompasses both lateral epicondylitis, involving pathology at the origin of the common extensor tendon at the lateral epicondyle, and medial epicondylitis, involving the flexor-pronator muscle group origin at the medial epicondyle. The condition is restricted to mechanically-driven tendinous and periosteal pathology and explicitly excludes elbow pain attributable to peripheral nerve entrapment syndromes â€” including radial tunnel syndrome and cubital tunnel syndrome â€” as well as epicondylar inflammation or pain arising secondarily from systemic inflammatory or crystal arthropathies such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or gout.
clinical_rationale: Epicondylitis, encompassing both lateral and medial epicondylitis, is a mechanically driven tendinous and periosteal injury primarily arising from repetitive microtrauma or acute overloading at the elbow. It explicitly excludes non-mechanical causes like nerve entrapments, systemic inflammatory conditions, and crystal arthropathies. The provided definition excludes drug-induced inflammatory or crystal arthropathies (e.g., gout induced by urate metabolism inhibitors) and focuses solely on mechanically induced epicondylitis. As such, without evidence attributing epicondylitis directly to medication exposure, the condition does not meet the criteria for a pharmacovigilance outcome. Diagnosis typically occurs in outpatient settings following clinical history and physical examination, with imaging rarely required unless atypical presentations or systemic causes are suspected.

source_definition: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder defined by a persistent, endogenous predisposition of the brain to generate recurrent, unprovoked seizures, operationally characterized by the occurrence of two or more unprovoked seizure events separated by at least 24 hours. The phenotype encompasses all seizure-onset classifications â€” focal, generalized, and unknown onset â€” and all idiopathic or cryptogenic etiological categories, without restriction by syndrome subtype, severity, or treatment status. Explicitly excluded are: acute symptomatic (provoked) seizures occurring in direct temporal relation to an identifiable and reversible precipitant (e.g., acute metabolic derangement, toxic exposure, CNS infection, or acute structural injury); psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES); syncopal episodes with convulsive features; and febrile seizures. Furthermore, epilepsy arising as a direct and expected sequela of a known structural lesion (e.g., post-stroke epilepsy, cortical dysplasia, tuberous sclerosis) or an identifiable chronic metabolic disorder is excluded, restricting the phenotype to epilepsy in which no definitive causative structural or metabolic etiology has been established.
clinical_rationale: Epilepsy as defined excludes acute symptomatic seizures and seizures with a reversible cause, focusing on unprovoked, endogenous seizure predisposition. The exclusion of acute symptomatic seizures prevents misclassification of seizures attributable to drugs or toxins. However, the phenotype does encompass idiopathic or cryptogenic epilepsy, which could be exacerbated or influenced indirectly by medication side effects (e.g., worsening seizure threshold or drug interactions). While the definition excludes epilepsy directly attributable to structural or metabolic etiologies, drug causality for new-onset epilepsy within the defined scope is not established, leading to the 'NO' classification for pharmacovigilance. Epilepsy is a chronic condition characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures, making its clinical course persistent and relapsing. Diagnosis may occur in acute or outpatient settings depending on the severity or presentation, and requires diagnostic EEG or imaging to confirm the condition. Active treatment is expected, given the need for seizure control, and ongoing follow-up and management are critical for monitoring treatment efficacy and managing potential sequelae.

source_definition: Epistaxis is an acute episode of hemorrhage arising from the vascular mucosa of the nasal cavity, encompassing bleeding from both the anterior nasal septum (Kiesselbach's plexus) and the posterior nasal passages (sphenopalatine arterial territory). The phenotype includes episodes of all clinical severities â€” from brief, self-limiting bleeds to prolonged hemorrhage requiring medical intervention â€” and encompasses all underlying etiologies, including idiopathic or spontaneous bleeding, direct mechanical or traumatic causes, iatrogenic causes (including anticoagulant use or procedural injury), and disease-associated causes such as coagulopathies, hypertension, vascular malformations, or neoplastic processes. Each discrete bleeding event constitutes an independent phenotype occurrence. Explicitly excluded are: bleeding that merely presents at the nares but originates from non-nasal structures (e.g., nasopharyngeal tumors, skull base hemorrhage, hemoptysis, or hematemesis draining anteriorly), and blood-tinged nasal secretions without frank mucosal hemorrhage.
clinical_rationale: Epistaxis is relevant in pharmacovigilance as certain medications, notably antiplatelet agents (e.g., aspirin, clopidogrel) and anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin, DOACs), can increase bleeding risk in the nasal vessels, particularly in older patients with other risk factors such as hypertension. The description clearly specifies discrete episodes, which aligns well with common clinical documentation practices. While the direct drug-induced cases constitute a significant subpopulation, this phenotype broadly includes all causes of epistaxis (e.g., traumatic, idiopathic, or disease-related), making it a conditional safety outcome. Diagnosis may be made clinically, as the symptoms are typically overt and do not necessitate additional testing or procedures when the source of hemorrhage is clear. However, severe or recurrent episodes may require intervention, which could involve cautery, nasal packing, or posterior packing. Condition-specific follow-up is not universally required except in recurring cases with underlying pathology.

source_definition: Epstein-Barr virus infection, as defined here, represents the initial encounter between a host and the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV; human herpesvirus 4), encompassing the full spectrum of primary infection from asymptomatic seroconversion to the classic infectious mononucleosis syndrome characterized by fever, pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, and atypical lymphocytosis. The phenotype applies to hosts of all immune statuses, including immunocompromised individuals. It is defined on a syndromic basis and does not require pathogen-specific laboratory confirmation, thereby capturing clinically diagnosed infectious mononucleosis attributed to EBV as well as cases where EBV is the presumed but unverified etiology. Excluded from this phenotype are EBV reactivation events in previously seropositive individuals, latent EBV infection, chronic active EBV infection, and all downstream EBV-associated malignant or lymphoproliferative conditions â€” including Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease, and EBV-driven hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis â€” which are regarded as distinct clinical entities.
clinical_rationale: Epstein-Barr virus infection can be drug-attributable in cases where immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., calcineurin inhibitors, anti-TNF agents) predispose to primary infection by attenuating immune surveillance, or where treatments such as cytotoxic chemotherapy increase susceptibility to opportunistic infections. The phenotype, as defined here, excludes reactivation and chronic active EBV infection but includes primary infection without laboratory confirmation, which results in clinical breadth but diagnostic uncertainty. Clinical manifestations like infectious mononucleosis are transient, resolving with supportive management, while ER/hospitalization is more likely in severe presentations (e.g., acute airway compromise). Diagnosis is typically clinical but can involve laboratory tests (e.g., heterophile antibody testing, EBV-specific serology) for confirmation of symptomatic cases. Due to possible laboratory underreporting in non-confirmed cases, reliance on clinical diagnosis may decrease coding specificity.

source_definition: Erectile dysfunction is a male sexual dysfunction characterized by the inability to achieve or maintain a penile erection of sufficient rigidity for satisfactory sexual activity, ranging in severity from mild reduction in erectile quality to complete absence of erectile response. The condition encompasses dysfunction arising from any pathophysiological mechanism, including impaired arterial inflow or venous occlusion, disruption of autonomic or somatic neural pathways innervating erectile tissue, hormonal dysregulation, psychogenic inhibition, and pharmacological interference with the erectile reflex arc. It includes erectile impairment occurring as a secondary manifestation of systemic or local conditions such as diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, hypogonadism, pelvic surgery, or spinal cord injury. Explicitly excluded from this phenotype are other domains of male sexual dysfunction â€” specifically disorders of ejaculation, orgasm, and sexual desire â€” in which the capacity for penile erection is preserved.
clinical_rationale: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is a male-specific sexual dysfunction encompassing a broad spectrum of severity and mechanisms. Drugs are a documented cause of ED, commonly via mechanisms such as hormonal dysregulation (e.g., anti-androgens, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors), diminished blood flow (e.g., beta-blockers, antihypertensives, diuretics), or neuronal interference (e.g., SSRIs, antipsychotics, sedatives). Discontinuation or adjustment of causative medications can improve ED, which supports its relevance as a pharmacovigilance outcome. This definition explicitly excludes other male sexual dysfunctions like disorders of ejaculation or libido, maintaining a focus on penile erection capability. Most cases are likely diagnosed and managed in outpatient care due to its chronic and non-life-threatening nature.

source_definition: Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp is a chronic, non-infectious, sterile inflammatory condition of the scalp characterized by the development of superficial pustules, erosions, and crusting on a background of atrophic or chronically sun-damaged scalp skin, with the potential to progress to scarring alopecia if untreated. The condition may arise idiopathically in susceptible individuals â€” typically elderly patients with actinically damaged scalp â€” or may be precipitated by local tissue injury including topical immunomodulatory therapies (e.g., imiquimod, 5-fluorouracil), ionizing radiation, surgical procedures, or cryotherapy. The underlying pathophysiology reflects a dysregulated sterile neutrophilic and inflammatory response within atrophic scalp tissue rather than microbial invasion, immune-mediated subepidermal blistering, or neoplastic transformation. Explicitly excluded from this phenotype are infectious pustular or erosive scalp conditions driven by bacterial, fungal, or other microbial etiologies (e.g., folliculitis, impetigo, kerion); autoimmune blistering disorders involving the scalp (e.g., pemphigus vulgaris, mucous membrane pemphigoid); and malignant or neoplastic conditions presenting with erosive scalp lesions (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma, extramammary Paget's disease of the scalp).
clinical_rationale: Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp can be precipitated by local tissue injury, including topical immunomodulatory drugs like imiquimod and 5-fluorouracil, ionizing radiation, surgical procedures, or cryotherapy, which makes it a plausible drug-attributable phenotype. However, it also arises idiopathically in elderly patients with chronically actinic-damaged scalp tissue, limiting its specificity as a pure pharmacovigilance signal without further refinement. The condition progresses chronically with relapses, and late-stage untreated cases can lead to scarring alopecia. Diagnosis is typically clinical, based on exclusion of infectious or neoplastic causes, but may sometimes be supported by histopathology. Incident diagnoses are made in outpatient settings, but more severe erosive cases may require acute care interventions. Broad age ranges reflect the potential for onset across adulthood and elderly age, but it primarily affects older adults.

source_definition: Erythema is a cutaneous clinical sign characterized by persistent, blanching redness of the skin resulting from abnormal dilation of superficial dermal capillaries and increased local blood flow as part of a pathological inflammatory or reactive tissue response. The redness is visible on inspection and transiently disappears under direct pressure (diascopy), distinguishing it from hemorrhagic discolorations such as petechiae, purpura, and ecchymosis, which arise from extravasated erythrocytes and do not blanche. The phenotype encompasses the full etiological spectrum of pathological erythema â€” including inflammatory, infectious, immune-mediated, physical, and drug-induced causes â€” and serves as the superordinate concept under which named erythema syndromes (e.g., Erythema Multiforme, erythema migrans, erythema nodosum) are subsumed as more specifically defined subtypes. Transient physiological skin flushing resulting from emotional stimuli, thermoregulation, or exercise is excluded, as these represent normal vasomotor responses without an underlying pathological process.
clinical_rationale: Erythema is a visible, blanching redness of the skin caused by abnormal dermal capillary dilation and increased blood flow due to pathological processes. It is broadly defined here to encompass all etiologies, including drug-induced reactions and immune-mediated conditions, but requires specification to narrow to drug-attributable outcomes. Examples like erythema multiforme and drug rashes are suitable under pharmacovigilance contexts, whereas many non-drug-related causes (e.g., infectious, autoimmune, or physical) fall outside this scope. Diagnostic coding typically reflects the presence of erythema without detailed cause attribution, limiting specificity in observational studies. The supplied description explicitly excludes transient physiological flushing, further refining the phenotype definition to pathological cases.

source_definition: Erythema Multiforme is an acute, self-limited hypersensitivity reaction of the skin and mucous membranes characterized by the abrupt onset of fixed, symmetrically distributed targetoid (iris) lesions â€” composed of concentric zones of color change with a dusky or blistered center â€” arising predominantly in response to infectious triggers, most commonly herpes simplex virus. The phenotype encompasses both EM minor, in which lesions are confined to the skin with absent or minimal mucosal involvement, and EM major, in which prominent involvement of one or more mucosal surfaces (oral, ocular, or genital) accompanies the cutaneous eruption. The condition is distinguished from urticaria by the fixed, non-migratory nature of lesions persisting for at least seven days, and from fixed drug eruption by its multifocal, symmetric distribution. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis are explicitly excluded as pathophysiologically and clinically distinct entities characterized by drug-driven epidermal necrosis, atypical flat targets without a raised border, and epidermal detachment â€” features that are absent in Erythema Multiforme.
clinical_rationale: Erythema Multiforme (EM) is primarily triggered by infections, notably herpes simplex virus, and rarely by medications. The phenotype explicitly excludes Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN), which are drug-attributable conditions. EM's typical infectious etiology makes it less relevant as a pharmacovigilance outcome; however, it occasionally has rare drug triggers, making it conditionally relevant under a narrowed reading of drug-attributable cases. The acute, self-limited nature of the condition classifies it as transient, with recurrent episodes possible due to repeat triggers. Diagnosis is usually made in outpatient settings based on clinical features, with no specific test required. Treatment often includes symptomatic relief, antiviral therapy in herpes-associated cases, and supportive care, particularly for mucosal involvement.

source_definition: Erythema Multiforme Major is an acute, self-limited, immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction of the skin and mucous membranes, distinguished from Erythema Multiforme Minor by the presence of clinically significant involvement of at least two distinct mucosal surfaces, most commonly the oral mucosa, conjunctivae, and genital mucosa. The hallmark cutaneous feature is the classic, raised target lesion exhibiting three concentric zones â€” a central dusky or vesiculobullous area, a surrounding pale edematous ring, and an outer erythematous halo â€” distributed predominantly on the acral surfaces and extensor extremities. Mucosal involvement manifests as painful erosions, hemorrhagic crusting (particularly of the lips), and pseudomembrane formation. Epidermal detachment, when present, involves less than 10% of body surface area. Systemic prodromal symptoms including fever, malaise, and arthralgia may accompany the eruption. No confirmed etiologic trigger is required; infectious causes such as herpes simplex virus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae are common precipitants but are not definitional. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome is explicitly excluded: it is characterized by flat atypical targets or widespread purpuric macules, predominantly drug-triggered pathophysiology, and diffuse full-thickness epidermal necrosis representing a pathophysiologically and morphologically distinct entity. Erythema Multiforme Minor and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis are likewise excluded on the basis of absent or insufficient mucosal involvement and extent of epidermal detachment, respectively.
clinical_rationale: Erythema Multiforme Major (EMM) represents an acute hypersensitivity reaction with characteristic target-like skin lesions and significant mucosal involvement. While multiple causes exist, drugs such as certain antibiotics and antiepileptics have been implicated as triggers, making it a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome. EMM is distinct from Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) due to its limited epidermal detachment (<10% BSA) and predominant infectious triggers, but drug causality, including that which overlaps with SJS/TEN medications, remains an important subset. EMM is generally an acute, self-resolving condition with a single episode of occurrence or rare recurrence following re-exposure to a trigger. Diagnosis requires clinical observation of hallmark skin and mucosal findings, potentially supported by biopsy in uncertain cases. The majority of incident cases are initially diagnosed in acute care settings due to the mucosal erosions and frequent systemic symptoms. In most cases, resolution occurs without leaving chronic sequelae.

source_definition: Esophageal motility disorder is a clinical condition characterized by objectively abnormal neuromuscular function of the esophageal body or esophagogastric junction, resulting in impaired, absent, premature, or excessively vigorous peristaltic contractions, or failure of appropriate lower esophageal sphincter relaxation. The category encompasses the full spectrum of recognized esophageal motor disorders, including achalasia and esophagogastric junction outflow obstruction, spastic and hypercontractile disorders such as diffuse esophageal spasm and jackhammer esophagus, and hypomotility disorders such as ineffective esophageal motility and absent contractility. Both idiopathic presentations and those arising as a manifestation of an underlying systemic condition â€” including connective tissue disease, autonomic neuropathy, or infectious etiology â€” are included. Excluded are conditions in which impaired esophageal transit is explained entirely by structural or mechanical obstruction (e.g., esophageal stricture, Schatzki ring, esophageal web, or extrinsic compression) in the absence of an independently identifiable motor dysfunction.
clinical_rationale: Esophageal motility disorders (EMDs) represent abnormal neuromuscular function within the esophageal body or esophagogastric junction and include etiologies such as achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, and hypomotility syndromes. Drug-attributable EMDs have been reported, particularly due to medications affecting smooth muscle function, such as calcium channel blockers, nitrates, or anticholinergic drugs, and conditions like drug-induced autonomic neuropathy. The clinical course of EMD varies by subtype: achalasia and other primary disorders are typically persistent once diagnosed, whereas transient impairment can occur in secondary presentations related to underlying systemic or infectious causes. Diagnosis commonly requires symptom evaluation (e.g., dysphagia) alongside objective testing such as high-resolution manometry or barium swallow studies. Compared to structural causes of impaired esophageal transit, motility disorders are distinctive in that their etiology lies in functional dysregulation.

source_definition: Esophagitis is an inflammatory condition of the esophageal mucosa arising from any biological mechanism, including acid-peptic injury due to gastroesophageal reflux, immune-mediated processes (such as eosinophilic infiltration), infectious agents (including fungal, viral, and bacterial pathogens), chemical or radiation-induced mucosal injury, and esophageal involvement as a manifestation of a systemic inflammatory or immune-mediated disease. The condition may present across the full severity spectrum, from superficial mucosal irritation to deep ulceration, and does not require a minimum severity threshold. Esophageal mucosal damage attributable solely to mechanical or physical trauma (including iatrogenic instrumentation injury) is excluded, as this represents a distinct pathophysiological entity without a primary biological inflammatory driver. Also excluded are Barrett's esophagus (a metaplastic sequela of chronic mucosal injury), esophageal malignancy (a neoplastic transformation), and functional esophageal disorders (such as functional heartburn or non-cardiac chest pain), which share symptom overlap but lack the defining pathological hallmark of mucosal inflammation.
clinical_rationale: Esophagitis has documented drug-attributable etiologies, including direct chemical injury from medications such as NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, tetracycline-class antibiotics, and iron supplements, as well as eosinophilic esophagitis potentially exacerbated by drug-mediated systemic immune reactions. While the clinical definition provided excludes mechanical trauma, drug-induced esophagitis remains a biologically plausible outcome of pharmacological exposures. Diagnosis often relies on endoscopic visualization or biopsy confirmation, meeting the threshold for requiring diagnostic testing. Cases may occur in both outpatient and acute care settings depending on severity, although outpatient diagnoses are more typical for mild to moderate disease. Treatment varies based on etiology, with acid suppression, topical steroids, or antimicrobials being initiated within 30 days in most cases.

source_definition: Essential hypertension is a chronic, primary hemodynamic disorder characterized by a persistent, pathological elevation of systemic arterial blood pressure at or above guideline-defined thresholds (â‰¥130/80 mmHg per ACC/AHA criteria or â‰¥140/90 mmHg per ESC/JNC 7 criteria), arising without an identifiable underlying secondary etiology such as renal artery stenosis, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, or Cushing's syndrome. The phenotype encompasses the full severity spectrum, including isolated systolic hypertension, and includes acute hypertensive urgency or emergency when these represent decompensation of a pre-existing chronic essential hypertensive state rather than a de novo acute presentation. Explicitly excluded are all transient or context-dependent blood pressure elevations, including gestational and pregnancy-induced hypertension, white-coat hypertension, masked hypertension, and drug-induced blood pressure elevation, as these represent distinct biological states with differing mechanisms, natural histories, and clinical implications.
clinical_rationale: Essential hypertension (primary hypertension) is a chronic disorder with multifactorial etiology and no singular identifiable secondary cause. While particular drugs, such as NSAIDs, corticosteroids, decongestants, and certain antidepressants, may lead to blood pressure elevation, the phenotype as described explicitly excludes drug-induced hypertension and other secondary causes. Thus, it is not primarily attributed to drug exposure and does not qualify as a pharmacovigilance outcome. However, blood pressure elevation could serve as a marker of adverse drug effects in other contexts. Essential hypertension typically requires long-term management with antihypertensive therapy and is associated with increased risks of cardiovascular complications. While acute hypertensive emergencies may arise in chronic essential hypertension, the condition is persistent by definition and never resolves completely.

source_definition: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency is a pathophysiological state characterized by insufficient secretion of pancreatic digestive enzymes â€” principally lipase, amylase, and proteases â€” from the exocrine pancreas, resulting in clinically manifest fat malabsorption evidenced by steatorrhea, unintentional weight loss, or fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies. The condition encompasses all degrees of clinically apparent enzyme insufficiency, from mild symptomatic malabsorption through severe nutritional compromise, and is inclusive of all underlying etiologies including chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, autoimmune pancreatitis, and surgical disruption of pancreatic anatomy. Non-pancreatic causes of fat malabsorption â€” such as celiac disease, intestinal Crohn's disease, short bowel syndrome, or primary bile acid deficiency â€” are excluded from this concept only when the non-pancreatic pathology fully and independently accounts for the observed malabsorption without evidence of concurrent pancreatic exocrine dysfunction.
clinical_rationale: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) is a condition with biological plausibility and documented drug associations, such as glucagon-like peptide receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and somatostatin analogues, which can impair pancreatic enzyme secretion. Additionally, EPI may result from conditions caused or exacerbated by drugs, such as chronic pancreatitis from alcohol or pancreatic surgery due to malignancies potentially linked to drug exposures. The clinical definition aligns well with the condition name, capturing the required focus on pancreatic contribution to malabsorption. Diagnosis is typically established by fecal elastase or other pancreatic function tests, although the presentation may include discrete symptoms like steatorrhea and weight loss. EPI is generally persistent once established, as underlying etiologies are usually chronic or irreversible. Treatment involves pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy, which is nearly always required for clinically evident cases.

source_definition: Facial nerve palsy, as defined here, is an acute-onset dysfunction of the peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) resulting in ipsilateral weakness or paralysis of all muscles of facial expression â€” including the frontalis, orbicularis oculi, and orbicularis oris â€” reflecting a lesion at or distal to the facial nucleus in the pons. The condition is idiopathic in etiology, with no identifiable infectious, structural, neoplastic, traumatic, or iatrogenic cause established after appropriate clinical evaluation; this excludes Ramsay Hunt syndrome, Lyme neuroborreliosis, otitis media with facial nerve involvement, parotid or temporal bone neoplasm, temporal bone fracture, and surgically-induced nerve injury. Associated features may include ipsilateral hyperacusis, reduced lacrimation or salivation, and altered taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue due to involvement of the chorda tympani and other CN VII branches. The phenotype captures any severity from mild unilateral paresis to complete bilateral facial paralysis, encompasses both first-ever and recurrent acute episodes, and explicitly excludes central (upper motor neuron) facial weakness, which characteristically spares the forehead musculature.
clinical_rationale: The description specifies idiopathic facial nerve palsy (often called Bell's palsy), excluding alternative causes such as trauma, infection, or neoplasm. While idiopathic facial nerve palsy is not usually drug-induced, there are rare reports linking it to specific drug classes, including immunomodulators and certain vaccines, suggesting drug exposure may play a conditional role. The condition is transient and recurrent, as resolution usually occurs and the label is shed, though distinct acute episodes may recur. Acute care is common but not exclusively typical, as many cases are diagnosed in ambulatory care settings. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, typically based on history and physical examination findings, with confirmatory testing used to rule out secondary causes rather than establish the diagnosis. Most cases receive active treatment, mainly corticosteroids, within 30 days, but not all require treatment. Long-term sequelae are uncommon, as the condition generally resolves fully within weeks or months.

source_definition: A fall is an unintentional event in which an individual comes to rest on the ground, floor, or a surface lower than their prior position, occurring from ground level or near-ground-level height (including descents from chairs, beds, or stairs), regardless of the precipitating mechanism or resulting injury. The phenotype encompasses falls attributable to any proximate cause, including impaired postural control, gait disturbance, loss of balance, environmental hazards, or an acute medical event such as syncope or seizure. Falls from significant elevation above standing height â€” such as those from ladders, scaffolding, or rooftops â€” are excluded, as these represent high-energy trauma events mechanistically distinct from the classical clinical construct of falling.
clinical_rationale: Falls are a significant pharmacovigilance outcome because they can result from drug-induced dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, sedation, and motor impairment, including effects of benzodiazepines, opioids, antihypertensives, and antipsychotics. This phenotype includes falls from ground level or near-ground-level height, which aligns with clinical observations of drug-related effects and excludes high-energy trauma events. While falls represent an acute event, there is a high risk for recurrence due to predisposing conditions and vulnerability in the affected population, resulting in a transient but recurrent clinical course. Diagnosis is often made in acute care settings, especially for falls resulting in injury. Falls may relate to underlying conditions of balance, neurological impairment, or syncope; thus, they require careful adjudication in observational data. Symptoms such as dizziness or imbalance may be coded separately, but are inconsistently recorded unless acute care documentation occurs. Exclusion of high-energy trauma from the definition reduces ambiguity and increases specificity for identifying this lower-energy fall phenotype.

source_definition: Fatigue is a subjective clinical symptom characterized by a persistent or unusual sense of tiredness, exhaustion, or diminished energy that is reported in a clinical context and is disproportionate to, or independent of, recent physical exertion. It encompasses the full spectrum of severity, from mild perceptions of reduced vitality to profound exhaustion, and is captured regardless of the underlying etiology, whether idiopathic, drug-related, or occurring in the context of a concurrent medical condition. Fatigue is conceptually distinct from somnolence or hypersomnia, which reflect pathological sleep drive or excessive daytime sleepiness arising from sleep-wake dysregulation, and from asthenia or objective muscle weakness, which represent a measurable loss of motor strength or physical capacity detectable on clinical examination.
clinical_rationale: Fatigue is a broad clinical symptom that can have multiple etiologies, including drug-induced causes such as sedatives, beta-blockers, anticonvulsants, and chemotherapy agents. It is a subjective symptom without a universal diagnostic threshold, making observational data challenging for reliable case capture. The distinction from somnolence or hypersomnia and objective motor weakness helps to narrow its scope. However, fatigue inherently lacks structured symptoms or a discrete biomarker, complicating validation in data models. Most incident recordings occur in outpatient settings unless caused by conditions requiring acute care, such as severe anemia or critical illness.

source_definition: Febrile neutropenia is an acute clinical syndrome defined by the concurrent occurrence of a clinically significant fever and a critically reduced absolute neutrophil count (ANC), regardless of the underlying etiology of the neutropenia. Neutropenia is defined as an ANC below 500 cells/Î¼L, or an ANC below 1,000 cells/Î¼L in the context of an anticipated decline to below 500 cells/Î¼L. Fever is defined as a single oral temperature of 38.3Â°C (101Â°F) or higher, or a sustained temperature of 38.0Â°C (100.4Â°F) or higher persisting for at least one hour. The syndrome encompasses acquired etiologies of neutropenia â€” including cytotoxic chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted or immunosuppressive therapies, hematologic malignancy with bone marrow infiltration, aplastic anemia, and drug-induced agranulocytosis â€” reflecting the shared pathophysiological state of severely impaired neutrophil-mediated host defense. All febrile presentations meeting the temperature threshold are included irrespective of whether the fever is subsequently attributed to infection, tumor necrosis, transfusion reaction, or drug hypersensitivity, as the clinical urgency is driven by the neutropenic state itself rather than a confirmed infectious etiology. Congenital and hereditary neutropenic syndromes â€” including Kostmann syndrome, cyclic neutropenia, and primary immunodeficiency-associated disorders â€” are explicitly excluded as distinct pathophysiological entities.
clinical_rationale: Febrile neutropenia is a drug-attributable syndrome in many cases, particularly through the effects of cytotoxic chemotherapy, targeted therapies, or immunosuppressive drugs causing acquired neutropenia, and is a recognized adverse event in pharmacovigilance. The clinical definition explicitly excludes hereditary neutropenic syndromes, focusing on acquired etiologies. The condition is acute in nature and transient, resolving once neutropenia and fever resolve, so subsequent episodes are considered separate events. Diagnostic criteria rely heavily on laboratory confirmation of neutropenia and documented fever to meet the definition. Febrile neutropenia is nearly always diagnosed and managed in acute care settings due to the urgency of intervention to prevent severe complications such as sepsis. The initial diagnosis is often triggered by the presence of fever but also requires laboratory confirmation of neutropenia.

source_definition: A febrile seizure is an acute, fever-provoked seizure occurring in a child between 6 months and 5 years of age who has no prior history of afebrile seizures and no established epilepsy diagnosis. The seizure is directly associated with a body temperature of 38Â°C (100.4Â°F) or greater and must not be attributable to an underlying central nervous system infection (such as bacterial meningitis or viral encephalitis), an acute metabolic disturbance (such as hypoglycemia or hyponatremia), or an acute structural neurological insult. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical spectrum: simple febrile seizures, which are generalized in onset, self-limiting, lasting fewer than 15 minutes, and occurring only once within a 24-hour period; and complex febrile seizures, which are distinguished by focal onset, duration of 15 minutes or longer, or recurrence within 24 hours. Both subtypes represent a provoked, age-dependent seizure response to fever in an otherwise neurologically normal child and are not considered manifestations of an underlying epileptic disorder.
clinical_rationale: Febrile seizures are not pharmacovigilance outcomes because they are primarily determined by the age-dependent neurological response to fever in otherwise normal children and are not intrinsically related to drug exposure or mechanisms. The description specifies clear diagnostic criteria, including the exclusion of CNS infection, metabolic disturbances, or structural insults as causative factors and the absence of underlying epilepsy. The age restriction is explicitly definitional at the time of the index event, as febrile seizures are specific to children between 6 months and 5 years of age. Diagnosis typically occurs in acute care settings given their sudden onset and association with fever-related illness.

source_definition: Fever is a clinical state characterized by a documented body temperature of 38.0Â°C (100.4Â°F) or greater, as recorded by any standard measurement method at any anatomical site. The phenotype is defined solely by the presence of this temperature threshold and is not restricted by underlying etiology, physiological mechanism, or duration; a single qualifying measurement is sufficient to establish the condition. All causes of temperature elevation are encompassed within this definition, including but not limited to infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic, drug-induced, and heat-related etiologies, with no etiologic or mechanistic exclusions applied.
clinical_rationale: Fever is an umbrella phenotype characterized by elevated body temperature (≥38.0°C), regardless of etiology, including drug-induced fever. Drug-induced fever can occur due to direct pyrogenic effects of drugs, hypersensitivity reactions, or idiosyncratic reactions. However, the definition includes non-drug-related causes, such as infections, autoimmune conditions, or heat-related illnesses, which may limit specificity as an isolated pharmacovigilance outcome unless further refinements or exclusions are applied. Fever often resolves transiently after the underlying cause is addressed without any long-term sequelae directly attributable to fever itself.

source_definition: Fibromyalgia is a chronic, widespread musculoskeletal pain disorder characterized by dysregulated central pain processing (central sensitization), in which amplified nociceptive signaling produces pain, allodynia, and hyperalgesia disproportionate to any identifiable peripheral tissue pathology. The condition must meet formal diagnostic criteria, specifically a widespread pain index of 7 or greater combined with a symptom severity score of 5 or greater (ACR 2010/2016), or an equivalent validated threshold, with symptoms present for at least three months. Associated features including fatigue, non-restorative sleep, and cognitive disturbance are recognized as integral expressions of the underlying central sensitization mechanism. Fibromyalgia may be diagnosed and included in this phenotype even when a comorbid systemic inflammatory or metabolic condition (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus) is present, provided the ACR diagnostic criteria are independently fulfilled and the widespread pain is not entirely attributable to the peripheral pathophysiology of that comorbid disease. Cases where diffuse pain is fully explained by active inflammatory arthropathy, hypothyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica, or inflammatory myopathy without independent ACR criteria fulfillment are excluded.
clinical_rationale: Fibromyalgia is characterized by dysregulated pain processing in the central nervous system, resulting in widespread musculoskeletal pain and associated symptoms such as fatigue and cognitive disturbances. While there has been some interest in drug-associated secondary fibromyalgia-like syndromes (e.g., medication-associated myalgia or arthralgia), fibromyalgia itself is not definitively established as an unambiguous pharmacovigilance outcome. Its pathophysiology primarily relates to central nervous system hypersensitivity rather than direct drug-induced pathology, and significant comorbidity with systemic inflammatory and metabolic conditions complicates assessing causality. Diagnostic reliance on patient-reported symptoms and lack of confirmatory objective tests further limit definitive attribution of fibromyalgia to medication use. The clinical definition provided is sufficiently detailed to exclude diffuse musculoskeletal pain fully explained by other conditions (e.g. hypothyroidism or inflammatory myopathies).

source_definition: Fistulizing Crohn's Disease is a penetrating subtype of Crohn's Disease characterized by the formation of abnormal inflammatory tracts arising from the transmural, granulomatous inflammation pathognomonic of Crohn's Disease. The phenotype encompasses all anatomical subtypes of fistulas â€” including perianal, enteroenteric, enterovesical, enterovaginal, and enterocutaneous â€” regardless of structural complexity, and includes associated perianal and intra-abdominal abscesses as direct manifestations of the same penetrating pathophysiological process. Both currently active fistulas and a prior history of fistulizing disease are within scope, with the temporal state recognized as a clinically meaningful modifier. The phenotype requires an established or strongly supported diagnosis of Crohn's Disease; patients with indeterminate or unclassified colitis (IBDU) who demonstrate fistulizing or penetrating behavior are included on the basis that transmural penetrating disease is biologically consistent with Crohn's pathobiology. Fistulas attributable to non-inflammatory-bowel-disease etiologies are explicitly excluded, including those arising from radiation enteritis, colorectal or pelvic malignancy, diverticular disease, cryptoglandular (idiopathic) perianal disease, infectious etiologies such as tuberculosis, and post-surgical or iatrogenic complications. Ulcerative colitis with perianal manifestations is excluded given its fundamentally mucosal, non-transmural pathophysiology.
clinical_rationale: Fistulizing Crohn's Disease, a severe complication of Crohn's Disease, is characterized by abnormal tracts resulting from transmural granulomatous inflammation. While specific drugs for Crohn's Disease can reduce inflammatory activity and prevent fistula formation, certain medications (e.g., infliximab) have been associated with rare cases of paradoxical inflammation or promotion of fistulizing behavior. Usual care for Crohn's Disease includes surveillance and reintervention for recurrent or persistent disease, including newly flaring fistulas. This condition is defined by its anatomy and pathobiology, and specific diagnostic procedures such as imaging, endoscopy, or surgical findings are often necessary to confirm the presence and location of fistulas. Management frequently includes medical therapies (e.g., antibiotics, immunomodulators, biologics) and, for severe cases, surgical intervention. Patients diagnosed with Fistulizing Crohn's Disease are likely to require long-term follow-up and monitoring for progression or associated complications.

source_definition: Follicular lymphoma is a systemic B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising from germinal center B cells and characterized by a predominant follicular growth pattern on histology. The phenotype encompasses all histologic grades (Grade 1 through Grade 3B), reflecting a spectrum from predominantly centrocytic, indolent disease to centroblast-rich variants that may behave more aggressively. Cases in which the lymphoma has undergone histologic transformation to a higher-grade process, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, are included as part of the natural disease course. The phenotype is restricted to nodal and systemic disease; anatomically and biologically distinct entities recognized as separate WHO classifications â€” including primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma, pediatric-type follicular lymphoma, and duodenal-type follicular lymphoma â€” are explicitly excluded on the basis of their divergent pathobiology, clinical course, and treatment paradigm.
clinical_rationale: Follicular lymphoma arises from germinal center B cells and has a well-established link to chemotherapy or radiation as potential contributing factors for secondary malignancies, including lymphoma. It also has the potential for histologic transformation into more aggressive subtypes. This phenotype includes all histologic grades of nodal and systemic follicular lymphoma but excludes distinct subtypes with different clinical courses and management strategies, as outlined in the description. The condition is persistent, as most cases require ongoing management even if not actively progressing, and there is a high likelihood of condition-specific follow-up or surveillance within one year of diagnosis. Diagnosis often relies on biopsy and histopathological analysis, making diagnostic procedures essential. Incident diagnoses are likely to be made in outpatient oncology settings or during specialist consultations, and active treatment is common soon after diagnosis.

source_definition: Foreign body in ear is defined as the physical presence of any non-endogenous material â€” whether animate (e.g., a living insect) or inanimate (e.g., a bead, food particle, cotton fragment, or displaced medical device) â€” lodged within any structure of the ear, including the external auditory canal, middle ear, or inner ear, irrespective of how the object came to be present. The defining characteristic is the objective existence of the foreign material within the ear; secondary sequelae such as otitis externa, tympanic membrane perforation, or hearing loss are not required for the condition to be present and are not considered part of this phenotype. Endogenous substances, including cerumen impaction, are explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Foreign body in ear is not inherently drug-attributable; it arises due to external causes such as accidental insertion or a traumatic event. No pharmacological agents are known to cause or directly predispose a person to foreign body lodgment in the ear. The condition is transient, as removal of the foreign body resolves the issue immediately, with no medically described recurrences due to the first event. The condition is most often detected in acute care settings (emergency department or urgent care), although some cases may be diagnosed in primary care or specialty ENT clinics. Both sexes are biologically susceptible. There are no specific age constraints, as this can occur at any age, but children are more likely to experience this due to behavioral patterns that increase the likelihood of foreign bodies lodging in the ear. Diagnosis is typically clinical and does not require laboratory tests or imaging, as direct visualization suffices. Management usually involves active removal of the foreign body by a medical professional, either with an instrument or specific treatments (e.g., suction, irrigation). Follow-up care is not routinely required unless there are complications, and symptoms may or may not be documented distinctly in the medical record, though their presence does help initiate diagnostic evaluation.

source_definition: Fournier gangrene is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening, polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, external genitalia (scrotum, penis, or vulva), and perianal soft tissues, characterized by synergistic infection involving a mixed consortium of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria that drives obliterative endarteritis, tissue ischemia, and spreading fascial necrosis. The condition includes all confirmed cases of fascial involvement regardless of anatomic extent or degree of systemic compromise. Excluded from this definition are perineal or genital soft-tissue necroses arising from non-infectious mechanisms such as blunt or penetrating trauma, vascular ischemia, or radiation injury in the absence of superimposed polymicrobial infection, as well as monomicrobial necrotizing infections of the perineal region and superficial perineal or scrotal cellulitis that has not progressed to deep fascial plane involvement.
clinical_rationale: Fournier gangrene is biologically plausible and supported as a pharmacovigilance outcome given documented cases of drug-related immunosuppression (e.g., corticosteroids, chemotherapy, anti-TNF therapy) leading to increased susceptibility to necrotizing fasciitis, including polymicrobial perineal involvement. The pathology involves synergistic aerobic and anaerobic infection with tissue ischemia and necrosis. This phenotype is defined to include only deep fascial infections of the perineum and exclude non-infectious necrosis, monomicrobial infections, and superficial cellulitis, reducing the risk of misclassification but increasing sensitivity to diagnostic uncertainty in coding. Most cases are initially diagnosed in acute care settings as life-threatening emergencies requiring immediate surgical and medical intervention.

source_definition: A fracture is a pathological disruption of the structural continuity of bone â€” cortical, trabecular, or both â€” regardless of the underlying etiology or mechanism. The phenotype encompasses the full etiological spectrum, including traumatic fractures resulting from acute external mechanical force applied to structurally normal or age-expected bone, pathological fractures occurring in bone weakened by an underlying disease process (such as primary or metastatic malignancy, metabolic bone disease, or Paget's disease), and stress or fatigue fractures arising from repetitive submaximal loading that exceeds the bone's remodeling capacity. Both complete fractures, in which cortical continuity is fully disrupted across the entire cross-section of bone, and incomplete fractures, in which partial structural integrity is maintained (including hairline, greenstick, torus/buckle, and stress-reaction fractures), are within scope. Osteochondral fractures involving a bone component are included. Explicitly excluded are bone contusions (bone marrow edema without cortical or trabecular discontinuity), dental fractures, and isolated cartilaginous injuries without concurrent skeletal bone involvement.
clinical_rationale: Fractures have multiple etiologies, including traumatic, pathological, and stress-related mechanisms. Drug-attributable mechanisms are plausible for certain types, such as increased fracture risk associated with glucocorticoids, bisphosphonates (atypical femoral fractures), and proton pump inhibitors (via calcium metabolism alteration). While traumatic fractures from external mechanical force are typically non-drug-related, pathological and stress fractures may be linked to pharmacologic effects or conditions aggravated by medications. For OMOP cohort definitions, distinguishing these subtypes may be necessary for pharmacovigilance research. The clinical course depends on the type of fracture — traumatic fractures are transient, with healing achieving resolution, whereas pathological or stress-induced fractures may recur or persist as part of underlying disease mechanisms. Most fractures are diagnosed in acute care settings, with exception for milder stress-related injuries. Radiological imaging is essential for definitive diagnosis, and treatment is typically required within 30 days. Fractures can necessitate follow-up for monitoring recovery and potential chronic sequelae, but this is not universal.

source_definition: A fragility fracture is a bone fracture occurring in a skeletally mature individual resulting from the combination of low-energy mechanical trauma â€” defined as forces insufficient to fracture structurally normal bone, such as a fall from standing height or less â€” and pathologically compromised bone integrity, arising from conditions such as osteoporosis or osteopenia. The phenotype is anatomically unrestricted, encompassing fractures at any skeletal site provided both precipitating conditions are present or clinically inferable. Explicitly excluded are fractures attributable primarily to high-energy trauma where mechanical force alone would be sufficient to fracture healthy bone; pathological fractures through bone infiltrated or destroyed by primary or metastatic malignancy, in which tumor biology rather than systemic bone fragility is the dominant etiological mechanism; periprosthetic fractures where biomechanical stress at the implant-bone interface is the primary driver; and fractures occurring in skeletally immature children and adolescents, whose bone fragility reflects distinct developmental or congenital etiologies rather than acquired metabolic bone disease.
clinical_rationale: Fragility fractures are typically linked to underlying conditions such as osteoporosis or osteopenia, which compromise bone integrity and result in fractures from low-energy traumas like falls. These fractures are relevant to pharmacovigilance, as certain medications (e.g., corticosteroids, aromatase inhibitors, anti-epileptic drugs, and PPIs) are known to contribute to bone fragility and thus increase the risk of these fractures. The condition is anatomically unrestricted and includes fractures at any skeletal site in adults with compromised bone integrity. The clinical definition excludes high-impact traumatic fractures, periprosthetic fractures, fractures in adolescents, or fractures due to cancer-related lytic lesions. In observational data, capturing fragility fractures can be challenging due to the need to distinguish them from traumatic fractures based on context rather than anatomy. However, the association with osteoporosis is often inferred from claims patterns and concurrent treatment. The course is transient and recurrent, as patients shed the label after healing but remain at heightened risk for future fractures. The majority of incident diagnoses are made in acute care settings due to the nature of fractures.

source_definition: Gastric ulcer is a discrete, full-thickness mucosal defect that penetrates through the muscularis mucosae and may extend into deeper layers of the stomach wall, arising from an imbalance between injurious factors â€” principally Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, or gastric acid hypersecretion â€” and the mucoprotective mechanisms of the gastric mucosa. The phenotype encompasses all anatomical subsites of the stomach, including the body, antrum, pyloric channel, and prepyloric region, and spans the full clinical spectrum from uncomplicated disease presenting with epigastric pain and endoscopically confirmed ulceration to complicated disease involving hemorrhage, perforation, or gastric outlet obstruction. Excluded from this concept are superficial gastric erosions that do not breach the muscularis mucosae, stress-related mucosal disease arising from systemic ischemia in the context of critical illness, and ulcerating gastric malignancies such as adenocarcinoma presenting as a malignant ulcer, all of which are pathophysiologically and clinically distinct from primary benign gastric ulcer disease.
clinical_rationale: Gastric ulcer is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome due to its established etiology involving nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). NSAIDs impair mucosal defense by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, leading to epithelial injury and ulcer formation, especially in the presence of coexisting risk factors such as Helicobacter pylori infection. Proton pump inhibitors or cytoprotective agents are commonly co-prescribed to mitigate the risk of NSAID-associated gastric ulcers. The clinical course is ordinarily transient, as ulcers heal with treatment, though complications like perforation or hemorrhage may arise. This phenotype excludes malignant ulcers and superficial erosions, which are distinct entities. Gastric ulcers vary in severity; uncomplicated cases may be diagnosed and managed in outpatient settings, while complicated cases requiring acute intervention are primarily encountered in hospital settings.

source_definition: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition characterized by the pathological retrograde movement of gastric contents into the esophagus, resulting in troublesome symptoms, demonstrable esophageal mucosal injury, or both. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical spectrum, including non-erosive reflux disease (NERD), in which characteristic symptoms such as heartburn and regurgitation occur in the absence of endoscopically visible mucosal damage; erosive esophagitis of any grade, defined by endoscopic evidence of acid-induced mucosal breaks; and GERD-related structural complications, including Barrett's esophagus â€” a metaplastic transformation of the distal esophageal epithelium representing adaptation to chronic acid exposure â€” and peptic stricture. Objective evidence may be established by endoscopic findings or by abnormal esophageal acid exposure on ambulatory pH or impedance-pH monitoring. Physiological reflux â€” defined as transient, asymptomatic episodes of gastric acid contact with the esophageal mucosa occurring without symptoms or mucosal injury, as observed in healthy individuals during the postprandial period â€” is explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: GERD is a chronic condition with a spectrum ranging from non-erosive reflux disease (NERD) to erosive esophagitis and complications such as Barrett's esophagus and peptic strictures. Drug-induced esophagitis is documented or plausible due to various mechanisms including reduced lower esophageal sphincter tone (e.g., calcium channel blockers, anticholinergics), delayed gastric emptying, or direct mucosal injury (e.g., NSAIDs, bisphosphonates). GERD is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome when attributed to an offending drug. Most patients diagnosed with GERD retain the diagnosis indefinitely, as it represents a chronic underlying physiological abnormality or propensity to reflux. A minority of patients develop GERD-related complications (e.g., Barrett’s esophagus), which represent clinical progression rather than resolution, supporting a persistent classification.
