Diagnosis is common in outpatient settings, though sometimes made in acute care contexts for severe complications like bleeding or stricture. GERD symptoms such as heartburn and regurgitation are frequently coded independently in structured data, and diagnostic confirmation often requires endoscopy or pH monitoring. Treatment with acid-suppressive therapy (e.g., proton pump inhibitors) within 30 days is nearly universal under routine care, and ongoing follow-up for symptom control or surveillance for complications is typically expected.

source_definition: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage is defined as the loss of blood originating from any anatomical segment of the gastrointestinal tract â€” encompassing the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, small intestine (jejunum and ileum), colon, rectum, and anus â€” that produces at least one clinically recognizable sign, including hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, or hematochezia. The phenotype encompasses bleeding arising from any underlying mechanism, including spontaneous pathological processes (e.g., peptic ulceration, vascular malformation, neoplasm, inflammatory bowel disease, portal hypertensive vasculopathy), direct physical trauma to the gastrointestinal tract, and iatrogenic or procedural causes (e.g., post-endoscopic or post-surgical bleeding). Occult blood loss detectable solely by laboratory testing in the absence of any overt clinical sign does not satisfy the threshold for this phenotype. Explicitly excluded are states that mimic gastrointestinal hemorrhage but do not represent true GI mucosal or vascular blood loss: hemoptysis of pulmonary origin that is swallowed and subsequently vomited or appears as melena; melena attributable to swallowed blood from epistaxis; and dark, tarry, or red-colored stool caused by ingested iron supplements, bismuth-containing compounds, or dietary pigments, in the absence of confirmed blood loss from the gastrointestinal tract.
clinical_rationale: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage encompasses a broad range of presentations and etiologies, including spontaneous pathology (e.g., peptic ulcers, malignancies, vascular lesions) and drug-induced causes (e.g., NSAIDs, anticoagulants, thrombolytics). Drug etiology is biologically plausible and documented, often through GI mucosal injury, impaired clotting, or interaction with vascular abnormalities. True gastrointestinal hemorrhage typically involves clinically recognizable signs like hematemesis or melena, and excludes mimics of GI bleeding (e.g., hemoptysis or dietary causes). Incident cases are commonly identified in the acute care setting, especially in severe cases, though mild episodes may be managed in outpatient settings. Thus, acute care codes are sensitive but may miss less severe outpatient presentations. Recorded symptoms such as hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia can be expected for most cases, and a diagnosis often requires endoscopy or imaging to confirm the source of the bleeding. Active treatment (e.g., transfusion, endoscopic intervention, discontinuation of the offending medication) is commonly initiated within 30 days of diagnosis. Condition-specific follow-up or surveillance is anticipated, especially for recurrent episodes or to monitor recovery and minimize future events.

source_definition: Gastrointestinal perforation is a full-thickness breach of the gastrointestinal wall occurring at any anatomic segment from the esophagus to the rectum, arising from pathologic processes (such as peptic ulcer disease, inflammatory bowel disease, ischemia, malignancy, or diverticular disease) or iatrogenic mechanisms, but excluding perforations caused by external physical trauma such as penetrating abdominal injury or ingested foreign bodies. The phenotype encompasses both free perforations with leakage of luminal contents into the peritoneal, retroperitoneal, or mediastinal space and contained perforations in which the defect is walled off by adjacent tissue or omentum, provided the full-thickness nature of the breach is objectively confirmed by radiologic evidence of free or extravasated gas or fluid, contrast extravasation, or direct visualization at endoscopy or surgery. Chronic fistulas â€” defined as epithelialized tracts forming a stable communication between two structures â€” are excluded; however, an acutely formed fistulous tract arising as a direct complication of a perforation event is considered part of this phenotype. Partial-thickness mucosal or submucosal defects, intestinal obstruction, and imaging findings of pneumatosis intestinalis without confirmed wall breach are not included.
clinical_rationale: Gastrointestinal perforation is a serious medical condition with a documented drug-attributable etiology. It has been associated with the use of medications such as NSAIDs (leading to peptic ulcer perforation), corticosteroids (compromising the integrity of the gastrointestinal wall), antiangiogenic agents, and immunosuppressants (exacerbating infections or IBD that can lead to perforations). The clinical definition provided ensures that only full-thickness breaches of the gastrointestinal wall are included while excluding external trauma, chronic fistulas, and partial-thickness defects, which strengthens phenotype specificity. Acute perforations typically require immediate management and are incident diagnoses almost always made in acute care settings. The natural course is transient for the acute perforation, although a minority of patients may develop chronic sequelae such as strictures or adhesions requiring additional care. High-quality imaging modalities or direct visualization are nearly universally required for diagnosis, given the severity and potential nonspecificity of presenting symptoms such as abdominal pain.

source_definition: Gaucher Disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder resulting from primary deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (encoded by GBA1), leading to pathological accumulation of glucosylceramide within macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. The phenotype encompasses all three recognized disease types: Type 1 (non-neuronopathic), characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, hematologic abnormalities including anemia and thrombocytopenia, and skeletal complications such as bone pain, osteopenia, and avascular necrosis; Type 2 (acute neuronopathic), defined by severe, rapidly progressive neurological deterioration with brainstem involvement presenting in infancy; and Type 3 (chronic neuronopathic), characterized by progressive central nervous system involvement alongside visceral and skeletal disease with a more protracted course. The phenotype requires that the glucosylceramide accumulation is attributable to primary GBA1 enzyme deficiency rather than secondary macrophage overload arising from high-turnover hematologic conditions such as chronic myeloid leukemia or hemolytic anemias. In addition, patients must exhibit at least one clinically manifest feature of the disease; individuals with confirmed GBA1 pathogenic variants who remain entirely asymptomatic are excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Gaucher Disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder due to a primary deficiency in glucocerebrosidase that leads to glucosylceramide accumulation in the macrophages, impacting multiple organ systems. It has no established drug-attributable etiology, as the underlying cause is purely genetic. The clinical course depends on the subtype: Type 1 is persistent with long-term management focused on enzyme replacement, Type 2 is progressive and rapidly fatal in infancy, while Type 3 is persistent and slowly progressive with chronic neurological deficits. As a genetic disorder, it affects both sexes equally, and onset can occur at any age. Diagnosis often requires enzymatic testing and genetic confirmation, particularly for distinguishing Gaucher Disease from other conditions involving macrophage activation and glucosylceramide accumulation. Pharmacovigilance for Gaucher-like syndromes secondary to drug-induced macrophage activation or hematologic abnormalities represents a valid use case but is distinct from a purely genetic Gaucher Disease definition.

source_definition: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a primary psychiatric condition characterized by persistent, excessive, and difficult-to-control worry spanning multiple life domains (e.g., work, health, finances, interpersonal relationships), present on more days than not for a minimum of six months. The worry is accompanied by at least three of the following associated symptoms: restlessness or feeling on edge, easy fatigability, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, or sleep disturbance. The anxiety and worry must cause clinically significant distress or meaningful functional impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of life. This phenotype excludes anxiety states directly attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (including stimulant intoxication or sedative/alcohol withdrawal) or a general medical condition (e.g., hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, cardiac arrhythmia). It further excludes presentations where the anxiety is better accounted for by another primary psychiatric disorder, including Panic Disorder, Social Anxiety Disorder, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, Major Depressive Disorder, or a Psychotic Disorder.
clinical_rationale: Generalized Anxiety Disorder is not directly attributable to drug exposure, as the diagnosis excludes substance-induced anxiety states or those caused by general medical conditions, including effects of medications. Consequently, it is not considered as a pharmacovigilance outcome. However, it may arise secondarily or worsen in certain contexts, such as medication withdrawal or chronic illness due to adverse drug experiences. Affected individuals carry the diagnostic label indefinitely unless fully remitted for a significant duration. Its onset typically occurs in outpatient settings, as symptoms rarely precipitate acute care presentations without complicating factors like suicidal ideation or physical complications. The diagnostic criteria rely heavily on clinical interview rather than objective tests, though scales and screening tools may be used to support the diagnosis.

source_definition: Generalized exfoliative dermatitis is an acquired inflammatory skin condition characterized by widespread erythema and desquamation involving at least 90% of the total body surface area, arising from dysregulated immune-mediated or hypersensitivity mechanisms. The condition encompasses presentations of any temporal course â€” acute, subacute, or chronic and recurrent â€” and may arise as an exacerbation of a pre-existing primary dermatosis (such as psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, or pityriasis rubra pilaris), as a systemic cutaneous hypersensitivity reaction to a drug or other exogenous agent, or without an identifiable cause (idiopathic erythroderma). The condition is defined by the clinical state of diffuse skin inflammation with scaling and exfoliation, and explicitly excludes erythroderma attributable to malignant or neoplastic processes (including cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and SÃ©zary syndrome), full-thickness epidermal necrolysis and detachment as seen in toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, skin involvement secondary to graft-versus-host disease, and congenital or genetic keratinization disorders presenting at birth.
clinical_rationale: Generalized exfoliative dermatitis is a severe inflammatory condition of the skin that can be precipitated by drug-induced hypersensitivity reactions, particularly to medications such as antibiotics (e.g., penicillins), antiepileptics, and allopurinol. Non-drug-attributable etiologies also exist, including exacerbations of underlying dermatoses such as psoriasis or atopic dermatitis, and idiopathic cases. Thus, while the definition inherently includes drug-attributable causes, it also covers non-drug-related etiologies and chronic conditions, necessitating a broader clinical reading. Discrete episodes may occur, particularly for acquired cases, making this suitable as a transient or recurrent phenotype. Acute presentations are usually managed in emergency or inpatient care settings due to the risks of complications, such as fluid imbalances, infections, and systemic inflammatory response. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by dermatological examination, and often involves ruling out similar erythroderma-like conditions (e.g., malignant causes or congenital disorders). There are no codable discrete symptoms expected; the condition is defined by its clinical appearance. Follow-up care and surveillance are frequently required to manage skin healing, monitor systemic involvement, and avoid recurrence.

source_definition: Generalized myasthenia gravis is a chronic autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission in which pathogenic autoantibodies â€” directed most commonly against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChR), or less commonly against muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) or lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4) â€” impair synaptic signal transmission at the neuromuscular junction, producing fatigable skeletal muscle weakness that extends beyond the extraocular muscles to involve limb, bulbar, and/or respiratory musculature, and that characteristically worsens with sustained activity and partially recovers with rest. The phenotype spans the full generalized severity spectrum, from mild or moderate limb and bulbar weakness through severe respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support (myasthenic crisis), and includes seronegative presentations in which autoimmune etiology is established through clinical features, electrophysiological findings, and immunotherapy responsiveness in the absence of detectable autoantibodies. Generalized MG arising in the context of thymoma or precipitated by exogenous immunological stimuli â€” including immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy â€” is included, as the autoimmune postsynaptic NMJ pathophysiology remains the defining feature irrespective of precipitant. Explicitly excluded are presynaptic NMJ disorders with mechanistically distinct etiologies, including Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (anti-VGCC antibody-mediated, typically paraneoplastic) and botulism (toxin-mediated presynaptic acetylcholine release blockade); congenital myasthenic syndromes arising from genetic, non-autoimmune NMJ defects; and motor neuron diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which may produce overlapping bulbar and limb weakness through an entirely different pathophysiological mechanism.
clinical_rationale: Generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) is an autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission characterized by autoantibodies that impair synaptic signaling at the neuromuscular junction. Specific drug classes, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, have been implicated in triggering gMG, making the condition a valid pharmacovigilance outcome when drug attribution is considered. It is clinically persistent but exhibits a relapsing course with potential for exacerbations like myasthenic crisis. Diagnostic confirmation generally requires clinical features, electrophysiological testing, and/or autoantibody detection. While symptom recognition may suggest presentation, characteristic symptoms are not always reliably documented as discrete structured records. Management often requires immunosuppressive therapy, and ongoing follow-up and surveillance for relapses or treatment-related complications is expected.

source_definition: Geographic atrophy is an advanced, irreversible form of retinal degeneration characterized by well-demarcated, full-thickness loss of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and secondary degeneration of the overlying photoreceptors confined to the macular region (posterior pole). The condition may arise from any underlying etiology, including age-related macular degeneration, drug-induced maculopathy (e.g., hydroxychloroquine toxicity), inherited retinal dystrophies (e.g., Stargardt disease, pattern dystrophies), and pathologic myopia. The phenotype encompasses macular GA regardless of concurrent or prior neovascular (wet) AMD, including atrophy arising secondary to choroidal neovascularization or its treatment. Only established, complete atrophic lesions are included; precursor states characterized by incomplete RPE loss (e.g., incomplete RPE and outer retinal atrophy, iRORA) are excluded. The phenotype requires the presence of macular GA in at least one eye; bilateral involvement is not required.
clinical_rationale: Geographic atrophy is an advanced form of retinal degeneration that can be caused by drugs such as hydroxychloroquine, which is associated with retinal pigment epithelial and photoreceptor toxicity, as well as inherited disorders and age-related macular degeneration. While the condition is irreversible, drug-induced forms of macular geographic atrophy have been documented in pharmacovigilance, making it a valid safety outcome under the drug-attributable subset. The complete loss of retinal pigment epithelium meets strict criteria for diagnosis and does not remit, making the clinical course persistent. Diagnoses are confirmed through objective imaging modalities such as fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography, and patients require active management within 30 days, typically to address vision-related sequelae or adjust treatment for the underlying cause. Long-term retinal surveillance and management of chronic visual impairment are standard parts of care.

source_definition: Gestational diabetes mellitus is a metabolic condition characterized by new-onset glucose intolerance or hyperglycemia arising during the second or third trimester of pregnancy â€” typically at or after 24 weeks of gestation â€” as a direct consequence of the progressive physiological insulin resistance induced by pregnancy-related hormones, principally human placental lactogen, progesterone, and cortisol. The glucose impairment must meet formally recognized pregnancy-specific diagnostic thresholds and may range in clinical severity from mild glucose intolerance managed through diet and lifestyle modification alone to hyperglycemia requiring pharmacologic intervention, as the definition is agnostic to management intensity. This condition is explicitly distinguished from overt diabetes mellitus that is merely first detected during pregnancy (wherein glucose values satisfy standard non-pregnant diagnostic criteria, implying pre-existing undiagnosed disease rather than a pregnancy-induced state), from hyperglycemia attributable to identifiable secondary causes extrinsic to the pregnancy itself (including but not limited to exogenous corticosteroid administration, acute pancreatitis, monogenic diabetes, or primary endocrine disorders), and from any form of diabetes mellitus that was clinically established prior to conception.
clinical_rationale: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a metabolic condition strictly confined to pregnancy, with glucose intolerance triggered by pregnancy-specific hormonal changes. Drug-attributable hyperglycemia is explicitly excluded from the diagnostic scope by definition, making GDM unsuitable as a direct pharmacovigilance outcome. Drugs such as corticosteroids may induce hyperglycemia during pregnancy, but such cases would be classified outside the GDM phenotype. GDM typically resolves postpartum, but the patient remains at increased risk for future type 2 diabetes or glucose intolerance, making the clinical course transient with potential recurrent episodes limited to subsequent pregnancies. Diagnosis requires glucose measurements meeting specific thresholds, performed between 24–28 gestational weeks, and incident cases are predominantly managed in outpatient obstetrical care. Follow-up care within one year focuses on postpartum glucose re-evaluation and future risk stratification.

source_definition: Glaucoma is a heterogeneous group of progressive optic neuropathies defined by characteristic structural deterioration of the optic nerve head â€” including enlargement of the optic cup, thinning of the neuroretinal rim, and loss of the retinal nerve fiber layer â€” with or without detectable visual field loss, the latter of which may be absent in early or suspect-stage disease. The phenotype encompasses all primary forms, including primary open-angle glaucoma, primary angle-closure glaucoma, and normal-tension glaucoma, as well as secondary forms in which glaucomatous optic neuropathy arises from an identifiable underlying condition such as uveitis, pseudoexfoliation syndrome, pigmentary dispersion, ocular trauma, neovascularization, or corticosteroid exposure, regardless of intraocular pressure level. Ocular hypertension â€” defined as elevated intraocular pressure in the absence of optic nerve damage or visual field loss â€” is explicitly excluded, as it represents a risk state rather than established disease. Non-glaucomatous optic neuropathies that may produce structural or functional findings superficially resembling glaucoma â€” including ischemic optic neuropathy, compressive optic neuropathy, optic neuritis, and hereditary optic neuropathies such as Leber hereditary optic neuropathy â€” are likewise excluded, as these arise from pathophysiological mechanisms entirely distinct from the glaucomatous disease process.
clinical_rationale: Glaucoma represents a broad category of optic neuropathies with diverse etiologies, including primary open-angle glaucoma, angle-closure glaucoma, and secondary causes such as corticosteroid-induced glaucoma. Secondary forms, such as those provoked by corticosteroid use, explicitly support pharmaceutical attribution and make glaucoma an important pharmacovigilance outcome under the provided definition. The course is persistent since the damage to the optic nerve is irreversible, and the diagnosis is retained for life, with ongoing management typically required to prevent further progression. Incident cases are primarily diagnosed in an outpatient care setting through routine eye exams and ophthalmological evaluation, though patients with secondary glaucomas (e.g., neovascular or traumatic glaucoma) may present in acute care with vision-threatening disease. Though visual field loss or pain may sometimes prompt initial presentation, symptoms are often absent early in disease, and diagnosis relies heavily on diagnostic testing such as intraocular pressure measurements, optic nerve imaging, and formal visual field testing. Long-term follow-up is essential for monitoring disease progression and response to therapy.

source_definition: Glomerulonephritis is an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the renal glomeruli that may manifest acutely, subacutely, or follow a chronic progressive course. The condition is characterized by glomerular inflammation producing at least one hallmark clinical or laboratory feature: glomerular hematuria (evidenced by dysmorphic erythrocytes or red blood cell casts in the urine), proteinuria of any degree, or impairment of renal function attributable to glomerular injury. The phenotype encompasses both primary forms, in which glomerular inflammation arises intrinsically without an identifiable systemic cause, and secondary forms, in which glomerular inflammation is a manifestation of an underlying systemic condition such as systemic lupus erythematosus, ANCA-associated vasculitis, or post-infectious immune complex deposition. Explicitly excluded are non-inflammatory glomerulopathies resulting from metabolic or hemodynamic injury â€” including diabetic glomerulosclerosis, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, and amyloidosis â€” as these involve structural glomerular damage without an immune-mediated inflammatory mechanism. Tubulointerstitial nephritis is also excluded, as it involves inflammation confined to the renal interstitium and tubular compartments and represents a distinct anatomical and pathophysiological entity.
clinical_rationale: Glomerulonephritis is an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the renal glomeruli that can be triggered by systemic autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, ANCA-associated vasculitis) and post-infectious immune complex deposition, but it can also occur as a primary disease without an identifiable systemic cause. Certain drugs (e.g., penicillamine, gold, hydralazine, and D-penicillamine) are recognized triggers of secondary glomerulonephritis via immune-mediated mechanisms. The condition is characterized by specific laboratory findings such as glomerular hematuria, proteinuria, or impaired renal function. Although glomerulonephritis may follow an acute or subacute course, many secondary forms and primary progressive forms lead to chronic kidney disease, making the disease persistent. However, recurrence is possible in cases of acute or subacute manifestations, depending on the cause, the presence of repeat injury, or relapsing systemic disease. Diagnosis requires laboratory evidence (e.g., urinalysis and/or renal biopsy), and while some mild cases may not necessitate immediate treatment, severe cases will require rapid intervention to prevent end-organ damage.

source_definition: Gout is a systemic metabolic disorder characterized by the pathological deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in articular, periarticular, and soft tissues, driven by sustained hyperuricemia arising from endogenous urate overproduction, impaired renal urate excretion, or identifiable exogenous causes such as diuretic use, calcineurin inhibitors, or states of elevated cellular turnover. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical spectrum of MSU crystal disease: acute gouty arthritis â€” episodic, intensely inflammatory mono- or oligoarthritis precipitated by MSU crystal shedding into the synovial space; inter-critical gout â€” clinically quiescent periods between flares during which the underlying metabolic disturbance and crystal burden persist; chronic tophaceous gout â€” persistent MSU crystal deposition forming macroscopic tophi in joints, tendons, bursae, and subcutaneous tissues, often accompanied by structural joint destruction and chronic inflammatory arthropathy; and renal manifestations directly attributable to urate crystal disease, including gouty nephropathy (urate crystal deposition within renal parenchyma) and uric acid nephrolithiasis. Diagnosis requires at least one clinical manifestation of MSU crystal disease; asymptomatic hyperuricemia alone is insufficient for inclusion. Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease and pseudogout are explicitly excluded, as they involve a distinct crystal type and pathophysiological mechanism independent of urate metabolism.
clinical_rationale: Gout is an appropriate pharmacovigilance outcome due to well-documented drug etiologies that contribute to hyperuricemia and MSU crystal deposition, such as diuretics, calcineurin inhibitors, and chemotherapy agents that promote cellular turnover. Specific episodes of acute gouty arthritis are transient, allowing for discrimination of individual events in recurrent cases. However, gout overall is clinically persistent due to sustained hyperuricemia and the ongoing risk of recurrent flares, inter-critical phases, chronic tophaceous involvement, and renal manifestations. The included definition appropriately excludes closely related conditions like pseudogout and CPPD, which are mechanistically distinct. The pathological basis of the disease is clear, but acute gouty arthritis should be differentiated from chronic gout for event-based analyses.

source_definition: Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) is an immune-mediated syndrome in which immunologically competent donor-derived lymphocytes recognize and mount an allogeneic attack against antigenically distinct host tissues, causing end-organ inflammation and injury. The phenotype encompasses both the acute form â€” characterized by cytokine-driven inflammatory injury predominantly affecting the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and liver, typically manifest within 100 days of the initiating exposure â€” and the chronic form, which presents as a fibroinflammatory syndrome with features resembling autoimmune and connective tissue disorders and may arise beyond 100 days or overlap temporally with acute disease. All severity grades are included, from localized, mild presentations to multi-organ, life-threatening disease. The phenotype extends across all clinical contexts in which viable donor lymphocytes are introduced into an immunologically susceptible host, including allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, passenger lymphocyte transfer from solid organ transplantation, and transfusion-associated GvHD arising from non-irradiated blood product administration. Excluded from this concept are the immunologically reciprocal process of host-versus-graft rejection, engraftment syndrome (a non-alloreactive inflammatory state following neutrophil engraftment), and conditions that mimic GvHD clinically but lack a donor-host allogeneic immune mechanism.
clinical_rationale: GvHD is a biologically plausible and well-documented pharmacovigilance outcome, arising in the context of transplantation, transfusion, or cellular therapy through donor-host immune interaction. Its link to specific exposures, including stem cell transplantation and transfusion, makes it etiologically relevant to drug and biologic safety surveillance. Both acute and chronic forms are included, with overlapping clinical presentations and distinctions in onset timing. Diagnostic criteria rely on clinical features and histopathologic findings but can be supported by characteristic symptoms such as rash or liver dysfunction. Given the detailed description of the phenotype encompassing a range of severity and associated exposures, the condition is persistent with episodic exacerbations in chronic disease or recurrent acute presentations. Acute presentations often arise in acute care settings, whereas chronic GvHD may first manifest in outpatient follow-up. Monitoring and management often continue long-term due to the risk of sequelae or progression.

source_definition: Granulocytopenia is an acquired hematologic state characterized by a pathological reduction in circulating granulocytes below the established normal lower limit, with neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count below approximately 1,500 cells/ÂµL) as the primary and clinically defining feature; concurrent reductions in eosinophils or basophils may coexist but are not required for the diagnosis. The condition spans a continuous severity spectrum from mild neutropenia through moderate and severe forms, encompassing agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count below 500 cells/ÂµL) as its most extreme expression. Granulocytopenia may arise from diverse acquired mechanisms including, but not limited to, cytotoxic or immunosuppressive drug effects, immune-mediated destruction, bone marrow suppression from infectious agents, nutritional deficiencies, or other systemic insults. The definition explicitly excludes granulocytopenia attributable to congenital or hereditary conditions (e.g., severe congenital neutropenia/Kostmann syndrome, cyclic neutropenia, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome), in which chronically reduced granulocyte counts represent a constitutive baseline rather than an acquired pathological state.
clinical_rationale: Granulocytopenia is a pharmacovigilance-relevant condition because it encompasses acquired neutropenia, which has documented drug-attributable etiologies through mechanisms such as bone marrow suppression (e.g., chemotherapy, clozapine), immune-mediated destruction (e.g., beta-lactam antibiotics), or toxic insult (e.g., gold salts). Congenital causes are explicitly excluded in the description, so only the acquired forms, which can result from drug exposure or other systemic insults, fall within scope. Usual care involves resolution of the acute episode but allows recurrence, with agranulocytosis as the most severe presentation. Diagnosis typically requires laboratory confirmation, and mild to moderate cases may present in outpatient settings, whereas severe cases requiring immediate intervention are likely diagnosed in the hospital. Follow-up is warranted for monitoring recovery and managing complications such as infection risk.

source_definition: Growth deficiency is a pathological state occurring in pediatric and adolescent individuals prior to the attainment of skeletal maturity, characterized by impaired linear growth manifesting as height or height velocity at least two standard deviations below the age- and sex-matched population mean. The condition encompasses all recognized pathophysiological mechanisms of growth failure, including hypothalamic-pituitary-somatotropic axis dysfunction, chromosomal disorders, skeletal dysplasias, and growth failure secondary to chronic systemic diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease, chronic kidney disease, or malabsorptive conditions. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is included within this phenotype, as it represents a clinically recognized deviation from expected growth tempo warranting evaluation and monitoring. Familial short stature, in which a child's linear growth trajectory reflects inherited genetic potential without an underlying pathological mechanism and predicted adult height is consistent with mid-parental height, is explicitly excluded as a normal biological variant rather than a pathological state.
clinical_rationale: Growth deficiency is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome under a conditional reading. While non-drug-related mechanisms such as genetic disorders and chronic systemic illnesses often drive growth failure, growth deficiency can also be caused by certain drugs. Corticosteroids, for example, are well-documented to suppress linear growth via inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary-somatotropic axis, as are high-dose methotrexate and cytotoxic chemotherapy in pediatric populations. Identifying growth deficiency in observational data is challenged by the need for serial height measurements or calculated growth velocity over time, as single diagnosis codes often subsume multiple etiologies or evaluation contexts. The provided description is consistent with this complexity. Familial short stature, a non-pathological variant, is explicitly excluded, and pharmacovigilance efforts should focus on acquired or reversible causes, particularly in children exposed to known growth-suppressing agents.

source_definition: Guillain-BarrÃ© syndrome is an acute, monophasic, immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy of the peripheral nervous system in which aberrant autoimmune activity â€” typically triggered by a preceding infectious illness â€” targets the myelin sheaths or axons of peripheral and cranial nerves. The phenotype encompasses all recognized pathological subtypes, including acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP), the axonal variants acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) and acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN), Miller Fisher syndrome, and other regional presentations, across the full range of clinical severity. The syndrome is characterized by progressive, bilateral weakness or sensorimotor dysfunction with reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes, with or without cranial nerve involvement, autonomic dysfunction, or respiratory compromise, where neurological deterioration occurs over a period of days up to a maximum of four weeks, after which progression halts and is followed by a plateau and subsequent partial or complete recovery. Cases in which neurological deterioration continues beyond eight weeks, or in which true clinical relapse occurs after a period of confirmed recovery, are excluded as they represent chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy rather than Guillain-BarrÃ© syndrome.
clinical_rationale: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy that has documented associations with drug exposures such as vaccines (e.g., influenza vaccines), biologics, and other triggers. Its etiology can include mimicking or dysregulated responses to infectious agents, including those possibly exacerbated by medications. The description excludes chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), focusing on the acute monophasic presentation characteristic of GBS. Incidence typically requires diagnostic testing such as nerve conduction studies, CSF analysis, and clinical examination. The presentation varies between subtypes, but most cases involve bilateral progressive weakness, sensorimotor dysfunction, and autonomic failure, often requiring hospital care and intensive monitoring. Cases are monophasic, with resolution or recovery expected after the acute phase, making it transient with minimal interepisode gap concerns.

source_definition: Guttate psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition driven by dysregulated T-cell activity along the IL-17/IL-23 axis, characterized by the acute or recurrent eruption of numerous small (typically less than 2 cm), discrete, erythematous, scaly papules and plaques distributed predominantly over the trunk and proximal extremities, often in a raindrop-like pattern. The condition reflects psoriasiform epidermal hyperproliferation with characteristic neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltration and is considered part of the psoriasis disease spectrum regardless of whether a precipitating trigger, prior psoriasis history, or specific body surface area involvement is identified. This phenotype explicitly excludes pityriasis rosea (a self-limited, herald-patchâ€“associated viral-linked exanthem), secondary syphilis (a systemic infectious condition with papulosquamous manifestations), pityriasis lichenoides chronica and pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (clonal T-cell disorders with lichenoid and necrotic features), and small-plaque parapsoriasis (a distinct chronic dermatosis of uncertain malignant potential), all of which may mimic the morphology of guttate psoriasis but differ fundamentally in pathophysiology, histology, and clinical behavior.
clinical_rationale: Guttate psoriasis is a recognized inflammatory skin condition within the psoriasis spectrum, with acute or recurrent episodes often triggered by infections, stress, or injury to the skin (Koebner phenomenon). Although psoriasis as a broader category is increasingly linked to biologics and other medications affecting immune modulation, guttate psoriasis itself is not well-documented as an independent drug-attributable entity. Its episodic nature and potential triggers, however, make it suitable for pharmacovigilance under the narrower reading of medication-induced or exacerbated guttate psoriasis. Diagnosis usually requires integration of clinical findings rather than definitive laboratory or histologic testing, though biopsy may occasionally be helpful. Skin symptoms such as erythematous scaly plaques are often highly visible and well-documented. Guttate psoriasis is frequently manageable on an outpatient basis, though severe or complicated cases may occur in acute care settings.

source_definition: Gynecomastia is the benign proliferation of glandular and ductal breast tissue in males, arising from a relative imbalance between estrogenic and androgenic activity at the breast tissue level. The condition encompasses all etiological subtypes, including physiological presentations across the lifespan (neonatal, pubertal, and senescent), idiopathic cases, drug- or hormone-mediated cases, and cases secondary to systemic conditions that alter the estrogen-to-androgen ratio (such as hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, hepatic dysfunction, or adrenal and testicular pathology). The defining feature is true glandular and stromal tissue proliferation, clinically detectable as a firm or rubbery subareolar disc or diffuse breast mound. This phenotype explicitly excludes pseudogynecomastia (lipomastia), defined as male breast enlargement attributable solely to adipose tissue deposition without underlying glandular proliferation, as this represents a distinct pathophysiological entity. Malignant male breast neoplasia is also excluded.
clinical_rationale: Gynecomastia encompasses both drug-related and non-drug-related subtypes. Medications such as antiandrogens, certain antipsychotics, estrogens, spironolactone, digoxin, and others are known to promote gynecomastia via hormonal disruption. While physiological and disease-mediated gynecomastia exist, the drug-induced form is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome and biologically plausible through established mechanisms of endocrine alteration. Most cases are diagnosed in an outpatient setting through clinical examination and history, without requiring invasive procedures. Acute phases of gynecomastia may resolve after intervention (such as discontinuation of the offending drug), while chronic cases may persist, particularly physiological gynecomastia during senescence or pubertal phases. Pseudogynecomastia is explicitly excluded in the definition.

source_definition: A hallucination is a false sensory perception arising in any modality â€” including auditory, visual, tactile, olfactory, or gustatory â€” that occurs in the complete absence of a corresponding external stimulus and is experienced by the individual as a genuine, externally originating percept, with full subjective conviction of its reality. The phenotype is agnostic to etiology and encompasses hallucinations arising from primary psychiatric illness, neurological dysfunction, systemic medical conditions, and substance intoxication or withdrawal. No minimum severity, duration, or degree of functional impairment is required for inclusion. Illusions â€” misperceptions of a real external stimulus â€” are explicitly excluded, as are pseudohallucinations in which the individual retains full insight that the perception is internally generated and not real. Hypnagogic and hypnopompic phenomena occurring at the physiological sleep-wake boundary are excluded unless they co-occur with other pathological features or arise in a context that cannot be attributed to normal sleep-state transition.
clinical_rationale: Hallucinations, as defined, encompass a broad range of false sensory perceptions across multiple etiologies, including substance-induced causes. Drug-attributable hallucinations are well-documented as side effects of various medications, notably corticosteroids, dopaminergic agents, psychedelic compounds, and psychoactive substances. These can manifest acutely during intoxication or withdrawal syndromes, establishing a plausible pharmacological mechanism for drug-induced hallucinations. The definition provided explicitly includes cases arising from substance exposure, highlighting its relevance for pharmacovigilance. While incident presentations can range from acute care (for severe cases) to outpatient settings for primary psychiatric or subtle sensory complaints, acute primary care is common for evaluation in urgent cases.

source_definition: Headache is defined as any pain, pressure, or discomfort perceived within the cranial vault, arising from any underlying mechanism, whether primary â€” in which the headache itself represents the disease process (e.g., migraine, tension-type, cluster, or other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias) â€” or secondary, in which the cranial pain is a manifestation of an identifiable underlying condition (e.g., intracranial hypertension, meningitis, cerebrovascular disease, systemic illness, or medication use). No minimum severity threshold is required; presentations of any intensity, from mild to severe, are included. The phenotype is restricted to pain localized to the head above the orbitomeatal line; isolated facial pain, cervicogenic pain, and orbital or ocular pain not accompanied by cranial headache are excluded.
clinical_rationale: Headache is a heterogeneous condition encompassing both primary headache disorders like migraines and secondary headaches caused by various underlying conditions, including drug-attributable mechanisms such as medication-overuse headache, intracranial hypertension triggered by corticosteroids, or headache induced by vasodilators or other drugs. As described, the definition integrates a wide breadth spanning multiple etiologies, some drug-attributable and others entirely unrelated to medications. Therefore, the suitability as a pharmacovigilance outcome depends on narrowing to drug-associated entities. Incident headache is predominantly diagnosed in outpatient or ambulatory care, except for acute severe presentations associated with secondary etiologies requiring urgent evaluation (e.g., meningitis or stroke). Symptoms are nearly universally documented, and diagnostic testing is typically required when secondary headache is suspected.

source_definition: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome arising from structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection, resulting in the heart's inability to deliver sufficient cardiac output to meet the metabolic demands of the body, or to do so only at the cost of elevated filling pressures. The phenotype encompasses the full temporal spectrum â€” first-onset, chronic stable, and acute decompensated presentations â€” and includes all ejection fraction categories: reduced (HFrEF), mildly reduced (HFmrEF), and preserved (HFpEF). All etiologies of intrinsic myocardial dysfunction are included, encompassing ischemic, hypertensive, valvular, dilated, restrictive, peripartum, toxic, septic, and stress-induced cardiomyopathies, as well as right ventricular failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension or primary pulmonary disease (cor pulmonale). Explicitly excluded are states that produce hemodynamic compromise or congestion through mechanisms other than intrinsic myocardial dysfunction: purely mechanical obstructive etiologies (cardiac tamponade, massive pulmonary embolism), volume-overload states in which cardiac pump function is preserved (e.g., iatrogenic fluid overload or fluid congestion in end-stage renal disease without myocardial impairment), high-output states driven by excessive systemic demand on a structurally normal heart (severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, arteriovenous fistula), and pericardial constriction (constrictive pericarditis) in which hemodynamic impairment is extrinsic to the myocardium.
clinical_rationale: Heart failure is a well-established pharmacovigilance outcome due to the known causal relationship between numerous drugs and the development or exacerbation of heart failure. Drugs such as certain chemotherapy agents (e.g., anthracyclines), NSAIDs, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and several other classes have been implicated via mechanisms including direct cardiotoxicity, negative inotropic effects, fluid retention, or blood pressure dysregulation. The phenotype described here includes acute and chronic forms of heart failure across all ejection fraction categories and etiologies, providing a comprehensive taxonomy. However, non-cardiac conditions producing hemodynamic compromise without myocardial dysfunction are explicitly excluded, ensuring diagnostic precision. The condition is persistent given that even stabilized patients retain the diagnostic label of 'heart failure,' and decompensations represent acute relapses. Diagnosis requires clinical evaluation and objective tests such as echocardiography or natriuretic peptide measurements, and treatment initiation or modification is almost universally needed. Incident diagnoses often occur in acute care settings, but outpatient findings also contribute significantly depending on the timing and acuity of symptom onset.

source_definition: Heavy menstrual bleeding is a gynecologic condition occurring in non-pregnant, non-postpartum individuals, characterized by menstrual blood loss of sufficient volume or duration to be perceived by the patient as excessive, to exceed an objective threshold (classically greater than 80 mL per menstrual cycle, or its clinical proxies such as passage of clots larger than 1 cm or saturation of one or more sanitary products per hour), or to cause measurable interference with physical, emotional, social, or material quality of life. The phenotype encompasses all etiological subtypes, including structural causes (endometrial polyps, adenomyosis, uterine leiomyomata, and endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy) and non-structural causes (coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, primary endometrial disorders, iatrogenic causes, and idiopathic presentations), as classified by the FIGO PALM-COEIN framework. Explicitly excluded are any episodes of uterine bleeding occurring in the context of a confirmed or suspected intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy, spontaneous or induced abortion, or the postpartum period, as these represent physiologically and clinically distinct bleeding states.
clinical_rationale: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) spans both drug-attributable and non-drug-attributable etiologies, making it a CONDITIONAL pharmacovigilance outcome. Drugs such as anticoagulants, hormonal contraceptives, and tamoxifen are known to induce or exacerbate heavy menstrual bleeding in predisposed individuals, while structural and non-iatrogenic causes (e.g., fibroids, endometrial disorders, coagulopathy) are independent of drug exposure. This definition explicitly excludes pregnancy-related bleeding, aligning it with the non-pregnant population typically observed. Episodic by nature, HMB can recur in discrete cycles but does not retain its diagnostic label intercycle after measurable resolution (transient recurrent). Incident diagnosis may occur in outpatient or acute settings, depending on severity and impact on quality of life. Diagnosis is primarily clinical but supported by imaging, hysteroscopy, or laboratory tests. Quality assurance in coding must account for exclusions and subtype framing.

source_definition: HELLP syndrome is a severe, pregnancy-associated multisystem disorder characterized by the simultaneous presence of all three components of its defining triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (hemolysis, evidenced by elevated lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, and peripheral schistocytes), hepatocellular injury manifesting as markedly elevated liver enzymes (particularly aspartate aminotransferase), and thrombocytopenia with a platelet nadir of 100,000/Î¼L or below, consistent with moderate-to-severe disease (Mississippi Classification Class I or II). The syndrome reflects placenta-mediated endothelial dysfunction and does not require concurrent preeclampsia for diagnosis, as a clinically recognized subset arises without classic hypertensive or proteinuric features. The phenotype encompasses both antepartum presentations â€” occurring most commonly in the second or third trimester â€” and postpartum presentations arising up to seven days following delivery, as both are expressions of the same underlying pathophysiology. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (arising from severe ADAMTS13 deficiency) and hemolytic uremic syndrome or atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (arising from Shiga toxin-mediated injury or complement dysregulation, respectively) are explicitly excluded, as their surface resemblance to HELLP reflects entirely distinct mechanisms unrelated to placental pathology. Concurrent acute fatty liver of pregnancy is not an exclusion criterion, given the recognized pathophysiological overlap between the two conditions in severe pregnancy-associated disease.
clinical_rationale: HELLP syndrome is a multisystem disorder exclusively associated with pregnancy, arising from placental endothelial dysfunction. It is biologically plausible as a pharmacovigilance outcome due to drug interactions that may exacerbate endothelial dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, or hepatocellular injury, such as antiplatelet medications, NSAIDs, or pre-eclampsia treatments. The condition is transient by definition, resolving entirely post-delivery or postpartum management without recurring episodes unless associated with subsequent pregnancies. Diagnostic criteria require laboratory confirmation including hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes, rendering objective testing indispensable. It is almost exclusively diagnosed in acute care settings due to its severity and urgent need for intervention. The condition requires immediate active management (often delivery), followed by postpartum surveillance for sequelae such as persistent hypertension or hepatic dysfunction; thus, follow-up for over a year is expected in most cases.

source_definition: Hematochezia is a gastrointestinal clinical sign characterized by the passage of grossly visible, bright red, undigested blood per rectum, which may appear as frank blood, blood-streaked stool, or blood clots. The blood originates from a source within the gastrointestinal tract â€” which may range from the anorectal region to the proximal GI tract in the setting of rapid hemorrhagic transit â€” and is identified by direct visual observation without the aid of chemical or laboratory testing. No minimum threshold of blood volume or hemodynamic consequence is required for the sign to be present. Hematochezia is explicitly distinguished from melena, in which digested blood produces dark, tarry, malodorous stool indicative of slower upper GI transit; from fecal occult blood, detectable only through chemical assay in the absence of gross discoloration; and from rectal bleeding attributable to non-gastrointestinal sources, including gynecological hemorrhage or urological bleeding that contaminates the perianal region or toilet contents.
clinical_rationale: Hematochezia itself is a clinical sign, not a discrete pathological condition, and it spans many potential etiologies including those that are drug-induced, structural, idiopathic, or external. Drug-induced gastrointestinal bleeding is a plausible narrower reading, typically attributable to anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, NSAIDs, or other agents causing mucosal injury or coagulopathy. However, hematochezia as described is agnostic to hemodynamic significance, volume, and proximal medical causes, making it overly broad as a stand-alone safety outcome without further specification. Because the description covers a clinical sign rather than an etiology, diagnostic codes may be a marker of various underlying conditions that range across settings and do not inherently establish causation or severity.

source_definition: A hematoma is a localized collection of extravasated blood that has accumulated within tissue spaces outside the vascular lumen, forming a contained, clotted, or organizing blood mass. The condition may arise at any anatomical site, including subcutaneous tissue, muscle, solid organs, the central nervous system, and other parenchymal or connective tissue compartments. No restriction is placed on clinical severity; the phenotype encompasses hematomas ranging from minor superficial collections to large, clinically significant lesions. The etiology is unrestricted and includes traumatic, spontaneous (e.g., resulting from coagulopathy, anticoagulant therapy, or vascular malformation), and iatrogenic (e.g., post-surgical or post-procedural) causes. Hematomas occurring adjacent to or within a primary pathological lesion are included when the blood collection is identifiable as a discrete, contained entity. Explicitly excluded are: hemorrhagic effusions representing blood within pre-formed anatomical cavities (hemothorax, hemoperitoneum, hemarthrosis), which represent a pathophysiologically distinct process from tissue-bound collections; and active or ongoing hemorrhage, as a hematoma by definition represents a contained, post-hemorrhagic state rather than an acute extravasation event still in progress.
clinical_rationale: Hematoma is a localized collection of extravasated blood that may arise from trauma, coagulopathy, anticoagulant therapy, vascular malformations, surgical or procedural interventions, and other causes. Drug etiology is plausible through anticoagulant-related bleeding or impaired coagulation from drugs like warfarin, DOACs, or heparin, and hematomas represent a known safety concern for these medications and related therapies. Clinically, hematomas resolve with time or intervention unless complicated by infection or compartment syndrome, and discrete recurrent hematomas in separate locations are possible. While hematomas may be mild and managed in outpatient settings, large or deep hematomas are commonly identified in acute care. Exclusion of ongoing hemorrhage and hemorrhagic effusions limits this phenotype to organized, contained blood collections. Presentation is variable, and characteristic signs may or may not be recorded discretely in structured data.

source_definition: Hematuria, as defined here, is a clinical sign characterized by the visible discoloration of urine to a red, pink, or brown hue consistent with the presence of blood or blood-derived pigments. This phenotype encompasses gross (macroscopic) presentations only and does not require microscopic or laboratory confirmation of red blood cell presence in urine. The definition is etiologically inclusive, capturing hematuria arising from any source within or external to the urinary tract, including but not limited to urological malignancy, urolithiasis, glomerulonephritis, urinary tract infection, coagulopathy, anticoagulant or other drug effects, and procedural or traumatic causes such as catheterization or cystoscopy. The phenotype further includes presentations of visibly bloody or discolored urine attributable to non-RBC pigmenturia, such as myoglobinuria secondary to rhabdomyolysis or hemoglobinuria secondary to intravascular hemolysis, insofar as these present as the clinical sign of gross urinary discoloration. Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria detected solely by urinalysis or dipstick without a macroscopic presentation is explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Hematuria, as gross (macroscopic) discoloration of urine, can be associated with multiple etiologies, including drug-induced causes via anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, and hemolytic agents like chemotherapy drugs. It is valid as a pharmacovigilance outcome under narrowly defined circumstances where drug causation can be established, such as anticoagulant-related bleeding. However, broader inclusion, encompassing traumatic or anatomical origins, reduces its direct utility in pharmacovigilance unless preceded by an etiologic filter. The condition is inherently transient as the macroscopic finding resolves with treatment or cessation of bleeding. Diagnosis is clinical, based on visible urine discoloration, and does not typically require confirmatory testing. Follow-up is variable, depending on etiology and severity. This definition includes some non-hematuria (non-RBC pigmenturia) cases like hemoglobinuria, complicating clinical specificity for pharmacovigilance.

source_definition: Hemochromatosis is a disorder characterized by pathological elevation of total body iron stores, evidenced by raised serum ferritin and/or transferrin saturation, arising from any mechanism that results in excessive iron accumulation. The phenotype encompasses hereditary forms driven by genetic dysregulation of iron absorption or cellular iron export, as well as secondary or acquired forms resulting from exogenous iron loading such as chronic transfusion therapy, dyserythropoietic conditions, or excessive dietary or parenteral iron intake. The diagnosis is established on biochemical grounds alone; clinically manifest end-organ iron deposition or damage â€” including hepatic fibrosis, cardiomyopathy, diabetes mellitus, arthropathy, or hypogonadism â€” may be present but is not required. All individuals with biochemically confirmed iron overload are included within this phenotype, irrespective of whether the elevation reflects a sustained disorder of iron homeostasis or an acute-phase response superimposed on another condition.
clinical_rationale: Hemochromatosis, including both hereditary and secondary forms, is a suitable pharmacovigilance outcome as certain drugs (e.g., intravenous iron, chronic blood transfusions for anemia) can induce or exacerbate iron overload. Additionally, its metabolic and biochemical nature makes it distinguishable clinically and with diagnostic tests such as serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, or liver biopsy. While hereditary hemochromatosis is a genetic condition and not drug-induced, this phenotype is broader, including both primary and secondary causes, such as drug- or intervention-related iron overload. This aligns the phenotype with pharmacovigilance interests under specific circumstances. The condition is persistent due to irreversible changes in iron metabolism, requiring lifelong surveillance and sometimes treatment, despite acute control of symptoms. Diagnosis may occur across settings depending on severity and organ involvement, though outpatient diagnosis for asymptomatic cases predominates.

source_definition: Hemolysis is defined as the pathological, acquired premature destruction of circulating red blood cells (RBCs) occurring at a rate that exceeds normal physiological RBC senescence and is detectable through clinical or laboratory evidence of RBC breakdown, including elevated lactate dehydrogenase, reduced or absent serum haptoglobin, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, free plasma hemoglobin, or hemoglobinuria. This phenotype encompasses both intravascular and extravascular RBC destruction and includes hemolysis arising from any acquired mechanism â€” among them immune-mediated processes (autoimmune, alloimmune, or drug-induced), microangiopathic mechanical destruction (as in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic uremic syndrome, HELLP syndrome, or disseminated intravascular coagulation), infectious etiologies (e.g., malaria, clostridial toxemia), and toxic or oxidative drug-induced injury. Hemolysis occurring as a secondary downstream consequence of another primary disease (e.g., hypersplenism from portal hypertension, hemolysis in Zieve syndrome) is included, as the phenotype characterizes the hemolytic state itself rather than its proximate cause. Explicitly excluded is the chronic baseline hemolysis intrinsic to hereditary or congenital RBC disorders (e.g., the constitutive hemolysis of sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis), as well as normal physiological RBC senescence and in vitro hemolysis arising from specimen collection or processing artifacts.
clinical_rationale: Hemolysis, as defined, is an acquired state of abnormal RBC destruction that can be drug-induced via mechanisms like immune-mediated hemolysis (e.g., hapten-mediated reactions or drug-induced autoimmune hemolytic anemia), oxidative stress from drugs (such as dapsone or sulfasalazine), or toxic injury. This makes it a valid pharmacovigilance outcome with multiple documented drug etiologies. The condition is transient because once the inciting factor is removed or treated, the hemolysis resolves. Although hemolysis can be secondary to a range of conditions, it represents a distinct clinical event when diagnosed and managed as such. Incident hemolysis is often recognized in the acute care setting due to its rapid onset and potential for severe manifestations such as hemoglobinuria, anemia, and jaundice, but less severe cases may be incidentally identified outpatient via laboratory findings. The description makes clear exclusions for in vitro hemolysis and constitutive chronic hemolysis from genetic disorders, constraining analysis to acquired states.

source_definition: Hemolytic Disease of the Fetus and Newborn is a condition in which maternal IgG alloantibodies, formed in response to fetal red blood cell antigens incompatible with those of the mother across any blood group system (including but not limited to ABO, Rh, Kell, and Duffy), cross the placenta and bind to fetal or neonatal erythrocytes, triggering immune-mediated hemolysis. The resulting condition encompasses the full spectrum of clinical severity, from mild neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and compensated hemolytic anemia to severe fetal anemia, hydrops fetalis, and perinatal death. The definition requires that maternal alloimmunization be a necessary and contributing pathophysiological driver; cases in which a co-existing non-alloimmune process (e.g., sepsis, polycythemia) amplifies but does not independently cause the hemolysis remain within scope, whereas cases in which such a process fully and independently accounts for the hemolysis are excluded. Explicitly out of scope are: non-immune hemolytic anemias arising from intrinsic erythrocyte defects (enzymatic, structural, or hemoglobin disorders); neonatal autoimmune hemolytic anemia driven by passively transferred maternal autoantibodies directed against self-antigens; and physiological jaundice of the newborn, which reflects normal neonatal bilirubin metabolism in the absence of immune-mediated red cell destruction.
clinical_rationale: Hemolytic Disease of the Fetus and Newborn is immune-mediated hemolysis triggered by maternal IgG alloantibodies against fetal blood group antigens. Drugs do not directly cause this condition; its etiology is rooted in maternal-fetal alloimmune incompatibility, making it unsuitable as a pharmacovigilance outcome. Its most severe manifestations, hydrops fetalis and perinatal death, can occur without discrete episodes, while lesser presentations like neonatal jaundice may resolve completely. Diagnosis often occurs during pregnancy or shortly after delivery, with acute care settings expected for severe cases. Testing, such as Coombs tests and bilirubin measurement, is essential to confirm diagnosis and manage severity. Follow-up care is needed especially for survivors of severe hemolysis with long-term effects like iron overload or kernicterus, but mild cases may resolve without ongoing management.

source_definition: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by the simultaneous presence of three core features: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, with the kidney representing the dominant organ of injury. The condition encompasses all recognized etiological subtypes, including Shiga toxin-producing organism-associated (typical) HUS, complement dysregulation-mediated atypical HUS, drug-induced, pneumococcal, and other secondary forms, provided the defining triad is present. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is excluded from this phenotype on clinical grounds when neurological manifestations predominate in the absence of significant acute kidney injury consistent with a TTP clinical profile; where ADAMTS13 testing has been performed, cases demonstrating severe ADAMTS13 deficiency (activity less than 10%) are additionally excluded regardless of clinical presentation. Pure immune thrombocytopenic purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and other non-microangiopathic causes of concurrent anemia and thrombocytopenia without the characteristic renal injury are outside the scope of this definition.
clinical_rationale: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury (AKI). Among its diverse etiologies, drug-induced HUS is a recognized subset, often implicating agents such as calcineurin inhibitors, chemotherapeutics like gemcitabine, or antiplatelet agents. While other forms of HUS, such as Shiga toxin-mediated ('typical') or complement dysregulation-driven ('atypical') HUS, may not involve pharmacologic etiology, the phenotype definition explicitly includes drug-induced cases alongside others with hallmark features. HUS is a transient condition with discrete episodes tied to specific insults, but recurrence is possible in atypical HUS or cases linked to repeat exposures or triggers. Diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation of hemolysis and renal injury, aligning with the need for diagnostic testing. Incident HUS usually requires acute care due to its severity, systemic involvement, and threat to organ function, making ED or inpatient settings typical for diagnosis. Complex care trajectories include short-term active treatment, such as plasma exchange, dialysis, or other organ support, and condition-specific follow-up to monitor for sequelae like chronic kidney disease or relapse in atypical cases.

source_definition: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by uncontrolled activation and proliferation of macrophages and cytotoxic T lymphocytes, resulting in excessive cytokine production and systemic immune-mediated tissue destruction. The syndrome encompasses two pathophysiological forms: primary (familial) HLH, driven by inherited defects in cytotoxic lymphocyte granule-mediated killing (e.g., mutations in PRF1, UNC13D, RAB27A, or STX11), and secondary (reactive/acquired) HLH, precipitated by an external stimulus such as infection (particularly Epstein-Barr virus or cytomegalovirus), hematologic malignancy, or systemic autoimmune/autoinflammatory disease â€” including macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) arising in conditions such as systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or systemic lupus erythematosus, which is treated as a clinical subtype within this phenotype rather than a distinct entity. Both forms share the same final common pathway of pathological immune hyperactivation. Clinical recognition requires fulfillment of â‰¥5 of 8 HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria: persistent fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias in â‰¥2 peripheral blood lineages, hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia, histopathological evidence of hemophagocytosis in bone marrow, spleen, lymph node, or liver, absent or markedly reduced NK-cell cytotoxic activity, hyperferritinemia (â‰¥500 Î¼g/L), and elevated soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor Î±-chain). The phenotype includes both active acute HLH episodes and documented prior history of HLH. No competing hyperinflammatory syndrome is categorically excluded; fulfillment of formal HLH-2004 criteria is the defining threshold regardless of the precipitating trigger.
clinical_rationale: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) can arise as a secondary outcome from various drug exposures, particularly chemotherapy agents and biological immunomodulators that dysregulate immune function. Secondary HLH is recognized in association with hematologic malignancies as well as infections that may be precipitated or exacerbated by drug-induced immunosuppression. Primary (familial) HLH is a genetic disorder and is not drug-attributable, but the phenotype defined here explicitly includes both primary and secondary forms under the shared HLH clinical criteria. Pharmacovigilance applicability is therefore conditional on restricting cohort logic to secondary/reactive HLH. Clinically, HLH is a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome that arises acutely, requires urgent recognition and treatment, and typically resolves with resolution of the underlying trigger, though some patients may experience recurrent episodes. Diagnosis is heavily reliant on fulfilling HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria, which mandates laboratory and histopathological tests; incident HLH is almost always recognized in the acute care setting due to its severity. Key triggers include drugs, infections, malignancies, and autoimmunity, with cytopenias, fevers, and splenomegaly being common presenting symptoms.

source_definition: Hemoptysis is the expectoration of blood or blood-tinged sputum originating from the lower respiratory tract, defined as airway structures and pulmonary parenchyma below the glottis. The condition spans the full severity continuum, from trace blood-streaking of sputum to frank, massive hemorrhage threatening airway patency and hemodynamic stability. It is etiologically agnostic, encompassing bleeding attributable to infectious processes (e.g., tuberculosis, necrotizing pneumonia, lung abscess), structural airway disease (e.g., bronchiectasis), primary or metastatic pulmonary malignancy, vascular anomalies (e.g., pulmonary arteriovenous malformations), thromboembolic disease, autoimmune or vasculitic injury to the pulmonary vasculature, and coagulopathic states. Explicitly excluded are: pseudohemoptysis, in which blood originates from the nasopharynx, oropharynx, or upper airway and is expectorated without arising from below the glottis; hematemesis, in which blood of gastrointestinal origin is vomited and may mimic expectoration; and blood-tinged secretions produced by passive hydrostatic congestion of the pulmonary capillary bed, such as the pink frothy sputum characteristic of acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, which reflects fluid transudation rather than active hemorrhage from respiratory structures.
clinical_rationale: Hemoptysis can be a pharmacovigilance outcome as it includes conditions with potential drug-attributable etiologies, such as coagulopathy (e.g., associated with anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents), drug-induced vasculitis, or pulmonary toxicity (e.g., certain chemotherapeutics). Its clinical definition spans a broad range of severities and underlying causes. The exclusion of pseudohemoptysis and hematemesis in the definition aligns the term with genuine pulmonary-origin bleeding. Recognizing hemoptysis as a distinct phenomenon may be challenging in observational data due to overlap with other causes of blood expectoration and the likely nonspecific coding under broader categories of respiratory symptoms.

source_definition: Hemorrhagic stroke is an acute cerebrovascular event characterized by spontaneous, non-traumatic intracranial hemorrhage arising from intrinsic vascular pathology â€” such as hypertensive small vessel rupture, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, arteriovenous malformation, intracranial aneurysm rupture, or anticoagulation-related bleeding from otherwise structurally normal vessels â€” resulting in sudden neurological deficit. The phenotype encompasses intracerebral hemorrhage (bleeding directly into brain parenchyma), subarachnoid hemorrhage (bleeding into the subarachnoid space), and spontaneous subdural hematoma occurring in the absence of precipitating trauma. Excluded from this phenotype are: all forms of traumatic intracranial hemorrhage caused by external mechanical force; hemorrhagic transformation of ischemic stroke, in which secondary bleeding occurs within an established ischemic infarct rather than as the primary initiating event; traumatic subdural and epidural hematomas; and intratumoral hemorrhage, in which bleeding originates from pathological tumor vasculature rather than diseased or structurally abnormal cerebral vessels.
clinical_rationale: Hemorrhagic stroke is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome, particularly when cases involve anticoagulant-related bleeding that occurs in the absence of trauma, a well-documented drug-attributable mechanism. Anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants), thrombocytopenia-inducing agents, or other drugs influencing hemostasis can precipitate intracranial hemorrhage. The clinical course is transient, as patients who survive no longer carry the diagnostic label of hemorrhagic stroke, though sequelae such as neurologic deficits may persist and are coded under other concepts. Intracranial events are overwhelmingly diagnosed in acute care settings due to the sudden onset of neurological symptoms. Imaging (CT or MRI) is required for diagnosis to differentiate types of intracranial hemorrhage and to exclude traumatic causes. Excluded from this definition are traumatic intracranial hemorrhages, hemorrhagic transformation of cerebral infarction, and hemorrhage secondary to tumors, which do not overlap the scope described. For recurrent events, an interepisode gap of 90 days is reasonable to eliminate residual or follow-up coding associated with the original episode.

source_definition: Hemorrhoids are a pathological condition of the normal hemorrhoidal vascular cushions â€” specialized submucosal structures composed of arteriovenous anastomoses, smooth muscle, and connective tissue located in the anal canal. The phenotype encompasses all anatomical subtypes, including internal hemorrhoids arising above the dentate line (classified Grade I through IV based on degree of prolapse), external hemorrhoids arising below the dentate line and covered by anoderm, and mixed hemorrhoids involving both compartments, regardless of whether the diagnosis is established in the context of symptoms (such as rectal bleeding, prolapse, pruritus, or pain) or as an incidental finding on clinical or endoscopic examination. This phenotype explicitly excludes anorectal varices, which represent dilated portosystemic collateral vessels driven by portal hypertension and are pathophysiologically distinct from primary hemorrhoidal vascular cushion disease. It further excludes rectal prolapse, a distinct anatomical entity involving full-thickness protrusion of the rectal wall that may mimic prolapsing internal hemorrhoids clinically but differs in underlying mechanism, anatomy, and management.
clinical_rationale: Hemorrhoids represent pathological changes to the hemorrhoidal vascular cushions and can present with symptoms such as bleeding, pain, prolapse, or pruritus, though some cases are diagnosed asymptomatically. Drug etiology is rare but plausible in specific scenarios, such as anticoagulant-induced bleeding exacerbating symptoms or medications causing constipation that aggravates hemorrhoidal disease. The course is generally transient, as patients often stop being described as having hemorrhoids once successfully treated; however, recurrence is possible due to risk factors like chronic straining, constipation, or venous stasis. Most incident cases are diagnosed in outpatient settings, but operative management may occasionally necessitate acute care. The description is appropriately focused on hemorrhoids as a vascular and anatomical condition, excluding unrelated entities such as anorectal varices or rectal prolapse.

source_definition: Hepatic Encephalopathy is a clinically apparent neuropsychiatric syndrome arising directly from hepatic insufficiency or portosystemic shunting, characterized by a spectrum of brain dysfunction ranging from mild personality change and cognitive impairment through disorientation, asterixis, and confusion to stupor and coma. The syndrome may occur in the context of acute liver failure, chronic liver disease of any underlying etiology, or non-cirrhotic portosystemic shunting, provided that the neuropsychiatric disturbance is causally attributable to hepatic dysfunction or aberrant portal-systemic circulation. Subclinical or covert forms detectable solely by formal psychometric or neurophysiological testing are excluded; a minimum threshold of clinically evident neurological or behavioral change is required. Encephalopathic states principally attributable to structural or primary neurological disease â€” including stroke, subdural hematoma, central nervous system infection, or primary psychiatric disorders â€” are excluded, as are metabolic encephalopathies driven by a distinct non-hepatic mechanism (including uremic, hypoglycemic, or Wernicke's encephalopathy), even when co-occurring in a patient with underlying liver disease.
