LBCL encompasses multiple nosological entities with shared clinical and morphological features, typified by aggressive behavior and requiring urgent treatment. The detailed description excludes entities like histologically transformed B-cell malignancies and MYC-driven lymphomas. LBCL clinical course is chronic (persistent) but prone to episodes of relapse and progression, necessitating active management and surveillance. Diagnosis typically requires biopsy and pathological evaluation, with ancillary molecular testing guiding treatment. LBCL entities are most commonly diagnosed in outpatient oncology settings, but diagnoses at relapse or severe presentations may occur in acute care settings.

source_definition: Left bundle branch block (LBBB) is a cardiac conduction abnormality arising from impaired or failed transmission of the electrical impulse through the left bundle branch of the His-Purkinje system, resulting in delayed and abnormal activation of the left ventricle. The phenotype encompasses both complete LBBB, characterized by a QRS duration of 120 milliseconds or greater with broad, notched or slurred R waves in lateral leads (I, aVL, V5â€“V6), absent septal Q waves, and secondary ST-T wave changes; and incomplete LBBB, defined by a QRS duration of 110 to 119 milliseconds with the same morphological features reflecting a lesser degree of conduction delay. The phenotype is restricted to persistent, intrinsic conduction disease and explicitly excludes QRS morphology that mimics LBBB as a consequence of right ventricular or biventricular pacing, where the delay is imposed by an external electrical stimulus rather than underlying His-Purkinje pathology. Rate-dependent (intermittent) LBBB, in which block manifests only above a critical heart rate threshold and resolves at lower rates, is also excluded, as this represents a functional phenomenon rather than fixed structural disease of the conduction system.
clinical_rationale: Left bundle branch block (LBBB) arises from intrinsic structural disease in the conduction system and typically reflects underlying cardiac pathology such as ischemic heart disease, cardiomyopathy, or fibrosis. Drug-induced etiologies are extremely rare and typically involve drugs with profound effects on cardiac conduction, such as sodium channel blockers or severe electrolyte disturbances secondary to medications. The condition is persistent once identified as intrinsic conduction disease but does not involve discrete relapsing episodes. Its diagnostic features on electrocardiogram (ECG) require objective testing, and symptomatic patients presenting for care typically undergo active management addressing underlying causes. However, LBBB itself is not inherently treated directly nor does it commonly serve as a primary pharmacovigilance outcome. Incident recognition occurs across care settings depending on acuity and underlying disease context.

source_definition: Lethargy is a pathological state characterized by a spectrum of reduced energy, motivation, and arousal â€” ranging from subjectively reported abnormal fatigue and diminished vigor to clinician-observed psychomotor slowing, decreased attentiveness, and reduced arousability, including states of obtundation. The phenotype encompasses both patient-reported experiences of abnormal tiredness or low energy and objective clinical findings of impaired alertness, and applies regardless of the underlying etiology, including lethargy occurring as a manifestation of a known primary condition. The upper boundary of this phenotype excludes deeper disorders of consciousness such as stupor and coma. Explicitly excluded are transient, physiologically expected states of fatigue â€” such as post-exertional tiredness or fatigue attributable solely to sleep deprivation â€” in the absence of an underlying pathological process.
clinical_rationale: Lethargy as defined includes a broad spectrum of diminished energy and alertness that can arise from diverse etiologies, including drug-induced effects (e.g., CNS depressants, sedatives, or medications triggering fatigue). Drugs capable of altering CNS arousal or energy levels are documented causes of lethargy, though non-drug causes (e.g., metabolic, infectious, or psychiatric conditions) are common as well. The definition provided excludes normal fatigue and deeper alterations in consciousness, anchoring it to pathological processes. This breadth makes lethargy valid as a pharmacovigilance outcome under a narrowed reading of drug-attributable lethargy but creates diagnostic ambiguity in claims data, where structured records are unlikely to delineate the etiology and severity. Important challenges include distinguishing drug-induced lethargy from fatigue due to systemic illness, depression, or sleep disorders and relying on subjective or non-specific presentations in structured data.

source_definition: Leukocytosis is a pathological or physiological state characterized by a true, biologically confirmed elevation of the total circulating white blood cell count above 11,000 cells per microliter (11 Ã— 10â¹/L) in adults, attributable to an increase in one or more leukocyte lineages â€” including neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils, individually or in combination. The phenotype encompasses all etiologies of genuine leukocyte expansion, including reactive causes (infection, inflammation, tissue injury, physiologic stress such as exercise or pregnancy), drug- or cytokine-mediated stimulation, and neoplastic clonal proliferation such as leukemia or myeloproliferative neoplasms. Confirmation requires at least two separate measurements demonstrating sustained elevation, except when a single markedly elevated value is clinically sufficient to warrant immediate medical action, such as in suspected hyperleukocytosis or blast crisis. Pseudoleukocytosis arising from laboratory or technical artifacts â€” including unlysed erythrocytes, platelet clumping, cryoglobulin precipitation, or nucleated red blood cells falsely inflating automated counts â€” is explicitly excluded, as these represent measurement error rather than a true increase in circulating leukocyte burden.
clinical_rationale: Leukocytosis is a heterogeneous condition with multiple potential etiologies, including drug-mediated causes such as corticosteroids, colony-stimulating factors (e.g., G-CSF), beta-agonists, and lithium. It is a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome when drug-induced or when drugs contribute to an underlying pathological process. However, it also includes non-drug causes such as infections, inflammation, and neoplastic disorders, as well as physiological states like pregnancy or exercise. The phenotype requires confirmation through laboratory tests and interpretation to separate true leukocytosis from pseudoleukocytosis artifacts. The condition is transient when resolving after the removal of the inciting cause or in the setting of a temporary reactive process, but it may be persistent in cases of underlying chronic or neoplastic conditions. Given the broad range of causes, its utility in pharmacovigilance requires careful attention to the specific population and exclusion of non-relevant etiologies.

source_definition: Leukopenia is a clinical state characterized by a reduction in the total circulating white blood cell count to below 4.0 Ã— 10â¹/L, as established by a single valid peripheral blood measurement. The definition is etiology-agnostic, encompassing all underlying mechanisms including drug-induced myelosuppression, acute infectious causes, autoimmune-mediated destruction, nutritional deficiencies, and primary bone marrow pathology, without restriction by causal attribution. It applies specifically to a reduction in the total leukocyte count; selective reductions confined to individual white cell lineages â€” such as neutropenia or lymphopenia â€” constitute distinct sub-phenotypes and do not satisfy this definition unless accompanied by a total WBC below the specified threshold. Cases in which a low reported WBC count is attributable to known pre-analytical laboratory artifacts, including EDTA-induced leukocyte clumping or cold agglutinin interference producing pseudoleukopenia, are explicitly excluded, as such findings do not represent a true reduction in circulating leukocytes.
clinical_rationale: Leukopenia is a reduction in total circulating white blood cell count below 4.0 × 10⁹/L as measured by peripheral blood testing, and it includes drug-induced causes such as myelosuppression from chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, or other hematotoxic drugs. Non-drug causes include infections, autoimmune destruction, bone marrow failure, and nutritional deficiencies. It is suitable for pharmacovigilance when specifically attributed to drug-induced etiology, but the definition provided spans both drug-attributable and non-drug causes. Additionally, the required laboratory confirmation ensures diagnostic objectivity but excludes pre-analytical artifacts. Etiology-agnostic leukopenia is conditional for pharmacovigilance, as drug-induced leukopenia represents a narrower reading. Recurrence is possible after resolution of a prior episode, and although the condition might result in chronic sequelae as a distinct diagnosis (e.g., persistent bone marrow disorders or secondary infections), most cases resolve without permanent labeling. Acute care settings account for a significant portion of incident cases, but outpatient diagnosis is also common, especially in mild cases or during routine hematology monitoring for underlying conditions.

source_definition: Lichen planus is a chronic, idiopathic, T-cellâ€“mediated inflammatory disorder characterized by a lichenoid tissue reaction pattern arising in immunocompetent, non-transplant hosts, and encompassing involvement of any combination of cutaneous surfaces, oral and genital mucosae, nails, and scalp (the latter presenting as lichen planopilaris). The condition is defined by its autoimmune pathophysiology â€” cytotoxic CD8+ T-cellâ€“driven apoptosis of basal keratinocytes â€” and is recognized clinically by violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped pruritic papules on the skin; lacy white Wickham's striae or erosions on mucosal surfaces; nail dystrophy and pterygium formation; and cicatricial alopecia of the scalp. All severity levels are included, from mild localized disease to severe erosive and ulcerative presentations. This phenotype explicitly excludes lichenoid tissue reactions attributable to exogenous triggers, including drug-induced lichenoid eruptions and the lichenoid manifestations of chronic graft-versus-host disease, as well as distinct dermatoses that may clinically resemble LP but differ in pathophysiology, such as lichen sclerosus and lichen simplex chronicus.
clinical_rationale: Lichen planus (LP) is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory condition characterized by cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell–mediated apoptosis of basal keratinocytes. While idiopathic LP is not directly associated with drug exposure, drug-induced lichenoid eruptions can closely mimic it but are excluded by this phenotype definition. The phenotype's exclusion of drug-attributable lichenoid eruptions precludes its use as a pharmacovigilance outcome for drug-safety studies. LP’s chronic and relapsing nature aligns with a persistent relapsing course. Diagnosis is typically made in outpatient settings based on clinical findings, supported by biopsy when necessary. LP may require follow-up for symptom management and prevention of complications such as scarring alopecia or secondary infections.

source_definition: Lichenoid eruption is an inflammatory condition of epithelial surfaces defined by a lichenoid tissue reaction pattern â€” characterized by band-like lymphocytic infiltration at the dermoepidermal junction with basal keratinocyte injury (interface dermatitis) and, clinically, by flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules or plaques â€” arising from any underlying etiology. The phenotype encompasses all recognized etiologic subtypes, including idiopathic lichen planus and its variants (cutaneous, oral, erosive, nail, and lichen planopilaris), drug-induced lichenoid reactions, graft-versus-host disease-associated lichenoid change, lichenoid contact dermatitis, and lichenoid keratosis, across any affected anatomical site including skin, oral and genital mucosa, esophagus, nails, and scalp. All severity grades are included, from mild localized papular eruptions to severe erosive or ulcerative disease. The phenotype explicitly excludes lichenification â€” a reactive epidermal thickening from chronic mechanical trauma or scratching â€” which lacks the defining lichenoid inflammatory mechanism. Also excluded are diseases in which a lichenoid histologic pattern represents an incidental or secondary finding rather than the defining pathologic process; conditions such as discoid lupus erythematosus or secondary syphilis are excluded even when lichenoid interface changes are noted on biopsy, as their diagnosis is established by other primary clinical and pathologic criteria.
clinical_rationale: Lichenoid eruption is a heterogeneous phenotype encompassing idiopathic lichen planus and its variants, drug-induced lichenoid reactions, and other causes. Drug-induced lichenoid eruptions are a documented pharmacovigilance outcome, attributed to various medications including antimalarials, beta-blockers, and ACE inhibitors. Mechanistically, drug-induced cases arise from immune-mediated interface dermatitis, while other subtypes may be idiopathic or related to non-drug causes (e.g., graft-versus-host disease). Usual care differentiates lichenoid eruption from diseases with incidental lichenoid histologic features (e.g., lupus) or distinct mechanisms (lichenification). The clinical course varies significantly: drug-induced cases tend to resolve upon withdrawal of the offending agent, while idiopathic and autoimmune cases may have recurrent or chronic courses. Symptom presentation (papules or plaques) often leads to outpatient diagnosis, though severe erosive or ulcerative forms may require acute care. Biopsy is near-universal for confirmation due to overlapping clinical presentations. Follow-up is necessary for oral or genital mucosal involvement, erosive cases, and management of chronic disease variants.

source_definition: Lightheadedness is a clinical state characterized by a subjective sensation of impending loss of consciousness, faintness, or spatial disorientation arising from transient reduction in cerebral perfusion, spanning the full spectrum from mild, self-resolving episodes to presyncope and episodes that culminate in brief loss of consciousness. The phenotype encompasses hemodynamically mediated presentations including those attributable to orthostatic hypotension, hypovolemia, reduced cardiac output, or vasovagal mechanisms. Explicitly excluded are sensations of rotational or linear motion arising from peripheral or central vestibular pathology, and episodes driven by psychogenic hyperventilation or anxiety-mediated hypocapnia. Lightheadedness that constitutes a fully explained, subordinate manifestation of a concurrently documented and active primary condition is also excluded, as such presentations are considered features of the underlying disease rather than an independent clinical state.
clinical_rationale: Lightheadedness is a subjective symptom rather than a definitive diagnosis and arises from diverse etiologies, including pharmacologic causes such as those related to orthostatic hypotension (e.g., antihypertensives, diuretics) or hypovolemia-inducing agents. Etiology may also include non-drug causes, such as vasovagal reflexes or cardiac output reduction. As noted in the description, non-hemodynamic conditions (vestibular issues, anxiety-driven episodes) and secondary sensations attributable to primary active diseases are excluded, so this phenotype focuses exclusively on hemodynamically mediated presentations. It is suitable as a pharmacovigilance outcome for drug-induced states under those mechanisms but not as a manifestation of non-drug causes. Presentation occurs across a spectrum of care settings, with mild self-resolving episodes often in outpatient care and severe or presyncopal presentations in acute care.

source_definition: Liver cirrhosis is an irreversible, end-stage pathological state of the liver characterized by diffuse replacement of normal hepatic parenchyma with fibrous scar tissue and regenerative nodules, resulting in permanent distortion of the hepatic lobular and vascular architecture. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical spectrum of disease, from asymptomatic compensated cirrhosis â€” in which hepatic synthetic function is relatively preserved and complications of portal hypertension are absent â€” through decompensated cirrhosis, marked by the presence of one or more major complications including ascites, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, or jaundice attributable to hepatocellular failure. The definition is etiology-neutral and applies regardless of the underlying primary cause (e.g., alcohol-related liver disease, chronic viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, or cholestatic liver disease). Explicitly excluded are: (1) pre-cirrhotic hepatic fibrosis stages that have not yet progressed to end-stage architectural destruction; (2) congestive hepatopathy and cardiac cirrhosis, in which hepatic structural changes arise secondary to right-sided heart failure and venous congestion rather than primary hepatic parenchymal injury; and (3) sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (hepatic veno-occlusive disease), which represents a distinct vascular pathophysiological entity not equivalent to cirrhotic architectural remodeling.
clinical_rationale: Liver cirrhosis is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome, as there are well-documented drug-attributable causal mechanisms including chronic hepatotoxicity from medications like methotrexate, amiodarone, or isoniazid. Additionally, cirrhosis can develop secondary to drug-induced chronic liver disease from repeated acute insults or immune-mediated injury. The condition is persistent due to its irreversible architectural destruction. Incident cirrhosis can occur in various care settings, with compensated cases often diagnosed in ambulatory care and decompensated cases typically presenting in acute care settings. The broad etiological inclusiveness of this definition poses no incompatibility with drug etiology, but secondary causes such as congestive hepatopathy or sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, which are explicitly excluded, aid specificity. Laboratory tests, imaging studies, and biopsy are critical for confirming the diagnosis, and complications often require active management and follow-up for at least a year.

source_definition: Liver necrosis is defined as the pathological, irreversible death of hepatocytes in non-neoplastic hepatic parenchyma, characterized by loss of membrane integrity, cytoplasmic swelling, and cell lysis as the result of an injurious process. The phenotype encompasses any extent of parenchymal hepatocellular death â€” from focal or spotty necrosis to zonal (centrilobular, midzonal, or periportal), submassive, or massive necrosis â€” and is etiology-agnostic, applying uniformly across all causative mechanisms including ischemic, toxic, drug-induced, viral, autoimmune, and metabolic processes. Excluded from this definition is necrosis confined to neoplastic hepatic tissue (e.g., tumor necrosis within hepatocellular carcinoma or hepatic metastases), which represents oncologic cell breakdown rather than a primary hepatocellular injury state. Also excluded is low-grade necroinflammatory activity used as a histologic grading feature in chronic liver diseases (e.g., interface hepatitis or piecemeal necrosis in chronic hepatitis activity scores or steatohepatitis staging systems), as this constitutes a chronic pathophysiological continuum distinct from identifiable, discrete necrotic events in the hepatic parenchyma.
clinical_rationale: Liver necrosis may result directly from drug exposures, particularly in cases of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) where hepatotoxicity leads to irreversible cell death. Mechanisms include direct toxicity (e.g., acetaminophen overdose), idiosyncratic reactions, or immune-mediated injury. Other etiologies such as viral, ischemic, or autoimmune processes are broader and unrelated to pharmacovigilance unless explicitly tied to drugs. The condition's clinical course is transient; once necrosis heals, the patient no longer retains the diagnostic label of 'liver necrosis,' though severe cases may result in chronic liver dysfunction under separate concepts like cirrhosis. Diagnosis typically requires imaging, laboratory tests, or biopsy findings, especially in non-severe or non-ischemic cases. Acute care setting predominates for substantial necrosis, such as massive or submassive necrosis, while smaller necrotic processes may be recognized in outpatient settings. The phenotype definition appropriately excludes chronic necroinflammatory grading systems and neoplastic tissue necrosis.

source_definition: Acquired Long QT syndrome is a non-heritable disorder of ventricular repolarization characterized by pathological prolongation of the QTc interval on electrocardiography arising from an extrinsic cause â€” including but not limited to pharmacological agents, electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia), or neurological insults â€” and manifesting clinically through at least one symptomatic arrhythmic event such as syncope, torsades de pointes, sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia, or sudden cardiac arrest. The presence of structural heart disease does not preclude the diagnosis, provided the symptomatic arrhythmic event is the presenting clinical feature. This definition explicitly excludes heritable channelopathies (Romano-Ward syndrome, Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome, and related congenital forms) and other ventricular arrhythmia syndromes that do not operate through QTc prolongation, including Brugada syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and short QT syndrome.
clinical_rationale: Acquired Long QT syndrome (LQTS) is a significant pharmacovigilance outcome due to its well-documented drug-attributable etiology, particularly through medications such as antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, macrolide antibiotics, and other QT-prolonging agents. It can also arise from reversible electrolyte disturbances or neurological insults. The definition provided excludes heritable forms of LQTS and other unrelated arrhythmia syndromes, which avoids ambiguity. Diagnosing acquired LQTS typically requires an ECG to confirm QTc interval prolongation. While symptom manifestations such as syncope and torsades de pointes may occur, these are not reliably coded prior to diagnosis in claims or EHR data. The condition requires prompt active treatment to address the underlying cause (e.g., drug discontinuation, electrolyte correction) and prevent life-threatening arrhythmias. Follow-up is critical to ensure the QTc interval normalizes and to prevent recurrence.

source_definition: Lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage is defined as any clinically evident bleeding originating from a source distal to the ligament of Treitz, encompassing the small bowel (jejunum and ileum), colon, and rectum. The condition is characterized by the passage of blood per rectum or the clinical detection of lower GI blood loss, and includes spontaneous, disease-driven, and iatrogenic or post-procedural causes of hemorrhage within these anatomical segments. This phenotype explicitly excludes bleeding originating from sources proximal to the ligament of Treitz â€” i.e., confirmed upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage â€” even when such bleeding presents as hematochezia due to brisk transit. It further excludes bleeding arising from perianal and anorectal structures, including hemorrhoids and anal fissures, which are considered a clinically and pathophysiologically distinct category of anorectal bleeding.
clinical_rationale: Lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage (LGIH) is a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome due to associated risks of drug-attributable etiologies, such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, and chemotherapeutic agents, all of which are well-documented to cause or exacerbate gastrointestinal bleeding. Clinically, LGIH is a transient condition, as the bleeding episode is typically resolved with medical or interventional treatment, and a new episode is generally considered distinct rather than a continuation. For observational data, diagnostic specificity and coding may vary; LGIH is often recognized in acute care settings such as the emergency department or during hospitalization. Confirmatory tests (e.g., lower gastrointestinal endoscopy, imaging, or lab findings for active bleeding) are often required to diagnose the condition accurately. Surveillance or recurrence post-resolution is uncommon unless underlying chronic or structural conditions persist, such as diverticulosis or malignancy.

source_definition: Lupus nephritis is a renal manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), defined by immune complex-mediated inflammation of the kidney occurring exclusively in patients with a confirmed SLE diagnosis. It encompasses the full histological spectrum of glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury as classified by the ISN/RPS system (Classes I through VI), ranging from minimal mesangial involvement to diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis and advanced sclerosis. The condition is characterized by the deposition of autoantibody-containing immune complexes within glomerular and tubulointerstitial structures, triggering complement activation and inflammatory cascades that result in proteinuria, hematuria, and, in severe or progressive cases, declining glomerular filtration and renal insufficiency. Excluded from this phenotype are renal disorders arising through distinct pathophysiological mechanisms in SLE patients, including thrombotic microangiopathy attributable to antiphospholipid syndrome, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, and diabetic nephropathy, as well as nephritis occurring in the context of drug-induced lupus or connective tissue disease overlap syndromes where formal SLE classification criteria are not met.
clinical_rationale: Lupus nephritis is a renal manifestation strictly tied to systemic lupus erythematosus and is mediated by immune complex deposition in the kidney, leading to inflammatory and complement-driven injuries within glomerular and tubulointerstitial structures. Drug-induced lupus is excluded from this phenotype, but there is documented evidence of drug-induced exacerbations of SLE itself, including renal flares, mediated by drugs such as hydralazine and procainamide. While lupus nephritis is not exclusively drug-attributable and depends on the underlying autoimmune pathophysiology of SLE, immunosuppressive medications used to treat SLE are well-documented to stabilize or worsen renal manifestations including lupus nephritis. The phenotype is persistent-relapsing due to the chronic nature of SLE and potential for renal flares, even after treatment-induced remission. ISN/RPS classification is essential for its diagnosis, typically requiring biopsy. Incident diagnosis may occur in outpatient or acute care settings, depending on the severity and clinical presentation (e.g., nephrotic syndrome or AKI).

source_definition: Lymphadenopathy is defined as abnormal enlargement of one or more lymph nodes â€” whether localized to a single anatomic region or generalized across two or more non-contiguous regions â€” identified through clinical examination or radiologic assessment. The phenotype is etiology-agnostic, encompassing nodal enlargement attributable to any underlying mechanism, including reactive or inflammatory responses (infectious, autoimmune, or drug-related), as well as neoplastic processes such as primary nodal malignancies (e.g., lymphoma, leukemia with nodal involvement) and metastatic disease. A single documented episode of nodal enlargement is sufficient to meet the definition, regardless of whether the finding is transient or sustained over time. Explicitly excluded from this phenotype are lymphedema, which represents impaired lymphatic fluid drainage rather than true nodal enlargement, and pseudolymphadenopathy, in which soft tissue masses, cysts, or other anatomic structures mimic the clinical or radiologic appearance of enlarged lymph nodes without representing pathology of the lymph node itself.
clinical_rationale: Lymphadenopathy encompasses nodal enlargement due to diverse causes, including reactive and inflammatory mechanisms (e.g., infection, autoimmune processes, or drug reactions like phenytoin-induced pseudolymphoma). Drug-attributable etiologies are documented, especially in cases of immune-mediated or reactive lymphadenopathy. However, the phenotype as defined is etiology-agnostic and includes neoplastic and metastatic causes which are not plausibly drug-induced, introducing heterogeneity in attribution for pharmacovigilance. The clinical course can range from transient events (e.g., infection-related) to persistent malignancies, making cohort definition highly dependent on the clinical context. Episodic lymphadenopathy linked to transient causes often resolves with treatment, while malignancy-related lymphadenopathy persists unless successfully treated. Incidental diagnosis can occur in outpatient or acute care settings, depending on the severity of symptoms or underlying cause.

source_definition: Lymphedema is a chronic condition of impaired lymphatic transport resulting in the pathological accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid within the tissues, arising from either idiopathic dysfunction of the lymphatic system with postnatal onset or acquired structural damage to lymphatic vessels or lymph nodes (e.g., from surgical disruption, radiation injury, malignant infiltration, trauma, or infectious processes such as filariasis). The condition encompasses any clinically recognized severity, from subclinical lymphatic insufficiency through irreversible fibrotic tissue changes, and may affect any anatomical region including the extremities, genitalia, face, head and neck, and trunk. Congenital lymphedema resulting from developmental malformation of the lymphatic system present at or shortly after birth is excluded. Edematous states arising solely from non-lymphatic systemic mechanisms â€” including cardiac congestion, hypoalbuminemia, nephrotic syndrome, or hepatic failure â€” are excluded. Pure lipedema, a disorder of pathological adipose deposition without primary lymphatic obstruction, is excluded; however, phlebolymphedema â€” a combined state in which chronic venous insufficiency has secondarily overwhelmed lymphatic capacity, resulting in identifiable lymphatic dysfunction â€” is included within this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Lymphedema can be caused by acquired damage to lymphatic vessels or nodes resulting from surgical operations (e.g., lymphadenectomy), radiation therapy, infections (e.g., filariasis), malignancy, or trauma, making it a pharmacovigilance outcome under a narrower reading centered on acquired causes. Drug-induced mechanisms, though rare, are biologically plausible via inflammation, fibrosis, or immune-mediated damage to lymphatic structures. The provided definition explicitly excludes congenital lymphedema and systemic edematous states unrelated to lymphatic dysfunction, narrowing the scope to acquired or idiopathic lymphedema with postnatal onset. Chronic venous insufficiency (phlebolymphedema) may also involve secondary lymphatic impairment. Diagnosis can be established through clinical signs and imaging (e.g., lymphoscintigraphy).

source_definition: Lymphoma is a malignant neoplasm arising from the clonal proliferation of lymphoid cells â€” including B-cells, T-cells, and NK-cells â€” that manifests primarily as a solid tumor mass within lymph nodes or extranodal lymphoid and non-lymphoid tissues. The phenotype encompasses both Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells within a reactive inflammatory infiltrate, and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a heterogeneous group of lymphoid malignancies lacking this defining histologic feature. The definition is restricted to active, incident disease in which the malignancy is currently present and has not achieved documented complete remission. Excluded from this definition are lymphoid malignancies that present predominantly as circulating neoplastic cells in the peripheral blood or bone marrow (e.g., chronic lymphocytic leukemia, lymphoblastic leukemia), as well as clonal plasma cell neoplasms (e.g., multiple myeloma, plasmacytoma), which, despite their shared lymphoid lineage, represent biologically and clinically distinct disease entities. Reactive, infectious, or inflammatory causes of lymphadenopathy are similarly outside the scope of this definition.
clinical_rationale: Lymphoma, including Hodgkin lymphoma and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, has documented drug-attributable etiologies, particularly in the context of immunosuppressive therapies (e.g., biologics targeting TNF-α, calcineurin inhibitors, and antilymphocyte monoclonal therapies). Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated lymphoproliferative disorders are also linked to iatrogenic immunosuppression following organ transplantation. The definition provided encompasses active, incident cases of lymphoma still requiring active management, distinguishing it from other lymphoid malignancies and plasma cell neoplasms. Diagnosis typically requires tissue biopsy and histologic confirmation. Incident cases are commonly recognized in outpatient specialty settings yet frequently involve escalation to acute care for biopsy, staging, or symptom management such as tumor lysis syndrome.

source_definition: Lymphopenia is an acquired reduction in the circulating absolute lymphocyte count below 1,000 cells per microliter in adults, reflecting a pathological decrease in the total peripheral blood lymphocyte pool. The condition arises through acquired mechanisms â€” including drug-induced immunosuppression, viral or bacterial infection, autoimmune-mediated lymphocyte depletion, malnutrition, or radiation exposure â€” and is established on the basis of a single confirmed laboratory measurement below this threshold, without a requirement for persistence across multiple time points. Lymphopenia attributable to primary or congenital immunodeficiencies, such as severe combined immunodeficiency or DiGeorge syndrome, is excluded, as these represent intrinsic developmental failures of lymphopoiesis rather than acquired perturbations of an otherwise competent lymphoid system. Lymphopenia occurring in the context of a concurrent hematologic or lymphoid malignancy is included within this phenotype, as the reduced lymphocyte count constitutes a clinically significant immune state irrespective of its oncologic co-etiology.
clinical_rationale: Lymphopenia is a drug-attributable outcome, commonly arising as a consequence of immunosuppressive medications (e.g., corticosteroids, chemotherapy agents) or other iatrogenic mechanisms such as radiation therapy. It can also result from infectious or autoimmune causes, malnutrition, or malignancy, but the phenotype excludes congenital immunodeficiencies that are not drug-attributable. The condition is transient because an acquired, isolated episode of lymphopenia resolves with removal of the underlying cause or appropriate treatment. It is typically diagnosed based on laboratory measurement of absolute lymphocyte count and does not usually require symptom documentation for detection. Follow-up or sequelae are less typical for isolated acquired lymphopenia, unless driven by its underlying disease.

source_definition: Macular edema is a pathological state characterized by the accumulation of intraretinal fluid within the macular region of the retina, resulting in measurable retinal thickening due to breakdown of the inner and/or outer blood-retinal barrier or impaired retinal fluid homeostasis. The condition encompasses all degrees of severity, from subclinical thickening detectable only by optical coherence tomography to overt edema associated with central visual acuity loss, and arises from any underlying etiology including but not limited to diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, uveitis, post-surgical inflammation, and retinal dystrophies. The phenotype is restricted to intraretinal fluid accumulation and explicitly excludes subretinal or sub-retinal pigment epithelium fluid accumulation secondary to choroidal neovascularization (as in neovascular age-related macular degeneration), apparent macular thickening caused by epiretinal membrane or vitreomacular traction without true fluid accumulation, and structural fluid-like spaces arising from macular schisis or retinoschisis.
clinical_rationale: Macular edema can be drug-induced, most notably by medications such as prostaglandin analogs, taxanes, nicotinic acid, glitazones, and certain biologics affecting VEGF pathways. The mechanism often involves disruption in the blood-retinal barrier or alteration in retinal vascular permeability. This phenotype is transient with potential for recurrence contingent on both treatment of the underlying cause and secondary insults. The description accurately excludes pathologies not involving intraretinal fluid accumulation, refining the concept to align with diagnostic conventions. Diagnosis is predominantly reliant on imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT), with distinct symptoms like visual acuity loss or distortion usually present but inconsistently documented as structured records. While active treatments, such as anti-VEGF injections or corticosteroids, are nearly always required, the diagnosis often involves follow-up imaging to ensure resolution and prevent recurrence.

source_definition: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a unipolar mood disorder characterized by one or more discrete Major Depressive Episodes, each defined by a minimum two-week period during which the individual experiences either persistent depressed mood or markedly diminished interest or pleasure in nearly all activities, accompanied by at least four additional neurovegetative, cognitive, or somatic symptoms from the DSM-5 criterion set â€” including significant weight or appetite change, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue or loss of energy, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, diminished concentration or indecisiveness, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation. The episode must cause clinically significant distress or functional impairment and must not be attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition. This phenotype encompasses presentations across the full severity spectrum (mild, moderate, and severe) but explicitly excludes depressive episodes occurring within the context of Bipolar I or Bipolar II Disorder, substance-induced depressive disorder, depressive disorder due to a general medical condition, Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia), adjustment disorder with depressed mood, and bereavement-related low mood that does not satisfy the full MDE symptom threshold and duration requirement.
clinical_rationale: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a clinically validated pharmacovigilance outcome as multiple drugs (e.g., corticosteroids, interferons, isotretinoin, some anticonvulsants, and certain antihypertensives) have documented associations with depressive syndromes. These cases are generally attributable to either direct pharmacological effects on neurotransmitter dynamics or secondary mechanisms such as exacerbation of underlying vulnerability. The clinical definition provided for MDD stipulates that episodes induced by substances or other medical conditions are excluded; however, drug-induced MDEs often mimic DSM-5 MDD criteria during presentation. While MDD is recurrent in a majority of patients, each Major Depressive Episode (MDE) has distinct onset and resolution, supporting 'TRANSIENT_RECURRENT' as the clinical course. Diagnosis is primarily made in outpatient care, though acute care settings may record severe presentations involving suicidality or psychosis. There is no sex-specific biological constraint, and while MDD spans all ages, diagnostic criteria (not definitionally restricted but practically rare) impose a skew toward adolescence and adulthood.

source_definition: Malaise is a subjective, non-specific constitutional symptom characterized by a diffuse and difficult-to-localize sense of general unwellness, discomfort, or feeling "off," that is not attributable solely to localized pain, effortful fatigue, or discrete physical weakness. It reflects a systemic perturbation of the individual's baseline sense of health and may manifest across any temporal dimension â€” from acute to chronic â€” and in association with any underlying pathophysiological process, including but not limited to infectious, inflammatory, metabolic, neoplastic, or iatrogenic etiologies. Malaise is distinguished from asthenia (generalized weakness/loss of strength) and fatigue (diminished capacity for sustained effort) by its qualitative character as a global sense of ill-being rather than a deficit in a specific physiological domain.
clinical_rationale: Malaise is described in the clinical definition as a nonspecific symptom reflecting an underlying systemic disturbance, including pathophysiological processes such as infectious, inflammatory, metabolic, neoplastic, or iatrogenic causes. While it can be associated with drug effects, particularly in the context of drug-induced systemic-inflammatory or toxic reactions, its non-specificity limits its utility as a direct pharmacovigilance outcome without further specification (e.g., malaise due to drug toxicity). No discrepancy exists between the name and the description; both cover a broad, undefined concept of systemic unwellness. It is a transient symptom that typically resolves if the underlying cause is addressed.

source_definition: Malignancy is defined as the presence of an active, invasive, histologically confirmed neoplasm characterized by uncontrolled clonal cellular proliferation with the capacity for local tissue invasion and, in many cases, distant metastasis. The phenotype encompasses the full spectrum of solid and hematologic malignancies, including melanoma, but explicitly excludes non-melanoma skin cancers (basal cell carcinoma and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the skin). To qualify as active, the malignancy must be diagnosed and not documented as having achieved complete remission or definitive cure; patients with stable disease, partial response, or those undergoing active oncologic management are included. Tumors of uncertain or borderline malignant potential are included when being managed with oncologic intent by a treating clinician. Pre-malignant conditions (e.g., myelodysplastic syndrome, high-grade dysplasia) and carcinoma in situ are excluded, as they lack histologically confirmed invasion and represent biologically distinct states that have not undergone frank malignant transformation.
clinical_rationale: The phenotype of malignancy represents a clinically and biologically heterogeneous group of neoplastic conditions with significant potential for drug-related etiology, including through mechanisms such as DNA damage, immune modulation, and hormonal pathways. Drugs such as immunosuppressants (e.g., calcineurin inhibitors), alkylating agents, and certain targeted therapies have well-documented associations with the development of malignancies. This definition excludes non-invasive and pre-malignant states but allows for the inclusion of tumors with histologically confirmed invasion and those managed with oncologic intent, highlighting the focus on active malignant disease. Given its clinical course, most malignancies are persistent conditions due to the lifelong relevance of the diagnosis and the need for ongoing surveillance or treatment, even in remission. Diagnosis typically occurs in the outpatient setting but can include acute care for certain presentations of advanced or aggressive tumors. Histological confirmation or diagnostic testing is essential for this phenotype, and active treatment and follow-up are standard parts of care in the vast majority of cases. However, the definition excludes cured or completely resolved malignancies, which helps demarcate active cases in the dataset.

source_definition: Malignant melanoma is an invasive malignant neoplasm arising from melanocytes, characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of atypical melanocytic cells with demonstrated breach of the basement membrane. The phenotype encompasses all primary anatomical sites of origin, including cutaneous (trunk, extremities, head and neck), acral lentiginous (palmar, plantar, and subungual), mucosal (oral, sinonasal, anorectal, and genitourinary), and uveal/ocular sites, reflecting the biological diversity of melanocyte distribution throughout the body. Metastatic melanoma presenting without an identifiable primary site is included, as the malignant melanocytic lineage and clinical management are equivalent to confirmed-primary disease. The phenotype excludes non-invasive melanocytic proliferations (melanoma in situ), benign melanocytic nevi regardless of degree of dysplasia, and all non-melanocytic cutaneous or ocular malignancies.
clinical_rationale: Malignant melanoma is biologically plausible as a pharmacovigilance outcome due to documented drug-inducible mechanisms like immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated secondary primary malignancies and potential indirect effects from chronic immunosuppression (e.g., after transplantation). Drugs contributing to immunogenic or mutagenic pathways may also accelerate the progression of melanoma. The provided clinical definition aligns with the broader scope of invasive melanoma across all anatomical sites, excluding non-invasive melanoma in situ or benign lesions. Incident diagnoses often present via specialized dermatology service or oncology, but critical care admission is rare unless metastatic or advanced.

source_definition: Mania refers to a discrete episode characterized by an abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased goal-directed activity or energy, representing a clear and observable departure from the individual's usual baseline. This phenotype encompasses the full manic spectrum: full manic episodes, in which the disturbance is of sufficient severity and duration (typically at least seven consecutive days, or any duration if hospitalization is required) to cause marked functional impairment, require inpatient care, or be accompanied by psychotic features; and hypomanic episodes, which are milder in intensity and duration (typically at least four consecutive days), do not require hospitalization, and are not associated with psychosis, but nonetheless constitute a noticeable change from baseline behavior. Associated features may include decreased need for sleep, inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, pressured speech, flight of ideas or racing thoughts, distractibility, and engagement in reckless or high-risk behaviors. This phenotype is inclusive of manic and hypomanic episodes arising from any proximate etiology, including primary bipolar spectrum disorders, general medical conditions, and substance use or withdrawal. Episodes in which manic or hypomanic features co-occur with a clinically significant concurrent depressive syndrome (mixed states) are explicitly excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Mania is recognized as a pharmacovigilance outcome since episodes can arise secondary to drug exposure, most notably as an adverse effect of corticosteroids, antidepressants, and stimulants. Physiological mechanisms include dopaminergic and adrenergic surge, alterations in serotonergic pathways, or direct neuropsychiatric toxicity. The clinical course is transient and episodic, with resolution expected after adequate treatment or removal of the offending agent, though recurrent episodes can occur in predisposed individuals, including those with bipolar disorder. The description is broad and encompasses both full manic episodes and hypomanic episodes, with formal inpatient or outpatient diagnostic criteria guiding recognition of new events. Diagnosis typically occurs in acute or emergency care settings during full manic episodes requiring urgent intervention, whereas milder cases (hypomania) are frequently observed in outpatient psychiatric care. Symptoms such as decreased need for sleep and reckless behavior are frequently documented separately, in claims or EHR systems, and confirmatory psychiatric evaluation is required for diagnosis.

source_definition: Mantle Cell Lymphoma is a mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising from antigen-experienced B-lymphocytes of the mantle zone, characteristically driven by overexpression of cyclin D1 resulting from the t(11;14)(q13;q32) chromosomal translocation, though a minor subset lacking cyclin D1 overexpression is included when immunophenotypic evidence â€” including SOX11 positivity, CD5 co-expression, and absence of CD23 â€” confirms mantle cell lineage. The phenotype encompasses the full clinicopathologic spectrum, including the classic aggressive nodal form presenting with widespread lymphadenopathy and extranodal involvement, and the indolent leukemic non-nodal form characterized by peripheral blood and bone marrow involvement with hypermutated immunoglobulin heavy chain variable genes and SOX11 negativity. All morphologic variants â€” conventional, blastoid, and pleomorphic â€” are included regardless of whether they represent de novo presentation or transformation from a prior MCL diagnosis. In-situ mantle cell neoplasia, a precursor state defined by cyclin D1-positive B-cells confined to the mantle zone without fulfilling diagnostic criteria for lymphoma, is explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Mantle Cell Lymphoma (MCL) is a non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma, driven primarily by the t(11;14)(q13;q32) translocation leading to cyclin D1 overexpression. Cyclin D1-negative MCL cases are included based on immunophenotypic confirmation. The condition has no exclusive drug-attributable etiology, although chemotherapy or immunosuppressive treatment can play a role in exacerbating or unmasking secondary lymphoid malignancies, these are not direct causative mechanisms. The breadth of clinicopathologic forms includes aggressive nodal and indolent leukemic variants, as well as morphologic variants like blastoid and pleomorphic types, which collectively result in a persistent diagnostic label under most clinical contexts due to ongoing management or surveillance needs. Due to its typically aggressive nature and systemic manifestations, initial diagnosis often occurs in acute care or specialty oncology settings. No sex-based or age-based biological constraints exist, as MCL affects both sexes and is most common in older adults but can occur at any age.

source_definition: Marginal zone lymphoma (MZL) is a clonal, neoplastic proliferation of mature B lymphocytes originating from the marginal zone compartment of secondary lymphoid organs, encompassing three anatomically and clinically distinct subtypes: extranodal MZL of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma), nodal MZL, and splenic MZL. All three subtypes share an indolent natural history characterized by slow growth and prolonged survival, though any may undergo histologic transformation into an aggressive large B-cell lymphoma, which remains within the scope of this phenotype as part of the MZL disease continuum. The condition is defined by confirmed neoplastic (clonal) B-cell proliferation and is agnostic to the underlying etiologic trigger (e.g., chronic bacterial, viral, or autoimmune antigenic stimulation). This phenotype explicitly excludes other indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas â€” including follicular lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma/WaldenstrÃ¶m's macroglobulinemia, and mantle cell lymphoma â€” as well as reactive, non-neoplastic marginal zone hyperplasia, which represents a polyclonal, self-limiting B-cell expansion without evidence of clonality.
clinical_rationale: Marginal zone lymphoma (MZL) is a mature clonal B-cell malignancy with an indolent clinical course. Drug-attributable etiologies have been described in the context of chronic immune stimulation due to the presence of viral infection (e.g., hepatitis C virus or Epstein-Barr virus) or bacterial infection (e.g., gastric Helicobacter pylori colonization driving MALT lymphoma), some of which may have an indirect connection to immunomodulatory drugs. However, there are no established direct drug-induced mechanisms for initiating MZL as a neoplastic event, and the primary pharmacovigilance interest may reside in potential drug-related triggers for histologic transformation into an aggressive B-cell lymphoma. Diagnosis requires confirmation of clonality and excludes several other indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes, as well as non-neoplastic marginal zone hyperplasia. While disease progression may lead to aggressive transformation, MZL itself is typically stable and requires lifelong management or surveillance at the chronic stage.

source_definition: Melanoma, as defined here, is a malignant neoplasm arising from the uncontrolled proliferation of melanocytes â€” pigment-producing cells of neural crest origin â€” that originate within the skin and demonstrate confirmed invasion into the dermis or deeper cutaneous layers. This phenotype encompasses all invasive histological subtypes of primary cutaneous origin, including superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, and acral lentiginous melanoma, across all stages of invasive disease (Stage I through Stage IV), inclusive of locally invasive primary tumors, regional lymph node involvement, in-transit metastases, and satellite lesions contiguous with the same cutaneous primary, as well as distant metastatic disease traceable to a primary cutaneous site. Excluded from this phenotype are melanoma in situ (Stage 0), which is confined to the epidermis and lacks dermal invasion and metastatic potential; melanomas arising from non-cutaneous anatomical sites such as uveal, mucosal, or occult primaries; and secondary cutaneous deposits representing metastatic spread from a non-cutaneous primary melanoma.
clinical_rationale: Melanoma is a malignant neoplasm of melanocytic origin with a biologically plausible drug-attributable etiology, as its development may be influenced by immunosuppressive therapies (e.g., those after organ transplantation or other chronic immunosuppression) and photosensitizing drugs that increase susceptibility to ultraviolet radiation damage. The provided definition excludes melanoma in situ and non-cutaneous primary sites, narrowing the focus to invasive cutaneous melanoma. The diagnostic process requires histopathological confirmation, commonly supported by tissue biopsy, and melanoma often demands active treatment across all stages, including surgical excision, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and systemic chemotherapy. Long-term follow-up is essential due to risk of recurrence, progression, or metastases even after initial treatment.

source_definition: Meniere's disease is a chronic disorder of the inner ear characterized by endolymphatic hydrops â€” an abnormal accumulation of endolymph within the membranous labyrinth â€” that manifests as a recurring spontaneous episodic syndrome. A case is defined as definite when a patient experiences at least two discrete, spontaneous episodes of vertigo each lasting between 20 minutes and 12 hours, accompanied by documented low-to-mid frequency sensorineural hearing loss on the affected side, and at least one ipsilateral fluctuating aural symptom (tinnitus or aural fullness) temporally associated with the vestibular episodes. The phenotype encompasses both idiopathic endolymphatic hydrops and secondary forms in which hydrops arises from an identifiable underlying etiology, provided the full clinical triad is present. Explicitly excluded are vestibular migraine, in which episodic vertigo is attributable to a migrainous mechanism and does not meet the sensorineural audiologic profile, and superior semicircular canal dehiscence, in which sound- or pressure-induced vestibular symptoms and low-frequency hearing changes arise from a structural bony defect of the temporal bone rather than endolymphatic pathology.
clinical_rationale: Meniere's disease is a chronic condition characterized by spontaneous vestibular episodes with associated auditory symptoms attributable to endolymphatic hydrops. While idiopathic and secondary forms are included in its phenotypic spectrum, drug-induced etiologies have been reported via mechanisms such as ototoxicity or vascular effects. Potential offenders include aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, and other agents with inner ear toxicity, creating plausibility for pharmacovigilance. This disease is episodic and relapsing, though structural changes or persistent hearing loss may stabilize. Diagnosis relies heavily on clinician-documented symptom clusters and audiologic testing, making observational coding challenging due to sparse symptom representation and audiologic results often captured outside standard data domains. Its predominantly outpatient diagnosis pattern reflects the non-emergent nature of typical episodes and their gradual resolution.

source_definition: Acute mesenteric ischemia is a sudden, life-threatening reduction in blood flow to the small intestine and proximal colon within the superior mesenteric artery territory, arising from a primary vascular event, that produces a spectrum of intestinal injury ranging from reversible mucosal ischemia to transmural bowel infarction and necrosis. The condition encompasses all spontaneously occurring primary vascular mechanisms of mesenteric insufficiency, including arterial occlusion from embolism or in situ thrombosis at sites of atherosclerotic disease, non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia due to low-flow states or vasospasm in the absence of mechanical arterial obstruction, and mesenteric venous thrombosis causing venous outflow obstruction and secondary arterial hypoperfusion. The phenotype explicitly excludes chronic mesenteric ischemia (intestinal angina), isolated colonic ischemia arising within the inferior mesenteric artery territory, iatrogenic or post-procedural mesenteric ischemia occurring as a direct complication of surgical or interventional procedures, and secondary intestinal ischemia resulting from mechanical obstruction such as strangulated hernias, volvulus, or intussusception.
clinical_rationale: Acute mesenteric ischemia is a life-threatening vascular condition with established drug-attributable mechanisms such as anticoagulant-induced bleeding precipitating low-flow states or thrombotic events from newer anticoagulants or platelet inhibitors. Vasospasm contributing to non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia has been described with vasopressors and ergot derivatives, making the condition attributable to pharmacologic exposures in certain scenarios. The cohort logic is transient and recurrent as different vascular events in distinct settings result in new episodes. The definition applies to primary vascular causes within the superior mesenteric artery territory, excluding mechanical obstructions, chronic ischemia, and secondary ischemia. Diagnosis is overwhelmingly acute care-based, as the presentation is severe and emergent, typified by abdominal pain and hemodynamic consequences. Accurate identification requires imaging or procedural confirmation, and patients generally require active intervention within 30 days, including revascularization or surgical resection.

source_definition: Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) is a chronic liver condition defined by hepatic steatosis â€” the pathological accumulation of fat within at least 5% of hepatocytes â€” arising in the context of underlying cardiometabolic dysfunction. The diagnosis requires the presence of at least one recognized cardiometabolic risk factor, including overweight or obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus or prediabetes, arterial hypertension, or dyslipidemia (elevated triglycerides and/or reduced HDL cholesterol). The phenotype encompasses the complete spectrum of metabolic steatotic liver disease: from uncomplicated hepatic steatosis, through metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) â€” characterized by hepatocellular injury, lobular inflammation, and hepatocellular ballooning â€” to progressive hepatic fibrosis and end-stage metabolic cirrhosis. The condition is etiologically distinguished from alcohol-associated liver disease by the restriction of alcohol use to no more than two standard drinks per day in men or one standard drink per day in women; individuals exceeding these thresholds are classified separately as MetALD or ALD and are excluded from this phenotype. Additionally excluded are all secondary and competing causes of hepatic steatosis, including drug-induced hepatic steatosis (e.g., from amiodarone, methotrexate, or tamoxifen), inherited metabolic disorders with direct hepatic lipid deposition (e.g., Wilson's disease, lipodystrophy, abetalipoproteinemia), prolonged parenteral nutrition-associated steatosis, and hepatic steatosis attributable to a concurrent primary liver disease such as viral hepatitis or autoimmune hepatitis.
clinical_rationale: MASLD is an umbrella term for a spectrum of chronic liver disease primarily arising from cardiometabolic dysfunction, including simple hepatic steatosis, steatohepatitis, progressive fibrosis, and metabolic cirrhosis. While MASLD excludes drug-induced hepatic steatosis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a subset of MASLD, may be relevant for pharmacovigilance as underlying hepatic vulnerability could increase susceptibility to drug toxicity or amplify disease progression under certain drug exposures. MASLD itself, due to exclusion of drug-induced causes and focus on metabolic-origin disease, is less suitable as a primary pharmacovigilance endpoint. The course is persistent and includes progressive stages, but these stages may manifest episodically in terms of complications or exacerbations. Diagnosis is expected primarily in outpatient settings due to the chronic and cardiometabolic risk factor-driven nature of the disease, with hospital encounters occurring for advanced complications like metabolic cirrhosis. Structured coding of symptoms like hepatic steatosis is inconsistent, but diagnostic criteria strongly rely on imaging, laboratory tests, and biometric profiling.

source_definition: Metabolic syndrome is a clinical state defined by the co-occurrence of three or more of the following five cardiometabolic abnormalities: central (abdominal) obesity, elevated fasting triglycerides, reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, elevated resting blood pressure, and elevated fasting plasma glucose. No single component is obligatory; any combination of three or more constitutes the syndrome. Pharmacologically managed components are counted as meeting their respective criterion regardless of whether current measured values fall within normal ranges, reflecting the underlying pathophysiological burden rather than treatment effect. The phenotype is inclusive of all etiological origins â€” whether arising as a primary clustering of cardiometabolic risk factors, as a consequence of an identifiable underlying condition such as an endocrine disorder or polycystic ovary syndrome, or as a secondary effect of medication exposure â€” provided the component thresholds are met. Isolated individual metabolic abnormalities that do not collectively satisfy the three-of-five threshold are excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Metabolic syndrome is a well-defined clustering of cardiometabolic components, which can arise spontaneously, due to underlying conditions (e.g., polycystic ovary syndrome, Cushing's syndrome), or as a consequence of medication exposures (e.g., corticosteroids, atypical antipsychotics). Its relevance as a pharmacovigilance outcome is conditional on recognizing it specifically as an acquired/metabolic state rather than congenital or primary genetic dyslipidemias or endocrinopathies. Its clinical course is persistent and requires ongoing management. Incident diagnoses usually occur in outpatient settings, although components may first present emergently (e.g., diabetes-related hyperglycemia or hypertensive crisis). Its diagnosis explicitly incorporates threshold-based clinical and/or laboratory measurements; symptoms may arise from its individual components, but these are not specific to the syndrome and unlikely to be discretely recorded as 'metabolic syndrome.' Management typically includes lifestyle modification and pharmacologic treatment of underlying components such as dyslipidemia, diabetes, or hypertension, and long-term follow-up is expected for risk-reduction and conditions stemming from the syndrome.

source_definition: Metastatic secondary malignancy is a pathological state in which malignant cells, originating from a primary neoplasm of any tissue type â€” including those of unknown primary origin â€” have disseminated via hematogenous or lymphatic routes and established viable tumor deposits at anatomically non-contiguous, distant organ sites. The condition is defined by the biological process of systemic tumor dissemination, encompassing invasion, intravasation, survival in circulation, extravasation, and colonization of distant tissues, and is restricted to distant metastatic spread equivalent to M1 staging. It explicitly excludes locoregional lymph node involvement, direct contiguous tumor extension into adjacent structures, independently arising second primary cancers, and treatment-induced malignancies. Cases in which the primary tumor site remains unidentified (cancer of unknown primary) are included, provided there is confirmation of the metastatic nature of the lesion.
clinical_rationale: Metastatic secondary malignancy is a biologically distinct condition signifying the systemic dissemination of malignant cells to non-contiguous, distant organ sites. Its exclusion of locoregional spread and independent second primaries distinguishes it from other neoplastic states. Drugs, particularly certain chemotherapeutic agents, have been implicated in altering tumor biology to facilitate metastasis, and immunosuppressive agents may increase metastatic risk. However, metastasis is predominantly a natural consequence of cancer biology, and while drugs can alter this trajectory, they are not the proximal origin. Treatment or supportive interventions, particularly in palliative care settings, focus primarily on managing complications or retarding metastatic progression. Most diagnoses are made in acute care or specialist settings, given the advanced disease state at presentation, though care transitions to outpatient for continued management. Codes for metastasis may persist throughout a patient's life course post-diagnosis, classifying it as a persistent condition.

source_definition: Microalbuminuria is a laboratory-confirmed state characterized by a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30 to 300 mg/g on a spot urine specimen, or a urinary albumin excretion rate of 30 to 300 mg per 24 hours, measured by a validated quantitative assay. This range demarcates a level of urinary albumin excretion above the upper limit of normal (less than 30 mg/g or less than 30 mg/day, defining normoalbuminuria) and below the threshold for macroalbuminuria or overt clinical proteinuria (greater than 300 mg/g or greater than 300 mg/day). The definition is agnostic to the underlying etiology, mechanism of albumin loss, and duration of the finding; any single confirmed measurement within this quantitative range constitutes the phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Microalbuminuria is a laboratory-defined state reflective of early kidney damage and increased cardiovascular risk. It can result from various causes, both drug-induced (e.g., NSAIDs, antiretroviral therapy, certain chemotherapies) and non-drug-related (e.g., diabetes, hypertension, glomerular diseases). While drug etiologies are plausible, particularly through mechanisms involving podocyte injury or altered hemodynamics, the definition encompasses both transient and chronic states and does not specify etiology. This requires narrowing the use case when applying it as a pharmacovigilance outcome. Diagnosed solely through quantitative urine studies, its detection mandates laboratory testing and is often incidentally discovered during outpatient visits or routine monitoring in at-risk populations.

source_definition: Migraine is a primary neurological disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate-to-severe headache, typically unilateral and pulsating in quality, and commonly accompanied by nausea, vomiting, phonophobia, and photophobia. The underlying pathophysiology involves cortical spreading depression, trigeminovascular activation, and neurogenic inflammation of the meningeal vasculature. This phenotype encompasses all recognized clinical subtypes, including migraine without aura, migraine with aura (encompassing visual, sensory, aphasic, motor, retinal, or brainstem aura), chronic migraine, hemiplegic migraine, and vestibular migraine, regardless of attack frequency or headache day burden. The definition is grounded in the positive clinical and pathophysiological features of the migraine disorder itself; no conditions are explicitly excluded, and differentiation from other headache types is achieved through the inherent specificity of the migraine diagnosis.
clinical_rationale: Migraine is a neurological disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate-to-severe headaches that often include systemic features such as nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. Drug attribution is documented for certain medications that can exacerbate or precipitate migraines, including overuse of analgesics (medication-overuse headache) and headache onset following exposure to nitrates or other vasodilators. Despite its chronic nature in some patients, migraine episodes typically resolve between attacks, making the clinical course transient recurrent. This phenotype encompasses all subtypes without exclusions, and differentiation from other headache disorders relies on the positive features of migraine rather than exclusions. Most cases initially present in outpatient settings unless associated with acute severe complications, but subtypes such as hemiplegic migraine may occasionally lead to acute care presentations. Pathophysiological mechanisms, including cortical spreading depression and trigeminovascular activation, support a plausible biological relationship to drug exposure.

source_definition: Mild cognitive impairment is a clinical state characterized by objective decline in one or more cognitive domains â€” including memory, executive function, language, or visuospatial ability â€” that is measurably greater than expected for an individual's age and educational background, yet does not impair the performance of activities of daily living. The condition encompasses all recognized subtypes, including amnestic and non-amnestic presentations, whether involving a single cognitive domain or multiple domains concurrently. Mild cognitive impairment is etiologically neutral and may reflect neurodegenerative, cerebrovascular, mixed, or undetermined pathophysiology. The diagnosis requires that the cognitive decline represent a persistent pattern of change, explicitly excluding acute or transient cognitive states such as delirium, in which impairment is precipitant-driven, fluctuating, and reversible. The upper conceptual boundary with dementia is defined by the strict preservation of functional independence: any cognitive-driven loss of the ability to independently perform instrumental activities of daily living reclassifies the state as dementia rather than mild cognitive impairment.
clinical_rationale: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) explicitly excludes transient states like delirium and requires objective cognitive decline without functional dependence, making it persistent by definition. It is considered a precursor to dementia, which may be neurodegenerative, cerebrovascular, or mixed in etiology. While specific drugs (e.g., anticholinergics, benzodiazepines) are known to impact cognition and can potentially contribute to MCI presentations via chronic use, the etiological pathways of MCI are diverse and often multifactorial. The condition is defined by persistent change, not by episodic or transient presentations, supporting the stable nature of its clinical course. Initial diagnosis mostly takes place in outpatient settings, given the absence of acute symptoms or immediate need for intervention. There is no single diagnostic test, but identification usually involves neuropsychological or cognitive assessment combined with clinical evaluation. Further management and surveillance are necessary, given the potential progression to dementia.

source_definition: Motion sickness is a self-limiting physiological syndrome occurring in individuals with a structurally and functionally normal vestibular system, precipitated by exposure to real physical motion â€” including vehicular, maritime, aerial, or other environmental movement involving actual acceleration or displacement. It arises from conflict among discordant sensory inputs from the vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive systems, producing a characteristic symptom complex that may include nausea, vomiting, pallor, diaphoresis, malaise, and dizziness, ranging in severity from mild and transient to severe and incapacitating, and resolving upon cessation of the provocative motion stimulus. The phenotype explicitly excludes vestibular symptoms and nausea arising from intrinsic pathology of the peripheral or central vestibular apparatus (e.g., benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, Meniere's disease, labyrinthitis, or vestibular neuritis), nausea and vomiting attributable to other primary medical conditions that coincidentally occur during motion, and any symptom states induced solely by visual or simulated motion in the absence of real physical movement.
clinical_rationale: Motion sickness arises from a sensory conflict in individuals with normal vestibular function, triggered by physical motion involving acceleration or displacement. It resolves upon cessation of the motion stimulus and does not involve intrinsic vestibular pathology. Motion sickness has no documented causality from drug exposure, though it may intersect with pharmacovigilance studies as a potential confounder in cases where drugs exacerbate nausea or dizziness under motion. Symptoms are well-documented as nausea, vomiting, pallor, malaise, and dizziness, but these are transient and resolve when the provoking stimulus ends. Ambulatory care is its most common setting; diagnoses outside outpatient care primarily occur in extreme cases requiring intervention for severe incapacitation, though these are rare. Diagnostic specificity can be challenging as symptoms overlap broadly with other causes of nausea and dizziness that must be excluded.

source_definition: A motor vehicle accident is an acute traumatic event in which an individual is involved in a collision with or within a motorized road-use vehicle. The concept encompasses all persons directly implicated in such an event, including occupants (drivers and passengers) of any motorized vehicle, as well as pedestrians and cyclists who are struck by a motorized vehicle. The phenotype is defined by the mechanical collision event itself and does not require a minimum injury severity threshold or documented physical harm for inclusion. Both unintentional collisions arising from traffic circumstances and intentional vehicle-involved events (e.g., vehicular assault) are included within this definition.
clinical_rationale: Motor vehicle accidents are external traumatic events unrelated to drug exposure. Although specific drug classes (e.g., sedatives, muscle relaxants, or substances of abuse) may contribute to reduced driver function and increase collision risk, the outcome itself is mechanistically defined by the collision and is not attributable to drug causality. The scope of the definition, which includes unintentional and intentional collisions as well as those without physical harm, further underscores that the mechanical event rather than a clinical condition is being described. As such, this concept is unsuitable as a drug safety outcome under OMOP CDM pharmacovigilance frameworks.

source_definition: Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia characterized by the clonal proliferation of neoplastic plasma cells within the bone marrow, producing active, symptomatic disease. The condition is defined by the presence of end-organ damage attributable to the underlying plasma cell clone â€” specifically hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, or osteolytic bone lesions (CRAB criteria) â€” or by myeloma-defining biomarkers indicating very high tumor burden, including clonal bone marrow plasma cell infiltration of 60% or greater, a serum involved-to-uninvolved free light chain ratio of 100 or greater, or more than one focal lesion on MRI. The definition encompasses all immunoglobulin subtypes (IgG, IgA, IgD, IgE, light chain only, and non-secretory variants) and all disease stages without restriction. Explicitly excluded are the precursor state of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), smoldering (asymptomatic) multiple myeloma, solitary plasmacytoma of bone or extramedullary sites, and plasma cell leukemia, each of which represents a distinct clinical and biological entity with different natural histories and management paradigms.
clinical_rationale: Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia implicated in drug-related outcomes due to potential acceleration or unmasking by immunomodulatory agents, chemotherapeutics, and chronic immunosuppression. However, it is predominantly a non-drug-attributable malignancy with multifactorial risk factors, including genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures. The condition is best classified as persistent, as the malignant plasma cell clone, once established, cannot be eradicated with current therapies. Diagnosis typically occurs in outpatient or oncology specialty settings, often after identifying symptoms or signs of end-organ damage or through work-up for suggestive findings such as renal impairment, anemia, or hypercalcemia. Histological and biomarker-based confirmation is routine.

source_definition: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic, primary, idiopathic, immune-mediated demyelinating and neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system, characterized by inflammation, demyelination, axonal injury, and gliosis occurring at multiple anatomical sites within the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves across time.
