The diagnosis requires fulfillment of McDonald Criteria, demonstrating dissemination of CNS lesions in both space and time through clinical presentation, neuroimaging, or cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the absence of a better alternative explanation. The phenotype encompasses all recognized disease courses, including relapsing-remitting, primary progressive, secondary progressive, and progressive-relapsing MS, without restriction by disability level or disease duration. Explicitly excluded are neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and MOG-IgG-associated disease (distinct antibody-mediated astrocytopathies), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (a typically monophasic post-infectious or post-immunization demyelinating process), and all forms of secondary CNS demyelination attributable to a defined systemic or infectious etiology such as vitamin B12 deficiency, CNS vasculitis, neurosarcoidosis, or infectious encephalomyelitis.
clinical_rationale: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, immune-mediated disease of the central nervous system with known relapsing and progressive forms of clinical manifestation. While MS itself is not directly caused by drug exposure, certain drugs (e.g., natalizumab, fingolimod) may influence its course. MS can be considered a pharmacovigilance outcome in cases where disease-modifying therapy leads to adverse events such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy or rebound relapses after discontinuation of specific drugs. However, MS as defined in this phenotype is idiopathic and primary. Diagnostic coding requires fulfillment of McDonald Criteria, typically integrating imaging and cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Since the disease encompasses relapsing-remitting and progressive forms, its clinical course is best characterized as persistent relapsing. Most diagnoses occur in outpatient neurology settings, though acute care may be involved in severe presentations or initial diagnostic workups.

source_definition: Muscle spasm is an involuntary, painful contraction of skeletal (striated) muscle that may occur as an acute, self-limiting episode or as a chronic or recurrent condition. The contraction arises from aberrant peripheral neuromuscular excitation or local muscle pathophysiology â€” including electrolyte disturbance, ischemia, overuse, or trauma â€” rather than from central or upper motor neuron-mediated dysregulation of muscle tone. All presentations are characterized by sudden, forceful muscle shortening accompanied by pain and, in some cases, visible or palpable hardening of the affected muscle. This phenotype explicitly excludes smooth muscle spasm (e.g., bronchospasm, intestinal colic, ureteral spasm), as well as neurologically-driven sustained tone disorders such as spasticity, lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity, and dystonia, which represent fundamentally distinct pathophysiological states.
clinical_rationale: Muscle spasm is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome under certain circumstances, as drugs can directly or indirectly contribute to the aberrant neuromuscular excitation or muscle pathophysiology described in the definition. For example, medications such as diuretics, which can induce electrolyte disturbances, or statins, which may cause muscle pathology, are implicated in inducing muscle spasms. The definition provided explicitly excludes smooth muscle spasm and neurologically-driven tone disorders, narrowing the phenotype to acute or chronic skeletal muscle spasm due to peripheral neuromuscular or local muscle causes. Acute episodes and recurrent presentations are common, and follow-up care is rarely expected. Diagnosis is often clinical, based on patient history and physical examination, with tests occasionally ordered to identify underlying causes. This outcome spans outpatient and acute care settings depending on severity or underlying cause.

source_definition: Muscle weakness is a clinical phenotype characterized by a reduction in the force-generating capacity of skeletal muscle, manifesting as patient-reported difficulty or inability to perform motor tasks, clinically observed limitation in movement or functional activity, or both. The phenotype spans the full severity continuum, from mild impairment of strenuous activities to profound paresis or paralysis. It is etiology-agnostic, encompassing weakness attributable to primary neuromuscular disorders â€” including myopathies, peripheral neuropathies, and motor neuron diseases â€” as well as weakness arising secondarily from systemic, metabolic, endocrine, or other non-neuromuscular conditions. Explicitly excluded are fatigue and asthenia, defined as a generalized sense of tiredness or reduced endurance without a true decrement in muscle force generation, and pain-limited effort, in which apparent motor limitation reflects voluntary inhibition of contraction due to pain rather than genuine neuromuscular impairment.
clinical_rationale: Muscle weakness, defined clinically as reduced force-generating capacity of skeletal muscles, has a broad etiological spectrum, including primary neuromuscular disorders and systemic conditions. Drug-induced muscle weakness is plausible through mechanisms such as myotoxicity (e.g., glucocorticoids, statins), neurotoxicity (e.g., vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy), metabolic disturbance (e.g., hyperkalemia or hypokalemia from RAAS modulators), or muscle deconditioning during prolonged drug-induced immobility (e.g., sedatives). The description excludes fatigue, asthenia, and pain-limited effort, focusing on reduction in actual muscle strength. As a symptom rather than a discrete disease entity, muscle weakness is transient and can recur with new insults but often lacks discrete recorded symptoms for specific attribution. Diagnosis tends to occur predominantly in outpatient settings, as it often reflects subacute or chronic conditions rather than emergency presentations. While diagnostic tests such as electromyography or serum creatine kinase may be ordered to identify the etiology, empirical diagnosis based on clinical features is common.

source_definition: Myalgia is a clinical state characterized by pain, aching, or discomfort perceived in or attributed to skeletal muscle tissue, of any severity and duration, arising from pathological or pharmacological causes. The phenotype encompasses muscle pain secondary to systemic disease, medication or toxic exposure, inflammatory, infectious, or metabolic processes, as well as idiopathic presentations. Cases in which the precise anatomical origin of pain â€” whether myogenic, neuropathic, or articular â€” is clinically ambiguous remain within scope. Explicitly excluded is pain that is purely physiological in origin, specifically delayed-onset muscle soreness following exercise or discomfort clearly and solely attributable to physical overexertion in the absence of any underlying pathological process.
clinical_rationale: Myalgia is a broad phenotype encompassing pathophysiological or pharmacological causes of muscle pain. While systemic disease (e.g., viral infections, autoimmune disorders), medications (e.g., statins, colchicine), and toxic exposures (e.g., alcohol, cocaine) are well-established contributors, other causes like trauma or referred pain may confound its attribution to drugs. Medication-induced myopathies and muscle dysfunction are particularly relevant in pharmacovigilance due to their frequency and severity (e.g., statin-induced myopathy). The description excludes physiological causes like delayed-onset muscle soreness, refining the focus to pathologic processes. Myalgia is transient and recurrent as diagnoses are episodic and shed upon resolution. Initial diagnoses are common in outpatient settings, though severe cases (e.g., rhabdomyolysis suspicion) may require acute care entry. Structured symptom data is often available (e.g., pain complaints), and laboratory tests (e.g., CK levels for suspected drug-induced myopathy) may contribute to diagnosis. Treatment is frequently directed within 30 days, especially for drug withdrawal or symptomatic relief, but extended follow-up for specific triggers like statins may occur.

source_definition: Myasthenia gravis is a chronic autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission characterized by pathogenic autoantibodies â€” most commonly directed against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChR), or less commonly against muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) or lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4) â€” that impair signal transmission at the neuromuscular junction, producing fatigable skeletal muscle weakness that worsens with sustained or repeated activity and partially recovers with rest. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical spectrum, from isolated ocular involvement (ptosis and/or diplopia) through generalized limb and bulbar weakness to acute respiratory failure (myasthenic crisis). Seronegative MG â€” lacking detectable autoantibodies by current assays but sharing the same clinical and physiological characteristics â€” is included, as is MG arising in the context of thymoma or triggered by exogenous immunological stimuli such as checkpoint inhibitor therapy, since the autoimmune postsynaptic NMJ pathophysiology remains the defining feature irrespective of precipitant. Explicitly excluded are presynaptic NMJ disorders with mechanistically distinct etiologies, including Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (anti-VGCC antibody-mediated, typically paraneoplastic) and botulism (toxin-mediated presynaptic acetylcholine release blockade); congenital myasthenic syndromes arising from genetic, non-autoimmune NMJ defects; and motor neuron diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which may produce overlapping bulbar and limb weakness through an entirely different pathophysiological mechanism.
clinical_rationale: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission, and its pathogenesis involves autoantibodies targeting postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, muscle-specific kinase, or LRP4, producing fatigable skeletal muscle weakness. MG can be associated with drug-induced autoimmunity, particularly from immune checkpoint inhibitors, making it a valid pharmacovigilance outcome under this mechanism. Its clinical course is persistent with potential relapsing episodes, as even well-managed patients retain the label of MG and can experience episodes of worsening weakness. Diagnoses span outpatient settings for milder forms (ocular MG) to acute care for generalized weakness or myasthenic crisis. Distinction is required from mechanistically distinct disorders like Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome and botulism. Diagnostic workup often includes antibody testing, electrodiagnostic studies, and chest imaging for possible thymoma.

source_definition: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder characterized by dysplastic maturation of one or more myeloid cell lines in the bone marrow, resulting in ineffective hematopoiesis and peripheral blood cytopenias affecting erythroid, myeloid, and/or megakaryocytic lineages. The condition encompasses the full clinical spectrum from low-risk, indolent disease to high-risk disease with excess blasts (up to 19% of marrow nucleated cells), and includes both de novo cases and those arising as a consequence of prior cytotoxic therapy or radiation exposure (therapy-related MDS). The phenotype is defined by the presence of clonal dysplasia as the underlying biological mechanism and explicitly excludes: acute myeloid leukemia, defined by a marrow blast burden of â‰¥20%; aplastic anemia, which represents immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic progenitors without clonal dysplasia; and reactive or nutritional cytopenias (e.g., vitamin B12 or folate deficiency) that may produce morphological pseudo-dysplasia in the absence of a clonal disorder.
clinical_rationale: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) has a documented association with drug exposure, particularly therapy-related MDS that arises after cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiation therapy for prior malignancies. This mechanism involves DNA damage and mutagenesis in hematopoietic stem cells. The disease is characterized by clonal hematopoiesis, ineffective bone marrow function, and peripheral cytopenias affecting various myeloid lineages; its disease definition excludes similar presentations caused by non-clonal mechanisms like nutritional deficiencies or immune-mediated destruction. Diagnosing MDS relies on laboratory findings, including marrow dysplasia, cytogenetics, and flow cytometry, nearly always requiring structured diagnostic procedures. It is typically managed by hematologists in an outpatient setting, though progression or complications such as neutropenic fever or anemia may require acute care. MDS is persistent and progressive, though risk stratification varies by disease subtype; it is not transient and often progresses to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) over time.

source_definition: Myocardial ischemia is a pathophysiological state in which the myocardium is subjected to insufficient oxygen delivery relative to its metabolic demands, producing cellular hypoxia that may be transient and reversible or sustained and progressing to irreversible myocardial necrosis. The phenotype encompasses both acute presentations â€” characterized by sudden coronary perfusion impairment due to plaque rupture, thrombosis, or vasospasm â€” and chronic, stable states arising from fixed obstructive coronary artery disease or persistent supply-demand mismatch. Both primary supply-side mechanisms (reduced coronary blood flow) and demand-side mechanisms (systemic conditions increasing myocardial oxygen requirements beyond a limited supply, such as severe anemia, tachyarrhythmia, or hemodynamic compromise) are included. Clinical qualification requires the presence of either ischemic symptoms (chest pain, dyspnea, or anginal equivalents) or objective evidence of ischemia (electrocardiographic changes, cardiac biomarker elevation, abnormal stress testing, or imaging-demonstrated perfusion deficit); both need not be present simultaneously. Myocardial infarction is subsumed within this phenotype as its most severe expression. Explicitly excluded are non-ischemic causes of myocardial injury: myocarditis (immune-mediated or infectious myocardial inflammation), Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy (catecholamine-mediated ventricular dysfunction without obstructive coronary pathology), and traumatic myocardial contusion, as these conditions do not arise from an oxygen supply-demand imbalance at the coronary level.
clinical_rationale: Myocardial ischemia is a well-documented pharmacovigilance outcome, as certain medications can impair oxygen supply-demand balance or induce coronary spasm. For example, sympathomimetics and vasoconstrictive agents can provoke ischemia via coronary vasospasm, while drugs like beta-blockers or systemic vasodilators can precipitate or worsen ischemia in specific settings of demand or supply imbalance. Further, anemia-inducing agents or drug-induced conditions like tachyarrhythmias affect myocardial oxygen demands, leading to ischemia. Acute events (e.g., those involving plaque rupture or thrombosis) are transient and distinct from chronic stable ischemia. Chronic ischemia due to supply-demand mismatches typically reflects persistent underlying ischemic heart disease driven by anatomical or physiological imbalances. Given these differing etiologies, the definition encompasses both transient recurrent episodes for acute presentations and persistent stable disease for chronic ischemia. Diagnosis often requires objective testing or recognizable symptoms, reinforcing reliance on both diagnostic codes and key bridging variables like cardiac biomarkers, ECG findings, or imaging for optimized case classification.

source_definition: Myocarditis is an inflammatory condition of the myocardium, characterized at the time of its initial clinical onset by immune-mediated or infectious injury to cardiac muscle cells, typically manifesting with some combination of chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmia, electrocardiographic abnormalities, elevated cardiac biomarkers reflecting myocyte necrosis, and functional cardiac impairment detectable by imaging. The phenotype encompasses the full severity spectrum at presentation, from mild acute myocarditis to hemodynamically compromising fulminant disease, as well as chronic or persistent myocardial inflammation recognized at first clinical identification. Concurrent pericardial inflammation is not exclusionary when myocardial involvement is present. The etiology may be viral, autoimmune, drug- or toxin-mediated, vaccine-associated, idiopathic, or attributable to a systemic inflammatory disease. Explicitly excluded are cases of myocardial injury caused solely by direct mechanical trauma â€” such as blunt cardiac contusion or operative injury â€” in which tissue damage occurs without a primary inflammatory or immune-mediated mechanism.
clinical_rationale: Myocarditis is a suitable pharmacovigilance outcome, as drug- and vaccine-associated myocarditis are established phenomena with documented mechanisms. Immunomodulatory drugs, chemotherapeutics, antibiotics, and vaccines (notably mRNA COVID-19 vaccines) can trigger immune-mediated or toxic myocardial injury. Viral myocarditis remains predominant overall, but the phenotype's scope — excluding purely traumatic causes and focusing on inflammatory mechanisms — aligns with pharmacovigilance interests. Diagnosing myocarditis typically combines clinical presentation, elevated cardiac biomarkers, ECG changes, and cardiac imaging, with endomyocardial biopsy reserved for severe or diagnostic-uncertain cases. Recognition may occur across all care settings depending on severity, though acute care is typically involved for severe cases. Drug etiology may be challenging to distinguish but is biologically plausible in the stated definition.

source_definition: Myoclonus is a pathologic neurological condition defined by the sudden, brief, shock-like involuntary contraction of one or more muscles (positive myoclonus), arising from aberrant neuronal discharge at any level of the neuraxis, including cortical, subcortical, brainstem, spinal, or peripheral generators. The condition encompasses both symptomatic forms â€” in which myoclonus is attributable to an identifiable underlying etiology such as metabolic disturbance, neurodegenerative disease, hypoxic-ischemic injury, medication exposure, or toxin â€” and idiopathic or essential forms in which no causative condition is identified but the myoclonus is recognized as pathologic by clinical assessment. A single clinically documented occurrence is sufficient for inclusion without a recurrence threshold. Explicitly excluded are: physiologic myoclonic phenomena such as hypnic jerks and hiccups; myoclonus occurring exclusively as an ictal manifestation of an epileptic seizure; and negative myoclonus (asterixis), which represents a brief lapse of sustained postural tone due to sudden inhibition of muscle activity rather than active muscular contraction.
clinical_rationale: Myoclonus is a result of abnormal neuronal discharges that cause involuntary muscle contractions. Symptomatic forms may result from drug etiologies, such as medication-induced myoclonus caused by SSRIs, opioids, or anesthetics. Metabolic disturbances, neurodegenerative diseases, and other secondary causes also contribute to its occurrence. Drug-induced cases are well-documented, making myoclonus a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome if the focus is restricted to acquired or symptomatic cases. The condition is clinically diverse, presenting as transient episodes or persistent states, depending on the cause. The definition explicitly includes all myoclonus recognized as pathological and excludes physiological or non-relevant forms (e.g., hypnic jerks, asterixis, ictal myoclonus). A diagnostic test may be necessary to identify secondary causes, while treatments may be warranted depending on the severity or underlying cause.

source_definition: Nail fungus (onychomycosis) is a fungal infection or clinically suspected fungal involvement of the nail unit â€” encompassing the nail plate, nail bed, nail matrix, and periungual tissue â€” of any anatomical location (fingernails and/or toenails), any causative organism (dermatophytes, non-dermatophyte molds, or yeasts such as Candida species), and any severity or clinical subtype, including distal lateral subungual, white superficial, proximal subungual, and total dystrophic forms. The condition is characterized by one or more of the following: nail plate discoloration, thickening, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, or structural nail deformity attributable to fungal pathology. Explicitly excluded are all non-infectious nail dystrophies regardless of diagnostic certainty, including psoriatic nail disease, traumatic onychodystrophy, lichen planus of the nail, nail-patella syndrome, and other structural or inflammatory disorders of the nail unit, even in cases where fungal co-involvement cannot be definitively ruled out.
clinical_rationale: Nail fungus, or onychomycosis, is a fungal infection with no documented drug-attributable causality, as its etiology is driven by fungal exposure, skin/nail microenvironment, and immune function rather than medication use. Drugs may play a minor permissive role in susceptibility through immune suppression (e.g., corticosteroids or immunosuppressants in immunocompromised patients), but the connection is indirect, and nail fungus is not generally recognized as a primary drug-induced outcome. The description clearly excludes non-infectious nail dystrophies and focuses solely on infectious fungal pathology, simplifying phenotyping by eliminating differential diagnoses and reducing false positives. Diagnostic confirmation often relies on clinical examination and fungal culture or direct microscopy, while symptoms like discoloration, onycholysis, or thickened nails may be visually apparent but inconsistently coded separately from the diagnosis itself.

source_definition: Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological disorder of hypothalamic sleep-wake regulation characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) as the cardinal feature. The phenotype encompasses Narcolepsy Type 1 (NT1), defined by EDS in conjunction with cataplexy and/or confirmed hypocretin-1 deficiency in cerebrospinal fluid, and Narcolepsy Type 2 (NT2), defined by EDS in the absence of cataplexy with normal or unmeasured CSF hypocretin levels. Cases may be identified through objective polysomnographic and multiple sleep latency testing meeting ICSD-3 criteria (mean sleep latency â‰¤8 minutes with â‰¥2 sleep-onset REM periods) or through a clinician-rendered diagnosis based on clinical presentation. The phenotype is restricted to primary (idiopathic) narcolepsy and explicitly excludes narcolepsy-like syndromes attributable to an identifiable secondary cause, including structural hypothalamic lesions, autoimmune encephalitides, demyelinating disease, or metabolic storage disorders. Disorders presenting with overlapping hypersomnolence but representing distinct clinical entitiesâ€”including idiopathic hypersomnia, Kleine-Levin syndrome, and hypersomnia secondary to medications or circadian disruptionâ€”are also excluded.
clinical_rationale: Narcolepsy is a chronic disorder of hypothalamic sleep-wake regulation, specifically idiopathic in the supplied definition and restricted to primary forms (Narcolepsy Type 1 and Type 2). Narcotic medications or other drugs are not established causes of primary narcolepsy, but medications may act as unmasking agents or aggravators of daytime sleepiness in susceptible individuals. Therefore, narcolepsy itself lacks a direct drug-attributable etiology, classifying it as non-pharmacovigilance-relevant. However, careful differentiation is required as sedating medications, especially in vulnerable populations, can induce symptomatic overlaps. Clinical identification is aided by polysomnographic or multiple sleep latency testing and/or specific clinical diagnostic criteria. The condition is chronic once established and requires long-term management.

source_definition: Nausea is a symptom defined as the subjective, consciously perceived sensation of an impending urge to vomit, arising from dysregulation of the complex afferent signaling network involving the gastrointestinal tract, the central nervous system (including the brainstem emetic center and the chemoreceptor trigger zone), and the autonomic nervous system. It is a non-specific symptom that may occur in isolation or in conjunction with vomiting, retching, or autonomic accompaniments such as diaphoresis, pallor, and hypersalivation. The phenotype encompasses all documented instances of this sensation regardless of severity, duration, frequency, or underlying etiology, including but not limited to gastrointestinal, neurological, metabolic, pharmacological, vestibular, and obstetric causes.
clinical_rationale: Nausea is a non-specific symptom that can result from a wide variety of underlying causes, including drugs. Drug-induced nausea is well documented and can occur via multiple mechanisms, such as direct effects on the gastrointestinal tract, activation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone, or vestibular dysregulation. Commonly implicated drugs include opioids, chemotherapeutic agents, and antibiotics. While nausea can occur in isolation, it often precedes vomiting or accompanies autonomic symptoms, making it highly likely to be recorded discretely in clinical data. The definition provided here is broad and includes all instances of nausea, regardless of etiology, severity, or setting; this warrants the conditional designation as a pharmacovigilance outcome, with a focus needed on drug-induced causes. The diagnosis is clinical and does not usually require confirmatory testing, but active treatment may be pursued depending on severity, and follow-up is rare for self-limited episodes unless the underlying cause remains unresolved.

source_definition: Neonatal jaundice is a clinical state defined by bilirubin-mediated yellow discoloration of the skin and sclerae arising from hyperbilirubinemia â€” whether unconjugated, conjugated, or mixed â€” occurring within the first 28 days of chronological life in term neonates, or within the equivalent physiologically adjusted neonatal period in preterm infants. The phenotype encompasses the full etiological spectrum, including physiological jaundice due to transitional immaturity of hepatic bilirubin conjugation, pathological jaundice from hemolytic conditions (such as ABO or Rh incompatibility or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency), breastfeeding- and breast milk-related jaundice, hepatocellular dysfunction, structural biliary anomalies (including biliary atresia and choledochal cysts), and jaundice occurring as a manifestation of systemic conditions such as neonatal sepsis, congenital infections, or inborn errors of metabolism. The underlying mechanism must be elevation of serum bilirubin; yellow skin discoloration attributable to non-bilirubin causes such as carotenemia, which characteristically spares the sclerae, is explicitly excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Neonatal jaundice spans a wide etiological spectrum with both physiological and pathological causes. Drug-induced neonatal jaundice is plausible, particularly in cases of maternal exposure to drugs causing hemolysis (e.g., sulfa drugs in G6PD-deficient neonates), drugs interfering with bilirubin conjugation (e.g., oxytocin), or hepatotoxic drugs. However, most cases are not drug-related, and physiological jaundice due to hepatic immaturity is most common. The phenotype description explicitly confines the condition to neonates within the first 28 days, aligning with standard neonatal period definitions. Diagnosis is made clinically, supported by serum bilirubin levels, and confirmation often requires laboratory testing to guide management and identify underlying etiologies. While acute care may be required for severe or pathological jaundice, routine cases are commonly diagnosed in outpatient settings.

source_definition: Neonatal thrombocytopenia is a hematologic condition characterized by a reduction in circulating platelet count below 150 Ã— 10â¹/L occurring in an infant during the birth hospitalization, irrespective of gestational age at delivery or chronological age at time of onset. The phenotype encompasses the full continuum of platelet reduction severity, from mild decreases just below the normal threshold to profound thrombocytopenia carrying substantial hemorrhagic risk. All underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are included â€” among them immune-mediated platelet destruction (alloimmune or autoimmune), consumptive processes driven by sepsis or systemic inflammatory states, hypoxic-ischemic injury, placental insufficiency, and congenital or genetic disorders of platelet production or function â€” as etiology is regarded as a separate clinical attribute rather than a defining criterion of the condition. The condition is considered resolved or no longer neonatal in character upon discharge from the birth hospitalization.
clinical_rationale: Neonatal thrombocytopenia is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome, as it has recognized drug-attributable etiologies including maternal drug exposures (e.g., antiplatelet agents, anticonvulsants, or medications affecting bone marrow function), neonatal drug toxicities, or drugs affecting maternal-fetal blood flow. The condition is inherently transient by definition, as its neonatal label is dropped with discharge from the birth hospitalization, though some infants with significant coagulopathy or severe underlying disorders may experience long-term sequelae. The condition is frequently diagnosed in the hospital given the routine monitoring of neonates in birth hospitalizations and typically requires laboratory confirmation. Platelet counts are monitored closely where abnormalities are detected, though mild cases may not require active intervention beyond surveillance. Severe cases, especially those involving hemorrhagic risk, often require urgent platelet transfusions or interventions targeting the underlying cause (e.g., treatment of maternal alloimmune thrombocytopenia or neonatal sepsis).

source_definition: Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome arising from glomerular filtration barrier dysfunction that results in pathological urinary protein loss, defined by the presence of massive proteinuria exceeding 3.5 grams per day in adults (or an equivalent protein-to-creatinine ratio) accompanied by hypoalbuminemia reflecting the systemic consequences of sustained urinary protein depletion. The syndrome may arise from intrinsic glomerular diseases â€” such as minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, or membranous nephropathy â€” or as a manifestation of systemic conditions that secondarily damage the glomerular barrier, including diabetic nephropathy, lupus nephritis, and amyloidosis; it is therefore defined at the syndrome level without requiring identification of a specific underlying etiology. Peripheral edema and hyperlipidemia or lipiduria, while recognized downstream consequences of hypoalbuminemia and altered lipid metabolism respectively, are not required diagnostic criteria. Pure nephritic syndrome â€” characterized by dominant inflammatory features including macroscopic hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, and azotemia with only mild-to-moderate proteinuria â€” is explicitly excluded; however, mixed nephrotic-nephritic presentations are included when the nephrotic component meets the quantitative proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia thresholds and is clinically dominant.
clinical_rationale: Nephrotic syndrome is a well-documented clinical syndrome arising from structural or functional damage to the glomerular filtration barrier. It can occur as a primary glomerular disease or as a secondary effect of systemic conditions. Drug-induced nephrotic syndrome is a recognized entity, with certain medications such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), penicillamine, gold, interferons, and pamidronate being established culprits. The clinical course is persistent-relapsing due to the chronic relapsing nature of the underlying glomerular diseases or persistent progression from systemic causes. Incidence is generally identified in outpatient or acute care settings, depending on whether associated complications warrant hospitalization. Proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia are requisite laboratory findings for diagnosis, and most cases require active treatment and long-term management to address the syndrome, prevent complications, and treat underlying causes. Some cases are associated with discrete recorded symptoms (e.g., edema), but these are not universal. Given its multifactorial origins, nephrotic syndrome is suitable as a pharmacovigilance outcome in cases of suspected drug-induced etiology.

source_definition: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening, pharmacologically precipitated neurological emergency characterized by the obligate presence of both hyperthermia and severe generalized muscle rigidity, accompanied by one or more supportive features including altered mental status (ranging from agitation to coma) and autonomic instability (such as diaphoresis, tachycardia, labile blood pressure, or urinary incontinence). The syndrome arises as an idiosyncratic response to any agent that reduces central dopaminergic tone, including dopamine receptor-blocking drugs (typical and atypical antipsychotics, antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine), dopamine-depleting agents (e.g., tetrabenazine), or abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic agonists in patients with Parkinson's disease or related disorders. The underlying pathophysiology reflects acute central dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal and hypothalamic pathways, producing the characteristic thermodyregulatory failure and extrapyramidal rigidity. This phenotype explicitly excludes serotonin syndrome, which is distinguished by serotonergic excess and presents with hyperreflexia, clonus, and a distinct drug exposure profile; malignant hyperthermia, a pharmacogenetic condition triggered by volatile anesthetic agents or succinylcholine via aberrant skeletal muscle calcium release; and lethal or malignant catatonia, a primary psychiatric emergency arising from the underlying psychiatric illness itself without a pharmacological precipitant.
clinical_rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening, drug-induced neurological emergency caused by central dopamine suppression, typically from dopamine receptor antagonists, dopaminergic depletion, or abrupt dopamine agonist withdrawal. Though rare, its etiology is pharmacologically well-established, making it a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. NMS is transient and resolves with specific intervention, including drug withdrawal and supportive care. While recurrence is possible with rechallenge, the implicated agents and clinical vigilance make distinct episodes identifiable. Incident diagnoses of NMS typically arise in acute care settings due to its emergent nature. Diagnostic sensitivity in observational data may rely on accurate coding rather than characteristic symptoms, as hyperthermia and rigidity are clinically evident but less reliably coded, and definitive diagnosis generally requires clinical judgment in conjunction with medication exposure history.

source_definition: Neutropenia is an acquired hematologic condition defined by a true, confirmed reduction in the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below 1,500 cells per microliter of circulating blood, irrespective of duration or severity grade. The phenotype encompasses all acquired mechanisms of neutrophil reduction, including drug- and chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression, immune-mediated neutrophil destruction, viral or infectious bone marrow suppression, and neutropenia arising as a secondary consequence of an underlying systemic disease such as autoimmune disorders, bone marrow failure syndromes, or nutritional deficiencies; in all such cases, the neutropenia itself is the phenomenon of interest. The condition is defined solely by the laboratory criterion of a documented ANC below threshold, without requiring the presence of clinical symptoms, active infection, or therapeutic intervention. Congenital and hereditary neutropenic syndromes â€” including Kostmann syndrome, cyclic neutropenia, and primary immunodeficiency-associated disorders â€” are explicitly excluded as distinct pathophysiological entities. Pseudoneutropenia, defined as a spuriously low ANC attributable to in vitro neutrophil margination or agglutination artifacts rather than a true reduction in circulating neutrophils, is also explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Neutropenia is a clinically relevant pharmacovigilance outcome due to its well-established association with drug-induced bone marrow suppression, particularly from chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, and antibiotics. It is a critical adverse event because it increases susceptibility to infections. The phenotype explicitly excludes congenital or hereditary syndromes and pseudoneutropenia, focusing on acquired neutropenia, the majority of which are potentially attributable to drugs, infections, or systemic diseases. Diagnosis relies on laboratory confirmation with an ANC below 1,500 cells per microliter. As neutropenia is defined as a condition of reduced neutrophils rather than its sequelae (e.g., febrile neutropenia), the definition captures the asymptomatic state as well as symptomatic cases. Its laboratory-defined nature means that diagnostic codes alone are likely to capture only the most clinically significant cases (e.g., severe or prolonged neutropenia, or episodes associated with complications like febrile neutropenia).

source_definition: Nicotine use is defined as the active, volitional, and current self-administration of nicotine through any recreational delivery route, including but not limited to combustible tobacco products (cigarettes, cigars, pipes), smokeless tobacco products (chewing tobacco, snuff, snus), and electronic nicotine delivery systems (e-cigarettes, vaping devices). The phenotype encompasses the full spectrum from habitual, non-dependent use to clinically established nicotine use disorder, characterized by compulsive use, tolerance, and withdrawal upon cessation. Nicotine replacement therapy (e.g., patches, gum, lozenges, inhalers) used exclusively in the context of a cessation attempt is excluded; however, concurrent use of NRT alongside ongoing recreational nicotine consumption is included, as this pattern reflects continued active use. Passive or involuntary nicotine exposure, such as inhalation of environmental tobacco smoke, is excluded, as the phenotype requires deliberate self-administration. Individuals who have ceased all nicotine use, regardless of prior duration or dependence severity, are excluded.
clinical_rationale: Nicotine use encompasses active self-administration through various routes, including tobacco smoking, smokeless tobacco, and electronic nicotine delivery systems. The phenotype explicitly includes habitual use and nicotine use disorder, but excludes passive exposure and former users who have discontinued. Nicotine use has pharmacovigilance relevance as it can significantly interact with drug metabolism, notably through CYP enzyme induction associated with smoking. It also contributes to conditions such as cardiovascular disease and malignancy, which may confound pharmacovigilance analyses. The clinical course is persistent in habitual or dependent users, given the lasting label under ongoing use. Diagnosis is predominantly clinical without mandatory testing, though survey-like assessments or self-reporting are common. Active nicotine use disproportionately affects ambulatory populations and a smaller fraction present to acute care in the context of associated complications (e.g., MI).

source_definition: Non-arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (NAION) is an acute ischemic injury to the anterior segment of the optic nerve, arising from interruption of perfusion through the short posterior ciliary arteries supplying the optic nerve head, in the absence of a vasculitic etiology such as giant cell arteritis. It presents as a sudden-onset, unilateral visual disturbance ranging across the full severity spectrum â€” from a mild, sectoral or altitudinal visual field defect to severe reduction in visual acuity â€” accompanied by optic disc edema during the acute phase. The phenotype encompasses both the spontaneous form, characterized by structural optic disc vulnerability (crowded disc, small cup-to-disc ratio) in the setting of chronic microvascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or obstructive sleep apnea, and cases precipitated by acute systemic hemodynamic compromise including perioperative hypotension or significant blood loss. Explicitly excluded are: arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy associated with giant cell arteritis; posterior ischemic optic neuropathy, which involves the retrobulbar optic nerve without optic disc edema at onset; and demyelinating optic neuritis, which involves immune-mediated inflammatory injury to the optic nerve rather than ischemic vascular occlusion.
clinical_rationale: NAION is an acute ischemic injury to the optic nerve, with a significant proportion of cases presenting spontaneously due to underlying disc anatomy and chronic microvascular risk factors like hypertension and diabetes. However, acute systemic hemodynamic insults, including hypotension or blood loss induced by medications (e.g., perioperative hypotension from anesthetics or excessive anticoagulation), are recognized precipitating factors. This drug-attributable causality supports its inclusion as a pharmacovigilance outcome. Diagnosis relies heavily on clinical presentation (sudden onset of visual disturbance and optic disc edema during acute phase), and exclusion of arteritic and other optic neuropathies is essential. Recurrence of NAION in the contralateral eye is possible but rare. The usual care setting is outpatient ophthalmology unless systemic complication drives simultaneous acute-care presentation.

source_definition: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) is a clonal malignancy of lymphoid tissue arising from neoplastic transformation of B-cells, T-cells, or NK-cells at varying stages of differentiation, presenting as a heterogeneous group of diseases that may involve lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow, or extranodal sites. The phenotype encompasses the full histologic spectrum, including both indolent subtypes (e.g., follicular lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma) and aggressive subtypes (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma), as well as entities at the leukemia-lymphoma interface â€” such as Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia â€” when the predominant clinical and pathologic presentation reflects lymphomatous rather than leukemic disease. Diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation through tissue biopsy demonstrating lymphoid neoplasm, inclusive of immunophenotypic characterization where performed. Hodgkin Lymphoma, defined by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells within a reactive inflammatory background, is explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) spans a biologically diverse group of lymphoid malignancies with clonal transformations of B-cells, T-cells, or NK-cells. Drug causality has been documented for certain therapies (e.g., alkylating agents and immunosuppressants) that increase risky clonal proliferation, as well as in secondary lymphomas after prior chemotherapy or immunosuppression. Epidemiologic criteria also support drug-attributable etiologies indirectly, via immunomodulation or delayed DNA repair. Diagnosis requires histopathologic evidence and typically biopsy, distinguishing NHL from Hodgkin's lymphoma excluded in this definition. The heterogeneity of clinical presentations means NHL cases can range from indolent outpatient recognition to diagnosis during hospitalization for advanced disease. In either case, diagnosis triggers long-term management, surveillance, or treatment sequelae, but the disease itself is persistent and relapsing due to the biology of neoplastic lymphoid proliferation.

source_definition: Non-infectious uveitis is an inflammatory condition of the uveal tract â€” encompassing the iris, ciliary body, choroid, and associated structures including the vitreous and retina â€” in which the inflammatory process is driven by immune-mediated, autoimmune, or idiopathic mechanisms rather than by a viable infectious pathogen (bacterial, viral, fungal, or parasitic). The phenotype includes all anatomical subtypes: anterior uveitis (iritis and iridocyclitis), intermediate uveitis (pars planitis and vitritis), posterior uveitis (choroiditis, chorioretinitis, and retinitis of immune origin), and panuveitis, regardless of whether the presentation is acute, recurrent, or chronic. Drug-induced uveal inflammation â€” where an iatrogenic immune response to a medication precipitates the inflammatory cascade â€” is included within this phenotype. Conditions that clinically mimic uveitis through neoplastic infiltration of the eye, including intraocular lymphoma, leukemic infiltration, and retinoblastoma (masquerade syndromes), are explicitly excluded, as these represent fundamentally distinct pathophysiological processes not rooted in immune-mediated uveal inflammation.
clinical_rationale: Non-infectious uveitis is a pharmacovigilance-relevant outcome because drug-induced uveitis is included in the phenotype, with documented etiologies linked to medications such as bisphosphonates, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and systemic biologic agents. The immune-mediated or idiopathic mechanisms underlying non-infectious uveitis align with established drug-attributable pathways, and the inclusion of drug-induced presentations ensures suitability for active safety surveillance. The description highlights anatomical subtypes and excludes mimics like masquerade syndromes. Uveitis can recur episodically or operate as a chronically managed condition with relapses, but it persists as a diagnostic label in recurrent forms, requiring treatment and surveillance in ophthalmology across a spectrum of severities from outpatients to acute care presentations for severe cases.

source_definition: Non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) is a primary malignant neoplasm arising from keratinocytes of the non-mucosal keratinized skin, encompassing two histologically distinct entities: basal cell carcinoma, originating from basal epithelial cells, and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, arising from suprabasal keratinocytes, both requiring histological confirmation of dermal invasion. The phenotype is restricted to de novo primary cutaneous tumors and explicitly excludes in-situ and precursor lesions (e.g., Bowen's disease, actinic keratosis), secondary cutaneous involvement from metastatic internal malignancies, and tumors arising at mucosal or transitional zone anatomical sites including the lip vermillion, perianal region, and anogenital skin. Melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, cutaneous lymphoma, and adnexal carcinomas are excluded on the basis of distinct cell of origin and pathophysiology.
clinical_rationale: Non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC) encompasses basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the keratinized skin, both of which are common and primarily linked to ultraviolet radiation exposure. Drugs such as voriconazole and immune checkpoint inhibitors have been associated with increased risk of NMSC, especially in immunocompromised patients, indicating plausible drug-induced etiologies. Diagnosis requires histological confirmation, and clinical management often involves surgical excision, topical therapies, or radiation for larger or metastatic lesions. The phenotype definition explicitly excludes in-situ lesions, precursor states, and mucosal or metastatic involvement, which narrows the scope to primary keratinocyte malignancies. Incident cases are typically detected in outpatient settings but may occasionally present in acute care for advanced complications or rare metastatic disease.

source_definition: A non-pathological fracture is a disruption in the structural continuity of bone occurring as a direct consequence of acute, high-energy mechanical trauma â€” specifically, a force of sufficient magnitude to fracture structurally intact bone in any individual. The defining criterion is the traumatic mechanism: the applied force must, by its nature and energy level, be objectively capable of fracturing normal bone, independent of the patient's systemic bone mineral density or disease status. Stress fractures and fatigue fractures arising from cumulative repetitive microtrauma are excluded, as they represent incremental mechanical failure rather than a single acute traumatic event. A fracture is further excluded when structural bone pathology â€” including malignant infiltration, osteomyelitis, metabolic bone disease, genetic bone disorders, or any lesion that directly compromises the mechanical integrity of the bone tissue â€” is present at or anatomically involves the fracture site, regardless of the energy of the precipitating trauma. Co-existing bone disease at sites anatomically remote from the fracture location does not alter the classification.
clinical_rationale: Non-pathological fractures are caused by acute, high-energy trauma to structurally normal bone, without the presence of predisposing pathological conditions affecting bone integrity at the fracture site. Such fractures are not commonly considered for pharmacovigilance surveillance because they are directly attributable to external mechanical forces rather than drug-related mechanisms. Drug-induced fractures are typically related to pathological states such as osteoporosis, which are specifically excluded by this definition. Therefore, as defined, these fractures do not represent drug-attributable outcomes. The classification explicitly excludes stress fractures, fatigue fractures, and fractures associated with bone pathology, narrowing the scope to acute trauma in structurally normal bone. These fractures are most often diagnosed in acute care settings such as emergency departments or trauma centers.

source_definition: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a primary malignant neoplasm arising from the epithelial cells of the lung parenchyma or bronchial airways, encompassing all histological subtypes that are distinguished from small cell lung cancer by their morphological and biological characteristics. Included subtypes are adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, sarcomatoid carcinoma, and large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC), the latter included in accordance with its high-grade aggressive behavior and treatment alignment with other NSCLC subtypes per contemporary classification. The phenotype encompasses disease at any stage of progression, from localized (Stage I) through locally advanced (Stage III) to distant metastatic disease (Stage IV). Explicitly excluded are small cell lung cancer, typical pulmonary carcinoid, and atypical pulmonary carcinoid, which represent distinct neuroendocrine entities with different pathophysiology, prognosis, and treatment. Also excluded are secondary malignant neoplasms of the lung â€” that is, metastatic deposits originating from a primary cancer at any other anatomical site â€” as these do not reflect the biology or natural history of primary lung malignancy.
clinical_rationale: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) can have drug-contributing etiologies, particularly from exposure to certain carcinogens in tobacco smoke or environmental toxins, as well as from targeted therapy or prior radiation therapy contributing to therapy-related secondary malignancies. Its inclusion as a pharmacovigilance outcome is supported under plausible drug-contributory mechanisms. NSCLC is a persistent condition but can exhibit distinct phases related to cancer progression or response to treatment, thus its clinical course is designated as persistent stable. NSCLC is typically diagnosed in symptomatic patients after advanced diagnostic imaging and biopsy, often in inpatient or acute care settings, though some cases may be detected during outpatient imaging for unrelated reasons. The phenotype name and clinical definition are consistent, with clear exclusions of carcinoid tumors and secondary malignancies, aligning with biological definitions.

source_definition: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is an acute ischemic event characterized by myocardial necrosis resulting from a spontaneous coronary artery event â€” specifically plaque rupture, plaque erosion, or intraluminal thrombosis (Type 1 mechanism) â€” in the absence of ST-segment elevation on the initial presenting electrocardiogram. The diagnosis requires a dynamic pattern of cardiac troponin elevation, defined as a rise and/or fall in serial measurements with at least one value exceeding the 99th percentile upper reference limit of a normal reference population, thereby distinguishing acute myocardial necrosis from chronic myocardial injury states. The clinical diagnosis does not require angiographic or imaging confirmation of a culprit coronary lesion. This phenotype explicitly excludes myocardial infarction attributable to supply-demand imbalance without a primary coronary plaque event (Type 2 MI), procedure-related myocardial injury (Types 4 and 5 MI), unstable angina (ischemic symptoms without biomarker elevation), ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and non-ischemic causes of troponin elevation such as myocarditis or sepsis-related myocardial injury.
clinical_rationale: NSTEMI is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome due to its etiologic connection to drug-induced events that can trigger or exacerbate acute coronary syndrome, such as plaque instability related to statin therapy, thrombosis induced by antiplatelet agents, or vasospasm attributed to drugs like cocaine or certain chemotherapeutics. The transient rise and fall of cardiac troponin levels with biomarker elevation defines the acute nature and episodic pattern of the condition. The focus on Type 1 MI excludes entities like Type 2 MI or non-ischemic troponin elevations, ensuring high specificity to coronary plaque-related events. Diagnosis is typically based on troponin dynamics combined with clinical symptoms and ECG findings, necessitating immediate acute care. Incident patients almost always present in emergency or inpatient settings, where multimodal management and treatment initiation occur promptly. The condition often leads to condition-specific follow-up within the first year, including secondary prevention and monitoring for recurrent episodes or progression to chronic coronary disease.

source_definition: Obesity is a chronic disease state characterized by an excess accumulation of body adipose tissue sufficient to impair health, defined by a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/mÂ² or greater in adults. The phenotype encompasses all severity grades, including Class I (BMI 30.0â€“34.9 kg/mÂ²), Class II (BMI 35.0â€“39.9 kg/mÂ²), and Class III obesity (BMI â‰¥ 40 kg/mÂ²), also referred to as severe or morbid obesity. No restriction is placed on underlying etiology; the phenotype includes obesity arising from any mechanism, including primary (essential) obesity driven by chronic energy imbalance and polygenic susceptibility, as well as secondary forms attributable to endocrine disorders (e.g., hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome), hypothalamic dysfunction, genetic or chromosomal syndromes (e.g., Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl syndrome), or medication-induced weight gain. The presence of obesity-related comorbidities or metabolic sequelae is not required for inclusion; the anthropometric threshold alone is sufficient to satisfy the phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Obesity is a chronic condition that can arise from primary mechanisms (energy imbalance and polygenic susceptibility) or secondary mechanisms, including medication-induced weight gain. Numerous drugs, such as corticosteroids, antipsychotics, antidepressants, and antiepileptic drugs, are known to contribute to obesity through mechanisms such as altered metabolism, increased appetite, or interference with fat oxidation. Obesity is a persistent condition once it develops, as it requires ongoing management and the label is typically retained even if weight loss occurs. Initial diagnosis is almost exclusively made in outpatient care based on anthropometric measurement like BMI, and no symptomatic presentation is required. Though it does not require laboratory tests or imaging, obesity often prompts active management within 30 days, typically through lifestyle intervention and in some cases pharmacologic or surgical treatment. Follow-up for managing comorbidities and weight-loss interventions is expected within the first year after diagnosis.

source_definition: Obsessive compulsive disorder is a primary psychiatric condition characterized by the persistent co-occurrence of obsessions â€” recurrent, intrusive, and unwanted thoughts, urges, or images that generate marked distress â€” and compulsions â€” repetitive behavioral or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or according to rigidly applied rules, aimed at reducing distress or preventing a dreaded outcome. Symptoms must be time-consuming, cause clinically significant distress, or result in meaningful impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning. This phenotype excludes all DSM-5 obsessive-compulsive spectrum disorders (including Body Dysmorphic Disorder, Hoarding Disorder, Trichotillomania, and Excoriation Disorder), which share compulsive features but represent distinct pathophysiological and clinical entities. It further excludes obsessive-compulsive symptoms that arise as a direct physiological consequence of a general medical condition (including neuroinflammatory conditions such as PANDAS/PANS or acquired brain injury) or substance use.
clinical_rationale: Obsessive compulsive disorder is primarily a psychiatric condition with considerable genetic, neurodevelopmental, and environmental contributions. Drug-induced onset or exacerbation is rare, but cases secondary to certain medications, such as antipsychotics, stimulants, and serotonergic drugs, have been reported in the literature. These secondary cases are excluded from this phenotype, which is limited to primary DSM-5 OCD based on psychological and behavioral criteria. OCD is persistent and does not remit with a discrete episode; most patients require ongoing management and are continuously labeled as having the condition. Diagnosis is most often made in an outpatient mental health or primary care setting but can occur in acute care settings for severe cases involving marked distress or risk. While obsessive and compulsive symptoms are characteristic, they may not consistently be recorded as separate coded entries. Formal diagnosis relies on clinical history and behavioral symptoms rather than diagnostic tests or procedures.

source_definition: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic sleep-related breathing disorder characterized by repetitive, partial or complete collapse of the upper airway during sleep due to loss of pharyngeal dilator muscle tone, resulting in recurrent apneas and hypopneas, intermittent nocturnal hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and sleep fragmentation. The disorder spans a clinical severity spectrum from mild to severe, defined by an apnea-hypopnea index of five or more events per hour of sleep. OSA may arise as a primary condition or secondary to anatomical, endocrine, or other systemic factors that compromise upper airway patency, and includes all such etiologically attributable cases provided the obstructive mechanism is present. Explicitly excluded are central sleep apnea, in which respiratory events result from absent or dysregulated central neural drive rather than mechanical obstruction; upper airway resistance syndrome, which involves increased airway resistance and arousal without meeting the apnea-hypopnea threshold; and primary snoring, which entails pharyngeal vibration without airflow limitation, apnea, or associated hypoxemia.
clinical_rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic condition with diverse etiologies, including obesity, anatomical factors, and endocrinopathies, that compromise upper airway patency. While it is often manageable, OSA is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome due to its potential drug-related contributors, such as sedative-hypnotics or opioids exacerbating airway collapse. The condition is persistent and requires long-term management with modalities like CPAP, mandibular advancement, or surgery. Diagnosis typically depends on objective sleep studies, such as polysomnography, to confirm apneas or hypopneas based on an apnea-hypopnea index threshold. Most incident diagnoses occur in outpatient settings, but severe cases may arise in acute care following life-threatening consequences such as hypoxemia. Symptoms such as snoring or hypersomnolence are common but may not always be discretely recorded as structured data. Etiologies and severity variation further complicate case capture.

source_definition: Oliguria is a clinical sign characterized by a pathological reduction in urine output below physiologically adequate levels, defined as less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour (or approximately 400â€“500 mL per day) in adults, and less than 1 mL/kg/hour in children. It represents a failure of the urinary system to produce sufficient urine volume to maintain normal fluid, electrolyte, and waste homeostasis. Oliguria may arise from any of three broad pathophysiological categories: pre-renal causes, in which systemic hypoperfusion reduces glomerular filtration (such as in hypovolemia, shock, or severe cardiac failure); intrinsic renal causes, in which parenchymal damage impairs tubular or glomerular function (such as in acute tubular necrosis or glomerulonephritis); or post-renal causes, in which mechanical obstruction impedes urinary flow (such as in ureteral obstruction or urinary retention). Anuria, defined as urine output below 50â€“100 mL per day reflecting near-complete or complete cessation of urine production, is included as the most severe expression of this same continuum. The phenotype is mechanism-agnostic and population-inclusive, capturing the output abnormality itself as the defining clinical feature across all age groups and care settings.
clinical_rationale: Oliguria is a significant clinical sign indicating pathological reductions in urine output. It is an important marker of kidney dysfunction, mediated by pre-renal states (hypovolemia, shock), intrinsic renal injury (acute tubular necrosis), or post-renal obstruction. Drugs can contribute to oliguria via mechanisms such as nephrotoxicity (aminoglycosides), hemodynamic disruption (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), or by exacerbating urinary obstruction. Though oliguria alone is not typically a primary diagnosis, it is often recorded as part of workup and monitoring for acute kidney injury (AKI). The concept is transient and linked to an underlying cause. Diagnosis typically occurs in acute care settings because oliguria is often associated with serious illnesses requiring urgent intervention. Importantly, some cases may lack specific diagnostic codes, as the phenotype may be captured through observations or laboratory values rather than definitive diagnoses.

source_definition: Onychomycosis due to dermatophyte is a chronic, superficial fungal infection of the toenail unit caused exclusively by dermatophyte organisms (principally Trichophyton rubrum and Trichophyton mentagrophytes), defined by pathological invasion of the nail plate, nail bed, and/or nail matrix. The phenotype encompasses all clinical presentation subtypes: distal and lateral subungual onychomycosis (distal-lateral subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, and nail discoloration), superficial white onychomycosis (chalky white plaques on the dorsal nail plate surface), proximal subungual onychomycosis (leukonychia originating at the proximal nail fold), and total dystrophic onychomycosis (complete structural destruction of the nail unit). The condition is restricted to the toenails and excludes fingernail involvement. Non-infectious conditions that produce morphologically similar nail changes â€” including psoriatic nail disease, traumatic onychodystrophy, and lichen planus of the nail â€” are explicitly excluded, as are onychomycoses attributable to Candida species or non-dermatophyte molds.
clinical_rationale: Onychomycosis due to dermatophyte is a fungal infection of the toenail unit caused exclusively by dermatophyte microorganisms, and it is recognized as a relevant pharmacovigilance outcome in the context of antifungal drugs or drugs that may alter the immune response. It is a chronic condition, persisting as long as the fungal infection remains untreated, making it persistent rather than transient. Toenail onychomycosis rarely results in urgent care visits; the majority of cases are diagnosed in outpatient settings due to its gradual onset and cosmetic or functional impairment rather than life-threatening impact. There are no biological age or sex constraints specific to this condition. Diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation of dermatophyte infection, as clinical presentation alone is insufficient to exclude non-infectious mimickers or other types of fungal onychomycosis. Therapy often involves prolonged antifungal treatment, and patients may receive ongoing monitoring or retreatment depending on the clinical response and recurrence rates. Given the chronicity of infection, long-term follow-up assessments are common. The description restricts the condition to toenail involvement, aligning with the nomenclature provided.

source_definition: Oral ulcer is a discrete, focal loss of the full thickness of the oral mucosal epithelium within the oral cavity proper â€” encompassing the buccal mucosa, gingiva, hard palate, floor of mouth, and tongue â€” resulting in exposure of the underlying lamina propria. The breach must be complete, extending through the basement membrane, thereby distinguishing true ulceration from superficial erosions in which epithelial integrity is only partially compromised. The phenotype encompasses ulcers arising from any endogenous pathophysiological mechanism, including infectious (viral, bacterial, fungal), immune-mediated (aphthous, autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease), drug-induced (including cytotoxic mucositis), nutritional deficiency-related, and neoplastic processes. Any lesion in which a zone of full-thickness mucosal breach is present qualifies, regardless of whether the surrounding mucosa is affected by a co-existing primary mucosal disease such as lichen planus or leukoplakia. Ulcers arising solely from exogenous mechanical injury â€” including self-inflicted biting, dental appliance trauma, or iatrogenic physical injury â€” are excluded. The lips and oropharynx are outside the anatomical boundary of this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Oral ulcers can arise from various mechanisms, including drug-induced mucositis from cytotoxic agents, immune-related adverse events, or direct mucosal toxicity, making them a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on physical examination of mucosal integrity, though underlying causes may necessitate further investigation. The description excludes exogenous trauma and confines the phenotype anatomically to the oral cavity proper, which clarifies the definition compared to the broader colloquial use of 'oral ulcer.' Drug-induced cases are typically transient, though recurrent episodes can occur in susceptible individuals, such as those undergoing repeated chemotherapy cycles. Documentation of characteristic symptoms like pain or soreness may be present but not uniformly coded as separate records, and diagnosis does not always require objective testing. Acute care is uncommon for uncomplicated cases, but severe drug-associated ulceration may still require urgent intervention.

source_definition: Orthostatic hypotension is a clinical syndrome characterized by a sustained reduction in blood pressure upon assumption of an upright posture, defined by a fall in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or a fall in diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg, occurring within three minutes of standing or head-up tilt. The condition represents a failure of the cardiovascular system to adequately compensate for the gravitational redistribution of intravascular volume during the transition from supine or seated to upright posture, resulting in transiently reduced cerebral and systemic perfusion pressure. This hemodynamic compromise is accompanied by one or more symptoms of cerebral or global hypoperfusion, including dizziness, lightheadedness, presyncope, syncope, blurred vision, weakness, fatigue, or cognitive slowing upon standing, thereby constituting a symptomatic hemodynamic event rather than an isolated measurement finding. The phenotype is etiology-agnostic, encompassing all pathophysiological mechanisms capable of producing this hemodynamic-symptomatic profile â€” including neurogenic autonomic failure (e.g., from Parkinson's disease, multiple system atrophy, or diabetic autonomic neuropathy), hypovolemia (e.g., dehydration or hemorrhage), impaired cardiac output, and pharmacologically mediated vasodilation or sympatholytic effects. Explicitly excluded are: initial orthostatic hypotension (blood pressure drop resolving within 15 seconds of standing), delayed orthostatic hypotension (drop occurring only after more than three minutes of upright posture), postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome in the absence of the requisite blood pressure drop, and reflex-mediated vasovagal syncope not fulfilling the orthostatic blood pressure threshold criteria.
clinical_rationale: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is a heterogeneous condition encompassing multiple etiologies, including neurogenic autonomic failure, hypovolemia, impaired cardiac output, and drug-induced mechanisms such as vasodilation or sympatholytic effects (e.g., antihypertensives, antipsychotics). Drug-induced OH, in particular, is well-documented as a pharmacovigilance outcome, occurring via direct hemodynamic alterations. Its clinical course is transient and episodic with resolution of symptoms once positional correction, hydration, or other acute measures are applied. Symptoms such as dizziness, syncope, or blurred vision are commonly reported but inconsistently coded separately. Diagnosis nearly always requires a positional blood pressure measurement, making diagnostic testing universal. Incident OH is typically recognized in both acute and ambulatory care contexts, making the 'acute care common' classification appropriate. The description's exclusion criteria, like initial and delayed orthostatic hypotension, support precise phenotype differentiation.

source_definition: Osteoarthritis of the knee is a chronic, progressive degenerative disease of the knee joint characterized by the pathological breakdown of articular cartilage, remodeling of subchondral bone, formation of osteophytes, and variable degrees of synovial inflammation, resulting in joint space narrowing, pain, stiffness, and functional impairment. The phenotype encompasses the full severity spectrum, from early-stage cartilage softening and mild radiographic changes through advanced bone-on-bone disease and severe functional disability. Both primary (idiopathic) osteoarthritis, arising from age-related mechanical wear and genetic predisposition, and secondary osteoarthritis, arising from prior joint injury, surgical intervention, obesity-related mechanical overload, or metabolic joint disease, are included. Explicitly excluded are inflammatory arthropathies â€” including rheumatoid arthritis, gout, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, and psoriatic arthritis â€” whose principal pathophysiology is autoimmune or crystal-mediated rather than degenerative, even when such conditions produce secondary structural changes in the knee joint.
clinical_rationale: Osteoarthritis of the knee is primarily a chronic degenerative condition caused by mechanical wear, age-related cartilage breakdown, and predispositional factors including obesity, prior joint injury, and genetic susceptibility. While the condition is not inherently drug-attributable, medications such as corticosteroids or fluoroquinolones may, in rare cases, accelerate joint degeneration indirectly through effects on cartilage, though this is not a primary etiology. The description provided explicitly excludes inflammatory causes of joint pathology, clarifying scope. Osteoarthritis is persistent and does not resolve but may have episodic symptomatic exacerbations. Modal incident diagnosis occurs in ambulatory care via clinical evaluation and imaging (radiographic evidence).

source_definition: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by compromised bone strength resulting from reduced bone mineral density and deterioration of bone microarchitecture, leading to increased susceptibility to fracture. The condition is defined by a bone mineral density T-score of âˆ’2.5 standard deviations or below at any standard measurement site (lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip), or by the occurrence of a low-trauma fragility fracture at a site typical of bone fragility such as the vertebrae, hip, distal radius, or proximal humerus. The phenotype encompasses all etiologic subtypes, including primary forms (postmenopausal, age-related, and idiopathic) and secondary forms arising from identifiable causes such as glucocorticoid exposure, primary hyperparathyroidism, hypogonadism, or malabsorption syndromes. Osteopenia (T-score between âˆ’1.0 and âˆ’2.5 in the absence of fragility fracture) is explicitly excluded, as are conditions with fundamentally distinct bone pathophysiology such as osteomalacia, Paget's disease of bone, osteogenesis imperfecta, and skeletal involvement from malignancy.
clinical_rationale: Osteoporosis is relevant to pharmacovigilance due to the well-documented association between certain drugs (e.g., glucocorticoids, aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation therapy) and bone loss, leading to an increased risk of fragility fractures. The clinical definition explicitly distinguishes osteoporosis from osteopenia and other bone pathologies, ensuring a focused cohort. Osteoporosis is a persistent condition once diagnosed because the label and ongoing management for fracture prevention apply indefinitely, even if bone mineral density improves. Diagnoses are often established in outpatient settings through dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) or following the management of fragility fractures, though severe cases with fractures may present to acute care. The etiology described spans primary and secondary causes, accommodating drug-induced mechanisms. Fragility fractures often follow as sequelae, necessitating long-term care.

source_definition: Ovarian cancer is a malignant neoplasm arising de novo from the cellular constituents of the ovary, encompassing all histologically confirmed invasive primary subtypes including epithelial carcinomas (such as serous, mucinous, endometrioid, and clear cell carcinomas), malignant germ cell tumors, and malignant sex cord-stromal tumors. The condition is defined by histopathological evidence of invasive malignancy with primary origin in ovarian tissue; tumors of borderline or low malignant potential, which lack frank invasion, are excluded. Secondary malignant involvement of the ovary arising from metastatic spread of a cancer originating in another anatomic site (e.g., Krukenberg tumors of gastric or colorectal origin) is explicitly excluded, as such presentations represent the primary cancer of the originating organ rather than a primary ovarian malignancy.
clinical_rationale: Ovarian cancer is biologically plausible as a pharmacovigilance outcome due to documented associations with certain medications, particularly hormonal therapies (e.g., increased risk with extended estrogen monotherapy and potentially decreased risk with combined oral contraceptives). Additionally, iatrogenic factors such as prior alkylating chemotherapy or pelvic radiation may contribute. The course is persistent stable, as histologically confirmed ovarian cancer requires ongoing management and surveillance, and the diagnostic label is not shed regardless of remission or cure. Diagnosis requires histopathological confirmation typically obtained via surgical exploration, and incident cases are commonly identified in acute or specialized care settings due to presenting symptoms or concerning imaging findings. Discrete symptoms such as abdominal pain or bloating may precede diagnosis, but these are non-specific and inconsistently recorded. Ovarian cancer mandates active treatment within 30 days of diagnosis, ranging from surgery to chemotherapy, and requires condition-specific follow-up for surveillance, treatment re-assessment, or sequelae (such as recurrence or secondary cancer) over the subsequent 365 days.

source_definition: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a chronic lower urinary tract syndrome characterized by the presence of urinary urgency â€” a sudden, compelling desire to void that is difficult to defer â€” occurring with or without urgency urinary incontinence, and typically accompanied by urinary frequency and nocturia, in the absence of a causative infectious, metabolic, or local pathological condition. The diagnosis may be established on the basis of the clinical symptom complex alone or by urodynamic demonstration of involuntary detrusor contractions during the bladder-filling phase (detrusor overactivity). The phenotype encompasses both the continent form (OAB-dry) and the incontinent form (OAB-wet). Explicitly excluded are: stress urinary incontinence driven by exertional increases in intra-abdominal pressure without an urgency component; neurogenic detrusor overactivity attributable to a diagnosed neurological disorder (e.g., multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, Parkinson's disease); urgency and frequency secondary to bladder outlet obstruction; and transient lower urinary tract symptoms caused by urinary tract infection.
clinical_rationale: Overactive bladder (OAB) can be attributed to drug-induced mechanisms, such as medications affecting bladder innervation or detrusor activity (e.g., cholinergic agents or diuretics), although it is more commonly idiopathic. The provided definition excludes causative infectious, metabolic, or pathological conditions. While OAB is typically managed symptomatically, some structured data may reflect urgency or frequency symptoms separately prior to coding the full syndrome. No explicit age constraints are established, but prevalence and severity increase with aging, especially in postmenopausal women. Diagnosis can often be clinical, though urodynamic testing may be employed for confirmation in ambiguous cases. Notably, exclusion criteria outlined in the definition clearly distinguish OAB from related conditions with differing etiologies, such as neurogenic detrusor overactivity or bladder outlet obstruction.
