source_definition: Pain is a subjective, patient-reported unpleasant sensory and/or emotional experience of any intensity and duration, arising from any anatomical location or bodily system. The phenotype encompasses all etiological categories, including nociceptive pain due to actual or threatened tissue damage, neuropathic pain arising from disease or injury of the somatosensory nervous system, inflammatory pain, visceral pain, and pain of psychogenic or somatoform origin in which no identifiable physiological basis can be established. Pain of iatrogenic origin â€” including expected post-procedural and post-surgical pain â€” is explicitly included within this concept. No minimum severity threshold is required; any patient-reported painful complaint qualifies for this phenotype, irrespective of body site, underlying mechanism, acuity, or chronicity.
clinical_rationale: The concept of pain includes a broad spectrum of etiologies—nociceptive, neuropathic, inflammatory, visceral, psychogenic, and iatrogenic. It explicitly includes iatrogenic (procedure- or treatment-related) pain, making it suitable as a pharmacovigilance outcome in the context of drug-related pain syndromes, even though many instances of pain are non-drug related or are due to obvious external causes such as injury. The definition's breadth, however, introduces significant challenges to routine observational data-based capture, as pain is an entirely subjective phenomenon. While the description specifies that any painful complaint should qualify for the phenotype, pain-related symptoms are often inconsistently detailed or underreported in structured data. Thus, ascertainment of pain incidents as a singular and comprehensive phenotype remains inherently difficult.

source_definition: Pallor is a clinical sign characterized by an abnormal paleness or loss of normal color in the skin, mucous membranes, or conjunctiva, detectable on physical examination regardless of the degree of severity or the underlying etiology. The sign reflects a reduction in the visibility of oxyhemoglobin in the superficial vasculature, as may occur in states of anemia, reduced peripheral perfusion, vasoconstriction, or systemic illness. Any anatomical site of observation qualifies. Excluded from this concept are cyanosis (bluish discoloration arising from deoxygenated hemoglobin), jaundice (yellow discoloration resulting from hyperbilirubinemia), structural depigmentation disorders such as vitiligo or albinism (which represent a constitutional absence of melanin rather than an acquired hemodynamic or hematologic change), and erythema or flushing (pathological redness reflecting vasodilation or inflammation, representing the physiological opposite of pallor).
clinical_rationale: Pallor is a nonspecific clinical sign rather than a definitive diagnosis and can reflect a multitude of underlying etiologies, some of which are drug-attributable (e.g., anemia due to marrow suppression or hemolysis caused by drugs). As a standalone sign, it lacks specificity and is thus not well-suited for pharmacovigilance independent of its etiology. Pallor is transient in its presentation, resolving when the underlying cause is treated, and a new episode reflects a different clinical insult. Diagnosis is typically clinical and does not require systematic testing, although underlying causes may. Symptom documentation in structured data for pallor is generally uncommon outside of specific contexts (e.g., anemia-related investigations).

source_definition: Palmoplantar pustulosis is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory dermatosis characterized by the recurrent eruption of sterile, intraepidermal neutrophilic pustules strictly confined to the palmar and plantar surfaces. It is considered a clinically and pathophysiologically distinct entity from psoriasis vulgaris, defined by dysregulated innate immune activation within the acrosyringeal epithelium of the eccrine sweat ducts, leading to neutrophilic infiltration and subcorneal pustule formation. The condition includes both idiopathic presentations and cases precipitated by pharmacological triggers such as TNF-Î± inhibitors, lithium, or iodides. It explicitly excludes infectious pustulosis of the palms and soles (whether bacterial or fungal in origin), dyshidrotic eczema (pompholyx), which arises from spongiotic eczematous pathology rather than neutrophilic intraepidermal pustulation, and acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau, which affects the periungual and distal digital surfaces rather than the palmar and plantar epithelium proper.
clinical_rationale: Palmoplantar pustulosis is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with both idiopathic and drug-induced etiologies. Drug causality is well-documented for agents such as TNF-α inhibitors, lithium, and iodides. Biologically, the pathogenesis involves dysregulated innate immune activation within eccrine sweat ducts, distinct from the mechanisms of psoriasis vulgaris and eczema. Episodes are characterized by recurrent neutrophilic pustules confined to the palmar and plantar surfaces, making the clinical course relapsing. Diagnosis usually occurs in ambulatory care based on physical examination, though skin biopsy may be performed to rule out mimics. Pharmacovigilance surveillance would focus on drug-attributable cases, not idiopathic presentations. Outcome capture in observational data is limited by variable coding practices and potential underdocumenting of recurrent flares.

source_definition: Palpitations is a symptom defined as an abnormal or distressing subjective awareness of one's own heartbeat, perceived as racing, pounding, fluttering, or skipping, of any intensity and duration. The phenotype is defined entirely by the patient's conscious, uncomfortable perception of cardiac activity and does not require objective confirmation of an underlying cardiac rhythm disturbance. All etiological contexts are included, encompassing cardiac arrhythmias, metabolic disturbances such as hyperthyroidism or anemia, psychogenic causes, and iatrogenic or substance-related triggers. Excluded from this phenotype is awareness of the heartbeat that occurs exclusively under conditions of vigorous physical exertion or acute emotional arousal in circumstances where the sensation is not perceived as abnormal or distressing by the individual and does not prompt any clinical evaluation or concern.
clinical_rationale: Palpitations are an abnormal subjective awareness of heartbeat, often prompted by arrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation, PVCs, sinus tachycardia), medical conditions (e.g., hyperthyroidism, anemia), drugs (e.g., stimulants, beta-agonists, antidepressants), or psychogenic states (panic disorder). The description spans multiple etiologies, several of which are drug-related or drug-exacerbated, making the phenotype potentially suitable for pharmacovigilance investigations. However, palpitations are symptom-defined and do not necessarily correspond to an underlying structural or electrophysiological abnormality. They are transient and recurrent due to their episodic nature. While structured coding of palpitations may exist, the subjective nature often limits their reliable capture in longitudinal databases.

source_definition: Pancreatic cancer is a malignant neoplasm arising from the exocrine cells of the pancreas, encompassing pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) as the predominant histological subtype, as well as rarer exocrine-origin carcinomas including acinar cell carcinoma and other exocrine variants. The phenotype requires histologically or cytologically confirmed invasive malignancy and spans the full spectrum of disease stage from localized resectable disease through locally advanced and metastatic presentations. This definition is restricted to primary pancreatic malignancies of exocrine origin and explicitly excludes pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs), pre-invasive or borderline lesions such as intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) without confirmed invasive transformation and pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs), and any secondary malignant involvement of the pancreas arising from metastatic spread or direct extension of a non-pancreatic primary tumor.
clinical_rationale: Pancreatic cancer, predominantly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), is established as a pharmacovigilance outcome because several drugs have been implicated as possible risk factors (e.g., incretin-based therapies such as GLP-1 receptor agonists). However, drug-induced pancreatic cancer is rare, and confounding by indication (e.g., diabetes mellitus) and reverse causality pose challenges in causal inference. The condition is typically persistent, as patients retain the diagnostic label due to the incurable nature of advanced disease or the need for long-term surveillance in suspected cured cases following treatment. Diagnosis often requires imaging and histological or cytological confirmation, and incidental diagnosis may also occur. Pancreatic cancer is more commonly seen in older adults but this age skew does not merit a hard age restriction. Cases are often first identified in either outpatient or acute care settings depending on the stage at diagnosis and presenting symptoms; advanced stages may present with obstructive jaundice or weight loss that can lead to hospitalization.

source_definition: Pancytopenia is a hematologic state characterized by the simultaneous reduction of all three major peripheral blood cell lineages â€” erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets â€” each falling below the lower limit of normal as established by institutional reference ranges, without requiring specific numeric thresholds. The condition may arise from any underlying mechanism, including but not limited to intrinsic bone marrow failure or hypoplasia, infiltration of the marrow by malignant or granulomatous processes, peripheral immune-mediated destruction, or pathological sequestration in the reticuloendothelial system. It encompasses cytopenias of both central (marrow-mediated) and peripheral origin and is not restricted to any particular etiology. Pancytopenia explicitly excludes states in which fewer than all three cell lineages are reduced concurrently, such as bicytopenia or isolated single-lineage cytopenias, as well as spurious tri-lineage reductions attributable to laboratory artifacts such as platelet clumping or cold agglutinin-induced erythrocyte agglutination that do not reflect a true in vivo hematologic state.
clinical_rationale: Pancytopenia is a broad clinical finding that may be a valid pharmacovigilance outcome when it arises from a drug-related etiology, such as bone marrow suppression from chemotherapy, immune-mediated destruction caused by drug hypersensitivity, or idiosyncratic reactions (e.g., aplastic anemia from chloramphenicol). However, this condition also includes non-drug-induced etiologies, such as malignancy, autoimmune diseases, infections, and congenital aplastic syndromes. Because the definition encompasses both drug-attributable and non-drug-attributable cases, it is valid as an outcome only with attention to these distinctions. Pancytopenia is clinically transient, resolving when the causative factor is addressed, although persistence or progression might indicate evolution to a more severe condition, such as chronic bone marrow failure or myelodysplastic syndrome. Laboratory data confirm the diagnosis, but the precision of claims- or EHR-based algorithms is limited by the dependence on manual verification of tri-lineage findings to rule out spurious results.

source_definition: Paralysis is a clinical state characterized by any clinically significant reduction or complete loss of voluntary motor function, spanning the full spectrum from partial impairment (paresis) to total abolition of movement (plegia). The phenotype is unrestricted with respect to anatomical distribution, encompassing focal, regional, and generalized patterns including monoplegia, hemiplegia, paraplegia, quadriplegia, cranial nerve motor deficits, and isolated limb or trunk paresis. All underlying etiological mechanisms are included: upper and lower motor neuron lesions of the central and peripheral nervous systems (e.g., stroke, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, Guillain-BarrÃ© syndrome), neuromuscular junction dysfunction (e.g., myasthenia gravis, botulism), primary muscle disease (e.g., periodic paralysis), and functional or psychogenic motor loss arising from conversion disorder or functional neurological symptom disorder, provided the deficit has received a clinical diagnosis. The phenotype is temporally unrestricted, encompassing transient presentations (e.g., post-ictal Todd's paralysis, TIA-associated motor deficits) as well as persistent or permanent motor loss.
clinical_rationale: Paralysis encompasses a wide variety of etiologies, some of which are drug-attributable via mechanisms such as iatrogenic botulism from botulinum toxin, acute neuromuscular weakness from aminoglycoside toxicity, myopathy from statins, periodic paralysis triggered by medications affecting electrolyte balance, or psychogenic paralysis in reaction to psychiatric drugs or trauma. However, many cases arise from genetic, traumatic, or structural causes (e.g., stroke, spinal cord injury) entirely independent of drug exposure. This broad scope makes paralysis a valid pharmacovigilance outcome only under a narrowed reading that excludes non-acquired, congenital, or trauma-driven etiologies while emphasizing drug-induced, neuromuscular, and transient causes. Clinically, incident diagnosis most often occurs in acute care settings due to the often abrupt and severe onset of major motor deficits. Symptoms such as reduced movement or weakness are rarely recorded discretely in structured data prior to diagnosis, as the deficit itself typically prompts direct diagnostic labeling. Diagnostic confirmation is commonly supported by imaging, nerve conduction studies, or labs. While some causes of paralysis resolve fully after treatment of their underlying mechanism, others persist, as in chronic paraplegia or quadriplegia due to irreversible injury.

source_definition: Paralytic ileus is an acute, transient state of functional intestinal dysmotility characterized by the failure of normal peristalsis throughout the small and/or large bowel in the absence of any intrinsic or extrinsic mechanical obstruction. It arises from neurogenic, humoral, or metabolic disruption of the enteric and autonomic nervous system â€” most commonly as a consequence of abdominal surgery, systemic sepsis, trauma, electrolyte disturbances, or pharmacologic agents â€” and presents clinically with abdominal distension, absence or marked reduction of bowel sounds, nausea, vomiting, and failure to pass flatus or stool. All presentations along the clinical severity spectrum are included, from mild self-resolving post-operative ileus to severe cases requiring active decompressive management. Explicitly excluded are: mechanical bowel obstruction caused by adhesions, herniation, intraluminal mass, or extrinsic compression; colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome), which represents a segmental colonic dysmotility with a distinct clinical and management profile; chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction (CIPO), a chronic neuromuscular disorder of the gut; and ileus attributable primarily to vascular occlusion or mesenteric ischemia, which constitutes a separate pathophysiological entity.
clinical_rationale: Paralytic ileus is a recognized pharmacovigilance outcome, as multiple pharmacologic agents, such as opioids, anticholinergics, and anesthetic drugs, are documented causes. The mechanism is neurogenic or humoral disruption of enteric and autonomic nervous system function. The condition is transient in nature and resolves either spontaneously or with appropriate management. As excluded entities like mechanical bowel obstruction and chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction (CIPO) have distinct pathophysiologies and are not drug-induced, they must be omitted from cohort logic. Incidental diagnoses predominantly occur in acute care settings due to the severity of symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, and abdominal distension, and typically require diagnostic imaging or clinical assessment to establish the absence of mechanical obstruction, confirming the functional nature of the ileus. Beyond the acute episode, long-term sequelae are rare, as paralytic ileus typically resolves completely once the primary cause is addressed.

source_definition: Parasomnia refers to any abnormal behavioral, experiential, or autonomic phenomenon arising during sleep onset, within sleep, or during arousals from sleep, encompassing disorders of incomplete arousal from NREM sleep (including confusional arousals, sleepwalking, and sleep terrors), REM-related disturbances (including REM sleep behavior disorder, nightmare disorder, and recurrent isolated sleep paralysis), and other sleep-related phenomena (including sleep enuresis, exploding head syndrome, and hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations not attributable to narcolepsy). The phenotype includes occurrences of any frequency or severity, and encompasses cases regardless of whether the etiology is idiopathic, secondary to a medical or neurological condition, or precipitated by a substance or medication. Abnormal nocturnal motor or experiential events caused by epileptiform neuronal discharges â€” including nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy â€” are explicitly excluded as they represent a distinct pathophysiological mechanism.
clinical_rationale: Parasomnias encompass a diverse group of conditions characterized by abnormal behaviors or experiences during sleep. This category includes both idiopathic conditions and those secondary to other disorders or induced by substances or medications. Drug-induced parasomnias, such as those linked to sedatives, hypnotics, or antidepressants (e.g., SSRIs and atypical antipsychotics), are documented, making parasomnia a valid pharmacovigilance outcome under a narrower interpretation focusing on drug-attributable causes. However, the definition provided includes idiopathic and secondary causes unrelated to drugs, requiring conditional categorization. Routine diagnosis often occurs in outpatient settings, and structured symptoms like sleepwalking or night terrors are commonly captured in clinical data. Confirmatory sleep studies are sometimes required for differential diagnosis, although many cases rely on clinical history. Most parasomnias are transient and episodic, but recurrent episodes can occur over time.

source_definition: Paresthesia is an abnormal spontaneous sensory experience characterized by positive sensory phenomena â€” including tingling, prickling, burning, or numbness â€” arising without an adequate external stimulus and recognized as a clinical complaint within a medical encounter. The condition encompasses presentations of any anatomical distribution and etiology, provided the sensation is not purely attributable to transient mechanical pressure on a nerve (e.g., positional limb compression). Paresthesia explicitly excludes pain-predominant sensory disturbances such as neuropathic pain and dysesthesia with allodynia, as well as negative sensory phenomena such as hypoesthesia or frank sensory loss, which represent distinct pathophysiological states along the sensory neuropathy spectrum.
clinical_rationale: Paresthesia is a broad sensory symptom that arises from multiple etiologies, including drug-induced neuropathy. Drug-induced causes, such as chemotherapy (e.g., platinum-based drugs, taxanes), are well-documented. However, cases not related to drug exposure may arise from primary neurological conditions, systemic diseases, autoimmune conditions, or other non-pharmacological origins. The clinical course of paresthesia depends on its etiology, and while some cases related to transient insults may resolve, chronic cases related to nerve damage or systemic disease may persist, making this condition clinically heterogeneous. In observational data, separate documentation of discrete symptoms such as tingling or numbness is inconsistent, and confirmatory testing is not typically required to establish the condition, as the diagnosis is often clinical and subjective.

source_definition: Idiopathic Parkinson disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder defined by the selective, progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and the pathological intraneuronal accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein in the form of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, which propagate through the nervous system in a largely stereotyped rostrocaudal pattern. The phenotype encompasses the full disease continuum, beginning with a prodromal phase in which non-motor manifestations â€” including hyposmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, constipation, and autonomic dysfunction â€” precede the cardinal motor syndrome by years to decades. The clinically established motor phase requires the presence of bradykinesia in combination with at least one of resting tremor, muscular rigidity, or postural and gait instability. As the disease advances, the phenotype includes the full spectrum of non-motor burden, extending to neuropsychiatric symptoms, sleep disturbances, autonomic failure, and cognitive impairment ranging from mild cognitive impairment to Parkinson disease dementia, the latter representing a late-stage expression of the same underlying Lewy body pathological process rather than a distinct disease entity. The phenotype explicitly excludes atypical parkinsonian syndromes with divergent pathophysiology and prognosis â€” including Multiple System Atrophy, Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, Dementia with Lewy Bodies, and Corticobasal Degeneration â€” as well as all secondary and acquired causes of parkinsonism, including drug-induced (e.g., dopamine receptor antagonists, antiemetics), vascular, toxic, post-infectious, and post-traumatic parkinsonism.
clinical_rationale: Idiopathic Parkinson disease is not a direct drug-attributable condition, as its etiology is largely genetic and age-related. However, secondary and acquired parkinsonism (such as drug-induced) is attributable to medications, but these are explicitly excluded from the phenotype definition provided. The described progressive course with prodromal, motor, and advanced disease phases identifies the phenotype as a neurodegenerative disease, fully consistent with its classification as persistent-stable. Accurate cohort definition requires careful exclusion of atypical parkinsonisms and acquired secondary conditions, which complicates observational case identification in the OMOP CDM. Diagnosis is predominantly clinical, guided by characteristic motor features and exclusion of mimics, though ancillary tests may support atypical cases. Incident diagnoses are typically made in ambulatory care settings, though acute care may be involved to rule out secondary parkinsonism when patients present with confusion or acute changes. Motor symptoms, such as resting tremor and bradykinesia, may appear as discrete recorded observations independently, but non-specificity is a limitation. Longitudinal follow-up for treatment efficacy, counseling, or monitoring of progression is expected in practically all cases.

source_definition: Parkinsonism is a clinical syndrome defined by the presence of bradykinesia in combination with at least one of the following cardinal motor features: resting tremor, muscular rigidity, or postural instability, as identified on neurological examination. The syndrome encompasses any clinically detectable degree of motor dysfunction meeting these criteria, including early, mild, or transient presentations. Parkinsonism is etiologically heterogeneous and includes all underlying causes: idiopathic Parkinson's disease (characterized by progressive nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurodegeneration with Lewy body pathology); atypical neurodegenerative parkinsonian syndromes (including multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration, and dementia with Lewy bodies); and secondary forms arising from pharmacological dopamine receptor blockade, vascular injury to the basal ganglia or their connections, toxic exposures, post-encephalitic sequelae, structural lesions, or metabolic disturbances. The unifying criterion is the syndromic clinical presentation; no specific etiology is excluded from this definition.
clinical_rationale: Parkinsonism is an etiologically heterogeneous syndrome that includes primary neurodegenerative conditions, such as Parkinson's disease, and secondary causes like dopamine receptor blockade (e.g., due to antipsychotics or antiemetics), vascular injury, toxins, or metabolic disturbances. Drugs are a well-established cause of secondary parkinsonism, and drug-induced cases typically resolve after withdrawal of the offending agent. Primary neurodegenerative parkinsonism, however, is progressive and chronic. Given this heterogeneity, parkinsonism as a whole is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome only under the narrower context of secondary (e.g., drug-induced) cases. Thus, the condition is classified as conditional in terms of drug-attributable etiology. Given that parkinsonism can involve progressive neurodegenerative conditions, it is typically a persistent stable condition once diagnosed, though it may undergo evolution in severity and symptoms over time. The diagnosis is usually made in outpatient neurology or primary care settings, except in cases of acute secondary parkinsonism where acute care settings may be involved. Post-diagnostic follow-up is routine for patients, especially in cases of progressive disease, and characteristic motor symptoms often prompt clinical attention.

source_definition: Pemphigus is a group of chronic autoimmune blistering disorders characterized by intraepidermal acantholysis â€” the loss of cell-to-cell adhesion within the epidermis or mucous membranes â€” mediated by pathogenic IgG autoantibodies directed against desmoglein adhesion proteins (primarily desmoglein 3, desmoglein 1, or both). This phenotype encompasses Pemphigus Vulgaris (suprabasal acantholysis with predominant mucosal and cutaneous involvement), Pemphigus Foliaceus (superficial subcorneal acantholysis restricted to the skin), and Pemphigus Vegetans (a Pemphigus Vulgaris variant with verrucous or vegetating plaques), across all severity levels from newly diagnosed or mild localized disease through severe extensive involvement. Drug-induced pemphigus, in which the same anti-desmoglein acantholytic mechanism is pharmacologically provoked, is included. Excluded are Paraneoplastic Pemphigus, which involves a distinct multi-antigen autoantibody profile associated with an underlying neoplasm, and all subepidermal autoimmune blistering disorders â€” including Bullous Pemphigoid, Pemphigoid Gestationis, Dermatitis Herpetiformis, and Linear IgA Bullous Dermatosis â€” which differ fundamentally in the anatomical plane of cleavage and autoantibody targets.
clinical_rationale: Pemphigus includes a spectrum of chronic autoimmune blistering disorders driven by pathogenic autoantibodies targeting desmoglein adhesion proteins. Its inclusion as a pharmacovigilance outcome is supported by the recognition of drug-induced pemphigus, where specific medications like thiol-containing drugs and penicillamine can trigger similar autoantibody-mediated pathology. The clinical course varies by severity; most cases require chronic management, and the diagnostic label persists, though the disease activity may relapse episodically. Treatment and follow-up are largely guided by severity, with diagnostic confirmation typically relying on skin biopsy and immunologic testing. Mild cases may present in outpatient settings, but severe cases often require acute care. Exclusion of paraneoplastic pemphigus focuses this phenotype on primary and drug-induced pemphigus forms. No age-specific criterion limits applicability due to its autoimmune nature, though incidence skews toward older adults.

source_definition: Peptic ulcer is a discrete, full-thickness mucosal defect that penetrates through the muscularis mucosae of the stomach or duodenum, arising from an imbalance between aggressive luminal factors (acid, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori infection, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use) and the normal mucoprotective mechanisms of the gastroduodenal mucosa. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical spectrum, from uncomplicated disease characterized by episodic epigastric pain and endoscopically confirmed ulceration, to complicated disease manifesting as acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, perforation, or gastric outlet obstruction. Excluded from this concept are superficial gastric erosions that do not breach the muscularis mucosae, stress-related mucosal disease arising from systemic ischemia in critically ill patients, and ulcerating gastric malignancies (e.g., adenocarcinoma presenting as a malignant ulcer), all of which share overlapping clinical features but are pathophysiologically and prognostically distinct from peptic ulcer disease.
clinical_rationale: Peptic ulcer is a suitable pharmacovigilance outcome, as the condition is frequently attributed to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which impair gastric mucosal defense, and is included as a boxed warning on many NSAID product labels. Helicobacter pylori infection, another key etiological factor, is independent of drug exposure. The clinical course of peptic ulcer is transient and episodes can recur due to risk factor re-exposure or incomplete resolution. Complicated peptic ulcer often leads to acute care presentations, especially in cases involving bleeding or perforation; however, uncomplicated cases may be diagnosed in outpatient settings. Diagnostic confirmation typically requires endoscopy or radiographic imaging, particularly for complications such as perforation or obstruction. Active treatment is usually documented within 30 days, ranging from acid suppression therapy to interventions for complications. Follow-up to confirm healing or manage complications (e.g., resolving hemorrhage, ongoing acid suppression, or eradication of H. pylori) is expected within 1 year.

source_definition: Perforation of the tympanic membrane is an acute, full-thickness disruption of the tympanic membrane â€” the thin, fibrous structure separating the external auditory canal from the middle ear cavity â€” resulting in loss of structural integrity from any underlying mechanism. Infectious perforations arise from pressure-driven rupture secondary to acute otitis media, in which accumulating purulent middle ear effusion exceeds the tensile capacity of the membrane. Traumatic perforations result from sudden mechanical forces applied to the membrane or the external ear canal air column, including barotrauma, blast injury, direct instrumentation, slap-type impact, or temporal bone fracture. Iatrogenic perforations encompass both intentionally created surgical openings (e.g., myringotomy, tympanostomy tube insertion) and unintended procedural disruptions occurring during or following medical interventions involving the ear. The clinical presentation typically includes acute otalgia, conductive hearing loss, tinnitus, and otorrhea, confirmed by otoscopic visualization of a visible membrane defect. Chronic non-healing perforations persisting beyond the expected acute healing period are excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Perforation of the tympanic membrane can arise from infectious causes (e.g., otitis media), trauma (e.g., barotrauma, blunt force), or iatrogenic causes (e.g., myringotomy, tympanostomy procedures). While the majority of cases are acute and self-healing, some perforations may require medical intervention, such as protective care to encourage healing or surgical repair in unresolved cases. Drug-induced etiologies are not documented, and the condition most commonly arises from external or mechanical causes. Given this etiology, the concept is not a relevant pharmacovigilance outcome unless specified differently in a more constrained scenario (e.g., examining ototoxic or procedural risks affecting the ear). The clinical course is typically transient with the condition resolving following appropriate care.

source_definition: Peripheral edema is the abnormal accumulation of fluid within the interstitial compartment of the peripheral tissues â€” most commonly the lower extremities, but also including the upper extremities â€” manifesting as clinically detectable swelling of any degree, from trace pitting to severe bilateral edema. The condition may arise from any systemic or local mechanism that disrupts the balance of transcapillary fluid exchange, including but not limited to elevated venous hydrostatic pressure, reduced plasma oncotic pressure, impaired lymphatic drainage, or increased capillary permeability due to systemic inflammatory states. All clinically recognized severity levels are included. Excluded from this phenotype are swelling states arising from direct tissue injury or localized infection (e.g., post-traumatic edema, cellulitis), as well as angioedema, which represents a pathophysiologically distinct mast-cell- or bradykinin-mediated process involving submucosal or subcutaneous vascular leak rather than generalized interstitial fluid imbalance.
clinical_rationale: Peripheral edema can be drug-induced via mechanisms such as fluid retention (e.g., corticosteroids, calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs), capillary permeability changes (immune modulators, cytokine therapies), or altered lymphatic drainage associated with some therapies. However, many etiologies are non-drug-related, including heart failure, venous disorders, liver disease, and systemic inflammatory conditions. Peripheral edema is transient and recurrent, as episodes typically resolve with treatment or removal of the underlying cause, such as discontinuation of the offending drug or management of the primary disease. Elevated venous pressure or capillary fluid exchange imbalances make the lower extremities the typical site, with variation based on specific pathophysiological mechanisms. The condition's exclusion separate angioedema or traumatic swelling simplifies its capture as a single conceptual unit, though its broad multifactorial etiology requires domain-aware drug associations.

source_definition: Peripheral neuropathy is a pathological state characterized by structural or functional damage to one or more nerves of the peripheral nervous system â€” defined as all neural tissue outside the brain and spinal cord â€” resulting in clinically manifest dysfunction of sensory and/or motor fibers. The condition encompasses any distribution pattern, including symmetric polyneuropathy, focal mononeuropathy, and asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex, and may follow an acute, subacute, or chronic course. All underlying etiologies are included, among them metabolic and endocrine derangements, toxic and drug-induced injury, immune-mediated and inflammatory processes, hereditary structural abnormalities, infectious causes, and focal compressive or ischemic insults, as well as idiopathic presentations. To meet this phenotype, the patient must demonstrate at least one clinical symptom (such as numbness, tingling, neuropathic pain, or weakness) or at least one objective sign (such as diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, reduced sensation on examination, or measurable motor deficit) attributable to peripheral nerve dysfunction. Pure autonomic neuropathies without any sensory or motor involvement are excluded. Conditions in which the presenting symptoms and signs are entirely explained by central nervous system pathology â€” including myelopathy, cortical lesions, or demyelinating disease confined to central pathways â€” are also excluded.
clinical_rationale: Peripheral neuropathy includes a broad spectrum of causes, many of which are drug-attributable. Neurotoxicity from medications such as chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., platinum compounds, vincristine), certain antibiotics (e.g., metronidazole), antiretrovirals, and others is well-documented. Established mechanisms include axonal transport disruption, mitochondrial toxicity, and direct nerve damage. While the definition provided spans acute, subacute, and chronic courses, the diagnosis of incident peripheral neuropathy aligns with a transient recurrent course when assessing reversible or episodic etiologies, especially under the pharmacovigilance scope. Accurate diagnosis requires clinical correlation with symptoms, objective signs, and exclusion of central nervous system origins. Initial presentation may occur across care settings, though outpatient recognition is most typical. Coding can be challenging due to overlap with metabolic, compressive, and idiopathic neuropathies, but the presence of symptomatic documentation often aids in case identification. Drug causality is plausible in both acute and chronic cases, warranting pharmacovigilance consideration.

source_definition: Peripheral vascular disease is a symptomatic disorder of the arterial or venous vasculature of the upper or lower extremities, characterized by clinically manifest impairment of blood flow resulting in ischemic, obstructive, or hemodynamic consequences. On the arterial side, the condition encompasses symptomatic reduction in limb perfusion due to any etiology â€” including atherosclerotic stenosis or occlusion, inflammatory arteriopathy, thromboembolism, or other obliterative processes â€” presenting as intermittent claudication, rest pain, ischemic ulceration, or gangrene. On the venous side, it includes symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency, acute deep venous thrombosis, and post-thrombotic syndrome manifesting as limb pain, edema, skin changes, or venous ulceration regardless of the underlying cause. The phenotype encompasses disease arising de novo or as a vascular complication of a systemic condition such as diabetes mellitus or connective tissue disease. Excluded are: asymptomatic or incidentally detected vascular abnormalities without clinical manifestation; disease confined to the cerebrovascular, coronary, mesenteric, renal, or splanchnic circulations; and non-vascular conditions that mimic limb ischemia or venous disease through neurological or musculoskeletal mechanisms.
clinical_rationale: Drug-related peripheral vascular disease (PVD) is plausible in both arterial and venous contexts through mechanisms such as drug-induced vasculitis (e.g., hydralazine), thrombosis (e.g., estrogen-containing contraceptives or chemotherapy agents), and vascular complications of systemic drug effects (e.g., corticosteroids leading to secondary diabetes or lipid abnormalities). The condition may result from de novo vascular disease or as a complication of systemic diseases aggravated by drug exposures. The condition is both persistent and episodic, given its chronic nature with potential for flare-ups such as acute ischemia or thrombosis. Both intermittent claudication and venous disease typically present in outpatient settings, but acute manifestations (e.g., arterial embolism or DVT) frequently lead to acute care diagnosis. The clinical definition here spans arterial and venous disease affecting the limbs, but narrows to exclude asymptomatic or unmanifest abnormalities, as well as non-vascular mimics.

source_definition: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is a rare papulosquamous dermatosis characterized by the triad of follicular hyperkeratotic papules with perifollicular orange-red erythema, confluent palmoplantar keratoderma, and pathognomonic islands of uninvolved skin within areas of diffuse cutaneous erythema. The condition encompasses all recognized clinical subtypes (Griffiths Types Iâ€“VI), including classic adult-onset, atypical adult, classic juvenile, limited juvenile, atypical juvenile/familial, and HIV-associated forms, and may range in extent from localized involvement to generalized erythroderma. Drug-induced cases that are clinically and histologically indistinguishable from idiopathic PRP are included regardless of whether a precipitating medication is identified. The diagnosis requires that clinically similar papulosquamous conditions â€” principally psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, and ichthyosiform dermatoses â€” have been considered and excluded on the basis of clinical, dermoscopic, and/or histopathologic assessment, as these entities may closely mimic the morphological features of PRP.
clinical_rationale: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is a rare dermatosis that can be idiopathic or drug-induced. The inclusion of drug-induced PRP within the definition reflects its suitability as a pharmacovigilance outcome. Drugs such as retinoids and immunomodulatory agents have been implicated in some cases. PRP requires differentiation from psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, and ichthyosiform dermatoses through clinical, dermoscopic, and histopathologic assessment, which ensures diagnostic specificity. While idiopathic PRP dominates, drug-induced PRP is biologically plausible and supported by case reports. Its clinical course varies across subtypes: some forms persist chronically, whereas others resolve within months. Care settings span outpatient diagnosis for milder cases and acute dermatologic consultation or hospitalization for generalized erythroderma.

source_definition: Plantar fasciitis is a clinical condition characterized by pain and tenderness localized to the inferior heel and proximal plantar surface of the foot, arising from degenerative or inflammatory pathology of the plantar fascia, most commonly at or near its insertion onto the calcaneal tuberosity. The condition encompasses both idiopathic and biomechanically-driven forms â€” resulting from repetitive mechanical stress, overuse, or intrinsic risk factors such as reduced ankle dorsiflexion, pes planus, or obesity â€” as well as secondary forms presenting as enthesitis in the context of systemic inflammatory disease, including seronegative spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and reactive arthritis. All severity grades are included, spanning acute and chronic refractory presentations. Coexistent peripheral nerve involvement, such as tarsal tunnel syndrome or medial calcaneal nerve entrapment, is not excluded when primary fascial pathology is present. The concept explicitly excludes acute traumatic plantar fascia rupture, calcaneal stress fractures, and bony heel pathology in which the primary disease process is skeletal rather than fascial in origin.
clinical_rationale: Plantar fasciitis is primarily driven by mechanical stress and degenerative/inflammatory pathology of the plantar fascia, with common risk factors including overuse, reduced ankle dorsiflexion, and obesity. Secondary forms are associated with enthesitis in systemic inflammatory diseases like ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and reactive arthritis. This description explicitly excludes traumatic rupture and calcaneal fractures, focusing entirely on fascial pathology. Drug causality is plausible in enthesitis-driven secondary forms, as these are documented side effects of drug classes such as fluoroquinolones and medications affecting collagen or connective tissue integrity. However, idiopathic and biomechanical primary plantar fasciitis lacks a documented drug etiology. This distinction makes the phenotype conditional as a pharmacovigilance outcome, with applicability to drug-induced inflammatory enthesitis forms. Most cases are diagnosed clinically in outpatient settings, though imaging may be obtained in complex or refractory presentations. Characteristic symptoms (e.g., heel pain, localized tenderness) are often coded separately. Follow-up care for refractory or chronic cases is common, though mild transient presentations may resolve without further observation or management.

source_definition: Plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris) is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disease of the skin characterized by dysregulated T-cell activation and keratinocyte hyperproliferation, resulting in well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered by adherent silvery-white scales, most commonly distributed on extensor surfaces, the scalp, and the lumbosacral region. The phenotype encompasses all disease severities, from limited mild involvement to widespread severe disease, without restriction by body surface area or treatment status. This definition is restricted to the chronic plaque morphological subtype and explicitly excludes other psoriasis variants including guttate, pustular (generalized or localized), inverse, and erythrodermic psoriasis. Psoriatic arthritis, which may coexist as part of the broader psoriatic disease spectrum, is not excluded but represents a distinct clinical entity beyond the cutaneous scope of this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Plaque psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disease with a well-characterized etiology involving dysregulated T-cells and keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Drug-induced psoriasis-like eruptions are well-documented for medications such as beta-blockers, lithium, and TNF inhibitors. While its chronic nature suggests ongoing monitoring or management, plaques are typically coded by the diagnosis alone without discrete records of presenting symptoms (e.g., scaling or erythema). As outlined, the phenotype specifically excludes guttate, pustular, erythrodermic, and inverse variants, focusing solely on the chronic plaque subtype. Psoriatic arthritis is clinically distinct but may overlap as part of the broader psoriatic spectrum, which adds complexity in diagnosis but does not alter the focus of the phenotype.

source_definition: Pleural effusion is a pathological state characterized by the abnormal accumulation of free fluid within the pleural space â€” the potential space between the visceral and parietal pleura â€” of sufficient volume to be detectable by physical examination (e.g., dullness to percussion, diminished breath sounds) or diagnostic imaging (e.g., chest radiograph, computed tomography, or thoracic ultrasonography). The phenotype encompasses all fluid subtypes and underlying etiologies, including transudative effusions arising from altered hydrostatic or oncotic pressure gradients (as in congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome), exudative effusions resulting from increased pleural membrane permeability (as in pneumonia, malignancy, or autoimmune disease), hemorrhagic effusions (hemothorax), and chylous effusions (chylothorax), regardless of the primary driving mechanism. The definition explicitly excludes adjacent pleural space pathology that does not constitute free fluid accumulation, including pleural thickening and fibrosis (solid tissue deposition), pneumothorax (pathological air accumulation in the pleural space), and primary or secondary pleural masses.
clinical_rationale: Pleural effusion is a heterogeneous entity with diverse causes, including transudative, exudative, hemorrhagic, or chylous subtypes. Drug-attributable causality is documented in certain forms, such as drug-induced lupus causing exudative effusion, chemotherapy-related or amiodarone-induced pleural effusion, and immune responses from specific drugs. While the majority of pleural effusions have non-drug-related etiology (e.g., heart failure, malignancy, liver disease), a narrower reading focusing on drug-induced pleural effusions could serve as a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. Diagnosis typically requires imaging or thoracentesis, and pleural effusions are predominantly identified during acute care settings due to respiratory compromise or incidental imaging findings. Fluid subtype differentiation and identification of underlying causes require diagnostic workups, and treatment frequently depends on addressing the underlying pathology.

source_definition: Pneumonia is an acute infectious inflammatory process of the lung parenchyma, characterized by the simultaneous presence of a new pulmonary infiltrate on imaging and clinical signs of infection, such as fever, productive cough, or leukocytosis. The phenotype spans all severity levels, from mild presentations amenable to outpatient management to severe cases requiring intensive care and mechanical ventilatory support. An infectious etiology must be the established clinical working diagnosis, although microbiological identification of a specific causative organism is not required. The concept encompasses pneumonia arising from any predisposing mechanism or host context, including aspiration pneumonia, post-obstructive pneumonia distal to structural lesions, and pneumonia occurring in immunocompromised individuals. Explicitly excluded are non-infectious mimics: cardiogenic pulmonary infiltrates secondary to hemodynamic causes such as congestive heart failure, and pulmonary infarction arising from pulmonary embolism, both of which may produce radiographic opacities and systemic inflammatory signs but do not constitute primary infectious parenchymal inflammation.
clinical_rationale: Pneumonia is a suitable pharmacovigilance outcome, as certain drugs may indirectly predispose to its development by impairing host defenses or altering respiratory mechanics (e.g., sedative-induced aspiration, immunosuppression from corticosteroids, chemotherapy, or biologics targeting immune pathways). The supplied definition makes infection a required etiology and explicitly excludes non-infectious mimics such as cardiogenic edema and pulmonary infarction. The condition may vary in severity and care setting, from outpatient-managed mild cases to critically ill patients requiring ICU-level care and mechanical ventilation. It is transient in the sense that an episode resolves (although it may recur), and distinctive symptoms such as cough, fever, and dyspnea are commonly documented alongside diagnostic imaging. A microbial diagnosis is often inferred rather than directly confirmed, and treatment initiation typically precedes high-accuracy microbiological identification. Reliable diagnosis depends heavily on imaging studies and clinical judgment.

source_definition: Pneumonitis is an inflammatory process of the lung parenchyma of non-infectious etiology, characterized by cellular infiltration and exudation within alveolar walls, interstitium, and surrounding lung tissue. The condition spans a full severity continuum, from subclinical presentations detectable only as radiographic ground-glass or interstitial opacities, through symptomatic disease manifesting as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxia, to severe respiratory compromise requiring medical intervention. Recognized etiological subtypes include drug-induced or iatrogenic injury, radiation-induced lung injury, aspiration of non-infectious material, and immune-mediated inflammation occurring in the setting of autoimmune or systemic connective tissue disorders (e.g., lupus pneumonitis, rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease). Infectious pneumonia â€” regardless of pathogen â€” is explicitly excluded. Pulmonary inflammation arising as a direct secondary consequence of a distinct primary cardiopulmonary process (e.g., hydrostatic pulmonary edema from heart failure, ARDS attributable to sepsis) is excluded, as is established pulmonary fibrosis representing a post-inflammatory fibrotic sequela (e.g., usual interstitial pneumonia pattern, end-stage honeycombing), which is considered a distinct downstream state rather than active pneumonitis.
clinical_rationale: Pneumonitis is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome under its drug-induced subtype, as numerous medications, including immune checkpoint inhibitors, methotrexate, and certain antimicrobials, have been implicated in inducing non-infectious inflammatory lung disease. The label excludes infectious pneumonia and post-inflammatory fibrosis, focusing instead on acute or subacute inflammation of the lung parenchyma due to non-infectious causes. The clinical course is transient for individual episodes but may recur, particularly in the case of repeated drug exposure or underlying autoimmune disorders. Diagnosis typically requires radiographic imaging combined with clinical correlation, often necessitating exclusion of infections or alternative causes via laboratory tests or biopsies. Both outpatient and acute settings can capture incident cases depending on severity, with hypoxia and respiratory compromise requiring acute care more often. Post-index follow-up is common to assess resolution, manage sequelae, or ensure avoidance of triggers.

source_definition: Pollakiuria is a clinical symptom characterized by a voiding frequency that exceeds the age-appropriate norm, manifesting as an abnormally elevated number of voluntary urination episodes throughout the day. Each voiding episode typically involves normal or reduced voided volumes, distinguishing this condition from polyuria, in which urinary frequency is a secondary consequence of pathologically elevated total daily urine output. Pollakiuria encompasses all etiologies â€” including but not limited to bladder hypersensitivity, lower urinary tract inflammation, structural or obstructive pathology, and neurogenic voiding dysfunction â€” without restriction by underlying cause. It is conceptually distinct from nocturia, which refers specifically to nocturnal voiding frequency as a separately defined clinical phenomenon, and from urgency urinary incontinence, in which involuntary urine loss accompanies or precedes the voiding episode. The defining feature is the increased frequency of volitional, continent voiding acts beyond what is developmentally and physiologically expected for the individual's age.
clinical_rationale: Pollakiuria is a symptomatic term denoting increased daytime urinary frequency without specifying the underlying etiology, and can result from various causes including pharmacological effects. Drug-induced pollakiuria is plausible via mechanisms such as bladder irritation, altered neurogenic signaling (e.g., medications affecting the central or peripheral nervous system), or hormonal effects. Notably, anticholinergics, diuretics, or bladder irritants may contribute. However, as a broad symptom description encompassing both drug and non-drug causes, pollakiuria as described requires narrowing to drug-attributable cases to qualify as a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. The clinical presentation often corresponds to outpatient care, and documentation typically includes subjective symptom description without discrete recorded markers for causative diagnosis, though urinalysis or imaging may be pursued to evaluate structural or inflammatory etiologies.

source_definition: Polymyositis is an inflammatory myopathy defined by active immune-mediated inflammation of skeletal muscle, presenting with symmetric proximal muscle weakness of any severity, predominantly affecting the shoulder and pelvic girdle musculature. The phenotype encompasses all active disease phases regardless of duration, and includes overlap myositis occurring in the setting of connective tissue diseases (such as systemic lupus erythematosus or systemic sclerosis), as well as cases where the clinical presentation is indistinguishable from idiopathic polymyositis despite an identifiable precipitant such as a drug or infectious agent. This phenotype excludes dermatomyositis (distinguished by characteristic cutaneous manifestations), inclusion body myositis (distinguished by distal muscle predominance and distinct histopathological features), non-inflammatory myopathies (including muscular dystrophies, metabolic myopathies, and endocrine myopathies), and rhabdomyolysis (acute non-immune-mediated muscle fiber breakdown secondary to trauma, exertion, or toxic injury).
clinical_rationale: Polymyositis is a recognized pharmacovigilance outcome, though rare in drug causality. Immune-mediated skeletal muscle inflammation has been reported with statins, checkpoint inhibitors, and other agents capable of triggering muscle-targeted autoimmunity. This phenotype spans idiopathic polymyositis, overlap myositis secondary to connective tissue diseases, and immune-mediated myositis with identifiable precipitants, including drug-induced cases. The exclusion of other distinct myopathies (dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, and non-inflammatory myopathies) focuses the definition on immune-mediated inflammatory muscle disease. Polymyositis is persistent due to ongoing disease labeling even if inflammation remits, and diagnosis requires supporting clinical findings, autoimmune serologies, and/or muscle biopsy. Incident cases are predominantly diagnosed in outpatient care but may also be recognized in acute care for severe weakness. Although weakness is symptomatic, discrete symptom coding is uncommon, and definitive diagnosis typically requires diagnostic testing and active treatment such as glucocorticoids or immunosuppressants.

source_definition: Portal hypertension is a pathophysiological state characterized by abnormally elevated pressure within the portal venous system, defined hemodynamically by a hepatic venous pressure gradient of 5 mmHg or greater. The condition arises from increased resistance to portal blood flow, increased portal venous inflow, or both, and may originate at any level of the portal circuit: pre-hepatic, due to obstruction of the portal or splenic vein proximal to the liver; intrahepatic, due to resistance within the hepatic parenchyma or sinusoids as seen in cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic liver disease; or post-hepatic, due to impaired hepatic venous outflow from hepatic vein or inferior vena cava obstruction, or from elevated central venous pressure transmitted to the hepatic veins by primary cardiac disease such as right-sided heart failure or constrictive pericarditis. The phenotype encompasses the full etiological and anatomical spectrum of portal hypertensive states and does not require the presence of clinically manifest complications such as gastroesophageal varices, ascites, or splenomegaly.
clinical_rationale: Portal hypertension is a complex state with a hemodynamic definition and multiple etiologies, including cirrhosis, hepatic vein obstruction, and systemic conditions like right-sided heart failure. Drug-induced portal hypertension is plausible but rare, mostly mediated by hepatic fibrosis (e.g., methotrexate, chemotherapy agents), or vascular injury (e.g., peliosis hepatis). While portal hypertension is persistent due to the underlying structural pathology, recurrence may apply only in narrow settings due to dynamic causal conditions such as transient cardiac dysfunction. Diagnosis typically requires advanced imaging or invasive hemodynamic studies, often ordered to investigate complications like varices or ascites. While definite pharmacovigilance relevance exists for cirrhotic drug etiologies, non-cirrhotic cases are less well-documented. Incident cases are commonly identified in acute care settings during evaluation for hemorrhage, ascites, or concurrent liver disease.

source_definition: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related psychiatric syndrome that develops following direct or indirect exposure to an event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. The disorder is defined by the persistent co-occurrence of all four symptom clusters: intrusion symptoms (e.g., involuntary distressing memories, flashbacks, trauma-related nightmares); persistent effortful avoidance of trauma-associated internal or external stimuli; negative alterations in cognition and mood (e.g., persistent negative affect, distorted self-blame, emotional numbing, persistent inability to experience positive emotions); and marked alterations in arousal and reactivity (e.g., hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, sleep disturbance, irritability). Symptoms must persist for more than one month, cause clinically significant distress or functional impairment, and not be attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition. All severity levels and subtypesâ€”including the dissociative subtype characterized by depersonalization or derealizationâ€”are encompassed. This definition explicitly excludes Acute Stress Disorder (symptom duration <1 month), Adjustment Disorder, and Prolonged Grief Disorder, as these represent distinct clinical entities that differ from PTSD in temporal course, symptom structure, or etiological mechanism.
clinical_rationale: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is well-established as a psychiatric condition related to exposure to traumatic events, which can include drug-associated etiologies. Certain medications, such as psychedelics or certain experimental treatments, have been associated with inducing or exacerbating PTSD-related symptoms in sensitive individuals under specific circumstances. PTSD is a persistent psychiatric syndrome diagnosed based on standardized criteria, and its diagnosis generally remains stable throughout life, even though symptom severity may fluctuate. Incident PTSD is primarily diagnosed in outpatient settings, although acute crisis episodes may occasionally present in acute care. Diagnostic criteria rely on clinical evaluation, supported by psychiatric measures and patient history rather than objective testing.

source_definition: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is an acute neurological syndrome arising from failure of cerebrovascular autoregulation, in which breakdown of the blood-brain barrier results in vasogenic edema that preferentially affects the posterior cerebral white matter, most prominently the parieto-occipital regions. The condition manifests across a full clinical spectrum, ranging from headache, visual disturbances, and confusion to seizures, status epilepticus, and impaired consciousness, and may be precipitated by any pathophysiological state capable of overwhelming autoregulatory capacity, including acute severe hypertension, eclampsia or preeclampsia, calcineurin inhibitor or cytotoxic drug exposure, sepsis, and systemic autoimmune disease. The phenotype is defined by the shared underlying mechanism of autoregulatory failure and associated vasogenic edema rather than by a specific etiology or trigger. Explicitly excluded are conditions producing posterior cerebral edema through structurally distinct mechanisms, including posterior circulation ischemic stroke, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and space-occupying intracranial lesions. Confirmation of clinical or radiological reversibility is not required for inclusion, as follow-up documentation may be absent in real-world settings.
clinical_rationale: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is an acute neurological condition associated with autoregulatory failure that leads to vasogenic cerebral edema, primarily affecting the posterior white matter. Drug-attributable etiologies are well documented, including calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., cyclosporine), cytotoxic chemotherapies, and certain immunosuppressants. While the majority of cases resolve with removal or management of the inciting factor, some may lead to permanent neurological sequelae. Given its acute onset and links to drug exposures, this is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. Diagnosis typically relies on characteristic clinical presentations combined with brain imaging findings, most commonly MRI, to confirm the presence of vasogenic edema. The description includes a wide range of severities and potential triggers, underscoring the need for operational specificity. Symptom documentation in structured data may vary depending on care setting but usually forms part of the diagnostic approach for PRES.

source_definition: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy-specific hypertensive syndrome defined by the new onset of elevated blood pressure (systolic â‰¥140 mmHg or diastolic â‰¥90 mmHg) in combination with significant proteinuria (â‰¥300 mg per 24-hour period or equivalent), arising after 20 weeks of gestation in a woman with no history of pre-existing hypertension, or presenting de novo within six weeks postpartum. The syndrome reflects underlying systemic endothelial dysfunction and abnormal placentation, and encompasses the full severity spectrum from mild hypertensive-proteinuric disease through presentations with severe features (blood pressure â‰¥160/110 mmHg or severe proteinuria). Eclampsia â€” defined as new-onset grand mal seizures not attributable to another neurological cause occurring in the context of the syndrome â€” is included as the most severe neurological manifestation of the same pathophysiological continuum. HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count) is included when it co-occurs with confirmed hypertension and proteinuria, representing severe end-organ expression of the underlying endothelial injury. Explicitly excluded are: superimposed preeclampsia arising in women with documented pre-existing or chronic hypertension; isolated gestational hypertension without proteinuria; and HELLP syndrome occurring in the absence of hypertension and proteinuria.
clinical_rationale: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy-related hypertensive disorder with endothelial dysfunction and abnormal placentation as pathophysiological underpinnings. It is a pharmacovigilance-relevant outcome due to established associations with drug exposure, including agents affecting placental development or endothelial function. Known drug-related etiologies include angiogenesis inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and immunosuppressants like cyclosporine. The clinical course is transient, as the syndrome resolves after delivery or termination of pregnancy, but complications can occur postpartum. Diagnosis typically requires laboratory evidence of proteinuria, and incident cases are often identified in acute care settings due to their maternal or fetal risk. HELLP syndrome and eclampsia are related entities that fall within the preeclampsia spectrum, while isolated gestational hypertension and superimposed preeclampsia on chronic hypertension are excluded by the supplied definition.

source_definition: Primary adrenal insufficiency is an acquired disorder characterized by the structural failure of the adrenal cortex to produce adequate quantities of both glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), resulting in a compensatory elevation of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The phenotype encompasses the chronic disease state â€” presenting with fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia â€” as well as acute adrenal crisis, a life-threatening decompensation precipitated by physiological stress and defined by severe hypotension, vomiting, and circulatory collapse. Recognized etiologies include autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex (Addison's disease), infectious infiltration (e.g., tuberculosis, fungal infections), adrenal hemorrhage or infarction, and infiltrative diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis, malignant infiltration). Excluded from this phenotype are central adrenal insufficiency arising from pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction; congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which represents an inherited biosynthetic enzyme defect rather than acquired cortical destruction; critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI), a reversible functional state of relative cortisol deficiency without structural adrenal pathology; and bilateral adrenalectomy, representing intentional surgical removal rather than disease-driven gland failure.
clinical_rationale: Primary adrenal insufficiency arises from acquired destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, and is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome due to documented drug-induced etiologies such as autoimmune adrenalitis triggered by immune checkpoint inhibitors, and adrenal hemorrhage or infarction as a rare adverse effect of anticoagulant use. The phenotype encompasses both chronic adrenal insufficiency and acute adrenal crisis, which may manifest as severe hypotension, vomiting, and circulatory collapse. Central adrenal insufficiency, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, CIRCI, and bilateral adrenalectomy are explicitly excluded. Diagnosis typically involves laboratory confirmation of cortisol deficiency and elevated ACTH levels alongside clinical features, and acute care is often needed for adrenal crises. Chronic primary adrenal insufficiency is a stable condition requiring lifelong hormonal replacement, while adrenal crises represent transient decompensations based on physiological stress.

source_definition: Primary angle-closure glaucoma is a form of glaucomatous optic neuropathy in which obstruction of aqueous humor outflow results from apposition or adhesion of the peripheral iris to the trabecular meshwork, causing sustained or episodic elevation of intraocular pressure that produces characteristic optic nerve head damage â€” including neuroretinal rim loss and optic disc cupping â€” with corresponding visual field defects. The designation "primary" signifies that the angle closure arises from inherent anatomical predisposition, typically shallow anterior chamber depth, short axial length, relative anterior lens position, or pupillary block, and not from an identifiable, mechanistically distinct pathological process such as neovascularization of the angle, uveitic posterior synechiae, anterior segment dysgenesis, or traumatic or lens-related displacement. The phenotype encompasses both acute presentations â€” characterized by a sudden, symptomatic angle-closure crisis with markedly elevated intraocular pressure â€” and chronic presentations, in which progressive synechial closure produces insidious optic nerve damage, provided that glaucomatous optic neuropathy is confirmed in either form. Incidental ocular findings that coexist but do not serve as the mechanistic driver of angle closure do not preclude classification within this phenotype. Cases of angle-closure suspect or primary angle closure without documented optic nerve involvement are explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Primary angle-closure glaucoma is well-defined as a form of glaucomatous optic neuropathy caused by anatomical predisposition to angle closure, leading to elevated intraocular pressure and characteristic optic nerve damage. This phenotype excludes non-glaucomatous forms of angle closure, such as those caused by secondary pathologies or those without documented optic nerve involvement. Medications, such as anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, and sulfonamides, are known to precipitate acute angle-closure episodes in susceptible individuals, making the acute presentation of primary angle-closure glaucoma a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. Chronic presentations are largely driven by anatomy rather than drug exposure. The clinical definition provided clearly distinguishes drug-attributable crises from chronic disease progression, warranting a conditional designation as a pharmacovigilance outcome.

source_definition: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic, progressive autoimmune liver disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of the small intrahepatic bile ducts (interlobular and septal bile ducts), resulting in sustained cholestasis, portal inflammation, and progressive hepatic fibrosis that may advance to biliary cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease. The phenotype encompasses the full disease spectrum â€” from asymptomatic biochemical cholestasis (typically an isolated elevation of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase) through symptomatic disease (fatigue, pruritus, jaundice) and advanced cirrhotic stages. Diagnosis requires at least two of three accepted criteria: a cholestatic biochemical profile; the presence of anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA, particularly the M2 subtype) or, in AMA-negative cases, PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies (anti-sp100, anti-gp210); or compatible liver histology demonstrating non-suppurative destructive cholangitis and interlobular bile duct loss. AMA-negative cases fulfilling biochemical and histological criteria are included. Patients with concurrent autoimmune hepatitis features meeting criteria for PBC-AIH overlap syndrome are included within this phenotype. Explicitly excluded are primary sclerosing cholangitis â€” a mechanistically and anatomically distinct large- and medium-duct cholangiopathy â€” and secondary biliary cirrhosis arising from mechanical biliary obstruction such as choledocholithiasis, biliary strictures, or post-surgical bile duct injury.
clinical_rationale: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a well-documented autoimmune condition that has established links to drug-induced etiologies. Certain medications, such as nitrofurantoin and minocycline, have been associated with drug-induced autoimmune liver diseases resembling or causing PBC. The condition involves immune-mediated destruction of interlobular bile ducts, leading to sustained cholestasis, hepatic inflammation, fibrosis, and potentially cirrhosis. Diagnostic criteria require a cholestatic biochemical profile, specific autoantibodies, or compatible liver histology. Its chronic nature makes it a persistent condition with possible progression to advanced liver disease. The provided description encompasses a wide range of disease stages, from subclinical biochemical abnormalities to end-stage liver disease, but explicitly excludes primary sclerosing cholangitis and secondary biliary cirrhosis of mechanical origin. Thus, it is appropriate as a pharmacovigilance outcome when drug causality is considered. Laboratory testing for cholestatic markers (elevated alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyltransferase) and autoantibodies is essential for confirming the diagnosis.

source_definition: Primary malignancy is defined as the incident, newly diagnosed occurrence of an invasive neoplasm arising at its anatomical site of origin, encompassing both solid tumors (including carcinomas, sarcomas, and other tissue-derived malignancies) and hematologic malignancies (including leukemias, lymphomas, and plasma cell disorders). The phenotype requires confirmation of invasive growth, defined as the extension of malignant cells beyond the basement membrane or equivalent structural boundary, thereby excluding all pre-invasive and in situ lesions. Non-melanoma skin cancers (basal cell carcinoma and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the skin) are explicitly excluded on the basis of their distinct biological behavior, near-universal underreporting, and divergent clinical trajectory relative to other malignancies. The phenotype is restricted to first-ever, incident diagnoses; local or distant recurrences of a previously identified malignancy and subsequent second primary tumors arising in patients with a prior cancer history are not captured under this definition.
clinical_rationale: Primary malignancies encompass a broad spectrum of invasive neoplasms, both solid tumors and hematologic cancers, and can serve as pharmacovigilance outcomes in drug safety surveillance due to documented associations with carcinogenicity, drug-mediated immunosuppression, and DNA damage. Drugs like chemotherapeutic agents, immunosuppressants, and radiation-sensitizing medications are recognized for their potential carcinogenic effects. The exclusion of non-melanoma skin cancers simplifies cohort logic and aligns with routine underreporting for these conditions. The focus on invasive neoplasms excludes pre-invasive or in situ lesions due to their distinct biological behavior and clinical management. The definition specifies inclusion of first-ever diagnoses, highlighting the importance of ensuring no prior cancer history at index for accurate cohort creation.

source_definition: Primary open-angle glaucoma is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy characterized by the concurrent presence of characteristic structural deterioration of the optic nerve head â€” including enlargement of the optic cup, thinning of the neuroretinal rim, and loss of the retinal nerve fiber layer â€” together with reproducible visual field defects consistent with glaucomatous damage, occurring in an eye with an open, unoccludable anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy. The condition is primary in nature, meaning no identifiable underlying etiology accounts for the optic nerve injury; secondary open-angle glaucomas arising from pseudoexfoliation syndrome, pigmentary dispersion, uveitis, ocular trauma, neovascularization, or corticosteroid exposure are explicitly excluded. Intraocular pressure level is not a defining criterion, and normal-tension glaucoma â€” in which the full structural and functional phenotype is present despite IOP within the statistically normal range â€” is encompassed within this definition. Ocular hypertension, defined as elevated IOP without optic nerve damage or visual field loss, is excluded as a risk state rather than established disease. Pre-perimetric presentations in which structural damage exists without detectable functional loss are likewise excluded. Non-glaucomatous optic neuropathies that may produce superficially similar structural or functional findings â€” including ischemic, compressive, inflammatory, and hereditary optic neuropathies â€” are excluded on the basis of distinct pathophysiological mechanisms.
clinical_rationale: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic optic neuropathy with progressive structural and functional damage, unrelated to secondary causes like corticosteroid exposure. It excludes secondary open-angle glaucomas and pre-perimetric states where structural damage lacks functional loss. Although corticosteroid exposure is a well-documented risk factor for secondary open-angle glaucoma, primary open-angle glaucoma explicitly arises without identifiable etiologic factors, limiting attribution of causality to drugs. POAG is a lifelong, progressive disease requiring sustained management, often diagnosed in outpatient settings via characteristic optic nerve structural changes and visual field tests. Symptoms are usually silent until advanced stages, making it difficult to identify discrete recorded symptoms prior to diagnosis. Diagnosis necessitates specialized ophthalmologic examination and testing, confirming characteristic optic nerve head changes and excluding other neuropathies. Patients nearly always require ongoing treatment and follow-up, including intraocular pressure-lowering therapies, to prevent disease progression.

source_definition: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic, idiopathic, fibro-inflammatory disease of the large bile ducts â€” intrahepatic, extrahepatic, or both â€” characterized by progressive periductal inflammation and fibrosis that leads to multifocal biliary strictures and upstream ductal dilation as demonstrated by cholangiography. The disease follows a progressive course spanning from an asymptomatic phase marked by cholestatic liver enzyme elevation through to biliary cirrhosis, portal hypertension, hepatic decompensation, and end-stage liver failure. The phenotype encompasses all disease stages along this continuum. Cases in which a secondary etiology for bile duct injury â€” including choledocholithiasis, post-surgical or ischemic strictures, recurrent pyogenic cholangitis, AIDS cholangiopathy, or toxic bile duct injury â€” has been definitively established are excluded; cases in which such etiologies have not been formally evaluated or remain uncertain at the time of diagnosis are retained within scope.
