Sclerosing cholangitis attributable to IgG4-related systemic disease is excluded only when that diagnosis has been formally established through serologic or histopathologic criteria. Small-duct PSC, in which cholangiographic findings are absent and diagnosis rests on liver biopsy alone, is outside the scope of this phenotype. Concurrent autoimmune hepatitis features (PSCâ€“AIH overlap syndrome) do not disqualify a case from inclusion, as the primary biliary pathology remains PSC.
clinical_rationale: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic fibro-inflammatory bile duct disease associated with progressive damage leading to liver failure. The etiology is idiopathic, but drug-induced cases are recognized as sclerosing cholangitis rather than primary, necessitating exclusion of toxic bile duct injury and other secondary causes. This makes PSC unsuitable as a direct pharmacovigilance outcome unless restricted to specific secondary or toxigenic subtypes, which are outside the phenotype scope as defined. PSC follows a persistent, progressive course with no clinical resolution, making the label permanent. Incident diagnosis may occur in outpatient settings for asymptomatic cases with cholestatic labs, but acute biliary decompensation is frequently recognized in acute care. Exclusion of secondary etiologies is critical for specificity, underscoring reliance on diagnostic imaging and histopathology.

source_definition: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a severe, progressive demyelinating disease of the central nervous system caused by reactivation and lytic infection of oligodendrocytes by the JC virus (JCV; human polyomavirus 2) in the setting of significantly impaired cellular immunity. The condition arises exclusively in individuals with deficient cell-mediated immune surveillance, irrespective of the underlying etiology of immunosuppression, including but not limited to HIV/AIDS, hematological malignancies, solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and iatrogenic immunosuppression from therapeutic agents. Pathologically, the disease is characterized by multifocal, asymmetric destruction of cerebral white matter due to direct viral cytolysis of oligodendrocytes, manifesting clinically as progressive, often asymmetric neurological deficits such as motor weakness, cognitive decline, visual disturbances, ataxia, and aphasia. Diagnosis is established on a confirmed basis by detection of JCV DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid via polymerase chain reaction or by histopathological or immunohistochemical demonstration of JCV on brain biopsy, or on a probable basis when characteristic multifocal white matter lesions on neuroimaging â€” typically T1-hypointense and T2/FLAIR-hyperintense without mass effect in classical presentations â€” are present alongside a compatible and progressive clinical syndrome in a known immunocompromised host. This definition explicitly excludes PML-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (PML-IRIS), which constitutes a distinct pathophysiological state arising from dysregulated immune recovery following treatment of the underlying immunosuppression rather than from ongoing unchecked viral replication.
clinical_rationale: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a known pharmacovigilance outcome due to its association with iatrogenic immunosuppression. Its occurrence is linked to several immunosuppressive therapies, including monoclonal antibodies like natalizumab, rituximab, and efalizumab, as documented in safety communications and literature. The condition is highly specific to immune-compromised individuals and progresses relentlessly without immune recovery. PML resolves only in cases where immune system reconstitution is achieved, and in such cases, the clinical challenge becomes differentiating PML from PML-IRIS. Its diagnosis critically relies on neuroimaging and laboratory testing (e.g., detection of JC virus DNA), which are required for confirmation. Given its pathogenesis and reliance on effective immunosuppression for onset, it is appropriate to classify it as persistent and stable, given that resolution requires a complete turnaround in immune function rather than natural history. Most cases are diagnosed in hospitalized settings, reflecting the severity of presentation and the need for specialty care.

source_definition: Prostate cancer is a primary malignant neoplasm arising from the glandular epithelial cells of the prostate gland, characterized histologically as invasive adenocarcinoma originating within the prostatic tissue. The phenotype encompasses the full continuum of invasive disease, from organ-confined localized tumors through locally advanced disease with extraprostatic extension or seminal vesicle invasion, to distant metastatic spread, and includes all histological grades from well-differentiated (Gleason score 6 / Grade Group 1) to poorly differentiated (Gleason score 9â€“10 / Grade Group 5). The definition is restricted to confirmed invasive adenocarcinoma of prostatic origin and explicitly excludes pre-malignant precursor lesions such as high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (HGPIN) and atypical small acinar proliferation (ASAP), rare non-glandular prostatic malignancies including neuroendocrine carcinoma, ductal adenocarcinoma, and urothelial carcinoma, and secondary malignancies involving the prostate via direct extension or hematogenous/lymphatic metastasis from a non-prostatic primary tumor.
clinical_rationale: Prostate cancer, specifically invasive adenocarcinoma arising from glandular epithelial cells of the prostate, has been associated with certain pharmacological agents. Antiandrogens and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors have complex roles in disease progression and detection, with some studies suggesting potential modulation of cancer risk. Rare cases of secondary prostate malignancies from chemotherapeutic agents or radiation-induced transformations have also been reported. The definition explicitly excludes pre-malignant lesions and secondary prostate involvement from non-prostatic primaries, ensuring a focus on primary invasive adenocarcinoma. The condition is usually long-term once diagnosed and is characterized by a persistent course, though disease stages and management intensity may vary. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, imaging studies, and histological confirmation are essential for diagnosis. This phenotype is well-suited for pharmacovigilance surveillance within its defined scope.

source_definition: Prostatitis is a clinical syndrome encompassing all recognized forms of prostatic inflammation, classified according to the NIH taxonomy into four categories: acute bacterial prostatitis (Category I), characterized by sudden-onset systemic infection with bacterial invasion of the prostate; chronic bacterial prostatitis (Category II), defined by recurrent urinary tract infection with persistent prostatic bacterial colonization; chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (Category III), characterized by pelvic pain lasting three or more months with or without evidence of leukocytosis in prostatic secretions, in the absence of identifiable uropathogens; and asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis (Category IV), defined by the incidental detection of prostatic inflammation on histology or semen analysis without patient-reported symptoms. The phenotype includes all etiologies of prostatic inflammation â€” infectious, autoimmune, iatrogenic (including radiation- and procedure-induced), and granulomatous forms secondary to systemic disease such as tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, or intravesical BCG therapy â€” as well as complications arising directly from prostatic inflammation, including prostatic abscess and inflammation associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Excluded from this phenotype are: prostatic inflammation identified solely as an incidental finding in the context of a primary diagnosis of prostate cancer, where the dominant pathological process is neoplastic rather than inflammatory; and inflammation or infection confined to anatomically distinct adjacent structures, including the epididymis, testis, and urethra, in the absence of concurrent prostatic involvement.
clinical_rationale: Prostatitis is a broad syndrome encompassing infectious and non-infectious etiologies, several of which may plausibly arise from or be exacerbated by pharmacological exposures. Drug-induced manifestations include granulomatous prostatitis (e.g., secondary to intravesical BCG therapy), autoimmune-related prostatic inflammation (potentially triggered by immune checkpoint inhibitors), and bacterial prostatitis secondary to antimicrobial resistance patterns influenced by prior drug use. Acute bacterial prostatitis is reliably transient and incident cases are commonly detected in acute care settings, whereas chronic pelvic pain syndrome exhibits a relapsing course in some patients. Coding captures are expected to be heterogeneous across the NIH categories, and careful attention to explanatory conditions (e.g., prostate cancer) is necessary to ensure face validity of records selected for surveillance applications.

source_definition: Proteinuria is defined as the persistent, pathological excretion of protein in the urine at clinically significant levels, typically exceeding 300â€“500 mg per day or a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of â‰¥0.3, and extending through nephrotic-range excretion at levels â‰¥3.5 g per day. The phenotype encompasses the full spectrum of protein excretion arising from any underlying pathophysiological mechanism, including disruption of glomerular filtration barrier integrity, impaired tubular reabsorption of filtered proteins, and systemic overflow of low-molecular-weight proteins that saturate tubular handling capacity. Proteinuria occurring as a renal manifestation of systemic disease â€” including but not limited to diabetes mellitus, hypertension, systemic lupus erythematosus, and amyloidosis â€” is included within this phenotype. Transient and functional protein excretion that is self-limiting and not reflective of an underlying structural or pathological renal process, such as orthostatic, exercise-induced, or febrile proteinuria, is explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Proteinuria reflects pathological kidney involvement, often secondary to systemic diseases or drug toxicity. Drug-induced proteinuria is plausible through mechanisms such as nephrotoxicity from NSAIDs, anti-VEGF agents, bisphosphonates, or cisplatin. Although transient and functional types of proteinuria are excluded by this definition, persistent proteinuria as described is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome with a documented etiologic link to medications. The condition is persistent unless treated, with disease management focusing on controlling the underlying cause and halting renal progression. It is commonly diagnosed in outpatient settings through urine tests, though severe cases may present in acute care due to complications. Symptom codes for proteinuria are seldom uniquely distinct from the diagnosis itself, and the condition virtually always requires confirmatory diagnostic testing. Expected sequelae include chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal failure, necessitating follow-up.

source_definition: Prurigo Nodularis is a chronic neuroimmune inflammatory skin disorder characterized by the presence of multiple intensely pruritic, firm, hyperkeratotic papules and nodules, distributed predominantly on the extensor surfaces of the extremities and trunk, arising from a self-perpetuating itch-scratch cycle driven by dysregulated peripheral and central sensitization of cutaneous sensory neurons. The condition encompasses the full clinical spectrum of disease burden, from limited nodular presentations to widespread, disfiguring eruptions, and includes both idiopathic cases and those arising secondary to an underlying systemic or dermatologic trigger such as atopic dermatitis, chronic renal insufficiency, hepatic disease, or HIV infection. Prurigo Nodularis is defined by its chronic, neuroimmune pathophysiology and is explicitly distinguished from nodular scabies and other infestation-driven nodular hypersensitivity reactions, which resolve upon eradication of the causative organism, and from hypertrophic lichen planus, which represents a distinct lichenoid interface dermatitis with CD8+ T-cell-mediated keratinocyte destruction and a characteristically different clinical distribution.
clinical_rationale: Prurigo nodularis is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by an itch-scratch cycle. While idiopathic cases of prurigo nodularis are common, secondary forms of the disease can arise as a consequence of systemic or dermatologic conditions, including underlying chronic conditions such as chronic renal insufficiency or hepatic disease. Drug-induced etiology has been reported in connection with certain medications, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors or targeted therapies used in cancer treatments, which are known to cause severe pruritic reactions and may contribute to the formation of nodular lesions through immune dysregulation. However, evidence linking medications specifically to prurigo nodularis, rather than generalized pruritus or other dermatologic side effects, is more scarce. This condition is persistent and primarily managed chronically through symptomatic treatments to alleviate pruritus and to control inflammation. A substantial fraction of cases present in outpatient care due to their chronic nature and severe pruritic symptoms, although complex or refractory cases may necessitate dermatology specialty care. Differential diagnosis is critical to distinguish prurigo nodularis from nodular scabies, hypertrophic lichen planus, or other conditions with similar clinical presentations.

source_definition: Pruritus is a subjective, unpleasant cutaneous sensation that elicits the desire or reflex to scratch, arising from the activation of peripheral pruritoceptive nerve fibers and their central processing pathways. The phenotype encompasses itch of any underlying origin â€” including primary dermatological, systemic, neuropathic, psychogenic, or mixed etiologies â€” and is not restricted by duration or severity, provided the sensation constitutes a clinically recognized symptom beyond normal, transient physiological itch that resolves spontaneously following a benign stimulus. Excluded from this definition are qualitatively distinct cutaneous sensory disturbances â€” specifically dysesthesia, burning, stinging, or formication (crawling sensations) â€” which, though they may co-occur with pruritus, represent separate neurophysiological phenomena and do not constitute itch in the pruritoceptive sense.
clinical_rationale: Pruritus is a highly nonspecific symptom arising from diverse etiologies, including drug reactions (e.g., opioid-induced itch), systemic disease (e.g., cholestasis, uremia), skin conditions (e.g., eczema, psoriasis), neuropathic causes (e.g., post-herpetic itch), and psychogenic factors. Drug-induced pruritus can occur via histaminergic and non-histaminergic pathways, making it a valid pharmacovigilance outcome under a narrowed scope focused on acquired or drug-related causes. Routine clinical documentation of pruritus is common but not universally standardized, as it may be recorded as the definitive symptom without specification of the underlying cause. It is an ambulatory-care-dominant presentation with broad variability in severity and diagnostic approach. While diagnostic tests may be employed to identify underlying causes, they are not required solely to recognize the presence of pruritus as a symptom.

source_definition: Pseudoaldosteronism is an acquired syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess caused by exogenous exposure to substances that either inhibit renal 11Î²-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11Î²-HSD2) â€” thereby allowing endogenous cortisol to occupy and activate mineralocorticoid receptors â€” or directly activate mineralocorticoid receptors through non-aldosterone ligands. Causative agents include glycyrrhizin-containing products (licorice, herbal preparations, chewing tobacco), carbenoxolone, and exogenous mineralocorticoid compounds regardless of therapeutic intent. The syndrome is biochemically defined by hypokalemia and/or suppressed plasma renin activity in the presence of low or inappropriately normal serum aldosterone, a pattern that distinguishes it from primary and secondary hyperaldosteronism where aldosterone is elevated. Clinical features such as hypertension and metabolic alkalosis are characteristic but not required for diagnosis. Heritable monogenic syndromes producing a similar biochemical phenotype (e.g., Liddle syndrome, apparent mineralocorticoid excess due to genetic 11Î²-HSD2 deficiency) are excluded from this concept.
clinical_rationale: Pseudoaldosteronism is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome because it is caused by exogenous substances such as glycyrrhizin in licorice and tobacco, carbenoxolone, and exogenous mineralocorticoid compounds. The mechanism involves inhibition of renal 11β-HSD2 or direct activation of mineralocorticoid receptors, leading to a biochemical phenotype that includes hypokalemia and suppressed plasma renin activity in the context of low or inappropriately normal serum aldosterone. This acquired condition excludes monogenic syndromes like Liddle syndrome and genetic 11β-HSD2 deficiency, which are non-drug-related and thus outside the scope of drug safety surveillance. Diagnosis relies on biochemical criteria rather than discrete symptoms, and while hypertension and metabolic alkalosis are characteristic, they are not universally present.

source_definition: Psoriatic arthritis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory arthropathy that occurs in association with psoriatic skin or nail disease, characterized by inflammation affecting peripheral joints, axial structures, entheses, and/or digits (dactylitis), in any combination and at any severity. The diagnosis requires documented inflammatory involvement of at least one musculoskeletal structure beyond the skin; psoriasis alone, in the absence of joint or entheseal pathology, does not constitute this phenotype. The condition is seronegative in nature, and cases where seropositive rheumatoid arthritis provides the primary explanation for joint inflammation â€” even in the presence of co-existing psoriasis â€” are excluded. Arthritis arising as a reactive or post-infectious process, including other seronegative spondyloarthropathies triggered by identifiable infectious etiologies, is likewise excluded.
clinical_rationale: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a validated pharmacovigilance outcome due to known drug-attributable triggers, including immune checkpoint inhibitors and drug-induced psoriasis that progresses to PsA. The condition typically follows a chronic pattern but involves recurrent episodes of inflammation in affected joints or other musculoskeletal structures. Diagnosis is predominantly clinical but supported by imaging or laboratory tests to confirm synovitis, dactylitis, or enthesitis, and to differentiate PsA from other arthropathies. The associated psoriasis makes outpatient diagnosis likely unless symptoms are severe or disabling. The definition excludes non-inflammatory joint pain or arthritis arising from infections or seropositive (e.g., rheumatoid) processes, which reinforces diagnostic specificity.

source_definition: Psychosis is a discrete, acute clinical episode characterized by the active presence of one or more positive psychotic symptoms â€” including hallucinations (perceptions without an external stimulus), delusions (fixed false beliefs resistant to contrary evidence), or formal thought disorder with markedly disorganized thinking or speech â€” representing a demonstrable break from an individual's baseline reality testing. The phenotype requires that these symptoms be currently active at the time of clinical assessment; patients in full remission or presenting with only residual or attenuated symptoms do not meet this definition. No restriction is placed on severity: presentations of any clinically recognized intensity qualify, provided active symptomatology is documented. No restriction is placed on underlying etiology: episodes attributable to primary psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, brief psychotic disorder, schizoaffective disorder), mood disorders with psychotic features (e.g., bipolar disorder with psychotic features, psychotic major depressive disorder), substance or medication intoxication or withdrawal, or identifiable general medical conditions (e.g., autoimmune encephalitis, severe metabolic disturbance, or infectious processes producing psychotic features) are all encompassed within this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: The definition describes psychosis as an acute, episodic condition marked by active positive psychotic symptoms, with no etiology restriction. Drug-attributable psychosis is well-documented, particularly through mechanisms such as intoxication from stimulants, hallucinogens, and cannabinoids, or withdrawal from alcohol/sedative-hypnotics. Additionally, medications such as corticosteroids, dopamine agonists, and anticholinergics are known to induce psychosis. This makes psychosis an appropriate pharmacovigilance outcome under this definition. Episodes resolve fully unless the underlying causative factor persists, and recurrent episodes arising from a new insult are genuine new events. Although severe cases may present in acute settings, diagnosis can occur in outpatient care for less severe presentations or follow-up visits. Definitive diagnosis relies on clinical assessment, with tests used primarily to exclude or identify secondary causes. Active treatment typically involves pharmacotherapy or stabilization within 30 days, and sequelae or recurrence may equally require follow-up.

source_definition: Ptosis of the eyelid is an acquired condition characterized by abnormal downward displacement of the upper eyelid margin resulting from dysfunction or structural failure of the eyelid-elevating mechanism, specifically the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, its aponeurosis, or the accessory Mueller's muscle. The condition encompasses all acquired etiologies, including neurogenic causes (such as dysfunction of the oculomotor nerve, sympathetic pathway disruption, or impaired neuromuscular transmission), myogenic causes (such as primary or systemic muscular disease affecting the levator), aponeurotic dehiscence or disinsertion (including involutional and post-surgical forms), mechanical ptosis due to lid mass, infiltration, or scarring, and traumatic injury to the levator complex. The phenotype includes presentations of any degree of severity, from a mildly reduced palpebral aperture to complete occlusion of the visual axis. Excluded are congenital forms of ptosis arising from developmental dysgenesis of the levator, as well as all conditions producing apparent lid drooping without true pathology of the elevating mechanism, such as dermatochalasis, enophthalmos, hypoglobus, or contralateral eyelid retraction creating a pseudoptosis appearance.
clinical_rationale: Acquired ptosis has documented drug-attributable etiologies, particularly neurogenic and myogenic causes. Neurogenic ptosis can result from botulinum toxin exposure or neurologic drug side effects affecting the oculomotor nerve or sympathetic pathway. Myogenic ptosis is associated with systemic muscular dysfunction, including drug-induced myopathies or impaired neuromuscular transmission (e.g., aminoglycosides or fluroquinolones). Aponeurotic ptosis is generally unrelated to pharmacologic exposures, being more commonly involutional or post-surgical. This condition spans episodic and chronic manifestations, and the described scope only includes acquired ptosis, excluding congenital and pseudoptosis. Diagnosis usually occurs in outpatient care due to gradual onset and non-emergent nature, although acute neurogenic presentations may involve acute care settings. Symptoms like eyelid drooping may be recorded, but objective testing or imaging is typically unnecessary except when pseudoptosis or secondary causes must be ruled out.

source_definition: Pulmonary arterial hypertension, restricted to its idiopathic and heritable forms (IPAH/HPAH), is a rare, progressive disease of the pulmonary vasculature defined by obliterative remodeling of the small pre-capillary pulmonary arteries and arterioles â€” encompassing intimal proliferation, medial hypertrophy, adventitial fibrosis, and plexiform lesion formation â€” arising in the absence of any identifiable associated systemic condition, drug or toxin exposure, or extrinsic hemodynamic driver. The pathological process produces a sustained elevation of pulmonary vascular resistance, resulting in progressive right ventricular pressure overload, right heart failure, and reduced systemic cardiac output. The phenotype is characterized by a pre-capillary hemodynamic pattern and is explicitly distinguished from pulmonary hypertension attributable to left heart disease, parenchymal lung disease, or chronic thromboembolic obstruction. Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease and pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, which represent distinct venopathic and capillaropathic processes, are likewise excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: The provided description strictly narrows pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) to its idiopathic and heritable forms (IPAH/HPAH), explicitly excluding drug-, toxin-, or systemic-condition-associated PAH. No drug-attributable mechanism is implicated within the definition, and the phenotype excludes pharmacovigilance-relevant categories such as drug-induced PAH documented for agents like anorexigens. These idiopathic/heritable forms are predominantly genetic and unrelated to exposure. PAH is managed as a chronic disease, characterized by persistence rather than discrete episodes. Diagnosis requires invasive hemodynamic testing (right heart catheterization), and incident cases typically arise in outpatient specialty care given the slow progression of symptoms. Additional structured symptomatic codes such as exertional dyspnea or fatigue are infrequent due to diagnostic delays.

source_definition: Pulmonary edema is a pathological state characterized by the abnormal accumulation of fluid within the pulmonary interstitium and/or alveolar spaces, resulting from either elevated pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure (cardiogenic) or increased alveolar-capillary membrane permeability (non-cardiogenic), and manifesting across a full spectrum of clinical severity with objective evidence of fluid accumulation such as auscultatory findings, hypoxemia, or radiographic interstitial or alveolar opacification. The condition encompasses presentations secondary to any identifiable primary etiology, including but not limited to left ventricular failure, sepsis, renal failure, hepatic dysfunction, and toxic inhalation injury. Explicitly excluded from this definition are: pleural effusion, in which fluid collects in the pleural space rather than within the lung parenchyma; pulmonary hemorrhage, in which alveolar flooding is due to extravasation of blood rather than fluid transudation or permeability-driven edema; atelectasis, a mechanical collapse of lung units without interstitial or alveolar fluid accumulation; and infectious pulmonary infiltrates (pneumonia), in which alveolar consolidation results from an infectious inflammatory exudate rather than hydrostatic or permeability-driven fluid dynamics.
clinical_rationale: Pulmonary edema is a heterogeneous condition with multiple etiologies, including cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic causes, many of which are drug-inducible. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema can arise due to drug-related myocardial depression (e.g., anthracyclines), arrhythmias, or acute hypertensive crises. Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema may be associated with drug hypersensitivity reactions, direct alveolar toxicity, or increased alveolar-capillary permeability such as observed with chemotherapy agents, opioids, or illicit stimulants. Its presentation spans acute settings with clear objective findings aligning well with cohort criteria. Diagnosis typically requires imaging or clinical evidence of fluid accumulation, and treatment usually targets the underlying cause alongside specific therapies for fluid overload or oxygenation. Pulmonary edema is transient as a diagnosis and episodes are distinctly separable, though some cases may lead to chronic sequelae recorded under alternative conditions such as heart failure.

source_definition: Pulmonary embolism is an acute or subacute pathophysiologic state characterized by the mechanical obstruction of one or more pulmonary arteries or their branches by embolic material of any origin, including but not limited to dislodged venous thrombus, fat particles, air, tumor fragments, or amniotic fluid. The obstruction results in impaired pulmonary perfusion, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and, in proportion to the degree of vascular occlusion, varying degrees of right ventricular pressure overload, hypoxemia, and hemodynamic compromise ranging from clinically silent or mildly symptomatic presentations to massive cardiopulmonary collapse. This phenotype encompasses the full severity spectrum â€” from subsegmental and low-risk PE through submassive presentations with right ventricular dysfunction to massive PE with sustained hemodynamic instability â€” but explicitly excludes chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), which represents a distinct, irreversible pathophysiologic end-state arising from unresolved chronic clot burden.
clinical_rationale: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a mechanistically plausible pharmacovigilance outcome, particularly for drugs affecting coagulation (e.g., oral contraceptives, hormone replacement therapy, and certain cancer therapies). PE is an acute condition with episodes resolving either spontaneously or with treatment, including anticoagulation or thrombolysis, typically administered during acute hospitalization or emergent care. Recurrence after resolution represents a new embolic event. Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is excluded by the definition provided, reinforcing the transient and episodic character of the acute forms of PE. Most incident cases are diagnosed in acute care, supported by imaging studies, such as CT pulmonary angiography or ventilation-perfusion scanning.

source_definition: Pulmonary fibrosis is a pathological state characterized by the irreversible replacement of normal lung architecture â€” including the pulmonary parenchyma (alveolar walls and interstitium) and/or the pleura â€” with excess fibrous connective tissue, resulting from aberrant wound-healing responses regardless of the initiating etiology. The condition encompasses fibrotic lung disease of any identified or unidentified cause, including but not limited to idiopathic forms, fibrosis secondary to systemic connective tissue diseases, occupational and environmental exposures, drug- or radiation-induced injury, and chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis with established fibrotic remodeling; it includes fibrosis at any demonstrable stage, from incidental radiologic findings to advanced disease with architectural distortion. Explicitly excluded are non-fibrotic interstitial lung diseases in which the predominant pathology is reversible inflammation rather than permanent fibrogenesis, including acute and subacute hypersensitivity pneumonitis without fibrosis, cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, and eosinophilic pneumonia.
clinical_rationale: Pulmonary fibrosis is a recognized pharmacovigilance outcome, as it can result from drug toxicity caused by agents like amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin, and immune checkpoint inhibitors. These drugs can lead to aberrant wound-healing responses in the lung parenchyma, causing irreversible fibrotic remodeling. The clinical definition provided explicitly excludes non-fibrotic interstitial lung diseases, ensuring that coding and cohort logic focuses specifically on the chronic fibrotic disease rather than reversible etiologies. Pulmonary fibrosis is inherently irreversibly progressive, making the disease persistent throughout the patient's life after diagnosis. It is often incidentally identified via imaging or respiratory symptoms, with usual care increasingly reliant on diagnostic imaging and/or histopathology to confirm etiology and stage the disease. Drugs may contribute as primary causes or accelerants of fibrosis; therefore, monitoring for drug-attributable cases is critical to patient safety.

source_definition: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic state defined by an elevation of mean pulmonary arterial pressure to 20 mmHg or above at rest, irrespective of the underlying etiology, acuity, or reversibility. The condition encompasses three primary hemodynamic subtypes: pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension, in which increased resistance originates within the pulmonary vasculature proximal to the capillary bed; post-capillary pulmonary hypertension, in which elevated mean pulmonary arterial pressure is passively transmitted from increased left atrial or left ventricular filling pressures; and combined pre- and post-capillary pulmonary hypertension, in which reactive pulmonary vasoconstriction is superimposed on post-capillary congestion. High-output pulmonary hypertension â€” in which the pressure threshold is reached solely due to markedly elevated cardiac output in the setting of normal pulmonary vascular resistance and normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure â€” is additionally recognized as a mechanistically distinct subtype. The definition applies equally to acute, transient, and sustained presentations and does not require a specific underlying disease process, functional severity classification, or minimum duration of elevation.
clinical_rationale: Pulmonary hypertension may be drug-attributable in specific scenarios such as anorectic drugs (e.g., fenfluramine), alkylating agents, interferons, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors inducing pre-capillary pulmonary arterial hypertension, or chemotherapy agents exacerbating post-capillary pulmonary hypertension through cardiotoxicity. This definition encompasses transient and chronic forms irrespective of cause, making it suitable for surveillance. Routine diagnosis requires invasive hemodynamic assessment via right heart catheterization, supported by echocardiography for screening, confirming that objective testing is necessary. Incident diagnosis occurs in both outpatient and acute care settings depending on underlying etiology and acuity. Discrete symptoms like breathlessness may be recorded alongside or before diagnosis in clinical practice but are nonspecific and inconsistently documented. Drugs are not always implicated, as genetic, environmental, and secondary causes predominate. Cohort construction needs clear guidance to separate incident cases from chronic management records in longitudinal data.

source_definition: Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is an acquired disorder of erythropoiesis characterized by a near-complete absence of erythroid precursors â€” specifically pronormoblasts and subsequent maturation stages â€” in an otherwise cellular bone marrow, resulting in severe normocytic, normochromic anemia with profound reticulocytopenia in the peripheral blood, while white cell and platelet lineages remain intact. The condition must be sustained, with the erythroid failure persisting for at least four weeks, thereby distinguishing it from self-limited aplastic crises. The phenotype encompasses all recognized acquired etiologies, including idiopathic autoimmune-mediated PRCA, thymoma-associated PRCA, large granular lymphocyte leukemia-associated PRCA, drug-induced PRCA (including anti-erythropoietin antibody-mediated cases), and PRCA due to chronic persistent viral infection in immunocompromised hosts. Explicitly excluded are congenital erythroid hypoplasia (Diamond-Blackfan Anemia), transient aplastic crises, and global bone marrow failure syndromes such as aplastic anemia in which erythroid suppression occurs in the context of broader pancytopenia and marrow hypocellularity.
clinical_rationale: Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a clinically distinct acquired disorder of erythropoiesis that can result from drugs, in particular, anti-erythropoietin antibody-mediated mechanisms or cytotoxicity. The clinical phenotype excludes congenital, transient, and pancytopenic conditions, narrowing the focus to sustained erythroid failure with normocytic, normochromic anemia and reticulocytopenia. Drug-induced PRCA is well-documented, with anti-erythropoietin cases particularly associated with exogenous erythropoietin therapy in chronic kidney disease. Incident PRCA is generally recognized through severe anemia and bone marrow biopsy diagnostic findings. Chronic sequelae, treatment outcomes, and therapeutic surveillance may occur beyond the acute diagnostic window.

source_definition: Pyelonephritis, as operationalized in this phenotype, encompasses infectious inflammation of the urinary tract â€” including the lower tract (urethra and bladder) and upper tract (ureters, renal pelvis, and renal parenchyma) â€” caused by any infectious organism, including bacterial, fungal, viral, or parasitic agents, across both acute episodic and chronic recurrent or persistent presentations. The phenotype includes uncomplicated cases in anatomically and immunologically normal hosts as well as complicated cases in the presence of urinary obstruction, structural anomalies, urolithiasis, diabetes, immunosuppression, pregnancy, or other host factors that increase severity or risk of treatment failure. Infection may arise via the ascending route from the lower urinary tract or via hematogenous seeding of the kidney or urinary tract, provided that the infectious urinary involvement represents a primary clinical concern and not merely an incidental complication of a distant systemic infection or bacteremia. Non-infectious inflammatory conditions of the renal parenchyma, including acute interstitial nephritis of autoimmune or drug-induced etiology, are explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Pyelonephritis is a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome, as drugs such as glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and certain antimicrobials can increase susceptibility to infection or treatment failure. This phenotype is defined broadly to encompass both acute and chronic presentations, inclusive of complicated infections in at-risk populations (e.g., pregnancy, diabetes, immunosuppression). Excluded from the phenotype are non-infectious inflammatory conditions like drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis, which require a separate cohort definition. Pyelonephritis is frequently diagnosed in acute care settings when systemic signs occur, but less severe presentations may be recognized in ambulatory care; therefore, the expected care setting straddles both. The inclusion of the lower urinary tract affects coding sensitivity, which may capture patients under broader UTI labels, especially in outpatient settings.

source_definition: Radial styloid tenosynovitis (De Quervain's tenosynovitis) is an inflammatory condition of the tendon sheath of the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, specifically affecting the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons as they pass through the fibro-osseous tunnel overlying the radial styloid process. The condition encompasses the full clinical spectrum from acute reactive inflammation of the tendon sheath to chronic stenosing tenosynovitis characterized by fibrous thickening and narrowing of the compartment, and includes cases arising from any underlying etiology, including idiopathic onset, repetitive mechanical overuse, pregnancy- or lactation-associated hormonal changes, systemic inflammatory arthropathies, and post-traumatic causes. It is defined by localized pain, swelling, and tenderness at the radial styloid with reproduction of symptoms on resisted thumb abduction or ulnar deviation of the wrist, reflecting pathology intrinsic to the tendon sheath and peritendinous structures of the first dorsal compartment. This phenotype explicitly excludes first carpometacarpal joint osteoarthritis, which represents a distinct articular cartilage and subchondral bone disease of the basal thumb joint, and intersection syndrome, which involves the second dorsal compartment tendons at a more proximal anatomical site.
clinical_rationale: Radial styloid tenosynovitis (De Quervain's tenosynovitis) has plausible drug-attributable etiologies through systemic inflammatory responses triggered by medications, such as biologics for autoimmune conditions potentially exacerbating local inflammation, and hormonal changes associated with pregnancy or lactation. However, the condition is more commonly associated with mechanical overuse, idiopathic onset, or systemic inflammatory arthropathies. Drugs are less commonly implicated, making its suitability as a pharmacovigilance outcome conditional based on the etiology. The description specifies exclusion of conditions that may overlap anatomically, such as first carpometacarpal joint osteoarthritis and intersection syndrome. Incidence is typically observed and managed in outpatient settings.

source_definition: Rash is an episodic or reactive cutaneous eruption of any morphologyâ€”including macules, papules, plaques, urticaria, vesicles, bullae, pustules, and petechiaeâ€”arising from a biological mechanism such as immune activation, inflammatory response, infectious process, or toxic exposure, and spanning any degree of severity from localized mild erythema to extensive cutaneous involvement. Mucosal involvement of the oral, genital, or ocular mucosa is included when it occurs concurrently with a skin-surface eruption as part of the same pathophysiological event. The phenotype excludes cutaneous changes attributable solely to mechanical or physical insult, including pressure-induced skin breakdown, frostbite, and radiation dermatitis. It further excludes chronic dermatological conditions in which the rash constitutes the defining and persistent hallmark of an underlying skin disease, such as psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and rosacea; episodic or reactive cutaneous eruptions occurring as secondary manifestations of systemic disease are included.
clinical_rationale: Rash as defined here includes a wide range of causes, including drug-induced hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., urticaria, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome), which are established pharmacovigilance outcomes. The definition appropriately excludes chronic dermatological conditions, mechanical or physical skin injuries, and persistent primary skin diseases, focusing specifically on episodic or reactive eruptions. The broad scope of the term 'rash' makes it conditional as a pharmacovigilance outcome; only drug-attributable etiologies are relevant for active drug safety surveillance. Although rashes may occur incidentally or be unrelated to drug exposure, structured diagnostic codes and characteristic symptoms (e.g., urticaria/erythema) help clarify attribution in observational data. Diagnostic testing is rarely required to identify or confirm rashes themselves unless their morphology overlaps syndromes demanding systemic cause evaluation (e.g., blistering disorders or petechiae).

source_definition: Raynaud's phenomenon is a condition characterized by episodic, reversible vasospasm of the digital arteries and arterioles of the fingers and/or toes, manifesting as at least one well-demarcated phase of pallor or cyanosis triggered by exposure to cold or emotional stress, with restoration of normal perfusion upon rewarming or resolution of the stressor. The phenotype encompasses both primary Raynaud's disease, in which no underlying systemic etiology is identified, and secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, in which vasospasm is attributable to an identifiable underlying condition such as systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, or drug or chemical exposure. A complete triphasic color sequence is not required; monophasic or biphasic presentations meeting the core vasospastic attack criteria are included. The definition is confined to the vasospastic attack itself and excludes ischemic end-organ complications such as digital ulcers or gangrene, which are considered downstream sequelae. Explicitly excluded from this phenotype are acrocyanosis â€” a persistent, non-episodic low-flow state lacking the discrete attack pattern â€” and peripheral arterial disease or critical limb ischemia, which represent fixed occlusive arterial insufficiency rather than reversible vasospasm.
clinical_rationale: Raynaud's phenomenon (RP) can be classified as primary (idiopathic) or secondary to an underlying condition, including drug exposure (e.g., beta-blockers, bleomycin, cocaine, and ergotamines). Secondary RP is thus a valid pharmacovigilance outcome under a narrower reading. The episodic and reversible nature of RP makes its clinical course transient and recurrent, as individual vasospastic attacks resolve and recur in response to triggers like cold or stress. Symptomatology, such as color changes, is central to diagnosis, but discrete recorded symptoms are uncommon as documentation often conflates symptoms with the definitive diagnosis. Diagnostic confirmation typically does not require advanced testing unless secondary causes are suspected, in which case additional investigations may occur. Treatment is directed at preventing attacks or mitigating symptoms, especially in severe or secondary cases. Follow-up occurs mainly for secondary RP due to underlying conditions or severe ischemic complications, rather than for primary RP.

source_definition: Renal impairment is a pathological state characterized by any detectable reduction in kidney function below the expected physiological baseline for an individual, encompassing both acute, potentially reversible decrements and chronic, sustained loss of function. The condition may arise from any mechanism that compromises glomerular filtration, tubular function, or overall renal homeostatic capacity, including pre-renal causes driven by systemic hemodynamic insufficiency, intrinsic renal causes resulting from direct injury or disease within kidney parenchyma (glomerular, tubular, vascular, or interstitial), and post-renal causes attributable to urinary tract obstruction. Secondary kidney dysfunction occurring as a downstream consequence of primary pathology in another organ system â€” such as cardiorenal syndrome, hepatorenal syndrome, or sepsis-associated acute kidney injury â€” is included, provided the functional impairment is distinguishable from the primary disease state. Excluded from this phenotype are reductions in absolute glomerular filtration rate that are attributable solely to congenital or anatomical reduction in nephron mass, such as a compensated solitary kidney functioning normally per remaining nephron unit, as these represent a structural baseline rather than an acquired or pathological departure from expected function.
clinical_rationale: Renal impairment, as defined, encompasses both acute and chronic reductions in kidney function. Acute renal impairment (e.g., acute kidney injury) is a known pharmacovigilance outcome through mechanisms such as nephrotoxins, ischemic injury, and immune-mediated acute interstitial nephritis. Chronic renal impairment (e.g., chronic kidney disease) has a well-documented relationship with drug-induced progression, such as via cumulative nephrotoxic exposure or deteriorating filtration and homeostasis over time. Because the definition spans both acute and chronic forms, it is a pharmacovigilance outcome under either setting. Due to the breadth of mechanisms and etiologies (including pre-renal and post-renal causes), acute presentations often occur in acute care settings, while detection of chronic kidney disease tends toward outpatient contexts. The clinical course often depends on the underlying etiology, with acute forms being transient and recurrent, and chronic forms being persistent and progressive. For operational purposes, the broader phenotype can align more closely with the acute-onset manifestations when evaluating drug-induced effects.

source_definition: Renal tubular disorder is a clinically manifest, acquired dysfunction of renal tubular transport capacity affecting one or more segments of the nephron tubule â€” including the proximal tubule, distal tubule, or collecting duct â€” in which tubular epithelial cells fail to appropriately reabsorb or secrete one or more solutes such as bicarbonate, phosphate, glucose, amino acids, uric acid, potassium, or hydrogen ions. The disorder arises as a direct consequence of a tubule-targeting insult, such as nephrotoxic medications, heavy metal exposure, or paraprotein deposition, and presents with overt clinical features reflective of the affected transport pathway, including metabolic acidosis, solute wasting (e.g., euglycemic glucosuria, aminoaciduria, renal phosphate wasting), electrolyte disturbances, or impaired urinary acidification. This phenotype excludes inherited or congenital tubulopathies of genetic origin, tubular dysfunction occurring as a downstream consequence of primary glomerular disease, tubular impairment arising in the context of acute tubular necrosis or acute kidney injury, dysfunction attributable to systemic metabolic disturbances such as hypercalcemia, and subclinical or incidentally detected laboratory abnormalities without accompanying clinical manifestation.
clinical_rationale: Renal tubular disorders, as defined here, are acquired and arise as a direct consequence of nephrotoxic insults such as medications (e.g., aminoglycosides, cisplatin, or ifosfamide), heavy metals, or paraprotein deposition. The exclusion of inherited/congenital tubulopathies and dysfunction secondary to systemic conditions ensures that the phenotype focuses on acquired, etiologically distinct cases. Drugs and toxins are a well-documented causal mechanism, making this phenotype suitable for pharmacovigilance. Tubular dysfunction typically leads to overt clinical features such as metabolic acidosis or solute wasting, though these may require objective diagnostic tests to establish the diagnosis. Diagnosis largely occurs in acute or specialized care settings due to the severity and complexity of presentation. Many cases resolve if the offending insult is removed or treated, with the label no longer applied after resolution, though some cases may progress to chronic kidney disease or leave residual impairment.

source_definition: Respiratory depression is a clinical state characterized by a pathological reduction in respiratory rate below age-appropriate normative thresholds, regardless of underlying etiology, spanning a severity spectrum from mild through moderate to severe. In adults, mild depression is defined as a respiratory rate below 12 breaths per minute, moderate as below 10 breaths per minute, and severe as below 8 breaths per minute or any level of respiratory rate suppression requiring active clinical intervention; in pediatric populations, equivalent severity tiers are applied relative to established age-specific normative ranges (e.g., neonates, infants, toddlers, school-age children, and adolescents). Apnea â€” the complete absence of breathing â€” is encompassed within this phenotype as the most extreme expression of respiratory depression rather than a categorically separate entity. The definition is etiology-agnostic, capturing rate-based respiratory suppression arising from any mechanism, including central nervous system depression, metabolic or toxic insults, neurological injury, neuromuscular compromise, or other pathophysiological processes.
clinical_rationale: Respiratory depression is a suitable pharmacovigilance outcome due to its well-documented drug etiology, including central nervous system depressants (e.g., opioids, benzodiazepines) and neuromuscular blockers, among others. Its pathophysiology includes direct suppression of respiratory centers, toxicity, or paralysis of respiratory muscles. Since the phenotype definition includes all severity tiers of respiratory rate suppression, ranging from mild to severe, it captures cases likely to be diagnosed across diverse settings. The inclusion of apnea further broadens coverage by accounting for its most extreme manifestation. Resolution typically results in shedding of the diagnosis unless the underlying etiology produces irreversible sequelae, such as chronic neuromuscular disease or brain injury. Most cases requiring intervention occur in acute care settings, although mild cases may present in outpatient care, making acute care common rather than purely expected. Known challenges include sensitivity to setting and potential definition differences between individuals experiencing reversible suppression and those with structural or chronic causes of respiratory insufficiency.

source_definition: Respiratory failure is a clinical state in which the respiratory system is unable to maintain adequate gas exchange, manifesting as hypoxemia (partial pressure of arterial oxygen below 60 mmHg or oxygen saturation below 90% on room air; Type I), hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis (partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide above 45 mmHg; Type II), or both. The phenotype encompasses all time courses â€” acute onset, chronic persistence, and acute decompensation superimposed on chronic disease â€” and includes failure arising from any underlying etiology, including intrinsic pulmonary disease, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, central nervous system depression, and neuromuscular dysfunction. In settings where arterial blood gas confirmation is unavailable, the requirement for invasive mechanical ventilation or non-invasive positive pressure ventilation serves as an accepted clinical proxy for gas exchange failure. Pure respiratory distress characterized by symptomatic dyspnea or increased work of breathing that does not meet gas exchange thresholds and does not necessitate respiratory support is explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Respiratory failure is a well-documented potential pharmacovigilance outcome, with known drug etiologies including opioids, sedatives, and anesthetics causing respiratory depression; certain chemotherapeutics inducing pulmonary fibrosis; and immune checkpoint inhibitors leading to pneumonitis. The definition provided explicitly encompasses all time courses (acute, chronic, and acute-on-chronic) and includes any underlying cause, necessitating a broad and inclusive approach to cohort definition. Acute incidents of respiratory failure are predominantly diagnosed in acute care settings. While chronic respiratory failure may persist over time, acute episodes are usually transient and may recur, particularly in patients with underlying chronic disease.

source_definition: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection is an acute infectious disease caused by active replication of the human respiratory syncytial virus, confirmed by direct virological methods â€” including nucleic acid amplification testing (e.g., PCR), rapid antigen detection, or viral culture â€” from a respiratory specimen obtained during the episode of interest. The phenotype encompasses the full clinical spectrum, from asymptomatic laboratory-confirmed infection through mild upper respiratory tract illness (rhinorrhea, pharyngitis, cough) to lower respiratory tract disease (bronchiolitis, pneumonia) and severe respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support. Serological evidence of prior RSV exposure, such as RSV IgG seropositivity, does not constitute case-defining evidence, as it reflects historical immunological exposure rather than active viral replication. Concurrent detection of other respiratory pathogens does not exclude a case; RSV co-infection is recognized as clinically and epidemiologically meaningful. No restriction is placed on host age, immune status, or care setting â€” the phenotype applies across all populations in whom direct virological confirmation of active RSV infection is present.
clinical_rationale: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection is primarily infectious and is not typically a pharmacovigilance outcome but rather a concern in epidemiology and public health surveillance. While certain pharmacotherapies or immune-suppressive drugs may increase susceptibility to respiratory infections, the infection itself cannot be directly attributed to drug exposure. The phenotype explicitly requires virological confirmation of active RSV replication and includes asymptomatic cases, which makes it unsuitable in most pharmacovigilance contexts that rely on symptomatic disease outcomes. Diagnosis usually requires laboratory testing, and severe cases are often seen in acute care settings, particularly in pediatric and older adult populations at higher risk of complications.

source_definition: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) is a chronic sensorimotor neurological disorder defined by the presence of all four cardinal diagnostic criteria established by the International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG): an uncomfortable and irresistible urge to move the legs, typically accompanied by unpleasant sensory phenomena; onset or worsening of symptoms during periods of rest or inactivity; partial or complete relief of symptoms with movement; and a circadian pattern in which symptoms are exclusively or predominantly present in the evening or nighttime hours. This phenotype encompasses the full spectrum of clinical severity from mild to severe presentations, and includes both primary (idiopathic) and secondary (symptomatic) forms â€” including those attributable to iron deficiency, end-stage renal disease, pregnancy, or other identifiable underlying conditions â€” provided the four IRLSSG criteria are satisfied. Explicitly excluded are conditions in which the urge to move or limb discomfort is more fully explained by an alternative diagnosis: akathisia (drug-induced or disease-related generalized motor restlessness lacking the characteristic rest-worsening and circadian pattern); peripheral neuropathy with dysesthesias arising from nerve damage that does not follow the sensorimotor pattern of RLS; and vascular insufficiency or nocturnal leg cramps characterized by pain or cramping of mechanical or vascular origin without the defining urge-to-move phenomenology.
clinical_rationale: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) can have secondary etiologies attributable to drug exposures, including dopaminergic agents, antidepressants, antipsychotics, and antihistamines, which are thought to alter dopaminergic function or exacerbate underlying iron deficiency. The IRLSSG criteria ensure specificity, excluding alternative diagnoses like akathisia and neuropathies. While primary (idiopathic) RLS is not drug-induced, secondary forms linked to end-stage renal disease or iron deficiency may also serve as safety outcomes for drugs linked to worsening kidney function or disrupting iron homeostasis. RLS is chronic, persistent, and tends to progress or worsen with time, though symptom intensity can vary episodically. Diagnosis is generally clinical, based on history and physical exam, with laboratory investigations used to confirm secondary causes. Incident diagnoses are most often documented in outpatient settings, as RLS does not typically require acute intervention. Treatment is directed at symptom control, often with pharmacotherapy, and long-term follow-up is common in severe cases.

source_definition: Reye's syndrome is an acute, non-inflammatory encephalopathy occurring concurrently with hepatic microvesicular steatosis, without histological evidence of hepatic inflammation, reflecting generalized impairment of mitochondrial function. The syndrome spans a full clinical severity spectrum, from mild lethargy, vomiting, and biochemical hepatic dysfunction (stage I) through progressive cerebral edema, altered consciousness, decerebrate posturing, and coma (stages IIâ€“V), accompanied by characteristic metabolic derangements including hyperammonemia, elevated transaminases, and hypoglycemia in the absence of jaundice. The condition arises in association with antecedent viral illness (most commonly influenza or varicella) and/or salicylate exposure, and may affect patients of any age. Excluded from this phenotype are Reye-like syndromes attributable to identifiable inborn errors of metabolism (e.g., fatty acid oxidation disorders, urea cycle defects, organic acidemias), hepatic encephalopathy secondary to inflammatory liver disease, and toxic encephalopathies of distinct drug etiology (e.g., valproate-induced hepatotoxic encephalopathy).
clinical_rationale: Reye's syndrome is a known potential adverse outcome related to salicylate exposure, particularly in children following viral illnesses such as influenza or varicella. The mechanism involves mitochondrial dysfunction leading to hepatic microvesicular steatosis and non-inflammatory encephalopathy. The exclusion of Reye-like syndromes due to known inborn errors of metabolism, inflammatory liver disease, or other toxic encephalopathies reinforces the specificity of this phenotype as a distinct condition associated with salicylates. While rare, it is relevant in pharmacovigilance given its historical association with aspirin use in pediatric populations. Diagnosis typically requires laboratory confirmation of characteristic metabolic derangements, and care is usually initiated in acute settings because of the severity of the neurological and hepatic manifestations.

source_definition: Rhabdomyolysis is an acute pathophysiological state characterized by necrosis and breakdown of skeletal muscle fibers, resulting in the release of intracellular muscle contents â€” including myoglobin, creatine kinase, electrolytes (notably potassium and phosphate), and other sarcoplasmic proteins â€” into the systemic circulation. The condition encompasses the full clinical spectrum, from asymptomatic elevation of muscle-derived enzymes to severe systemic illness marked by myalgias, muscle weakness, and pigmenturia (myoglobinuria). It may be precipitated by any acquired mechanism, including but not limited to exertion, drug or toxin exposure (e.g., statins, alcohol, illicit substances), infectious or inflammatory processes, seizure activity, or hyperthermia. The phenotype is explicitly restricted to skeletal muscle injury; primary cardiac muscle pathology â€” including myocarditis, myocardial infarction, or other myocardial necrosis â€” constitutes a distinct competing biological state and is excluded even when associated with elevated total creatine kinase. Rhabdomyolysis attributable to mechanical traumatic injury (e.g., crush syndrome) or to underlying hereditary or metabolic myopathies is likewise excluded from this definition.
clinical_rationale: Rhabdomyolysis can result from a variety of causes, including drug exposures such as statins, alcohol, and illicit substances. Statins are well-documented to cause skeletal muscle breakdown in susceptible individuals due to drug-induced myopathy and increased muscle toxicity. This phenotype excludes rhabdomyolysis due to genetic, metabolic, or traumatic causes, focusing on acquired mechanisms, which include drug and toxin exposures, making it a valid pharmacovigilance outcome. The clinical course is typically transient with resolution once the causative factor is removed, though severe cases can lead to complications like acute kidney injury. Diagnosis involves laboratory findings, such as elevated creatine kinase, and is frequently confirmed or suspected during acute care settings due to the acute nature and potential severity of symptoms.

source_definition: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune inflammatory disease characterized by persistent synovitis, typically affecting peripheral joints in a symmetric polyarticular distribution, driven by aberrant immune activation resulting in progressive cartilage degradation and periarticular bone erosion. This phenotype encompasses all confirmed cases of RA regardless of current disease activity state or treatment status, capturing both seropositive cases (defined by the presence of rheumatoid factor and/or anti-citrullinated protein antibodies) and seronegative cases diagnosed on clinical and radiographic grounds alone. The phenotype applies across the full age spectrum, including both adult-onset and juvenile-onset presentations. Extra-articular systemic manifestationsâ€”such as rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, vasculitis, and secondary sicca featuresâ€”are considered part of the disease spectrum and are not exclusionary. This phenotype does not require evidence of active joint inflammation at the time of identification and includes patients in pharmacological or spontaneous remission.
clinical_rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease with both joint-specific and systemic manifestations. Drug-attributable etiologies include drug-induced arthritis mimicking RA, but the condition itself is inherently autoimmune—a distinction critical in pharmacovigilance. RA encompasses persistent disease even when managed into remission, and discrete episodes like flares do not erase the primary chronic diagnosis. Cohort logic must avoid transient definitions or event resetting with remission. Diagnosis occurs across care settings but depends on clinical judgment supplemented with serological and imaging tests. The inclusion of juvenile-onset RA in the phenotype expands capture age, though criteria remain zero-bound for overall RA documentation.

source_definition: Right bundle branch block (RBBB) is a cardiac conduction abnormality characterized by delayed or absent propagation of the electrical impulse through the right bundle branch of the His-Purkinje system, resulting in delayed and abnormal depolarization of the right ventricle. The phenotype encompasses both complete RBBB, defined by a QRS complex duration of 120 milliseconds or greater, and incomplete RBBB, defined by a QRS duration of 110 to 119 milliseconds, provided both manifest the characteristic electrocardiographic morphology: an RSR' or rSR' pattern in the right precordial leads (V1â€“V2) and a wide, slurred terminal S wave in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5â€“V6). The phenotype is defined purely by this electrophysiological conduction pattern and is inclusive of all etiologies, encompassing RBBB arising from intrinsic conduction system degeneration, structural cardiac disease (including coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, and congenital heart disease), acute right ventricular strain (such as that caused by pulmonary embolism), metabolic or electrolyte disturbances, and iatrogenic or procedural causes. No restriction is placed on whether the block is persistent or intermittent, nor on the presence or absence of underlying structural heart disease.
clinical_rationale: Right bundle branch block (RBBB) is an electrophysiological phenotype commonly defined by ECG criteria. While intrinsic conduction degeneration and structural heart disease account for most cases, RBBB can also arise from drug-attributable mechanisms such as class I antiarrhythmic toxicity or local damage during catheter-based electrophysiological procedures. Thus, RBBB has plausible iatrogenic or drug-associated etiologies in selected cases. The condition is generally persistent and stable in intrinsic or structural etiologies, though acute causes, like pulmonary embolism or drug-induced cases, may resolve. RBBB diagnosis requires ECG testing, and it is often identified incidentally in outpatient care but may also accompany acute presentations like pulmonary embolism or myocardial infarction in inpatient settings. Drug-induced cases may have corresponding medication records and resolution upon de-challenge, aiding causality assessment. Formal monitoring or follow-up is uncommon unless underlying cardiac pathology mandates it.

source_definition: Right heart failure is a clinical syndrome arising from primary right ventricular (RV) pathology, characterized by the inability of the right ventricle to maintain adequate pulmonary blood flow and systemic venous drainage at normal filling pressures. The phenotype encompasses both acute presentations and chronic persistent states, and includes any degree of RV dysfunction that produces clinical manifestations of systemic venous congestion â€” such as peripheral edema, elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatic congestion, ascites, and reduced exercise tolerance. Underlying etiologies are restricted to those in which the right ventricle is the primary seat of disease, including but not limited to pulmonary arterial hypertension, cor pulmonale due to chronic lung disease, right ventricular myocardial infarction, and primary cardiomyopathies predominantly affecting the right ventricle. Excluded from this phenotype are cases in which RV dysfunction develops principally as a secondary consequence of left ventricular failure or chronically elevated left-sided filling pressures, including biventricular heart failure and congestive heart failure in which left heart disease constitutes the dominant hemodynamic driver.
clinical_rationale: Right heart failure (RHF) is a clinical syndrome with diverse etiologies, including pulmonary arterial hypertension, cor pulmonale from lung disease, RV myocardial infarction, and primary RV cardiomyopathies. Drug-induced RHF is plausible through mechanisms such as pulmonary arterial vasoconstriction (some chemotherapeutics, illicit drugs) or direct myocardial toxicity, though robust evidence is limited. Chronic RHF, while persistent, often fluctuates in severity and may present acute-on-chronic exacerbations requiring focused management and possible hospital interventions. RHF typically requires diagnostic imaging or invasive hemodynamic assessment (e.g., echocardiography, right-heart catheterization) to confirm RV dysfunction and identify etiologies. Initial diagnosis may span acute care settings for severe presentations or outpatient settings for milder or chronic forms. While systemic venous congestion typically presents characteristic clinical features (e.g., peripheral edema, elevated JVP), these findings are inconsistently coded in structured data. Follow-up is likely and associated with significant morbidity, with management requiring ongoing surveillance.

source_definition: Sarcoidosis is a systemic inflammatory disorder of unknown etiology characterized by the formation of non-caseating granulomas in one or more organ systems. The condition may involve any organ, including but not limited to the lungs, mediastinal and peripheral lymph nodes, skin, eyes, heart, nervous system, liver, kidneys, and musculoskeletal system, with pulmonary involvement being the most common presentation. The phenotype encompasses any individual with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of sarcoidosis, whether established by histological demonstration of non-caseating granulomas on tissue biopsy or by clinical assessment comprising compatible presentation, characteristic imaging findings, and appropriate exclusion of alternative diagnoses without tissue confirmation. No restriction is placed on disease activity; both currently active disease and historically resolved or quiescent cases are included. No organ-specific scope is required, and no exclusions are applied based on co-existing conditions.
clinical_rationale: Sarcoidosis has an unknown etiology but certain drugs, including interferons, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, and immune checkpoint inhibitors, have been associated with sarcoidosis-like reactions or de novo disease. Thus, it can serve as a pharmacovigilance outcome under the narrower reading of drug-induced or drug-attributable sarcoidosis-like reaction, as spontaneous sarcoidosis is not directly drug-attributable. Most cases are characterized by non-caseating granulomas and can involve both persistent inflammatory disease requiring management and quiescent states with historical records but no ongoing relapse. This makes the phenotype broad in scope, encompassing persistent and resolved disease forms. Pulmonary involvement is most common, and diagnosis may occur in outpatient or acute care settings depending on the severity and organ involvement. Diagnosis nearly always requires imaging, biopsy, or exclusionary testing, and follow-up is required to monitor sequelae, relapses, or progression.

source_definition: Sarcopenia is a skeletal muscle disorder characterized by a clinically significant reduction in skeletal muscle mass accompanied by impaired muscle strength, reduced physical performance, or both. The condition spans a continuum of severity: a probable stage defined by measurable functional impairment (low grip strength or slow gait speed) alone; a confirmed stage requiring objective evidence of both low muscle mass and functional deficit; and a severe stage in which low muscle mass, low strength, and poor physical performance are all present. The phenotype encompasses both primary sarcopenia, arising from the biological processes of aging, and secondary sarcopenia, in which an identifiable contributing cause such as chronic disease, physical inactivity, or inadequate nutritional intake drives or accelerates muscle loss. Cachexia â€” a distinct syndrome of systemic inflammation-driven catabolism with involuntary total body weight loss â€” is explicitly excluded, as is frailty, a broader multi-system geriatric vulnerability state that, while frequently co-occurring, is not equivalent to a primary deficit in skeletal muscle structure and function.
clinical_rationale: Sarcopenia can have secondary etiologies linked to medication use, particularly prolonged high-dose corticosteroids, certain chemotherapeutic agents, and some other drugs that contribute to muscle breakdown or reduced muscle anabolism. This makes sarcopenia a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome. The condition includes both primary, age-related causes as well as secondary causes, which can make attribution challenging in observational data, but the provided description emphasizes this distinction, offering a basis for focusing on secondary sarcopenia when studying drug-etiologic pathways. Differential diagnoses such as cachexia or frailty, which are excluded by definition, must be carefully separated. The diagnostic process often requires functional assessments and imaging to confirm low muscle mass, as well as clinical evaluations to determine functional impairment or loss of performance.

source_definition: Schizoaffective disorder is a chronic psychiatric condition characterized by the co-occurrence of psychotic symptoms â€” including hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking â€” alongside clinically significant mood episodes that are either manic or major depressive in nature. The defining clinical feature is that psychotic symptoms are not confined to periods of mood disturbance; they persist for a meaningful duration in the absence of an active mood episode, establishing the psychotic syndrome as an independent component of the illness rather than a secondary feature of a primary mood disorder. Both the bipolar type, in which at least one manic or mixed episode is present, and the depressive type, in which only major depressive episodes occur, are included. The phenotype is defined syndromically and encompasses presentations regardless of underlying etiology, including those associated with substance use or concurrent medical conditions. This is a lifetime definition, applying to any individual who has at any point met the full clinical criteria, irrespective of current symptom status. Excluded are presentations in which mood symptoms are incidental to a primary schizophrenia-spectrum illness, and those in which psychosis arises exclusively within the context of mood episodes attributable to bipolar disorder or major depressive disorder.
clinical_rationale: Schizoaffective disorder is a syndromic psychiatric condition characterized by chronic psychosis and significant mood disturbances. It is a lifetime diagnosis that persists whether or not the illness is actively symptomatic. While medications including antipsychotics and mood stabilizers are standard in treatment, it is primarily a condition with genetic, neurobiological, and environmental determinants rather than direct drug causation. Drug toxicity or withdrawal can mimic or exacerbate psychotic and mood symptoms, but these presentations are considered secondary and excluded from the supplied definition. Pharmacovigilance typically involves monitoring drug-induced psychiatric syndromes (e.g., mood changes, akathisia, substance-induced hallucinations) rather than syndromically persistent diagnoses like schizoaffective disorder.

source_definition: Schizophrenia is a chronic, relapsing-remitting primary psychotic disorder characterized by the persistent or recurrent presence of positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thought or speech), negative symptoms (affective flattening, alogia, avolition, and anhedonia), and cognitive impairment, encompassing all clinical subtypes and spanning all phases of illness including acute exacerbation, partial remission, and clinical stability. The disorder arises as a primary psychiatric condition and is not attributable to the direct physiological effects of a substance (including intoxication or withdrawal) or to an identifiable neurological, metabolic, or systemic medical etiology. Explicitly excluded are all other primary psychotic and schizophrenia-spectrum disorders â€” including schizoaffective disorder, schizophreniform disorder, brief psychotic disorder, and delusional disorder â€” as well as psychotic features that represent a secondary manifestation of a primary mood disorder, such as bipolar disorder with psychotic features or major depressive disorder with psychotic features.
clinical_rationale: Schizophrenia is a primary psychotic disorder characterized by a constellation of positive and negative symptoms and cognitive impairment, with a chronic and relapsing-remitting course. The description explicitly excludes secondary psychoses caused by drug intoxication, withdrawal, or other medical causes, narrowing the scope away from drug-induced psychotic disorders. While some medications may worsen or unmask pre-existing schizophrenia symptoms, and antipsychotics play a central role in treatment, schizophrenia is not documented as being caused or induced by pharmacologic exposures. Thus, it is not a pharmacovigilance outcome unless a more specific subtype were identified, such as drug-induced psychotic disorder. The condition is diagnosed most often in ambulatory psychiatric settings, though acute exacerbations may require hospitalization or emergency care for management of psychosis. Diagnosis typically requires exclusion of secondary causes via clinical assessments and imaging/laboratory studies. Routine management requires long-term antipsychotic treatment and frequent follow-ups in psychiatric care settings.
