Explicitly excluded are: embolism to the cerebral circulation (ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack); embolism to the coronary circulation (acute myocardial infarction); in-situ atherothrombosis at the site of arterial occlusion without an identifiable proximal embolic source; paradoxical embolism in which a venous thrombus traverses an intracardiac or intrapulmonary shunt to enter the systemic circulation; and all non-thrombotic embolic material, including air, fat, cholesterol crystals, tumor fragments, and septic emboli.
clinical_rationale: Systemic embolism is a plausible pharmacovigilance outcome, as various drugs could increase the risk by promoting thromboembolism, such as oral contraceptives, hormone replacement therapy, and cancer therapies. It specifically refers to embolism of thrombotic origin from the left-sided systemic arterial circulation, excluding cerebral, coronary, and in-situ atherothrombotic events, as well as non-thrombotic embolic phenomena. The condition is acute, with discrete episodes that resolve or lead to irreversible ischemic damage. Diagnosis relies on objective evidence of an occlusive embolic mechanism, typically detected via imaging or other diagnostic procedures, and the condition often requires immediate medical or surgical treatment. It is primarily identified and managed in acute care settings, given the severity and the need for urgent intervention to restore perfusion.

source_definition: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, relapsing-remitting, multisystem autoimmune disease characterized by a fundamental breakdown in self-tolerance, resulting in the production of pathogenic autoantibodies â€” particularly against double-stranded DNA and other nuclear antigens â€” with resultant immune complex formation and deposition across multiple organ systems. The phenotype encompasses any individual who meets established classification criteria for SLE at any point in time, regardless of current disease activity, and includes the full spectrum of disease severity from mild hematologic or serositic involvement to cutaneous-predominant presentations that fulfill systemic criteria. The phenotype explicitly excludes: (1) drug-induced lupus-like syndromes, which are mechanistically distinct, typically reversible, and lack the characteristic autoantibody profile of idiopathic SLE; (2) isolated cutaneous (discoid) lupus erythematosus that has not progressed to fulfill systemic classification criteria; and (3) undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) and mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), which share clinical and serologic features with SLE but do not independently satisfy full SLE classification requirements.
clinical_rationale: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease with complex etiology, including potential drug exacerbation or triggering in genetically predisposed individuals. While drug-induced lupus is excluded from this phenotype, it is plausible that some drugs may exacerbate idiopathic SLE flares or onset. SLE is inherently relapsing-remitting; patients carry the diagnostic label lifelong once classified, irrespective of disease activity. Incident SLE is usually detected in outpatient care but patients often present to acute care settings during systemic or severe flares. Because the phenotype requires meeting systemic SLE criteria, isolated drug-induced lupus, discoid lupus, and UCTD/MCTD are explicitly excluded. The diagnosis typically relies on a combination of clinical features and confirmatory serologic testing, particularly anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies.

source_definition: Systemic sclerosis is a chronic, progressive autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by the triad of immune dysregulation, obliterative vasculopathy, and fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. It encompasses two major subtypes: limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), in which skin fibrosis is restricted to the face and the extremities distal to the elbows and knees, and diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc), in which fibrosis extends proximally to involve the trunk and is associated with earlier and more severe visceral disease, including interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, scleroderma renal crisis, and gastrointestinal dysmotility. Both subtypes are driven by primary autoimmune pathophysiology and are characterized by circulating disease-specific autoantibodies. Excluded from this definition are all scleroderma-like fibrotic states attributable to an identified exogenous or iatrogenic cause, including toxic oil syndrome, eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, drug-induced fibrosis, nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, and sclerodermatous graft-versus-host disease, as well as localized forms of scleroderma confined to the skin without systemic involvement.
clinical_rationale: Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune connective tissue disorder driven by immune dysregulation, vasculopathy, and tissue fibrosis, which can involve multiple organ systems, including the skin, lungs, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and cardiovascular system. The provided clinical definition excludes drug-induced and exogenous fibrotic conditions (e.g., toxic oil syndrome, nephrogenic systemic fibrosis), which have distinct pathophysiologic mechanisms. While systemic sclerosis itself is not drug-induced, certain drugs may exacerbate organ-specific complications of the disease, such as scleroderma renal crisis triggered by glucocorticoids or cyclophosphamide-related pulmonary fibrosis. Its chronic and progressive nature means the label is retained for life, and ongoing care for organ-specific complications is expected. Most incident cases are diagnosed in outpatient rheumatology or specialty care settings, but acute care may occur during severe crises like renal crisis or pulmonary hypertension requiring hospitalization.

source_definition: T-cell lymphoma is a malignant neoplasm arising from mature, post-thymic (peripheral) T-lymphocytes or natural killer (NK) cells, confirmed by histopathologic examination demonstrating clonal lymphoid proliferation with T-cell or NK-cell immunophenotype. The phenotype encompasses all stages of systemic disease (Ann Arbor Stages I through IV), including both nodal and extranodal sites of involvement, and captures the full spectrum of lymphomatous and leukemic clinical presentations arising from mature T/NK-cell lineage, including entities such as peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS), angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL), anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL), T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL), and T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia (T-LGL). Excluded from this phenotype are: precursor T-cell neoplasms (T-lymphoblastic lymphoma and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia), which arise from immature thymic precursors and are biologically distinct; primarily cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (e.g., mycosis fungoides, SÃ©zary syndrome) confined to the skin without systemic transformation or dissemination; reactive or atypical T-cell proliferations without confirmed clonal malignancy; and all B-cell and Hodgkin lymphomas.
clinical_rationale: T-cell lymphoma is a biologically plausible pharmacovigilance outcome due to reported associations with immunosuppressive therapies, including monoclonal antibodies and TNF inhibitors, which may alter T-cell function or surveillance. Specific drug classes linked with lymphomas also raise concern, such as alkylating agents. Diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation with T-cell or NK-cell immunophenotype, making the condition dependent on diagnostic testing and largely managed in specialized care centers. The label 'T-cell lymphoma' encompasses diverse subtypes and disease presentations with a typically persistent nature; recurrence or progression is captured under the same diagnostic designation. Excluded subtypes like purely cutaneous lymphomas should not be considered within the pharmacovigilance scope unless systemic transformation occurs, requiring clear phenotyping logic to align with the definition provided.

source_definition: Tachycardia, as an adverse clinical outcome, is defined as a sustained resting heart rate of 100 beats per minute or greater occurring in the absence of recognized physiologic stimuli such as physical exertion or acute emotional arousal. The phenotype encompasses all underlying mechanisms and etiologies, including primary cardiac arrhythmias â€” such as pathological sinus tachycardia, supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation or flutter with rapid ventricular response â€” as well as tachycardia arising as a manifestation of systemic disorders, including but not limited to sepsis, pulmonary embolism, severe anemia, and hyperthyroidism. The condition is characterized by an abnormal and clinically significant elevation in heart rate defined by its pathological context rather than its mechanism alone, and functions as a broad adverse outcome indicator irrespective of whether a concurrent specific arrhythmia diagnosis is present. Purely physiologic compensatory heart rate elevations attributable to exercise, transient pain, or emotional stimuli are explicitly excluded.
clinical_rationale: Tachycardia as defined here is a broad syndrome of sustained elevated heart rate in the absence of recognized physiologic stimuli. Pathological sinus tachycardia and secondary arrhythmias are valid outcomes under specific contexts, and drug-induced tachycardia is well documented due to mechanisms such as beta-agonist overstimulation, QT interval prolongation, or anticholinergic toxicity. However, the inclusion of systemic causes like sepsis, hyperthyroidism, and anemia introduces etiologies not directly attributable to drug exposure. Therefore, tachycardia is a pharmacovigilance outcome only under a narrower reading focused on arrhythmia or drug-induced mechanisms. The clinical course varies by etiology; arrhythmias may be recurrent, whereas tachycardia secondary to systemic causes often resolves transiently with treatment of the underlying disorder. While it may be captured across all care settings depending on severity, acute care recognition is common in cases with systemic instability or arrhythmic threats.

source_definition: Takayasu's arteritis is a primary granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis characterized by transmural inflammation of the aorta and its major branches, occurring in individuals with an age of disease onset under 50 years. The condition encompasses the full disease spectrum: the early systemic inflammatory phase, marked by constitutional symptoms (fever, malaise, weight loss), elevated acute-phase reactants, and imaging evidence of arterial wall thickening or edema; and the late fibrotic and occlusive phase, characterized by established stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysmal dilation of the aorta or its primary branches, with clinical manifestations such as limb claudication, diminished or absent pulses, asymmetric blood pressure, renovascular hypertension, or aortic regurgitation. The phenotype captures any case carrying a clinician-assigned diagnosis of Takayasu's arteritis regardless of whether a secondary systemic autoimmune, infectious, or other underlying etiology is also present. Large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis presenting at age 50 or older is excluded as Giant Cell Arteritis and falls outside this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Takayasu's arteritis (TA) is primarily a large-vessel vasculitis with a granulomatous inflammatory mechanism. While its exact etiology remains idiopathic, drug-induced autoimmunity leading to vasculitis is biologically plausible, though rare, and case reports have documented drug-associated vasculitis involving large vessels. The description clarifies the importance of age of onset (<50 years) and categorically excludes Giant Cell Arteritis. The course of TA can involve both an early inflammatory phase and a late fibrotic/occlusive phase, with patients generally retaining the diagnosis once established. Due to systemic symptoms and severe manifestations, incident diagnoses are commonly made in acute care settings, though early-phase cases may present as outpatient evaluations of constitutional symptoms. Diagnosis requires imaging studies, and active treatment (e.g., immunosuppression) is expected during disease flares. Follow-up is essential given the risk of progressive vascular damage and sequelae such as aortic regurgitation or renovascular hypertension.

source_definition: Thrombocytopenia is a hematologic state characterized by a true reduction in the circulating platelet count below 150 Ã— 10â¹/L, as measured in peripheral blood. The condition encompasses all underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms that result in genuine platelet deficiency, including but not limited to impaired megakaryocytic production (e.g., bone marrow suppression or infiltration), accelerated peripheral destruction (e.g., immune-mediated, drug-induced, or consumptive processes), and abnormal platelet distribution or sequestration (e.g., hypersplenism). This definition is agnostic to etiology, severity subtype, and clinical symptomatology, capturing the full spectrum from mild to severe thrombocytopenia across all patient populations and clinical contexts. Explicitly excluded is pseudothrombocytopenia, an in vitro artifact in which platelet clumping â€” most commonly EDTA-dependent â€” produces a spuriously low automated platelet count that does not reflect a true reduction in circulating platelet levels.
clinical_rationale: Thrombocytopenia is described as a reduction in circulating platelet count below 150 × 10⁹/L, irrespective of the underlying mechanism or etiology. The description includes drug-induced thrombocytopenia, which is well-documented across multiple drug classes (e.g., heparin-induced, immune-mediated from antibiotics, chemotherapy-induced from bone marrow suppression). Drug-attributable cases are explicitly valid pharmacovigilance outcomes, though the broader definition encompasses non-drug causes such as genetic disorders, hypersplenism, or systemic diseases. Thrombocytopenia is an episodic, transient condition in most instances, as cases may resolve with treatment, withdrawal of an offending drug, or recovery from an underlying insult; however, recurrence is possible. Initial diagnoses can occur in acute or outpatient settings depending on severity and symptoms, but severe thrombocytopenia is more likely to be detected in acute care contexts due to bleeding or platelet-related complications.

source_definition: Thrombosis is the pathological formation of a blood clot (thrombus) at a discrete intravascular site â€” within either the venous or arterial circulation â€” resulting in partial or complete occlusion of that vessel at the point of formation. The diagnosis requires objective confirmation by an appropriate diagnostic modality and encompasses both clinically symptomatic events and thrombi detected incidentally. All biologically-driven etiological mechanisms are included in scope, encompassing spontaneous and idiopathic events, inherited thrombophilias (e.g., Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency), acquired prothrombotic states (e.g., antiphospholipid syndrome), immune-mediated thrombosis (e.g., heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, VITT), and thrombosis occurring as a biological consequence of systemic conditions such as malignancy, myeloproliferative neoplasms, infection, or disseminated intravascular coagulation. Thrombosis attributable to an iatrogenic or procedural cause â€” including device-associated, catheter-related, post-surgical, or immobilization-induced events â€” is excluded, as such thrombi arise from external mechanical triggers rather than intrinsic pathobiological processes. Embolic phenomena â€” wherein a clot or other occlusive material originating at a remote intravascular site travels to obstruct a distant vessel â€” are excluded; only in-situ thrombus formation at the local site of pathological coagulation activation qualifies as thrombosis under this definition.
clinical_rationale: Thrombosis, the pathologic formation of an intravascular blood clot, has well-documented drug-attributable etiologies, including drugs that induce immune thrombotic processes (e.g., heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia), and therapies that influence coagulation or platelet aggregation (e.g., estrogen-containing contraceptives, cancer therapies, or antiphospholipid treatments). The phenotype is biologically diverse, including spontaneous, acquired, and inherited mechanisms. Thrombosis is a recurrent condition where episodes are distinct and require diagnostic confirmation, commonly by imaging modalities or laboratory tests. This phenotype excludes iatrogenic thrombosis (e.g., catheter- or surgery-related) and embolic phenomena, narrowing its application to intrinsic pathobiological mechanisms. While venous thromboembolism is frequently incident in acute-care settings, arterial thrombosis may present across various contexts, leading to a classification of acute care as common rather than expected for incident events.

source_definition: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a pathological syndrome defined by microvascular endothelial injury leading to the formation of platelet-rich thrombi within small vessels, producing the characteristic hematological picture of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) and thrombocytopenia. MAHA requires the presence of fragmented red blood cells (schistocytes) with biochemical evidence of hemolysis and a negative direct antiglobulin test (DAT), thereby distinguishing it from immune-mediated hemolytic states. Thrombocytopenia reflects consumptive platelet loss within the microvasculature. End-organ damage â€” including renal insufficiency, neurological dysfunction, or cardiac injury â€” arising from microvascular ischemia is a supportive but non-obligatory feature when the hematological core criteria are satisfied. The syndrome encompasses all etiological forms, including TTP (ADAMTS13 deficiency), typical HUS (Shiga toxin-mediated), atypical HUS (complement dysregulation), drug-induced TMA, transplant-associated TMA, autoimmune-associated TMA, and malignancy-associated TMA. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is excluded when it constitutes the primary diagnosis; however, co-existent DIC does not preclude TMA when the dominant clinical and laboratory picture reflects microvascular thrombosis. Evans syndrome and other immune-mediated causes of thrombocytopenia and hemolysis are excluded on mechanistic grounds. HELLP syndrome in the setting of preeclampsia is excluded as a distinct obstetric entity; pregnancy-associated cases qualify only when a specific TMA mechanism â€” such as TTP or atypical HUS triggered by pregnancy â€” is operative.
clinical_rationale: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a pathological syndrome distinguished by endothelial injury, resulting in microvascular thrombosis, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Drug-induced TMA is a well-recognized and established safety outcome, with specific medications like quinine, mitomycin C, calcineurin inhibitors, and some chemotherapeutics implicated via mechanisms such as endothelial toxicity and complement dysregulation. Other etiologies, such as complement dysregulation (e.g., atypical HUS) and Shiga toxin-mediated HUS can occur without drug involvement, making drug etiology a conditional subset within the broad TMA category. Diagnosis typically requires laboratory evidence of hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes. Detecting drug-related TMA in observational data is particularly challenging due to etiological heterogeneity, overlap with other conditions (e.g., DIC, HELLP), and the need for specialized diagnostic testing. TMA is typically acute and urgent, with diagnosis frequently occurring in hospitalized patients, but recurrent episodes are possible within the broader natural history, particularly with syndromes like recurrent TTP.

source_definition: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) is an acquired, immune-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by the clinical syndrome of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, arising from autoantibody-mediated suppression or inhibition of ADAMTS13, the von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease. Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency leads to accumulation of ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers, spontaneous platelet aggregation, and formation of platelet-rich microthrombi in the microvasculature, producing end-organ ischemia most notably affecting the central nervous system, kidneys, and heart. Diagnosis is established on clinical grounds and does not require laboratory confirmation of ADAMTS13 activity below 10%. The phenotype is restricted to idiopathic (primary) immune-mediated cases and explicitly excludes congenital TTP caused by biallelic ADAMTS13 gene mutations, as well as all secondary thrombotic microangiopathies regardless of ADAMTS13 status, including those arising in the context of pregnancy (HELLP syndrome, obstetric TTP), malignancy, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and systemic autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus or antiphospholipid syndrome. Shiga toxin-mediated hemolytic uremic syndrome, complement-mediated atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and drug-induced thrombotic microangiopathies are also excluded.
clinical_rationale: The phenotype description explicitly focuses on idiopathic immune-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), which arises from severe acquired ADAMTS13 deficiency secondary to anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies. Importantly, it excludes congenital TTP, drug-induced thrombotic microangiopathies, and all secondary thrombotic microangiopathies (e.g., pregnancy-related HELLP syndrome) regardless of ADAMTS13 status. Immune-mediated TTP has documented drug-attributable etiology, most notably from ticlopidine and clopidogrel, which have been associated with direct immune-mediated mechanisms in case studies and regulatory warnings. This condition is life-threatening, with a clinical course that requires immediate plasma exchange therapy, steroids, and/or rituximab upon diagnosis. The diagnosis is often made in acute care settings based on clinical grounds, as marked ADAMTS13 deficiency testing, while confirmatory, is not required acutely. Autoantibody generation against ADAMTS13 constitutes a biologically plausible mechanism for drug-induced instances, substantiating its role as a pharmacovigilance outcome.

source_definition: Thyroid adenoma, as defined here, is a histologically confirmed, solitary, encapsulated benign neoplasm of follicular epithelial cell origin arising within the thyroid gland, characterized by a complete fibrous capsule and the absence of capsular or vascular invasion. The phenotype encompasses both non-functioning (hormonally quiescent, euthyroid) and autonomously hyperfunctioning (toxic) variants, the latter defined by independent thyroid hormone secretion with resultant TSH suppression. Inclusion requires histopathological confirmation demonstrating a true neoplastic proliferation; non-neoplastic adenomatoid or hyperplastic nodules arising within the context of multinodular goiter are explicitly excluded on the basis of their non-clonal, polyclonal proliferative origin. Follicular thyroid carcinoma is excluded by the requirement for intact capsular architecture and the absence of any evidence of invasive growth. HÃ¼rthle cell (oncocytic follicular) neoplasms are excluded as a distinct histological entity. Both sporadic and hereditary syndrome-associated follicular adenomas are included, as syndromic origin does not alter the fundamental neoplastic and histological character of the lesion.
clinical_rationale: Thyroid adenoma is a benign neoplasm of the thyroid gland, histologically distinct from thyroid carcinoma and multinodular goiter. The clinical scope, which includes both euthyroid and toxic variants, is independent of etiology; however, the hyperfunctioning (toxic) variant can lead to clinically relevant thyrotoxicosis. Drugs such as iodine-containing agents or amiodarone can influence thyroid function but do not directly induce thyroid adenoma, as the condition is driven by neoplastic proliferation, not drug exposure. Thus, the phenotype is NOT a pharmacovigilance outcome. Incidental findings are common in outpatient or screening contexts; symptomatic toxic adenomas may first be recognized in either outpatient care or acute care settings due to hyperthyroid symptoms. Histopathological confirmation is required for definitive diagnosis, with routine thyroid function testing useful for detecting autonomous hyperfunction.

source_definition: Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune inflammatory and remodeling disorder of the orbital and periorbital tissues driven by TSH-receptor autoantibody-mediated activation of orbital fibroblasts, occurring in the context of established or concurrent thyroid autoimmune disease, including Graves' disease or Hashimoto's thyroiditis, or in the presence of detectable thyroid autoantibodies. The condition encompasses the full severity spectrum from mild signs such as lid retraction, periorbital edema, or minimal proptosis, through moderate-to-severe disease with significant proptosis, restrictive diplopia, or corneal exposure, to sight-threatening disease caused by dysthyroid optic neuropathy or severe corneal breakdown. The phenotype includes both the active inflammatory phase, characterized by ongoing orbital inflammation, tissue expansion due to glycosaminoglycan deposition and extraocular muscle enlargement, and clinical activity signs, and the inactive quiescent phase, characterized by stable fibrotic orbital remodeling without active inflammation. Excluded are orbital inflammatory conditions without thyroid autoimmune disease association, including idiopathic orbital inflammatory pseudotumor, IgG4-related orbital disease, infectious orbital cellulitis, and orbital neoplasms, as well as clinically identical orbital disease occurring in entirely euthyroid, antibody-negative individuals with no evidence of thyroid autoimmunity.
clinical_rationale: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is a recognized autoimmune orbital disorder strongly associated with thyroid autoimmune diseases such as Graves' disease, driven by TSH-receptor autoantibody-mediated orbital fibroblast activation leading to inflammation and tissue remodeling. While TED itself is not primarily drug-induced, it can be exacerbated or contributed to by treatments such as radioactive iodine therapy, glucocorticoids, or thyroid surgery. Drug-induced orbital inflammatory conditions without thyroid autoimmunity are excluded and are not part of this phenotype. Given its persistence due to fibrotic remodeling in the quiescent phase, TED is a chronic condition with relapsing activity. Incident diagnosis occurs most commonly in outpatient care, but severe cases may involve acute settings. Testing is nearly universal, comprising imaging, autoimmune antibody titers, and thyroid function tests.

source_definition: Thyroid storm is an acute, life-threatening hypermetabolic crisis arising from extreme excess of circulating thyroid hormones, regardless of the underlying etiology of hyperthyroidism. It is characterized by severe, multi-system end-organ dysfunction, manifesting as one or more of the following: central nervous system disturbance (agitation, confusion, delirium, seizure, or coma), cardiovascular compromise (tachyarrhythmia, high-output cardiac failure, or hemodynamic instability), marked hyperpyrexia, or hepatic and gastrointestinal dysfunction (jaundice, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea). This distinction from severe but compensated thyrotoxicosis is essential: the diagnosis requires evidence of end-organ decompensation, not biochemical hormone excess alone. The presence of an identifiable physiological precipitant is not required; the phenotype is defined entirely by the clinical state of hypermetabolic decompensation with multi-organ involvement.
clinical_rationale: Thyroid storm is a hypermetabolic emergency requiring urgent recognition and intervention. Drug causality is established in precipitating underlying hyperthyroidism (e.g., amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis) and triggering thyroid storm in predisposed patients (e.g., discontinuation of antithyroid drugs or iodine-containing contrast media). The clinical course is transient and acute, as the diagnosis applies strictly to an episode of decompensation, after which the label is shed upon recovery. Incident cases nearly always present in acute care settings due to their life-threatening severity and multi-system dysfunction. Diagnostic codes for thyroid storm have high specificity but limited sensitivity, as the diagnosis relies on clinical judgment often supplemented by biochemical markers and imaging. The definition explicitly excludes non-decompensated thyrotoxicosis, underscoring the need for clinical evidence of organ-specific failure. This supports pharmacovigilance relevance since certain drugs can act as precipitants or contributors to the acute decompensation.

source_definition: Thyroiditis is a clinically evident inflammatory condition of the thyroid gland characterized by immune-mediated, infectious, granulomatous, fibroinflammatory, or exogenous-agent-induced injury to thyroid parenchyma, presenting with at least one of the following: symptomatic thyroid dysfunction (thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism), anterior neck pain or tenderness attributable to thyroid inflammation, or objective evidence of thyroid inflammation on imaging or histopathology. The phenotype encompasses all mechanistic subtypes, including chronic autoimmune (lymphocytic) thyroiditis, subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, postpartum thyroiditis, suppurative (infectious) thyroiditis, drug-induced thyroiditis (e.g., from checkpoint inhibitors, amiodarone, or lithium), radiation-induced thyroiditis, and fibrosing (Riedel's) thyroiditis. Explicitly excluded are non-inflammatory causes of thyroid dysfunction â€” including central or secondary hypothyroidism arising from pituitary or hypothalamic pathology, autonomous nodular thyroid function (toxic multinodular goiter), and Graves' disease, in which thyrotoxicosis is mediated by TSH-receptor-stimulating autoantibodies without a primary inflammatory thyroid process â€” as well as subclinical or incidentally detected thyroid autoimmunity without clinical manifestation of thyroid inflammation.
clinical_rationale: Thyroiditis is a diverse group of inflammatory conditions of the thyroid gland with multiple potential etiologies, including drug-induced mechanisms. Many drugs, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., nivolumab, pembrolizumab), amiodarone, lithium, and interferon-alpha, have been associated with thyroiditis through direct inflammatory mechanisms or immune dysregulation. The clinical course varies by subtype, but many cases, particularly those with subacute or drug-induced thyroiditis, are transient and can recur with repeat insults or drug re-challenges. Incident cases of thyroiditis are generally recognized and managed in the outpatient setting unless there is severe thyrotoxicosis, pain, or complications necessitating acute care. Diagnosis frequently involves clinical assessment and confirmatory laboratory (e.g., TSH, T4) and imaging studies (e.g., thyroid ultrasound). Initially treated cases may involve pain management, thyroid hormone replacement, or antithyroid therapies depending on the clinical presentation. While symptoms such as neck pain or thyroid dysfunction are common, they may not always appear as discrete structured records distinct from the thyroiditis diagnosis, and follow-up care is often necessary depending on the cause and progression of the thyroiditis.

source_definition: Thyrotoxicosis is a pathological state characterized by an excess of circulating thyroid hormones â€” elevated free thyroxine (fT4) and/or free triiodothyronine (fT3) â€” accompanied by suppression of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), reflecting the physiological consequences of hormone excess on the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis. The condition encompasses all pathological etiologies, including autonomous endogenous overproduction (as in Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, or solitary toxic adenoma), passive hormone release from inflammatory glandular destruction (as in subacute, postpartum, or silent thyroiditis), and excess from exogenous sources (including iatrogenic over-replacement and factitious ingestion). Clinical manifestations arise from the hypermetabolic and adrenergic-potentiation effects of hormone excess and may include tachycardia, heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, and anxiety, with severe cases progressing to thyroid storm. Subclinical thyrotoxicosis â€” defined by TSH suppression with thyroid hormone levels remaining within the reference range â€” is explicitly excluded, as is the transient, physiological hCG-mediated thyroid hormone elevation of the first trimester of pregnancy.
clinical_rationale: Thyrotoxicosis has both endogenous and exogenous causes, including drug-induced mechanisms such as exogenous over-replacement of thyroid hormones or factitious ingestion. Regulatory warnings exist for thyroid hormone preparations and amiodarone, which may induce thyrotoxicosis via complex iodine-mediated mechanisms. The condition's clinical manifestations are characteristic and arise from adrenergic and hypermetabolic effects of excess thyroid hormone. Most cases are transient and resolve either through withdrawal of causative agents, normalization following thyroiditis resolution, or definitive treatment like thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine ablation. Thyroid storm is a life-threatening complication that typically requires acute care settings. Diagnostic confirmation almost universally involves laboratory evidence of suppressed TSH and elevated free thyroid hormones, making objective testing central to case ascertainment. Persistent sequelae such as hypothyroidism or cardiac complications may occur in some cases and require long-term follow-up.

source_definition: Tinea pedis is a superficial fungal infection of the skin of the foot caused exclusively by dermatophyte fungi â€” primarily Trichophyton rubrum, Trichophyton mentagrophytes, and Epidermophyton floccosum â€” characterized by pathological invasion of the stratum corneum by these keratinophilic organisms. The condition encompasses all clinically recognized morphological subtypes, including interdigital tinea pedis (maceration, scaling, and fissuring of the web spaces), moccasin-type tinea pedis (diffuse hyperkeratosis and scaling of the plantar surface and lateral foot borders), vesiculobullous tinea pedis (inflammatory blistering typically involving the arch or instep), and ulcerative tinea pedis (progressive web-space ulceration, often with secondary bacterial superinfection). This phenotype is restricted to symptomatic, clinically manifest infection and excludes asymptomatic dermatophyte colonization. Explicitly excluded are non-dermatophyte fungal foot infections (e.g., cutaneous candidiasis, non-dermatophyte mold infections), as well as morphologically similar but pathophysiologically distinct entities including dyshidrotic eczema (pompholyx), palmoplantar psoriasis, allergic or irritant contact dermatitis of the foot, and bacterial interdigital intertrigo or erythrasma caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum.
clinical_rationale: Tinea pedis has no direct drug-attributable etiology and is exclusively caused by dermatophyte fungi. There is no mechanism for drugs to induce this fungal infection. It often manifests as interdigital maceration or plantar scaling and can be complicated by secondary bacterial infections requiring treatment. Diagnosis is based on clinical appearance, with confirmatory testing such as microscopy or culture being used in selected cases. It is transient and resolves with treatment, but reinfection is common. Incident cases are generally diagnosed in outpatient settings as the condition is not life-threatening and does not require emergent care. Symptoms, often including scaling, fissuring, or blistering, are readily observable and documented. Active treatment is required to eradicate the infection. Post-treatment surveillance is not typically necessary within one year unless reinfection occurs.

source_definition: Torsade de Pointes is an acquired form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia defined by a distinctive electrocardiographic pattern in which successive QRS complexes appear to twist around the isoelectric baseline, progressively cycling in amplitude and axis over a sequence of three or more beats, in the setting of a pathologically prolonged QT interval that is attributable to an exogenous or reversible trigger â€” such as a pharmacological agent, electrolyte disturbance (e.g., hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia), or metabolic insult â€” rather than an inherited channelopathy. Electrocardiographic documentation of both the characteristic twisting morphology and QT prolongation is required for inclusion; the QT prolongation must represent an acquired alteration of ventricular repolarization, not a baseline heritable trait. Episodes of any duration qualify provided the ECG criteria are met, including brief self-terminating runs. Explicitly excluded are: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia occurring in the absence of QT prolongation (e.g., catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, ischemia-associated polymorphic VT with normal QT interval); Torsade de Pointes arising in the context of congenital Long QT syndrome (e.g., LQT1, LQT2, LQT3, or related inherited channelopathies); monomorphic ventricular tachycardia; and ventricular fibrillation that cannot be confirmed to have originated as a TdP episode.
clinical_rationale: Torsade de Pointes (TdP) is a significant pharmacovigilance outcome due to its strong association with specific medications that can prolong the cardiac QT interval, such as antiarrhythmic drugs, antipsychotics, certain antibiotics, and other QT-prolonging agents. The clinical definition explicitly focuses on the acquired form of TdP, which is triggered by exogenous factors like medications or electrolytic and metabolic disturbances. It excludes other causes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, such as congenital Long QT syndromes or ischemia. Since it is a transient ventricular arrhythmia and requires specific electrocardiographic findings for diagnosis, its detection relies on both clinician judgment and appropriate diagnostic testing. Episodes are self-terminating or lead to immediate clinical deterioration, thus it is transient when considered as an episode, though significant monitoring is typically warranted. Given its strong linkage to iatrogenic triggers like drugs and the need for QT prolongation documentation by ECG, it is a critical endpoint for pharmacovigilance studies investigating drug safety related to cardiac adverse events.

source_definition: Toxic epidermal necrolysis is a severe, acute, immune-mediated mucocutaneous disorder characterized by widespread full-thickness epidermal necrosis and detachment involving more than 30% of the total body surface area, driven by extensive cytotoxic T-lymphocyte- and natural killer cell-mediated keratinocyte apoptosis. The condition may arise from any identifiable trigger â€” including drug exposure, infection, or idiopathic causes â€” and is defined entirely by its pathophysiological presentation rather than etiology. It is distinguished from Stevens-Johnson syndrome (less than 10% BSA involvement) and SJS/TEN overlap (10â€“30% BSA) strictly by the extent of epidermal detachment. Excluded from this concept are: staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, in which bacterial exotoxin-mediated subcorneal cleavage produces superficial, non-immune-driven epidermal separation; thermal and chemical burns, which represent mechanical rather than immunological epidermal destruction; and cutaneous graft-versus-host disease, in which allogeneic T-cell activity in the post-transplant setting produces histologically similar epidermal necrosis through a fundamentally distinct pathophysiological mechanism.
clinical_rationale: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is a severe, immune-mediated dermatologic emergency. Drug-induced TEN is well-documented, with causative drugs including anticonvulsants, antibiotics, and NSAIDs, among others. The distinction between TEN and Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) lies in the extent of epidermal detachment (>30% BSA for TEN). While non-drug etiologies exist (e.g., infections or idiopathic causes), the immune-mediated pathophysiology of drug-induced TEN makes it highly relevant for pharmacovigilance studies. Clinically, incident cases almost universally present in acute care settings due to their life-threatening severity and are typically diagnosed based on clinical presentation and histopathological confirmation. Drug exposure history is critical for identifying cases related to medications.

source_definition: Transient Global Amnesia is an acute, self-resolving neurological episode characterized by the sudden onset of profound anterograde amnesia â€” the inability to encode new memories â€” accompanied by variable retrograde amnesia spanning hours to days prior to episode onset. During the episode, the patient retains personal identity, procedural memory, and other higher cognitive functions, and typically exhibits repetitive questioning as a behavioral hallmark. All memory deficits resolve completely within 24 hours of onset, with no residual anterograde impairment. The diagnosis requires the absence of focal neurological signs and the exclusion of competing etiologies, specifically seizure-related amnesia (Transient Epileptic Amnesia), acute cerebrovascular ischemia (TIA or stroke), head trauma causing post-traumatic amnesia, and drug- or alcohol-induced blackouts.
clinical_rationale: Transient Global Amnesia (TGA) is characterized by acute, temporary anterograde and partial retrograde amnesia that resolves within 24 hours, with no residual deficits. The diagnosis is exclusionary and requires ruling out competing causes such as epilepsy, stroke, trauma, or substance-related effects. While TGA may sometimes follow triggers such as emotional stress, physical exertion, or even certain medications, there is no established direct drug-attributable etiology or biologically plausible drug-triggered mechanism. Episodes are transient and self-limiting, making pharmacovigilance relevance indirect at best, as the episode is usually unrelated to medications and further complicated by exclusion challenges. It is most commonly diagnosed in the emergency department, often fulfilling an urgent diagnostic need to differentiate it from more serious conditions like stroke.

source_definition: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is an acute, self-limiting episode of focal neurological dysfunction arising from temporary interruption of blood flow to a discrete region of the brain, spinal cord, or retina, in which all neurological deficits resolve completely within 24 hours of onset. The underlying vascular mechanism may be of any cerebrovascular etiology, including cardioembolic, large-artery atherosclerotic, small-vessel, arterial dissection, or cryptogenic origin. This phenotype explicitly excludes conditions that produce transient focal neurological deficits through non-ischemic mechanisms, including epileptic events with postictal (Todd's) paralysis, hemiplegic migraine with aura, hypoglycemia-induced focal neurological deficits, syncopal episodes with transient neurological features, and structural lesions such as subdural hematoma or intracranial mass effect. Classification does not require neuroimaging confirmation of infarct absence; the temporal resolution criterion of symptom duration under 24 hours is sufficient.
clinical_rationale: Transient ischemic attack (TIA) represents an acute, self-limiting cerebrovascular event often linked to transient interruption of blood flow due to embolic, thrombotic, or other vascular etiologies. Drug causality is plausible in cases of arterial dissection, cardioembolic events (e.g., atrial fibrillation provoked by medications), or iatrogenic hypercoagulability. However, non-vascular mimics of transient focal neurological deficits must be carefully excluded, as the phenotype definition is vascular-specific. It is a transient condition where the label is shed once the episode resolves within 24 hours, and any subsequent event constitutes a genuinely new onset. While incident diagnosis may occur in outpatient settings due to symptom resolution before ED presentation, most cases arise in or are referred to acute care settings given the urgency of ruling out stroke. No repeat testing is required to confirm symptom resolution, and treatment often includes preventive interventions rather than acute symptom resolution strategies.

source_definition: Transverse myelitis is an inflammatory disorder of the spinal cord characterized by dysfunction of motor, sensory, and/or autonomic pathways below the level of the affected spinal cord segment(s), arising from immune-mediated inflammation of the cord parenchyma, regardless of onset tempo. The condition encompasses both complete presentations â€” with bilateral, symmetric motor and sensory deficits and a defined sensory level â€” and incomplete presentations â€” with asymmetric or partial neurological deficits. The phenotype is etiologically inclusive, capturing idiopathic transverse myelitis as well as myelitis occurring in the context of established demyelinating diseases (including multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder), post-infectious or parainfectious immune activation, and systemic autoimmune conditions (such as systemic lupus erythematosus and SjÃ¶gren's syndrome). The phenotype explicitly excludes myelopathy attributable to mechanical spinal cord compression (e.g., intervertebral disc herniation, neoplastic invasion, epidural abscess or hematoma, or vertebral fracture), vascular injury (including spinal cord infarction, arteriovenous malformation-related myelopathy, and other ischemic or hemorrhagic causes), and toxic or metabolic insults (including subacute combined degeneration from nutritional deficiencies, radiation-induced myelopathy, and chemotherapy-associated myelopathy).
clinical_rationale: Transverse myelitis is a complex condition with immune-mediated inflammation of the spinal cord parenchyma. It may arise idiopathically or in association with systemic autoimmune disorders (e.g., lupus, Sjögren's syndrome), demyelinating diseases (e.g., multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder), or post-infectious immune activation. Drug-induced transverse myelitis is plausibly mechanistic in some cases, with known immune-mediated mechanisms for certain drugs (e.g., immune checkpoint inhibitors). The description appropriately excludes non-inflammatory etiologies such as trauma, ischemia, mechanical compression, and nutritional/toxic causes, ensuring focus on immune-mediated inflammation.

source_definition: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is an acquired disruption of normal brain structure or function caused by the application of an external physical force to the head or body, spanning the full continuum of severity from mild injury (concussion, characterized by transient neurological dysfunction with or without brief loss of consciousness and without obligate structural lesion) through moderate and severe injury (characterized by prolonged alteration of consciousness, post-traumatic amnesia, and/or demonstrable structural damage to brain parenchyma). All biomechanical mechanisms of injury are included: blunt or closed head injury from acceleration-deceleration or direct impact forces, penetrating injury such as projectile or impalement wounds, and blast-related injury from pressure-wave exposure. The phenotype encompasses the secondary pathophysiological cascade initiated by the primary insult â€” including cerebral edema, post-traumatic ischemia, raised intracranial pressure, and transtentorial or subfalcine herniation â€” as these represent direct biological consequences of the traumatic event rather than independent disease processes. Birth-related mechanical brain injury sustained during delivery and iatrogenic brain injury arising from surgical or procedural intervention are also included, as both fulfill the defining criterion of brain dysfunction attributable to an external physical force. Explicitly excluded are all non-traumatic acquired brain injuries, including ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke of vascular origin, hypoxic-anoxic encephalopathy, metabolic or toxic encephalopathy, and infectious or autoimmune encephalitis, none of which involve an external mechanical force as their primary etiology.
clinical_rationale: Traumatic brain injury is caused by external mechanical forces and includes a well-documented spectrum of secondary pathologies such as cerebral edema, post-traumatic ischemia, and herniation. Drug-related causation is not biologically plausible for the primary insult but could influence secondary outcomes (e.g., anticoagulant use exacerbating intracranial bleeding, or sedative-induced impairment contributing to falls that cause TBI). As the focus is on the mechanical cause, this phenotype is not suitable as a direct pharmacovigilance outcome. Incident TBI is typically diagnosed in acute care settings, often requiring imaging for severity classification. Recurrence is rare but possible in the setting of repeated or new trauma, making the clinical course transient and episodic. Structured symptom documentation prior to diagnosis (e.g., headache, altered consciousness) is uncommon, as symptoms are often subsumed under the primary injury code.

source_definition: Tremor is a symptom defined by rhythmic, involuntary oscillatory movement of one or more body parts, arising from alternating or synchronous contractions of antagonistic muscle groups. The phenotype encompasses all detectable tremor regardless of etiology, including physiologic tremor enhanced by metabolic stressors, drugs, or anxiety, as well as tremor occurring as a manifestation of neurological, systemic, or psychiatric disease. No minimum severity threshold is required; the tremor need only be clinically detectable. All activation states are included â€” resting, postural, kinetic, and intention tremor â€” across all anatomical distributions including limb, head, jaw, voice, and trunk. Asterixis and dystonic tremor are considered within scope given their oscillatory phenomenology, which overlaps with tremor classification in established clinical taxonomy. Explicitly excluded are non-rhythmic involuntary movement disorders: myoclonus, characterized by sudden, brief, shock-like jerks; chorea, characterized by irregular, flowing, non-patterned movements; and tics, which are stereotyped, semi-voluntary, and suppressible â€” all of which are distinct from true tremor in both neural mechanism and clinical phenomenology.
clinical_rationale: Tremor is a rhythmic, involuntary oscillatory movement that can be drug-attributable, particularly as a dose- or exposure-dependent adverse effect of medications such as beta-adrenergic agonists, antipsychotics, antidepressants (e.g., SSRIs), or antiemetics (e.g., metoclopramide). Tremor can also present as an exacerbation of physiologic tremor in response to metabolic stressors, substance withdrawal, or toxins. The definition is broad, encompassing all anatomical distributions, activation states, and types of tremor, which limits specificity for pharmacovigilance. Non-rhythmic movement disorders such as chorea or tics are excluded based on their distinct neural mechanisms. As tremor is not typically associated with discrete disease episodes but rather reflects persistent or recurrent patterns tied to underlying causes, it is generally persistent unless clearly linked to a transient trigger.

source_definition: Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused exclusively by organisms of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (including M. tuberculosis, M. bovis, and M. africanum), encompassing the full clinical spectrum from latent TB infection (LTBI) to active TB disease. In LTBI, the host immune response contains the pathogen within granulomatous structures without active tissue destruction, active replication, or clinical symptoms. Active TB disease arises when this containment fails â€” either through primary progressive infection or reactivation â€” resulting in pathogen-driven granulomatous inflammation, caseous necrosis, and overt clinical illness. Active disease may involve any anatomical site, including pulmonary parenchyma, pleura, lymph nodes, meninges, bones, joints, genitourinary tract, and disseminated (miliary) forms. Infections caused by non-tuberculous mycobacteria, regardless of clinical or radiographic similarity to TB, are explicitly excluded from this phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Tuberculosis (TB) can occur in active or latent forms, and only active disease is clinically symptomatic. Drugs, particularly immunosuppressants like TNF-alpha inhibitors, are documented to precipitate reactivation of latent TB, making TB relevant as a pharmacovigilance outcome. Active TB disease is typically persistent until adequately treated, with a prolonged course and organ-specific sequelae expected. Diagnosis generally requires microbiologic or histopathologic confirmation, and active treatment is expected within 30 days due to the contagious and progressive nature of the disease. Incident cases are often diagnosed in outpatient settings but severe presentations may require acute care. The provided definition appropriately excludes non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections as a confounding condition.

source_definition: Tumor flare reaction is a transient, self-limiting paradoxical worsening of tumor-related clinical signs and symptoms â€” including but not limited to localized pain, soft tissue swelling, erythema, and hypercalcemia â€” and/or an apparent worsening of radiological findings or tumor biomarkers (such as PSA or tumor marker elevation, or increased lesion activity on imaging), occurring in temporal proximity to the initiation of systemic anti-cancer therapy of any class. The phenomenon reflects a transient biological response at the tumor site or in surrogate markers prior to therapeutic benefit, and is distinguished from true disease progression by its self-limiting course and subsequent objective response or disease stabilization. Cytokine release syndrome, a systemic immune toxicity driven by supraphysiologic immune activation independent of tumor site behavior, and tumor lysis syndrome, a metabolic emergency resulting from rapid tumor cell death, are explicitly excluded from this concept.
clinical_rationale: Tumor flare reaction is a paradoxical transient worsening of tumor-related symptoms or surrogate markers triggered by systemic anti-cancer therapy. Although transient and self-limiting, it represents an important distinction from true disease progression and reflects underlying biological activity at the tumor site following therapy initiation. There is no documented direct drug-causative association independent of treatment context, making its relevance in drug safety surveillance conditional upon evaluating tumor flare within the scope of anti-cancer therapy initiation. Symptoms like localized pain and swelling may be recorded, along with radiological findings or marker elevation, but discrete symptom documentation is inconsistent and often subsumed within the tumor flare diagnosis itself. Objective imaging or biomarker monitoring is required to verify the diagnosis, and active treatment is contraindicated; instead, supportive observation is typical until resolution. Long-term sequelae are unlikely after the flare resolves, provided therapy is effective against the underlying tumor.

source_definition: Tumour Lysis Syndrome is a metabolic emergency arising from the rapid, large-scale lysis of neoplastic cells â€” of any histologic type, whether hematologic or solid â€” releasing intracellular contents (potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acid catabolites, principally uric acid) into the systemic circulation in quantities that exceed the body's normal homeostatic and excretory capacity. The syndrome encompasses the full spectrum from laboratory TLS, defined by clinically meaningful rises from an established pre-event baseline in two or more of serum uric acid, potassium, or phosphate, or a reciprocal fall in calcium attributable to tumor cell lysis, through clinical TLS, in which those metabolic derangements produce at least one organ-level consequence such as acute kidney injury, life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia, seizure, neuromuscular irritability, or death. Either spontaneous lysis driven by intrinsic tumor proliferation kinetics or lysis precipitated by cytotoxic, cytoreductive, targeted, or immunologic therapy falls within scope. Metabolic abnormalities present at baseline and wholly explained by pre-existing non-neoplastic conditions â€” including chronic kidney disease, gout, or adrenal insufficiency â€” are excluded. Rhabdomyolysis, which can produce an overlapping metabolic profile through skeletal muscle lysis, is excluded only when it represents the sole mechanism for the observed derangements; cases in which tumor cell lysis is a concurrent contributing mechanism remain within the phenotype.
clinical_rationale: Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS) is a recognized drug-attributable pharmacovigilance outcome due to its frequent association with cytotoxic, cytoreductive, targeted, or immunologic therapy for cancer. Its pathophysiology involves rapid lysis of tumor cells, leading to severe metabolic derangements such as hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, and hypocalcemia that can progress to organ-level consequences including acute kidney injury and cardiac arrhythmias. This makes TLS a biologically plausible and clinically relevant outcome for drug safety surveillance. Incident TLS typically manifests as an acute metabolic emergency requiring urgent intervention, and its criteria distinguish it from baseline metabolic abnormalities unrelated to tumor cell lysis. It is most commonly recognized in acute care settings such as inpatient or emergency departments due to its severity.

source_definition: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is a chronic, autoimmune condition defined by immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells, resulting in progressive and ultimately absolute insulin deficiency. The phenotype encompasses the full biological continuum of disease, beginning with the presymptomatic stages in which islet autoimmunity is confirmed by the presence of two or more circulating autoantibodies targeting islet antigens â€” including glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies (GADA), islet antigen-2 autoantibodies (IA-2A), zinc transporter 8 autoantibodies (ZnT8A), and insulin autoantibodies (IAA) â€” in the absence of glycemic abnormality, and extending through the clinical stage characterized by hyperglycemia meeting established diagnostic thresholds. This phenotype includes all autoimmune-mediated diabetes regardless of age of onset or rate of beta-cell loss, and therefore encompasses Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), which shares the same pathophysiological mechanism of immune-mediated beta-cell destruction. Explicitly excluded are all forms of diabetes arising through non-autoimmune mechanisms, including pancreatogenic diabetes (Type 3c) resulting from structural or inflammatory damage to the exocrine pancreas, monogenic diabetes attributable to genetic defects in beta-cell function (e.g., MODY), and ketosis-prone Type 2 diabetes mellitus, which may present with episodic insulin deficiency but lacks confirmed autoimmune etiology.
clinical_rationale: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is a chronic, autoimmune condition resulting in progressive and absolute insulin deficiency. It has a known drug-related context, primarily through immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., anti-PD-1 agents) that can trigger autoimmune diabetes. The phenotype is persistent, as diagnosis implies lifelong disease management with insulin therapy and monitoring. Diagnosis is typically established in outpatient care settings, though some patients may present acutely with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) requiring hospitalization. Both sexes are affected, with no age constraint as autoimmune diabetes can onset at any age, even though pediatric onset is more common. Explicit exclusion of non-autoimmune diabetes types ensures this is conceptually narrow. Reliable diagnostic workflows include laboratory confirmation of hyperglycemia, autoantibodies, and glucose tolerance tests, followed by long-term condition-specific care.

source_definition: Type 1 Myocardial Infarction is an acute, incident clinical event defined by myocardial cell death resulting from spontaneous disruption of an atherosclerotic coronary plaque â€” through rupture, erosion, or intraplaque hemorrhage â€” or from spontaneous coronary artery dissection, leading to thrombotic reduction or occlusion of coronary blood flow and consequent ischemic necrosis of myocardial tissue. The diagnosis requires evidence of acute myocardial necrosis, as reflected by a rise and/or fall in cardiac biomarkers (preferably high-sensitivity troponin) with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit, in conjunction with clinical features consistent with myocardial ischemia (ischemic symptoms, new ECG changes, or new wall motion abnormality). Both ST-elevation and non-ST-elevation presentations are included. Angiographic confirmation of obstructive coronary artery disease is not required. This definition explicitly excludes: Type 2 MI arising from myocardial oxygen supply-demand imbalance without plaque disruption; unstable angina in the absence of biomarker-confirmed necrosis; myocarditis and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy as non-ischemic and neurogenic causes of troponin elevation respectively; procedure-associated MI (Types 3, 4, and 5); and any previously established or historical MI diagnosis not representing an acute incident event.
clinical_rationale: Type 1 MI is directly relevant to pharmacovigilance as certain drugs can precipitate acute coronary plaque disruption or increase thrombotic risk. Examples include NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, and drugs inducing vasospasm (e.g., 5-HT1 receptor agonists). The clinical course is transient and recurrent; once resolved, the incident event loses its acute diagnostic label, though it may leave chronic sequelae such as ischemic cardiomyopathy. The minimum interepisode gap of 28 days is based on WHO MONICA criteria and commonly separates acute events. Diagnosis nearly always occurs in acute care settings due to the urgency of ischemic symptoms. Diagnosis depends on hallmark evidence of myocardial necrosis (elevation in cardiac biomarkers) correlated with signs of coronary ischemia, and the condition requires immediate management, though the cohort definition must exclude Type 2 MI, unstable angina, and historical MI. The exclusion of historical events constrains eligibility to incident acute presentations, directly aligning with the observational needs for pharmacovigilance studies.

source_definition: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus is a chronic, progressive metabolic disorder characterized by peripheral insulin resistance coupled with a relative, progressive decline in pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretory capacity, resulting in sustained impairment of glucose homeostasis and overt hyperglycemia. The condition arises from a polygenic predisposition interacting with environmental and lifestyle factors, and encompasses the full clinical spectrum from newly diagnosed, diet-controlled disease to advanced states requiring pharmacological or insulin-based management. It is distinguished from all forms of diabetes driven by absolute insulin deficiency or autoimmune beta-cell destruction, including Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), and monogenic diabetes (e.g., MODY). Also excluded are all forms of secondary diabetes attributable to a discrete structural or endocrine primary cause, including pancreatogenic diabetes, endocrinopathy-associated hyperglycemia (e.g., Cushing's syndrome, acromegaly), and drug- or toxin-induced glucose dysregulation. Gestational diabetes mellitus and transient stress hyperglycemia are likewise excluded as distinct, situationally determined states not reflecting the underlying chronic pathophysiological process.
clinical_rationale: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) is not drug-induced in etiology but is recognized as a chronic metabolic disorder resulting from genetic predisposition coupled with lifestyle and environmental factors. While certain drugs (e.g., corticosteroids, antipsychotics) can result in secondary hyperglycemia or worsen glycemic control in individuals with T2DM, these mechanisms are distinct from the primary pathophysiology of T2DM. The provided definition clearly excludes drug-induced diabetes or transient hyperglycemia, narrowing the phenotype to cases intrinsic to the chronic metabolic dysregulation of insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction. T2DM is persistent due to its progressive and incurable nature, though it may be stable in well-controlled cases. The diagnostic process often involves laboratory confirmation (e.g., fasting glucose, HbA1c), and the condition is most often identified in outpatient care settings. Symptoms such as polyuria, polydipsia, and fatigue are variably present and not always separately documented in structured records.

source_definition: Type B lactic acidosis is a metabolic disorder characterized by an elevated blood L-lactate concentration of 5 mmol/L or greater accompanied by a systemic arterial pH below 7.35, arising from pathophysiological mechanisms that are not solely attributable to generalized tissue hypoperfusion or systemic hypoxia. The condition encompasses all recognized Type B etiological subtypes: Type B1, in which lactic acidosis occurs in association with systemic diseases such as malignancy, hepatic failure, or non-shock sepsis; Type B2, in which lactic acidosis results from exposure to drugs or exogenous toxins that impair mitochondrial function or cellular lactate metabolism (e.g., metformin, linezolid, or nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors); and Type B3, in which lactic acidosis arises from inborn errors of metabolism, including mitochondrial myopathies and inherited enzyme deficiencies affecting the pyruvate-lactate pathway. Cases in which a Type B mechanism is identifiable and contributory are included even when concurrent tissue hypoperfusion is present as a co-occurring process. Lactic acidosis solely caused by tissue hypoperfusion or systemic hypoxia (Type A) is excluded, as is D-lactic acidosis â€” a biochemically distinct syndrome produced by intestinal bacterial fermentation that generates D-lactate undetectable by standard clinical L-lactate assays.
clinical_rationale: Type B lactic acidosis is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome when it arises as Type B2, induced by drug exposures such as metformin, nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors, or linezolid, which impair mitochondrial function or cellular lactate metabolism. The condition also includes etiologies unrelated to drugs, such as systemic diseases (Type B1), inherited metabolic errors (Type B3), or mixed mechanisms, making it a pharmacovigilance outcome only under a more specific reading of the condition. Type B lactic acidosis is transient, as the condition resolves once the inciting factor is removed or treated, though the clinical course can vary widely depending on the underlying cause and comorbidities. Diagnostic confirmation generally requires laboratory confirmation of elevated L-lactate and arterial pH, and patients typically present acutely in inpatient or emergency settings. Acute treatment, including addressing the underlying cause, is nearly always required, and follow-up monitoring is common to prevent recurrence or address ongoing risk factors.

source_definition: Type I acute respiratory failure is a clinical state of acute hypoxemic failure characterized by a clinically significant reduction in arterial oxygen tension â€” manifested as a PaO2 below 60 mmHg on room air, an arterial oxygen saturation below 90%, a PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 300 mmHg, or the acute requirement for supplemental oxygen or ventilatory support to sustain adequate oxygenation â€” arising from intrinsic pulmonary parenchymal or pulmonary vascular dysfunction, including mechanisms such as ventilation-perfusion mismatch, intrapulmonary shunting, and diffusion impairment. Arterial carbon dioxide tension is normal or reduced, distinguishing this entity from hypercapnic (Type II) respiratory failure. Hypoxemia attributable primarily to cardiogenic or hemodynamic mechanisms â€” including pulmonary edema driven by left ventricular failure or distributive shock states â€” is explicitly excluded. The phenotype encompasses both de novo presentations in patients with previously normal oxygenation and acute deteriorations superimposed on established chronic pulmonary disease, with the latter recognized as a distinct acute-on-chronic subtype defined by oxygenation decline beyond the patient's known baseline.
clinical_rationale: Type I acute respiratory failure is a critical condition with documented drug-attributable etiologies, including drug-induced pulmonary toxicity (e.g., bleomycin, amiodarone), acute pulmonary edema secondary to fluid retention from certain medications (such as chemotherapeutics and NSAIDs), and mechanisms such as acute lung injury in sepsis or hypersensitivity pneumonia triggered by medication. It is transient in nature, as patients typically recover or progress to other diagnoses such as chronic respiratory conditions if severe sequelae occur. This phenotype generally occurs in acute care settings due to its life-threatening nature, with diagnosis often requiring arterial blood gas measurement and substantial clinical intervention. Acute-on-chronic presentations are possible but fall under the scope of acute care. While characteristic respiratory symptoms such as dyspnea may precede diagnosis, these are often nonspecific and not separately coded in structured data, relying more on diagnostic testing to confirm hypoxemia.

source_definition: Ulcerative colitis is a chronic, idiopathic, immune-mediated inflammatory condition characterized by diffuse, continuous mucosal and submucosal inflammation of the large intestine, invariably involving the rectum and extending proximally to a variable degree â€” from isolated proctitis through left-sided colitis to extensive pancolitis. The phenotype captures the confirmed, established diagnosis of ulcerative colitis irrespective of current disease activity, encompassing patients in active flare, in clinical or endoscopic remission, or on maintenance therapy. The pathophysiology is restricted to idiopathic immune dysregulation of the colonic mucosa and is explicitly distinguished from Crohn's disease, which involves transmural inflammation and potential involvement of any gastrointestinal segment, and from indeterminate colitis, in which IBD subtype cannot be definitively established. All non-IBD colitis etiologies are excluded from this phenotype, including infectious colitis of bacterial, viral, or parasitic origin; ischemic colitis arising from vascular insufficiency of the colon; microscopic colitis in its collagenous and lymphocytic subtypes; and drug-induced colitis including immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated colitis.
clinical_rationale: Ulcerative colitis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease restricted to the colonic mucosa and submucosa, with proximal extent variable from isolated proctitis to pancolitis. While it is primarily idiopathic, drug-induced forms (e.g., checkpoint inhibitor-associated colitis) and non-IBD colitides are excluded by the definition. Drug causality is indirectly relevant due to pharmacological triggers of disease exacerbation, such as NSAIDs worsening colonic inflammation or inadequate immunosuppressive therapy precipitating flares. Incident flare episodes are clinically distinct and recurrences are separable after a sufficient gap, but as this phenotype follows confirmed diagnoses of ulcerative colitis regardless of activity status, the disease overall is persistent-relapsing. Diagnosis spans outpatient through acute care settings depending on flare severity. Biologically, ulcerative colitis is possible in both sexes and across all age groups, but onset skews toward young adults. Structured records of presenting symptoms such as diarrhea, rectal bleeding, or abdominal pain are inconsistently captured, and diagnostic confirmation universally requires endoscopy or histopathology. Active treatment occurs in most patients during flare episodes, but patients in remission under maintenance therapy are captured by this phenotype without needing new treatment post-index.

source_definition: Undernutrition is a pathological state arising from insufficient intake, impaired absorption, or excessive loss of one or more essential macro- or micronutrients, resulting in a measurable deficit relative to physiological requirements. It encompasses a continuum of severity â€” from mild micronutrient insufficiency, through moderate deficits characterized by functional decline and unintentional weight loss, to severe protein-energy malnutrition manifesting as significant muscle wasting, edema, or the clinical syndromes of marasmus or kwashiorkor. The concept includes isolated micronutrient deficiencies and undernutrition driven by inflammatory or disease-associated metabolic states. It explicitly excludes states of overnutrition or excess adiposity, even when accompanied by coexisting micronutrient gaps, and excludes isolated fluid-electrolyte imbalances or dehydration states that occur without a concurrent deficit in macro- or micronutrient status.
clinical_rationale: Undernutrition represents a diverse pathological spectrum stemming from inadequate nutrient intake, absorption, or demands exceeding supply. It can result from drug effects such as appetite suppression (e.g., glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists), impaired absorption (e.g., chronic use of orlistat), or altered metabolism (e.g., corticosteroid-induced hypermetabolic states). Drugs may also exacerbate nutrient loss (e.g., diuretic-associated potassium/magnesium depletion). The condition spans a broad clinical range, from mild and chronic to severe presentations (e.g., protein-energy malnutrition). Its diagnostic coding may intersect with related conditions like micronutrient deficiencies or cachexia, making phenotyping a challenge in the context of a heterogeneous population.

source_definition: Unstable angina is an acute ischemic coronary syndrome characterized by a destabilizing pattern of anginal symptoms â€” including new-onset exertional chest pain of at least Canadian Cardiovascular Society Class III severity, angina occurring at rest or with minimal physical activity, or previously stable angina that has escalated in frequency, duration, or intensity (crescendo pattern) â€” arising from reversible myocardial ischemia in the absence of detectable cardiomyocyte necrosis. The underlying pathophysiology encompasses atherosclerotic plaque disruption, partial coronary thrombosis, or dynamic obstruction resulting in transient but severe impairment of myocardial oxygen supply. The condition is explicitly distinguished from non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and ST-elevation myocardial infarction by the absence of elevated cardiac biomarkers (e.g., troponin), confirming that myocardial cell death has not occurred. Demand ischemia secondary to non-coronary systemic conditions (e.g., severe anemia, sepsis, or tachyarrhythmia) is excluded, as is stable exertional angina that has not undergone clinical destabilization.
clinical_rationale: Unstable angina is a valid pharmacovigilance outcome associated with drugs that induce or exacerbate coronary ischemia (e.g., vasodilators leading to coronary steal phenomenon, sympathomimetics increasing myocardial oxygen demand). The definition explicitly excludes myocardial infarction by biomarker criteria and focuses on acute coronary ischemia symptoms occurring without cardiomyocyte necrosis. Diagnosis primarily depends on clinical presentation and testing (e.g., ECG for ischemic changes) and is usually adjudicated in acute care settings due to its life-threatening nature. Direct complications, follow-up testing, and risk stratification extend beyond the acute episode, but discrete coding may be less sensitive than clinical diagnosis. Dynamic symptoms like chest pain may appear in structured data as well. Evidence for drug attribution is strong, warranting high confidence.

source_definition: Upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage is defined as any confirmed loss of blood originating from a mucosal or vascular source within the gastrointestinal tract proximal to the ligament of Treitz, encompassing the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. The hemorrhage may manifest as overt bleeding â€” presenting clinically as hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, or melena â€” or as objectively confirmed occult bleeding, such as iron-deficiency anemia in conjunction with endoscopic identification of an actively bleeding or recently bled upper gastrointestinal lesion. No minimum severity threshold is required; the phenotype spans the full spectrum from minor mucosal oozing to life-threatening hemorrhage. All underlying etiologies are encompassed, including non-variceal causes (peptic ulcer disease, Mallory-Weiss tears, erosive gastroesophageal disease, vascular malformations, and gastrointestinal malignancy) and variceal causes arising from portal hypertension (esophageal or gastric varices). Bleeding originating outside the gastrointestinal lumen â€” including oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal, or pulmonary hemorrhage that is swallowed and may clinically mimic upper gastrointestinal bleeding â€” is explicitly excluded from this definition.
clinical_rationale: Upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage (UGIH) is a known pharmacovigilance outcome, especially in association with drugs that compromise mucosal integrity (NSAIDs, corticosteroids), influence acid secretion (proton pump inhibitors, H2 antagonists during withdrawal), or impair coagulation (anticoagulants, antiplatelets, direct thrombin inhibitors). The definition includes all bleeding severities and etiologies, emphasizing mucosal or variceal sources proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Included manifestations span overt bleeding (hematemesis, melena) and occult bleeding diagnosed by anemia and endoscopic findings, ensuring broad capture. Due to potential for catastrophic hypovolemia, acute care recognition is typical, and diagnosis often requires endoscopic or imaging confirmation. The episodic nature supports independent recurrent case identification, while post-resolution iron deficiency and eradication of causative lesions mitigate frequent false recurrence under usual care workflows.
